title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
authors: Zhixu Li,Keqian Tang,Litian Gong,Jingyu Yao,Wenqian Zhang,Tianze Xu,Zehao Wang,Yuping Wang,Junge Zhang,Jiachen Li
comment: Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026); Project Website:this https URL
abstract: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.
introduction:
Household manipulation has been a long-standing goal in robotics and embodied AI, with the promise of improving daily life by enabling robots to perform chores from natural language instructions (e.g., “put an apple, bread, and milk on my plate”). Recent progress in generalist robotic manipulation has been driven in large part by Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [1, 2, 3, 4], which show strong generalization across diverse multimodal inputs [5, 6] and heterogeneous embodiments [7, 8]. However, real-world deployment demands more than completing the nominal task: embodied agents must also execute tasks in ways that align with the preferences, habits, and constraints of individual users, a requirement we refer to as personalization.

Preferences introduce diverse execution requirements for identical goals. For instance, placing a mug might require a specific handle orientation or a designated landing spot. Consequently, personalized manipulation must satisfy user-specific constraints on both what strategies are selected and how actions are performed. In this framework, preferences are treated as a learning dimension parallel to object-oriented task learning; the policy’s objective is to maximize preference adherence within a single trajectory without compromising fundamental task success.

Nevertheless, progress on personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) remains impeded by two major gaps.
First, PeRM lacks a shared formulation and standardized evaluation protocol across prior work.
Existing studies define personalization through diverse problem settings, including implicit preference alignment [9, 10], multi-user style adaptation [11], user-specific object-receptacle pairing [12], and helpful action prediction [13]; they also specify preferences through natural language [13, 14], few user examples [9], explicit preference functions [15], human speech [5], or numerical preference vectors [11].
Evaluation is similarly fragmented, spanning task success, user studies [13, 9, 11, 14], and preference-based scoring functions [16, 17], making methods difficult to compare and failure modes hard to diagnose.
Second, existing benchmarks typically emphasize high-level navigation or semantic selection over fine-grained manipulation preferences and multi-preference conflicts.
The closest preference-based RL benchmark [18] lacks robotic preference-learning datasets and multi-preference evaluation.
Other personalization benchmarks focus on object navigation or high-level receptacle selection [19, 20], while recent memory-based manipulation benchmarks [21, 22] do not distinguish task-instance memorization from genuine user-preference-driven personalization.

To address these gaps, we introduce a novel Personalized Robotic Manipulation Benchmark (LIBERO-PeRM), built using the popular LIBERO [23] framework. We elevate user preferences to a fundamental building block alongside tasks and layouts. Following the taxonomy of human preferences [24], we define a controlled taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering Motion Preference (trajectory constraints), Skill Preference (task strategies), and User Profile (semantic biases). The benchmark is restricted to preferences that can be expressed in language, instantiated without changing the original task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Within this scope, we provide 37 single-preference instances and 18 two-preference combinations.

LIBERO-PeRM features an extensible procedural generation pipeline that automatically instantiates tasks and their preference-conditioned variants within shared layouts. To support systematic training and evaluation, the pipeline simultaneously produces explicit preference satisfaction metrics and rich subtask-level metadata, including language instructions, goal images, and physical attributes.

For benchmarking, we construct five task suites with 312 preference-conditioned tasks and pipeline-generated, human-reviewed demonstrations, each targeting a core capability in personalized manipulation (Figure 1, top).
LIBERO-SinglePref evaluates single-preference learning; LIBERO-PrefScale evaluates scaling across data sizes, tasks, and layouts; LIBERO-PrefConflict evaluates preference-preference and task-preference conflicts; LIBERO-PrefCompose evaluates multi-preference composition; and LIBERO-ComprePref evaluates realistic preference-conditioned reasoning based on contextual language.
In LIBERO-PrefScale, we further provide no-preference data, unseen layouts, and different tasks to support in-domain evaluation, task/layout generalization, and preference-level generalization over different tasks in unseen layouts.

We use LIBERO-PeRM to conduct an initial study of five key research topics in personalized manipulation (see bottom row of Figure 1): 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how policies learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently policies acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose multiple preferences and behave under conflicts. These topics organize our experiments and highlight the core capabilities that robots must develop for reliable personalization.

Our contributions and findings are as follows:

We introduce a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, together with an automated pipeline that produces preference-conditioned demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics.

We construct five task suites, LIBERO-SinglePref, LIBERO-PrefScale, LIBERO-PrefConflict, LIBERO-PrefCompose, LIBERO-ComprePref, comprising 312 preference-conditioned tasks with pipeline-generated, human-reviewed demonstrations and evaluation protocols for controlled personalization studies.

Extensive experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training improves no-preference task success relative to sequential adaptation and contextual-prompt task success and preference satisfaction relative to preference-only LoRA, but weakens motion-preference learning; broader layout diversity and matched no-preference data also help, while preference generalization, decomposition, and execution under conflicts remain difficult.

1. We introduce a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, together with an automated pipeline that produces preference-conditioned demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics.

2. We construct five task suites, LIBERO-SinglePref, LIBERO-PrefScale, LIBERO-PrefConflict, LIBERO-PrefCompose, LIBERO-ComprePref, comprising 312 preference-conditioned tasks with pipeline-generated, human-reviewed demonstrations and evaluation protocols for controlled personalization studies.

3. Extensive experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training improves no-preference task success relative to sequential adaptation and contextual-prompt task success and preference satisfaction relative to preference-only LoRA, but weakens motion-preference learning; broader layout diversity and matched no-preference data also help, while preference generalization, decomposition, and execution under conflicts remain difficult.

title: Value as Memory: Online Value-Guided Post-training for General Robot Policies
authors: Wenye Yu,Yijin Chen,Kaiyi Xiong,Wenbo Han,Wendi Chen,Yang Jin,Han Xue,Jun Lv,Cewu Lu,Chuan Wen
abstract:
Real-world post-training of generalist robot policies faces two challenges: partial observability makes action selection ambiguous, while offline post-training methods delay feedback from deployment experience.
We present Value as Memory (VaM), a framework that addresses these challenges through value caching and online real-world reinforcement learning (RL).
Value caching conditions actions on recent value predictions as task-progress memory, while online updates enable timely policy improvement by combining offline demonstrations, off-policy interventions, and on-policy rollouts for sample-efficient adaptation.
As a result, VaM transitions from offline RL warmup to online autonomous learning with sparse rewards.
Across long-horizon tasks involving deformable objects and contact-rich manipulation, VaM yields a mean absolute success-rate gain of 29.4%29.4\% with value caching, while achieving a 32.8%32.8\% gain with online autonomous learning over matched offline training.
The evaluated online schedule performs 8×8\times as many policy iterations under the same gradient-step budget, with more than 2×2\times lower recorded time per gradient step with concurrent data collection and training.
introduction:
Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) enables generalist robot policies to learn from physical interaction and improve on deployment tasks (Chen et al., 2025b; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025).
Initialized from offline expert demonstrations, a policy aims to maximize cumulative task rewards (Luo et al., 2024; Frans et al., 2025) and optionally learns from human-intervention data during deployment (Luo et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026).

However, current real-world RL methods face limitations in data reuse and policy-update frequency.
On-policy updates primarily use fresh rollouts, limiting the reuse of historical experience (Chen et al., 2025a).
Iterated offline RL separates data collection from optimization, delaying feedback from newly encountered states (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025).
Besides, partial observability poses another challenge.
With limited observation histories, visually similar states may require different actions.
Meanwhile, value functions provide compact task-progress estimates, but typically serve as filtering scores or optimization weights (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Frans et al., 2025).
We therefore ask whether value estimates on observation histories can augment policy inputs to mitigate partial observability, and how an online RL system can exploit a learned value function to incorporate offline demonstrations, off-policy data, and on-policy rollouts for joint adaptation of the policy and value functions with high sample efficiency and rapid closed-loop feedback.

To this end, we introduce Value as Memory (VaM), an offline-to-online RL system with two key features.
First, we propose value caching, which extends value predictions beyond training supervision by supplying their recent history as an additional policy input.
Alongside visual and proprioceptive histories, this cache indicates whether estimated progress improves, stalls, or declines, helping distinguish states requiring different actions.
Second, VaM uses a hybrid training data scheme that combines offline demonstrations, off-policy trajectories, and current on-policy rollouts for sample-efficient joint adaptation of policy and value models.
Our training regime progresses from offline RL warmup through human-assisted collection to autonomous learning with sparse rewards.
Across real-world tasks involving deformable objects and contact-rich manipulations, VaM improves mean absolute success rate by 29.4%29.4\% over its variant without value caching.
It gains 32.8%32.8\% in mean absolute success rate over its offline RL counterpart under matched training budgets.
The evaluated online schedule performs 8×8\times as many policy iterations under the same gradient-step budget, with more than 2×2\times lower recorded time per gradient step with concurrent data collection and training.
These results support value caching for mitigating partial observability and our online RL system with a hybrid training data scheme for improving sample efficiency and policy iteration frequency.

Our contributions are twofold:

We propose value caching to condition policies on recent task-progress estimates, with theoretical analysis and real-world ablations supporting its role in mitigating action ambiguity under partial observability.

We develop an online RL framework that reuses offline demonstrations, off-policy trajectories, and current on-policy rollouts for joint policy and value adaptation, improving sample efficiency and policy iteration frequency.

title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
authors: Chenyuan Zhou,Yining Hong,Huang Huang,Yunfan Jiang,Wenlong Huang,David Held,Vitor Campagnolo Guizilini,Yue Wang,Li Fei-Fei,Jiajun Wu,Leonidas Guibas,Yejin Choi
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules.
We introduce T2-z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take.
During training, T2-z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction.
At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations.
Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.2015.20 to 7.007.00 and raises action success from 33.73%33.73\% to 72.96%72.96\%.
Its emergent latents capture structured
representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes.
Ablations further show that T2-z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.
introduction:
What a robot observes is insufficient to determine how the world will respond. Beneath visually similar scene configurations reside hidden environmental factors, such as friction, mass distribution, and unobserved human-defined interaction rules, that can fundamentally alter the consequences of the same action (fig. 1 (a)). Such factors are often revealed only through interaction with the target environments, as their influence becomes observable through the outcomes they induce. Explicitly representing these factors (Kumar et al., 2021), however, requires specifying in advance what factors may vary, their exact values, and how they should be parameterized, which is difficult to scale to unknown or compounded environmental variation. On the contrary, humans reason through “analysis by synthesis”  (Yuille and Kersten, 2006), using internal generative models not only to anticipate future outcomes, but also in reverse to infer latent structure that best accounts for what they observe. This raises a natural question: can hidden environmental factors be similarly captured in a latent representation that is directly optimized from test-time interactions?

We introduce T2-z for test-time optimization of environmental latents, which augments an action-conditioned robotic world model with a learnable environment latent 𝐳e\mathbf{z}_{e}. 𝐳e\mathbf{z}_{e} is a randomly-initialized compact representation that is expected to encode the unobserved factors governing how an environment responds to interaction, with no supervision about what environmental factors it should represent.
The world model predicts future visual observations conditioned jointly on the action and 𝐳e\mathbf{z}_{e}. We iteratively optimize the world model and 𝐳e\mathbf{z}_{e} in an alternating two-stage procedure: 1) world-model optimization: with 𝐳e\mathbf{z}_{e} fixed, we train the world model across all trajectories to learn shared action-conditioned dynamics across environments; 2) environment-latent optimization: with the world model frozen, we optimize the conditioned latent 𝐳e\mathbf{z}_{e} through prediction error, so that it captures underlying environment-specific variation not explained by the general world model alone. Both stages are optimized with the same flow-matching loss and alternated for multiple rounds until convergence, allowing the environment representation to emerge directly through prediction without predefined physical-factor supervision or a separate environment encoder.

At test time, the world model is frozen and T2-z turns environment inference into a direct
optimization problem. For a previously unseen environmental configuration,
we initialize a new 𝐳e\mathbf{z}_{e} and optimize 𝐳e\mathbf{z}_{e} to explain the outcomes of one or more observed test-time interactions.
Specifically, we update 𝐳e\mathbf{z}_{e} for multiple optimization steps through the same flow-matching objective used
during stage-two training, minimizing prediction error on the observed interactions. Because inference is optimization-based rather than amortized through a learned history encoder, T2-z is not tied to the trajectory count used for training and can flexibly incorporate any number of test-time trajectories.
Once optimized, the latent turns the frozen world model into an
environment-adapted test-time simulator, enabling prediction and comparison
of candidate action outcomes before execution.

We evaluate T2-z across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks. Quantitatively and qualitatively, T2-z improves world-model prediction across visual quality, physical prediction metrics (e.g., relevant object locations), and downstream action selection. T2-z reduces physical prediction error from 12.8612.86 to 4.804.80 in simulation and tracked-state error from 19.3019.30 to 10.8510.85 pixels in the real world, while improving action success from 37.9%37.9\% to 74.2%74.2\% and from 26.5%26.5\% to 70.8%70.8\%, respectively. PCA of the learned latents reveals structured representations that reflect the underlying environmental factors, including a multi-dimensional organization when more than one factors vary jointly, despite the model never knowing how many factors are present or what they represent (fig. 1(b)). In our multi-background setting, a unified latent structure emerges across diverse scene setups, revealing that the learned representation captures environmental dynamics without becoming entangled with scene appearance (fig. 1(d)). Ablations further show that T2-z can infer useful environment representations from as few as a single test-time interaction trajectory.

introduction:
Simulation has become a primary source of robot manipulation data, but building simulated
environments has long been the bottleneck: each one requires a task design, semantically
appropriate assets, a plausible layout, and a training signal, often all specified by hand
[38]. Generative simulation removes much of that cost. Coding agents now
synthesize scenes, articulations, and task specifications directly
[38, 39, 43, 37, 25], and language models author the reward functions that accompany them
[42, 48]. Environments are no longer scarce.

A central challenge remaining is deciding which environments to build next and what supervision will help the policy to learn from them.
Existing engines sample variation from hand-specified ranges [29], refine a scene until it is physically valid [39, 43],
or allocate budget by per-task success rate [10].
These signals indicate whether an
environment is valid and how well the current policy performs, but do not
by themselves measure how much the policy improves through training.
Without such feedback,
a generator risks spending its budget on environments the policy has already mastered or cannot yet learn to solve.

It records repairs needed to make scenes valid, together with policy failure diagnoses grounded in rollout evidence and localized to one generative factor and one trajectory phase. The memory tracks learning progress for recurring difficulty modes to guide subsequent generation.
This evidence is compiled into separate programs for scene generation and policy training, with the latter specifying subgoals and learning tools [38, 42].

As tasks involve longer sequences of dependent subtasks, sparse success signals can slow value learning, while designing effective dense rewards can require manual effort. We therefore introduce Text2potential, which compiles a failure diagnosis into a potential over the simulator state and uses it to densify value targets for action chunks [15, 7]. The resulting value estimates guide policy updates through weighted regression on the policy’s own rollouts, favoring action chunks with higher estimated value.

Across four manipulation tasks, CoDA achieves 27.6% out-of-distribution success, compared with 5.3% for the supervised fine-tuning baseline.
With the same budget for generating environments, a loop guided by per-task success rates achieves 18.1%, while open-loop variants yield 8.5%. Extending our loop to more rounds increases out-of-distribution success to 42.1%. Moreover, on LIBERO-Pro, training on source-task variants generated by CoDA increases success from 25% to 84% on position generalization and from 1% to 76% on task generalization. Finally, we observe that reusing memory across policy backbones transfers accumulated experience, enabling a second backbone to increase out-of-distribution success from 3.8% to 21.1%.

Closed-loop co-evolution.
We introduce CoDA, a framework that co-evolves a simulation data engine with a trainable action policy. Failure diagnoses grounded in policy rollouts guide environment generation and training, while measured learning progress determines which difficulties to revisit.

Shared heterogeneous memory. We introduce a memory shared by the generator and policy that combines episodic evidence, reusable difficulty modes, and procedural programs. The same diagnosis compiles into a generation program that recreates the difficulty and a training program that helps the policy overcome it. Both programs are indexed by difficulty mode, making them reusable across tasks.

Dense supervision through Text2potential. Text2potential compiles failure diagnoses into potentials over simulator states that provide dense targets for learning the value of action chunks [15]. Reward shaping requires potential evaluations only at chunk endpoints and preserves the policies that maximize the original task return.

Reusing memory across policy backbones also improves OpenVLA-OFT’s out-of-distribution success from 3.8% to 21.1% without additional environment generation.

title: Dexterity from Supervised Play
authors: Botao He,Yiming Dou,Yiannis Aloimonos,Jitendra Malik,Akash Sharma,Ruoshi Liu
abstract: How can robots autonomously collect the contact-rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present \dspfontDSP: Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world experiment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490×\times less interaction data. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-specific demonstrations or sim-to-real transfer.
introduction:
Humans, especially infants and children, develop dexterity from playing [1]. Play offers a task-agnostic source of interaction. Similarly, for robots, learning via playing holds tremendous potential for learning a rich physical understanding of the world required for dexterous manipulation without human supervision. In practice, however, play is a difficult behavior to engineer.

Prior works model play by manually defining explicit heuristics as guidance [2, 3, 4] and by engineering restrictive safety boundaries to prevent hardware damage [5]. However, play is inherently intuitive and difficult to formalize with hand-crafted rules, while manual safety constraints require excessive tuning that limits scalability.

In this work, our core hypothesis is that play is a behavior that can be modeled as a ‘goal-agnostic’ state-conditioned probabilistic model in a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and therefore be learned through a standard behavior cloning pipeline. In other words, even though a safe play behavior is hard to be defined explicitly with heuristics, it can easily be learned implicitly through demonstration data.

Therefore, we propose \dspfontDSP: Dexterity from Supervised Play, a
framework that turns minutes of human play into a policy that can continue
collecting robot interaction autonomously. An action-conditioned world model
learns from these data, while the same play policy provides candidate action
sequences for model-predictive control (MPC). As a preliminary acceleration
study, we also explore distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy
through self-play within the learned world model.

Our primary contribution is a framework for learning dexterous manipulation
from data collected by an autonomous play policy. We evaluate how autonomous
play supports world-model learning and goal-directed planning through four
technical contributions:

Supervised play. We formulate supervised play as a mechanism for turning a limited
human interaction prior into autonomous contact-rich data collection.

Scaling autonomous play data. We show that held-out
world-model prediction improves monotonically as the real-robot
autonomous-play dataset grows from 0.5 to 5 hours.

Play policy as an action prior. We show that using play policy as an action-proposal model for MPC significantly improves manipulation performance.

Self-play policy distillation. A method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through world-model self-play to accelerate inference.

Experimental results show \dspfontDSP reaches
within 0.60.6 rad on 91.4% of trials and within 0.40.4 rad on 72.7%, compared
with 53.9% and 25.8% for hindsight BC. PPO reaches 86.7% at both
thresholds after 344M counted frames, about 490 times the counted-frame
budget. Real world experiment shows \dspfontDSP is able to transfer to real world with matched performance.
We further validate \dspfontDSP on Push-T and visual in-hand manipulation, demonstrating that the framework generalizes across tasks and observation representations.
We also provide detailed analysis to carefully examine the characteristics of the proposed algorithm and the impacts of the
key design decisions. The code, data, and training details will
be publicly available for reproducing our results.

1. Supervised play. We formulate supervised play as a mechanism for turning a limited

2. Scaling autonomous play data. We show that held-out
world-model prediction improves monotonically as the real-robot
autonomous-play dataset grows from 0.5 to 5 hours.

3. Play policy as an action prior. We show that using play policy as an action-proposal model for MPC significantly improves manipulation performance.

4. Self-play policy distillation. A method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through world-model self-play to accelerate inference.

title: Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning for Path-Safe Target Reaching in Robotic Harvesting of Hydroponic Lettuce
authors: Al Bashir,Partho Ghose,Yibin Wang,Robert G. Hardin,Joshua Peeples,Genhua Niu,Azlan Zahid
abstract:
Robotic harvesting requires precise manipulation to ensure accurate positioning of the end-effector, especially in a constraint workspace. This study introduces the Path-Safe Approach Proximal Policy Optimization (PSA-PPO), a target-conditioned local reaching framework designed for robotic harvesting of nutrient film technique (NFT)-hydroponic lettuce in greenhouses. The proposed PSA-PPO preserves the standard clipped PPO objective while introducing a harvesting-oriented policy formulation that integrates target-conditioned observations, corridor-aware spatial constraints, trajectory-history-based safety encoding, and task-specific success criteria for constrained robotic manipulation. PSA-PPO was trained entirely in Isaac Lab and successfully transferred to a physical UR10e robotic arm without any real-world policy fine-tuning. In a controlled physical benchmark against 150 scheduled targets, PSA-PPO achieved the highest reaching rate of 94.7%, outperforming Cartesian+TOTG (86.0%), RRTConnect (88.0%), and RRT* (80.0%), while reducing median RMS jerk by 39.8–73.0% relative to the classical planners during the final approach segment. A formulation ablation evaluated over 200 simulation targets demonstrates that path-safety and side-corridor shaping are the principal drivers of harvesting-compatible performance: removing either term substantially degrades strict success even when terminal endpoint accuracy is preserved or improved, confirming that optimization toward the endpoint alone is an insufficient objective for constrained crop-proximal manipulation. Finally, PSA-PPO was integrated with an RGB-D vision module and an end-effector and evaluated as a complete greenhouse harvesting system across 144 lettuce harvesting attempts, achieving 94.4% vision-guided target reaching and 86.1% complete harvesting success.
These results position PSA-PPO as an effective simulation-trained harvesting motion controller that balances target-reaching reliability and low dynamic excitation.
introduction:
Reliable manipulator motion remains a critical challenge in robotic harvesting because crop localization, target approach, and physical crop interaction must be executed within highly constrained and variable agricultural environments [28, 21]. Unlike structured industrial manipulation, crop targets vary continuously in geometry, accessibility, and are surrounded by deformable plant material and cultivation infrastructure [14, 41, 10]. These constraints become especially important in controlled-environment agriculture, where dense crop layouts restrict manipulator workspace while increasing the requirement for repeatable autonomous operation [37].
Hydroponic lettuce presents a unique challenge in terms of manipulation. The harvesting tool must approach the stem–root region, just above the cultivation infrastructure, establish the right cutting angle, sever the plant, retain the detached lettuce, and transfer it without disturbing neighboring crops or rigid cultivation equipment [39]. Early research on lettuce harvesting demonstrated the effectiveness of machine-vision-guided manipulation within structured production systems [7]. More recent studies have continued to improve crop-specific harvesting mechanisms and the interactions of end effectors, highlighting the importance of combining crop localization with subsequent robotic actions [40, 3]. For instance, the field-tested Vegebot integrated learned perception, force-feedback control, and a specialized end effector designed for iceberg lettuce harvesting [5]. However, these studies do not address how to convert a vision-derived cutting point for lettuce into a repeatable motion that complies with the geometry and clearance constraints of a complex agricultural environment.

Manipulator motion in agricultural harvesting is still predominantly generated using inverse kinematics, sampling-based motion planning, trajectory optimization, or visual servoing.
Researchers have adapted these methods to crop-specific manipulation requirements. For example, Ma et al. [22] developed an improved BIT*-based planner [16] that jointly considered path quality, execution efficiency, and dynamic impact. Rong et al. [29] coordinated manipulator and lifting-joint motion to improve tomato-harvesting reachability, while Kang et al. [15] proposed a BIT*-based Time-Optimal and Path-Optimal (TOPO) planner that combines improved sampling and edge checking with path optimization to reduce planning time and generate shorter trajectories for selective broccoli harvesting. Recent studies have similarly modified Informed-RRT* [16] for smooth winter-jujube harvesting [11] and developed a sampling-based planner for high-quality motion generation in unstructured tea canopies [12]. At the system level, visual-servoing approaches [6] remain common for cucumber harvesting  [25, 13]. Classical planners [34, 23, 18] therefore provides strong geometric trajectory and can achieve high terminal precision, but agricultural manipulation requires simultaneous consideration of reachability, obstacle exposure, trajectory smoothness, perception uncertainty, execution robustness, and crop-specific approach geometry  [9, 41]. Additionally, these planners are vulnerable to singularities, sensitive to noise which often produce unstable motion and inefficient trajectories [19, 27].

Learning-based policy control offers a complementary approach for achieving smooth motion through learning loops between the robot agent and its environment. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [31] has become a widely used method in Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for continuous robotic control [35]. It uses a policy-gradient method that constrains policy updates through a clipped surrogate objective. However, this mechanism does not explicitly enforce geometric or trajectory-safety constraints; constraint-aware policy optimization remains a distinct problem [1]. For harvesting, a policy rewarded primarily for terminal target acquisition may reach the cutting point without preserving an acceptable approach direction, tool orientation, or intermediate clearance. Addressing this limitation requires a task formulation that represents the relevant spatial relationships, evaluates trajectory-level violations, and distinguishes terminal reaching from harvesting-compatible motion rather than relying on the standard PPO objective alone. A further significant challenge in DRL training is acquiring the necessary interaction experience of robot through trial and error. Policy optimization involves repeated robot motions and resets, substantial execution time, and potentially unsafe exploratory actions. These challenges are particularly critical in agricultural environments, where exploratory actions can damage delicate biological materials, harvesting infrastructure, or the manipulator itself [8, 35]. These limitations highlight the need to develop manipulation DRL policies without relying on exploratory policy optimization in a physical robot.

Simulation-based policy learning offers a fundamentally different development path. Instead of gathering the extensive interaction data required for policy optimization on a physical harvesting robot, both exploration and policy learning can be carried out in a virtual physics simulator, allowing the learned policy to be evaluated on hardware later. GPU-native simulation has made this approach increasingly feasible. For instance, NVIDIA Isaac Lab [24], a unified GPU-accelerated framework for reinforcement learning, showcases massively parallel robot-policy interactions directly on the GPU.

However, simulation-trained policies must overcome the reality gap yielded by imperfect dynamics, actuator behavior, sensing, and calibration variation. Previous research has addressed these discrepancies through visual and dynamics randomization  [36, 26] and physical parameter identification  [32]. For example, Subedi et al. [33] demonstrated simulation-only RL transfer for occlusion-aware plant manipulation by separating learned behavior from lower-level compliant control. Kim et al. [17] used visuomotor imitation learning for autonomous pepper harvesting in unstructured fields, while Rong et al. [30] combined position-based visual alignment with a corrective action policy for greenhouse tomato harvesting. However, there remains limited evidence for policies that simultaneously incorporate crop-specific approach geometry, trajectory-history clearance, simulation-only policy optimization, controlled physical comparison with multiple classical planners, and end-to-end harvesting in complex agricultural setups. Moreover, success in simulation alone does not guarantee physical reliability; evaluations of paired robots and policies have highlighted the importance of addressing control and observation discrepancies  [20]. For effective crop-proximal harvesting, it is essential to preserve the learned control interface while also accommodating the constraints of physical calibration and execution. This research gap is crucial to greenhouse-grown lettuce because successful reaching cannot be defined solely by the final tool center point (TCP) error. The cutter must approach the stem region from a suitable horizontal direction, remain compatible with the target-height geometry, preserve the required tool orientation, limit wrist–TCP descent near the cultivation structure, and avoid undesirably abrupt local motion. Hence, this control problem is consequently one of harvesting-compatible local constrained reaching, rather than generic point-to-point motion alone.

To address these gaps, this study develops Path-Safe Approach PPO (PSA-PPO), a target-conditioned local reaching formulation for hydroponic lettuce harvesting. Rather than modifying PPO’s optimization rule, PSA-PPO reformulates the learning task through geometry-conditioned safe initialization, target- and clearance-aware observations, coupled reaching and motion-safety rewards, and trajectory-history-dependent strict capture and termination criteria for collision-avoidance harvesting-specific trajectories. The policy is trained entirely in Isaac Lab and transferred without real-world policy fine-tuning, using calibrated target transformation, a frozen Cartesian deployment correction, and an independent ROS execution and safety interface. The study then examines whether harvesting-compatible behavior learned in simulation is retained on a physical UR10e, how it compares with
classical motion planners, and how it performs within a complete vision-guided greenhouse harvesting system.

The main contributions of this study are:

A target-conditioned path-safe local reaching formulation, named PSA-PPO, is developed for lettuce harvesting. It incorporates spatial constraints, trajectory-level safety awareness, and harvesting-specific task objectives.

The PSA-PPO is trained entirely in simulation, without any physical rollouts used for policy optimization or fine-tuning. The trained policy is evaluated against the identical 200 targets within the simulation, highlighting contributions such as path-safety shaping, side-corridor shaping, and motion regularization.

The simulation-trained policy is transferred to a physical UR10e robotic arm and is benchmarked against Cartesian+TOTG, RRTConnect, and RRT* algorithms over 150 common targets. This comparison assesses task reliability, terminal precision, target convergence, physical motion dynamics, joint tracking, and trajectory geometry, revealing the trade-offs involved in the controller.

PSA-PPO is integrated with an RGB-D-based lettuce vision module for target streaming and a end-effector mechanism in a complete greenhouse harvesting pipeline. Across 144 actual lettuce harvesting attempts, the system achieved 94.4% target reaching success.

title: Illumination-Aware Active Perception for Spacecraft Inspection
authors: Sagarika Rao Valluri,Benjamin Riviere
abstract:
Harsh and rapidly varying orbital illumination introduces failure modes during spacecraft inspection. Existing planners rely on line-of-sight inspection metrics which perform occlusion checks against a known target and conflate geometric visibility with task-relevant information.
These metrics overlook illumination effects including eclipse, self-shadowing, and specular reflection from spacecraft materials and tend to declare components as inspected despite the corresponding images lacking sufficient information.
We propose an inspection-planning framework that replaces geometric visibility with a learned measure of camera information derived from a classifier variational autoencoder (VAE) that operates directly on the captured image.
The encoder model is trained to classify spacecraft surface components from rendered patches, and its total latent variance is used to learn the varying illumination of said components, replacing binary visibility checks with a continuous, image-grounded quantity.
We evaluate the approach by implementing a Guidance, Navigation, and Control architecture in a photorealistic physics simulator, and vary lighting and viewing geometries with multiple orbits. We show that, although all approaches successfully maximize their own objective, our approach results in better illumination: a mean brightness of 0.570.57, with 81.6%81.6\% of observations above 0.250.25, compared with 0.020.02 (3.0%3.0\%) for geometric planning with an illumination band and 0.040.04 (6.0%6.0\%) for purely geometric planning.
introduction:
Autonomous inspection of resident space objects is essential for space situational awareness and is an important tool to execute proximity operations in constrained orbital environments. Inspection is necessary in missions like debris removal, satellite repair [1], and in-orbit assembly and manufacturing. Recent missions include the Remora mission conducted by Starfish Space and Impulse Space  [32], Qingzhou prototype spacecraft and Astroscale’s ADRAS‑J, a demonstration satellite that successfully captured close range pictures of space debris [2].

The primary objective of autonomous inspection is to maximize information gain of the target spacecraft in motion. This task comprises of gaining information about the target pose (in orbit, tumbling, undefined motion etc) and of specific component state on the target. Extensive research has been conducted by estimating target’s (relative) pose for navigation of non-cooperative targets [10] for single agent and multi agent inspection tasks [30]. These models have used camera data to train vision models to estimate pose by using navigation estimates to ensure target body is within the field of view. Given a target’s pose (inferred through above methods) autonomous methods are used to inspect state of components on the target using measurements like encounter geometry-incidence angle, range, visibility mask, and analytical models of illumination often amounting to a visibility check. Often, hierarchical models [22] are built with a Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) stack that explicitly sets an information metric to aid coverage and mapping of the target spacecraft.
Ultimately, the objective is to identify components by determining whether a surface element is a solar array, a radiator, or a docking interface, and if its condition is nominal or degraded. Without camera data, geometrical checks limit the planner’s ability to distinguish orbital viewpoints that yield photometrically informative measurements from those that do not, regularly admitting false positives/negatives during the inspection task.

To address this problem, we replace the geometrically computed metric with a learned metric that operates on image pixels directly from the onboard camera. Specifically, we train a classifier variational auto-encoder (VAE) [16] to classify target components from rendered imagery and learn corresponding illumination distributions.
During evaluation, the model’s latent variance is used for our inspection probability where it is high for dark, occluded, specular, or out-of-distribution patches and is low for well-resolved, in-distribution patches. To validate our solution, we implement an inspection-based Guidance, Navigation, and Control stack in the IsaacSim [24] a photorealistic simulator, and we compare closed loop performance of our learned metric to geometric and analytic baselines.
We find that the closed-loop system equipped with our learned model captures images with a mean brightness of 0.570.57, compared with 0.040.04 and 0.020.02 for the geometric and illumination-band baselines, with 81.6%81.6\% of observations above 0.250.25 versus 6.0%6.0\% and 3.0%3.0\% (an increase of approximately 7676 percentage points over the stronger baseline). We also find that its policy nearly matches the illumination-band baseline on that baseline’s own reward (193193 versus 197197 POI’s), while the reverse does not hold (100100 versus 190190 under our reward).

title: Mem4Act: Learning Effective Latent Memory for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
authors: Yun Zhang,Zhiyu Huang,Tianhui Cai,Chen Tang,Wei Wang,Jiaqi Ma
abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation fundamentally requires memory: agents must retain task-relevant information from past observations and interactions and use it to guide future actions. Existing approaches typically preserve raw historical observations, compressed visual tokens, or language summaries, but these representations either expose the action policy to increasingly long histories or risk discarding task-relevant temporal, semantic, and perceptual information. We introduce Mem4Act, a framework for learning effective latent memory as a fixed-size representation explicitly optimized for long-horizon robotic control. Mem4Act addresses three coupled challenges: how to efficiently cover long histories, what information memory should retain, and how to ensure the policy actually relies on memory. To this end, it organizes history via multi-granularity temporal aggregation, preserves complementary semantic and perceptual information through question-answering supervision and key-frame DINO feature reconstruction, and employs memory-first two-stage training to encourage greater use of memory by the action policy. The resulting memory captures both high-level task state and fine-grained perceptual evidence while providing a bounded interface to the action policy. Across RoboMME, RMBench, and four real-world manipulation tasks, Mem4Act achieves state-of-the-art performance on memory-dependent control, with success rates of 49.88%, 61.0%, and 81.5%, respectively. Extensive ablations further demonstrate the importance of temporal aggregation, complementary memory supervision, and memory-first training.
introduction:
Memory is fundamental to embodied intelligence: agents must remember past interactions and use them to guide future decisions (Yang et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026; Lei et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2026). Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance across diverse robotic tasks and embodiments (Reuss et al., 2025; Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Bu et al., 2025), yet most act primarily from the current observation. Under partial observability, however, decision-critical information may disappear long before it is needed. For example, in Fig. 1(a), block colors observed early become hidden after covering. Long-horizon manipulation tasks therefore require preserving and using the memory of past experiences.

A central challenge is how to turn past observations into effective memory for VLA models. Directly feeding the full history preserves detailed visual evidence and temporal context, but requires the large vision-language backbone to attend over an ever-growing sequence of visual tokens, leading to increasing computational and memory costs as well as potential causal confusion over long horizons. Existing methods reduce this burden through key-frame selection (Sridhar et al., 2025), per-frame token compression (Wang et al., 2026), or language summaries (Lei et al., 2025), but may sacrifice temporal coverage, fine-grained visual detail, or perceptual cues that become important only at later decision steps. We therefore distinguish historical context, which explicitly exposes past observations to the policy, from memory, which transforms and maintains information from prior interactions for future decisions. Under this definition, Mem4Act implements memory as a compact, fixed-capacity latent state that is continuously updated throughout the episode.

We argue that learning effective latent memory requires addressing three complementary challenges: coverage, content, and utilization (see Fig. 1(b)). Coverage asks how limited memory capacity should represent a long history. Without explicit temporal structure (Jang et al., 2025; Koo et al., 2026), memory tokens may redundantly encode similar periods while overlooking relevant events. Content asks whether memory preserves information that may become useful later. Under action supervision alone (Wang et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026), different histories can share the same immediate action while containing different information required later, providing weak supervision. Utilization asks whether the policy actually relies on memory. Because many actions can be predicted from the current observation alone, the policy may learn to ignore historical information, providing little incentive for memory to become decision-relevant. Together, effective memory therefore requires deciding where to attend, what to retain, and how to make the policy use it.

We introduce Mem4Act, a framework for learning effective latent memory in VLA models for long-horizon robotic control that addresses these challenges directly. For coverage, multi-granularity temporal attention organizes memory across temporal regions, progressively integrating local events into longer-term context. For content, semantic question answering directly supervises memory to preserve task-relevant facts, while key-frame DINO feature reconstruction (Siméoni et al., 2025) retains perceptual information from specific timesteps. For utilization, we adopt a memory-first training strategy that establishes informative memory representations before end-to-end action learning, encouraging the policy to exploit historical information rather than rely primarily on reactive cues.

We evaluate Mem4Act on 29 long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks: 16 single-arm tasks in RoboMME, 9 dual-arm tasks in RMBench, and 4 real-world dual-arm manipulation tasks. These tasks span diverse memory requirements, including temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory, as well as tasks that require recalling earlier observations and accumulating information across repeated interactions. Mem4Act achieves success rates of 49.88%, 61.0%, and 81.5% on RoboMME, RMBench, and real-world tasks, respectively, outperforming the strongest evaluated baselines while maintaining a fixed-size interface of 512 latent memory tokens. Extensive ablations further validate the effectiveness of its temporal structure, memory supervision, and training strategy. Our main contributions are:

Structured latent memory. We introduce multi-granularity temporal attention that allocates latent memory capacity across temporal scales, capturing local events and long-range context within a fixed-size latent memory interface.

Memory-specific supervision. We supervise latent memory learning with complementary semantic QA and key-frame perceptual feature reconstruction, encouraging retention of task-relevant historical information beyond action supervision alone.

Memory-first policy learning. We introduce a two-stage training strategy that first learns informative memory representations with auxiliary supervision and then jointly adapts memory and policy for control, improving both task performance and effective memory utilization.

title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards
authors: Helena Merker,Nick Walker,Andreea Bobu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin, TX.
abstract:
Reward learning typically assumes the human’s input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features—or aspects of the task—better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot.
Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn’t know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human’s attention on exactly those features.
In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to 30.8%30.8\% in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.
introduction:
When a human teaches a robot how to do a task, not every relevant aspect of the task—or feature—gets equal attention. For instance, while teaching a robot how to carry a knife across your cluttered kitchen, you might do a good job avoiding the hot stovetop or the rack hanging overhead, but struggle to consistently keep the knife away from every person or obstacle. Because humans have limited working memory and can’t focus on everything at once [1, 2], some features get carefully attended to while others are left underspecified. Recent work shows how the robot can detect, directly from its teaching data, which features were poorly supervised or entirely irrelevant to the task [3, 4]. We go a step further and ask: how should the robot work with the human to resolve that underspecification?

One approach is to ask the human for more demonstrations focused on the underspecified features [3]. But this places the burden on the human, who already struggled with attending to those features. We propose to shift this burden onto the robot: rather than ask the human to try again, the robot should itself ask targeted questions that resolve what it is uncertain about.

Preference queries, where the robot generates behavior options and the human just picks their preferred one, offer this kind of low-effort channel [5, 6, 7]. Active learning approaches select queries to maximally reduce uncertainty under a distribution over the human’s reward [6]. But when that distribution is initialized from imperfect teaching data [8], it inherits not just what the feedback got right but also its errors on the underspecified features. The robot then spends its early queries correcting a misaligned distribution before it can make progress on what it actually needs to learn.

Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn’t know can help it ask better questions. The robot’s diagnosis of what past teaching missed serves two roles. First, we use it to build an informed prior over the human’s reward: a Gaussian that is confident on the well-supervised features, flat on the underspecified ones, and near zero on irrelevant ones. This ensures preference queries are automatically directed at what needs resolving.
Second, we use it to supplement each query with an explanation that tells the human which features to focus on when answering, making the robot’s learning process transparent [9].
In Fig. 1, the robot communicates uncertainty about distance to human, and its query presents two options that vary along that feature. Together, these two components align what the robot asks with what the human attends to.

Our contributions are:
(1) an informed prior for active preference learning that corrects what the teaching data got wrong, automatically targeting queries at the underspecified features;
(2) an explanation mechanism that directs the human’s attention to those same features when answering, aligning what the robot asks with what the human attends to; and
(3) empirical validation in two simulated 7-DoF manipulation domains and a user study, where both components independently improve reward recovery and amplify each other, with the largest gains in the low-query regime.

title: Safe and Fuel-Efficient Motion Planning for Lunar Propulsive Drones
authors: Elena Wittemyer,Graco Gao
comment: This work has been submitted to the 2027 IEEE Aerospace Conference
abstract: Propulsive drones are a promising new technology for generating high-resolution terrain models of the Moon. In future lunar missions, propulsive drones will complete a series of hops across the lunar surface while capturing images with downward-facing cameras. We present an autonomous motion planning framework that uses a vision-guided optimal control strategy for performing safe, efficient hops between specified waypoints. The drone plans parabolic hops between waypoints generated by a global-level planner; if a nominal waypoint is unsafe or unreachable, the drone then completes a diversion maneuver to safely land. To evaluate the validity of potential landing sites, we develop a custom semantic segmentation model for identifying obstacles from aerial images, and we introduce an approach for rapidly calculating reachable terrain. We then use model predictive control (MPC) to robustly track hop trajectories that guide the drone towards safe landing sites. We test the optimal hop planner in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. Our results demonstrate that our unified motion planning framework yields safe, fuel-efficient hop trajectories which can be tracked rapidly and with low error via MPC.
introduction:
In a 2028 mission titled “MoonFall”, NASA plans to send a team of four propulsive drones to the Moon’s south pole to rapidly scout the lunar surface [1]. The drones will use their propulsion systems to complete short ‘hops’ across the surface of the Moon. In-flight, they will use multiple high-definition optical cameras to capture images of terrain that would be challenging to reach from the ground. With these images, the drones seek to build high-resolution models of the lunar surface, which are a critical resource for safe exploration of the Moon.
Scientists have developed terrain models for most of the lunar surface using orbital measurements [2]. At best, these digital elevation models (DEMs) have a resolution of about 1-5 m/pix; at worst, their resolution is about 60 m/pix [3]. Even the best DEMs do not have sufficient resolution to resolve smaller rocks or craters. Lunar landers often rely on these terrain models for choosing a landing site; these low-resolution models cannot provide enough information, so lunar landers must rely on sensor measurements moments before landing. Propulsive drones will generate terrain models at sub-meter resolutions, enabling safe landings for future spacecraft and supporting a sustained presence on the lunar south pole.

In this work, we consider the problem of autonomous motion planning for propulsive drone-based exploration of the lunar south pole. The first key challenge in motion planning for propulsive drones is landing site safety. At the moment a drone begins a hop, it does not know in advance where it is safe to land. Mid-flight, the drone must be able to identify a site that is not only free of obstacles like rocks or craters, but is also reachable under its dynamics model. It must then calculate and follow some feasible trajectory to reach this safe site. Moreover, it is important that each hop the drone completes is fuel efficient. The planned MoonFall drones have a limited fuel supply and are not designed to refuel; once they are low on fuel, the drones will permanently land and deploy a long-duration payload [1]. The more fuel efficient a drone’s hops are, the more terrain it can cover during its short flying lifespan. Critically, the drone must be able to determine landing site safety/reachability online and track efficient hop trajectories in real-time. We present a robust motion planning framework for propulsive drones which tackles the aforementioned challenges. Our motion planning framework begins with a series of global waypoints, which are chosen using low-resolution existing DEMs of the moon. Our optimal trajectory planner then generates hops between these waypoints. Midway through each hop, we calculate the set of landing sites that are both reachable and obstacle-free. If the next global waypoint is not reachable or safe, we calculate an optimal trajectory to the nearest valid landing site. This motion planning process is illustrated in Fig. 1. We test our motion planning framework in a high-fidelity lunar simulation developed by the Stanford NAVLab [4].

Our main contributions are as follows:

We design a motion planning architecture for fuel-efficient hop trajectories that are rapidly tracked using model predictive control.

We propose a strategy for calculating the set of reachable landing sites under the drone’s dynamics model in real-time.

We develop a lightweight semantic segmentation model trained on aerial images of simulated lunar terrain to identify rocks and craters in real-time.

1. We design a motion planning architecture for fuel-efficient hop trajectories that are rapidly tracked using model predictive control.

2. We propose a strategy for calculating the set of reachable landing sites under the drone’s dynamics model in real-time.

3. We develop a lightweight semantic segmentation model trained on aerial images of simulated lunar terrain to identify rocks and craters in real-time.

title: MOSS: Mode-Oriented Source Shaping for Robot Flow Matching Policies
authors: Zirun Ma,Jindou Jia,Tuo An,Jiaqi Bai,Jiahua Dong,Jianfei Yang
abstract: In robotic manipulation, the same observation often admits multiple feasible actions. Generative policies such as diffusion and flow matching naturally capture such multimodal behaviors, yet which mode is executed is left to random sampling and cannot be actively controlled. We propose Mode-Oriented Source Shaping (MOSS), which turns mode selection into an explicit choice of where generation starts. We first reveal, both empirically and theoretically, that deterministic flow transport induces mode-dependent structure in the source space. Under ideal deterministic ODE transport, distinct behavioral modes have distinct source-space preimages, while practical approximation errors can blur their boundaries due to imbalanced data, limited model capacity, and few inference steps. Motivated by this source-space structure, MOSS constructs semantically aligned mode-specific Gaussian sources that encode mode identity in the initial noise. A modality-strength estimator predicts the local degree of multimodality, which adaptively controls the geometry of the mode-specific sources. It contracts them toward a shared Gaussian where behaviors are similar and separates them near behavioral branching points. During deployment, the desired behavior is selected at inference simply by sampling from the corresponding component. Across 66 simulated and 33 real-world manipulation tasks, MOSS steers to the target mode up to 100%100\% of the time with high task success, recovers minority modes at over 90%90\% guidance rate under a :9010\!:\!90 imbalance dataset, and surpasses mode-conditioned flow policy by 43.343.3 points of guidance rate on real robots.
introduction:
Generative models have recently become a prominent paradigm in robot imitation learning (Pearce et al., 2023; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026). Unlike conventional policies that regress toward an optimal action, representative approaches such as Diffusion Policy (DP) (Chi et al., 2023) and Flow Matching (FM) (Lipman et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2026) generate action trajectories from random noise, allowing them to represent multiple feasible behaviors under the same observation, i.e., multimodal behaviors (Zhai et al., 2025). Here, a behavior mode denotes a semantically coherent family of action sequences that follow the same qualitative strategy for accomplishing the task (Chi et al., 2023). For instance, a robot may approach the same object from the left or the right, or interact with different targets in different orders, while still completing the task successfully. However, in existing generative policies, which mode is ultimately executed is largely determined implicitly by random sampling (Lipman et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026). This limits their applicability in settings that require user-specified preferences, test-time constraints, or human intervention (Zoellner et al., 2026; He et al., 2025).

Existing solutions fall into two categories. The straightforward one explicitly conditions the generative model on a mode indicator, in practice most often a language instruction, so that different conditions induce different action distributions (Yang et al., 2026; Zhang and Gienger, 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Such conditioning, however, often fails to steer the policy reliably when the training data are imbalanced (Fang et al., 2026), since high-dimensional visual scenes are strongly correlated with task execution, the model tends to learn scene-action shortcuts that bypass the weaker, low-dimensional language condition (Ren et al., 2026). The other line instead operates on the source distribution of FM, controlling multimodal behaviors by implicitly learning a set of Gaussian priors (Zhang et al., 2026; Machado et al., 2026). These priors, however, carry no explicit semantic correspondence to behavioral modes, so aligning them with user-defined modes still demands additional networks and laborious post-alignment (Zhang et al., 2026).

Toward a more reliable handle on mode selection, we first analyze how a well-trained FM policy behaves on multimodal tasks. We find that, even with a standard isotropic Gaussian source, the final behavior does not arise randomly from the entire noise space. Under deterministic Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) transport, different behavioral modes tend to occupy distinct, albeit noticeably entangled, regions of the source space. We further show theoretically that, under ideal transport conditions, such mode-specific initial-noise regions are guaranteed to be implicitly separated. In practice, however, imbalanced mode distributions, limited model capacity, and a restricted number of inference steps leave these partitions interleaved, weakly separated, or severely imbalanced, sometimes resulting in mode preference or even mode collapse (Zhai et al., 2025; Mazza et al., 2026). This raises a natural question: can we make the existing partitioning more explicit, and steer behavior directly through the initial distribution?

Based on this insight, we propose Mode-Oriented Source Shaping, termed MOSS, which enables controllable multimodal generation by dynamically shaping the source distribution of FM, as shown in Figure 1. Specifically, we first construct semantically defined mode-specific Gaussian sources, explicitly encoding mode identity into the initial noise and making the resulting control more robust to imbalanced mode distributions, limited model capacity, and limited inference steps. Since multiple modes typically arise only during certain critical phases rather than throughout the entire task (Jia et al., 2026a), a modality-strength estimator then predicts the local degree of multimodality from previous observation and action history, and uses it to continuously modulate the separability of the Gaussian components. When demonstrations from different modes behave alike, the components contract toward a shared Gaussian and maximize data sharing. As the robot approaches a behavioral branch, they gradually separate and give the initial noise a clear, stable mode identity.

MOSS provides several practical advantages beyond explicit mode selection. First, when different modes in the training demonstrations are highly imbalanced, the generation probabilities of standard FM tend to inherit the empirical data distribution. In contrast, our method can directly adjust the deployment probability of each mode by changing the source sampling distribution. Second, for data-scarce modes, we find that the proposed strategy can effectively leverage shared trajectory data from other modes, allowing the policy to learn more stable common motion structures while preserving clear mode boundaries, thereby improving both sample efficiency and task success for minority modes. Finally, compared with methods that apply strong guidance to shift the learned vector field at inference time, mode-specific sources still initialize transport from regions already established during training. This can potentially reduce trajectory-quality degradation caused by inference-time guidance (Yu et al., 2026), while naturally extending to currently emerging one-step denoising algorithms that do not support guidance (Ho and Salimans, 2022; Jia et al., 2026b).

We systematically evaluate our method on multiple robotic manipulation tasks with multimodal structure, including 66 simulation tasks and 33 real-world robot tasks. Compared with standard FM (Lipman et al., 2023), explicit mode-conditioned FM (Lei et al., 2026), and source-based methods (Zhang et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026), MOSS achieves up to 100%100\% target-mode steering while maintaining high task success rate (SR). Even under a highly imbalanced mode distribution (10:9010:90), our method can reliably recover the minority mode, achieving over 90%90\% guidance rate (GR). Ablations show that adaptive source geometry improves GR over fixed Gaussian separation by 1212-1414 percentage points in average GR at the same training budget. On real-world tasks, MOSS achieves an average GR/SR of 84.2%/85.3%84.2\%/85.3\%, outperforming mode-conditioned FM by 43.343.3 and 12.012.0 percentage points in average GR and SR, respectively. These results validate the effectiveness of source-space control under visual noise, limited demonstrations, and execution errors.

title: Whole-Body Dexterity
authors: Conor Mc Gartoll,An Dang,Pranay Thangeda,Arjun Gupta,Carolina Higuera,Nima Fazeli,Mustafa Mukadam,Manikantan Nambi
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Current humanoid dexterous manipulation remains largely confined to end-effectors and simple grasps, falling short of humans’ ability to engage the entire body by bracing and sliding bulky objects against the arms and torso. We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses the robot’s body and appendages as contact surfaces to grasp and manipulate objects. Our sim-to-real pipeline first generates a dataset of feasible whole-body grasps, then trains reinforcement-learning experts on a general any-to-any repositioning objective by sampling initial and goal grasps from the dataset, and distills these experts into a single policy that uses proprioception and object geometry. We show that the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, where it repositions a basketball and a cardboard box to regions around the torso and completes a long-horizon task that stows a box under one arm, carries it from a shelf to a table, and places it. The controller operates interactively, steered by coarse motion references from a human teleoperator. Across real-world whole-body manipulation tasks, the distilled controller completes 90% of trials, compared with 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.
introduction:
People rarely manipulate with their hands alone. We brace a box against the chest, cradle a basket across both arms, or tuck an object under one arm to free the other. These actions use the limbs and torso as a single highly dexterous manipulator.
We call this ability to reposition objects by continually changing supporting body contacts whole-body dexterous manipulation and apply it directly to humanoids.

Prior humanoid work has used this term for specific settings, such as coordinated whole-body control for manipulation with the hands [1, 2], while related loco-manipulation confines dexterity to the end-effectors [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] or to a sustained arm grasp on a bulky object [8, 9, 10]. None treats it as a general capability in which contact is established and released with any link to move an object across diverse regions of the body.

Viewed through this lens, whole-body dexterous manipulation has a useful parallel in dexterous hands, with the limbs and torso taking the roles of fingers and palm. Recent dexterous-hand work shows that strong capabilities emerge from learning to move objects through dense sequences of intermediate targets, whether by pre-training on anygrasp-to-anygrasp transitions [11] or by tracking hand–object subgoals from human motion through regrasps and finger gaiting [12].
Extending this principle to humanoids introduces a challenge: a dexterous hand with many fingers can often reposition some fingers while the others support the object [13, 14], whereas a humanoid using two arms has fewer independent supports. Releasing one arm may require the other to brace the object against the torso, and changing grasps can require rapid reconfiguration and rolling or sliding contact.
This additional complexity calls for a different approach to repositioning across body regions than these existing methods.

We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a framework for learning whole-body dexterous manipulation through mode-constrained re-grasping (Fig. 2) and deploying it on a real humanoid. We first generate a diverse set of whole-body grasps, then use them to initialize reinforcement-learning experts, WBD-EX. Experts learn to move objects between grasps toward goals specified by an object position and a target grasp mode: a left-arm, both-arm, or right-arm grasp. Transitions allow brief contact loss during movement but require a stable hold in the target mode at goals, so the experts learn how to hand off objects between arms, enabling repositioning across difficult regions such as behind the back and on top of the shoulders.
We distill expert trajectories into a controller that uses an object geometry descriptor to refine motion commands into stable whole-body object repositioning, without privileged object state.
Our main contributions are:

A whole-body grasp generation method defined over mode-typed contact configurations, formulated for arbitrary open-link articulated rigid-body systems and demonstrated on a humanoid robot.

A whole-body grasp generation method defined over mode-typed contact configurations, formulated for arbitrary open-link articulated rigid-body systems and demonstrated on a humanoid robot.

WBD-EX, per-object repositioning experts built on a mode-constrained re-grasping formulation that uses the diverse grasp dataset.

A distillation procedure that turns these experts into a controller conditioned on proprioception and object geometry, refining coarse commands into dexterous manipulation of diverse objects in simulation and on a real humanoid.
