title: REKI: Registering Knowledge in VLAs
authors: Juliette Marrie,Paul Pacaud,Adrien Ramanana Rahary,Shizhe Chen,Moritz Böhle
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size.
REKI consists of a vision–language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision–language data.
Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert’s cache.
This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer.
REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference.
We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: github.com/kyutai-labs/reki.
introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have become an effective paradigm for language-conditioned robot control.
A pretrained vision–language model (VLM) encodes camera views and instruction, based on which a smaller action expert predicts the next actions (Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026).

The strongest VLAs today are pretrained partly on proprietary data, and neither these data nor the pretraining pipelines are released (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026), making it hard to reproduce their results. Since each new model changes architecture, data and training recipe at once, gains cannot be traced back to a single choice.
With REKI, we release the full pipeline, from data curation to deployment.
REKI has a simple design, is pretrained on public data only and sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size.
It pairs a VLM with a flow-matching action expert, and a memory mechanism gives the policy access to its recent past.

Preserving past context can improve control (Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Chi et al., 2025), yet most VLAs predict actions from the current observation alone (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026).
Existing ways of incorporating such context, however, often introduce substantial overhead (Fig. 2): feeding past frames to the VLM adds their image tokens to every VLM pass (Jang et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026), recurrent methods require sequential training (Cherepanov et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026), and others introduce additional, dedicated memory modules to the policy (Shi et al., 2026; Koo et al., 2026).

REKI summarises past context through a small set of registers (Darcet et al., 2024) in the action expert.
The registers of each frame are cached across chunks (Fig. 3).
Each frame is thus encoded only once and no separate module, sequential unroll during training or test-time update mechanisms are necessary.
This yields clear gains at almost no overhead, and our 2.4B model REKI ranks first among VLAs pretrained on public data on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365 (Fig. 1), and generalises to real robots.

Our ablations show that memory consistently improves performance, with the most pronounced gains for the first past frame (Fig. 5).
Beyond task success, we find that memory stabilises action generation: without memory, the policy often oscillates between poses across action chunks, while with memory, such oscillations are about four times rarer (Fig. 5).

Our contributions are thus three-fold: (i) We introduce REKI, a 2.4B-parameter VLA pretrained on public data, which sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size. (ii) We introduce register tokens in the action expert to act as a memory, which can be cached efficiently, and analyse how this reduces the failure modes of the memoryless policy. We hope REKI serves as a strong and accessible baseline for future VLA research. To foster VLA research, we release the model weights and our optimised training and inference code, from data curation to deployment on a real robot.

title: Inertially Significant Humanoid Teleoperation via Whole Body Model Predictive Control and Online Parameter Estimation
authors: James Foster,Beomyeong Park,Luigi Penco,Robert Griffin
abstract: The effective deployment of humanoid robots in practical tasks of interest will require a capability of sensing and adapting to variations in inertial parameters, as occurs during heavy tool use or when carrying significant payload. Such payloads constitute a significant proportion of the combined payload-robot system, the effects of which cannot be ignored by delegating to feedback control. This paper showcases a general solution to this problem by integrating a whole body model predictive controller (WB-MPC) with an extended Kalman filter (EKF) for online estimation of fully physically consistent time-varying inertial parameters. These estimates are fed through to the WB-MPC’s full rigid body dynamics model, resulting in more accurate feedforward torques for task demands under external load. Additionally, a virtual reality (VR) interface is provided that enables an operator to provide task-specific references without regard to payload while delegating dynamic balance to the WB-MPC. The framework is validated with simulation and hardware experiments on a humanoid system.
introduction:
A key promise of humanoid robots lies in performing tasks that involve exerting significant force to manipulated objects, such as lifting a heavy tool or carrying a payload. In many such tasks, the inertia of the manipulated object is a significant fraction of the robot’s own.

A promising candidate solution is whole body model predictive control (WB-MPC), which iteratively solves a trajectory optimization over the robot’s full rigid body dynamics. It was first demonstrated on a humanoid in [1], and subsequent humanoid implementations have largely targeted locomotion [2, 3, 4]. Far fewer works apply WB-MPC to manipulation [5], and fewer still to objects whose inertia is significant relative to the robot. The closest is [6], which remains in simulation and estimates a modest payload inertia only after task execution. Other model-based approaches either add the load to a centroidal model explicitly [7], or absorb it implicitly through direct adaptive control laws bound to a reference model [8, 9]. Reinforcement learning (RL), meanwhile, has produced increasingly robust humanoid locomotion and manipulation [10, 11], but typically absorbs load variation in one of two ways. The first is domain randomization [12, 13], which trades nominal performance for robustness and tends toward conservative behavior; the second is a learned “extrinsics” estimator, whose abstract signals are tightly coupled to the policy that consumes them [14]. MPC and RL have recently been combined in [15], where a massively parallelized nonlinear centroidal MPC embedded inside policy training yields robust loco-manipulation.

A WB-MPC over the full rigid body dynamics can in principle directly command the feedforward effort an added payload demands, but only insofar as its rigid body dynamics model accurately captures the manipulated inertia [16]. A structure that underpins most identification methods for rigid body inertial parameters is that the inverse dynamics are linear with respect to the inertial parameters [17]. The system identification literature usually focuses on offline identification [18]; control-oriented online work has instead tended to focus on estimating gross quantities such as the center of mass and momentum [19], or a payload from previously identified dynamics coefficients [20] or a momentum observer [21]. For an estimate to be safely fed into a downstream controller, it must be fully physically consistent [22], which can be enforced via semidefinite programming [23], smooth nonlinear reparameterizations of the inertial parameters [24], or geometric methods [25, 26].

Model bias is also problematic when operating the robot via a virtual reality (VR) interface. VR provides operators with an intuitive control interface [27], and has become common both as a primary operation method and for data collection of learned control policies [28]. With some exceptions, VR operators typically do not have access to force feedback indicating a payload, and so may compensate to mitigate tracking offset, which is burdensome and deleterious to task performance. One such exception is the impressive but complex VR/haptic teleoperation suite in [29], where online inertial estimates are used to adjust the posture of a wheeled humanoid modeled as a cart-pole system, allowing the manipulation of heavy payloads relative to robot weight.

In this paper we propose a framework coupling three components to enable intuitive VR teleoperation of humanoids manipulating significant loads via WB-MPC. Firstly, a WB-MPC trades off dynamic balance objectives with tight tracking of operator-specified taskspace objectives. Secondly, an extended Kalman filter (EKF) coupled in closed-loop with the WB-MPC estimates fully physically consistent inertial parameters online and passes them to the WB-MPC’s rigid body dynamics model, allowing feedforward torque compensation of a priori unknown loads. We include EKF extensions that increase numerical robustness and aid interpretation: we regularize the estimate through a fictitious nominal measurement that keeps the estimate well-conditioned under the weak excitation of teleoperated motion, and estimate deviations from a well-characterized nominal body using a generalized log-Cholesky parameterization [24, 30]. Lastly, a minimal VR teleoperation interface, combined with the aforementioned WB-MPC and EKF, allows an operator to command desired motion without the burden of compensating for added payload, while dynamic balance control is delegated to the WB-MPC. We validate the framework on loaded trajectory tracking and balance tasks in simulation, and showcase VR teleoperation under load on hardware for a 2323 degree of freedom humanoid system (Fig. 1).

title: FastVLA: Task-Conditioned and Temporally Adaptive Visual Token Compression for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Jiuyi Xu,Chengyuan Qian,Zhengzhong Tu,Yang Sui,Yangming Shi
comment: Accepted by WACV 2027
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, but closed-loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high-resolution, often multi-view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency.
Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision-critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control-critical tokens.
We introduce FastVLA, a training-free, task-aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework.
At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task-to-vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance-distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration.
We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot.
In simulation, it reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59% and action latency by 9-32% (a 1.09×\times-1.46×\times speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing plug-and-play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines.
On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20% (1.25×\times speedup) at comparable success.
Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a compelling paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, enabling policies to predict low-level actions conditioned on natural-language tasks and visual observations [30, 15, 3, 22, 6].
By leveraging large-scale pretraining and large vision-language backbones, VLAs demonstrate strong generalization across objects, scenes, and task specifications, making them increasingly attractive for deployment in versatile manipulation systems.
Despite their impressive capabilities, deploying these models in closed-loop control is often limited by inference efficiency [8].
At every control step, high-resolution (e.g., 224×\times224) and frequently multi-view observations are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens [14, 10] that dominate the compute and latency of the vision-language-model (VLM) backbone during action prediction, far outweighing the few text tokens of a short task.

Yet not all visual tokens contribute equally to action prediction.
In a typical manipulation step, only a small subset of tokens carries decision-critical information (e.g., the target object/place or the gripper–object contact region), while the rest are redundant or even distracting [26, 27, 11].
Reducing the number of visual tokens processed by the large-language-model (LLM) backbone, without sacrificing task performance, has therefore become a key direction for accelerating VLA inference [20, 21, 25].

However, directly applying VLM-specific token compression methods [4, 7, 29] to robotic control is often suboptimal, because these methods are designed for single-shot vision-language understanding, where the objective is to preserve global semantic content for perception tasks such as detection, captioning, or generation.
Unlike image-based VLMs that process a single image, or video-based VLMs that encode a fixed sequence of frames, a VLA interacts with the environment through actions that directly shape its subsequent observations: at each step the agent receives a new observation conditioned on its previous action and predicts the next one.
Visual tokens are thus not representations of a static scene but components of a sequential decision process, which sets token compression for VLA apart from its VLM counterpart in two respects.
The first is that token relevance is governed by the task rather than by generic visual saliency (now standard practice in language-guided pruning), which we adopt as our importance signal rather than claim as a contribution.
The second, and the focus of this work, is that the amount of decision-critical visual information varies drastically across control steps: some steps (e.g., target localization) rely on broad scene context, whereas others (e.g., grasping or contact) depend on a small, localized region.
A single fixed compression rate is therefore inherently mismatched, wasting computation when the useful information is concentrated, and discarding necessary context when broader information is required.

Motivated by this, we propose FastVLA, a training-free visual token compression framework for efficient VLA inference whose core is a temporally adaptive, per-step compression rate.
At each step, FastVLA scores visual-token importance with task-to-vision attention which is a training-free signal that a controlled comparison shows is more reliable for action prediction than vision-only or fused attention and then, crucially, decides how many tokens to keep from the shape of the resulting importance distribution.
Specifically, it estimates the effective number of tokens the decision depends on via an inverse-Simpson uniformity measure, and maps this quantity through an online sliding-window calibration to a timestep-dependent compression rate: when the current step concentrates on few tokens relative to its recent history it prunes aggressively, and when the decision draws on broader context it prunes conservatively.
By allocating the token budget where each decision needs it, FastVLA reduces LLM-backbone computation, speeds up action prediction, and improves closed-loop responsiveness, without caches or training.

We evaluate FastVLA on three open-source VLA models including OpenVLA [15], OpenVLA-OFT [14], and CogACT [16], across the widely used LIBERO [18] and SIMPLER [17] benchmarks, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot.
In simulation, FastVLA reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59% and action latency by 9-32% (up to a 1.46×1.46\times speedup) while maintaining task success, yielding a comparable or even better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing training-free compression, pruning, and reuse baselines.
On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20% (1.25×1.25\times speedup) and raises the control frequency by up to 25% at comparable success.
In summary, our contributions are:

We propose FastVLA, a training-free, plug-and-play visual token compression framework that accelerates closed-loop VLA inference.

We design a step-adaptive compression policy that sets a timestep-dependent token budget from the inverse-Simpson uniformity of the importance distribution under online sliding-window calibration.

We validate FastVLA on OpenVLA/OpenVLA-OFT (LIBERO), CogACT (SIMPLER), and a physical Franka Research 3 robot, achieving substantial compute and latency reductions in simulation and a 1.25×1.25\times real-robot speedup with comparable task success.

1. We propose FastVLA, a training-free, plug-and-play visual token compression framework that accelerates closed-loop VLA inference.

2. We design a step-adaptive compression policy that sets a timestep-dependent token budget from the inverse-Simpson uniformity of the importance distribution under online sliding-window calibration.

3. We validate FastVLA on OpenVLA/OpenVLA-OFT (LIBERO), CogACT (SIMPLER), and a physical Franka Research 3 robot, achieving substantial compute and latency reductions in simulation and a 1.25×1.25\times real-robot speedup with comparable task success.

title: Compliant GMT: Making General Motion Tracking Compliant via Residual Reference Adaptation
authors: Venki Parsuram,Michelle Wang,Jin-Hyuk Hong,Pulkit Agrawal
comment: Project website:this https URL
abstract:
We propose Compliant GMT (C-GMT), a modular framework for full-body compliant responses in general motion tracking. As humanoid robots move into real world deployment, they not only need to perform any motion but also respond safely and robustly to interaction forces. Existing general motion tracking policies can imitate diverse motions but are trained to be stiff, leading to unexpected and unsafe behaviors under disturbance. Prior work in compliant humanoid control trades off compliance and generality. There exist examples of full-body compliant responses, but these are heavily curated to single-reference policies. On the other hand, general motion trackers (GMT) are trained to rigidly imitate massive motion capture datasets. Our key insight is to leverage the generality of pretrained GMTs for motion tracking while introducing compliance from a residual adapter that conditions on a history of proprioception. This enables our approach, C-GMT, to achieve both general motion tracking and whole-body compliant responses. Compared to state-of-the-art general motion trackers and single-motion compliant policies, C-GMT demonstrates competitive performance in both motion tracking accuracy and compliance adherence. We further demonstrate improved safety, robustness, and error tolerance in simulation and real-world G1 experiments.
Project website: https://venki1899.github.io/c-gmt/
introduction:
As humanoid robots move toward operation in human-centered environments, they must combine agile and robust whole-body control with the ability to interact safely and effectively with people and objects. General motion tracking (GMT) has emerged as the predominant approach for humanoid whole-body control, using a single policy trained on massive human motion capture datasets to imitate diverse and highly dynamic motion references while rejecting external disturbances [1, 2, 3]. Although this stiffness is desirable for free-space motion tracking, unexpected contacts during physical interaction will cause the policy to forcefully drive the robot toward its reference position, potentially damaging the robot or environment. This is a fundamental barrier to deploying humanoids alongside people.

A compliant robot mitigates these effects by yielding appropriately to external forces, improving safety and robustness. However, recent work on learned compliant humanoid control trades off generality and compliance. Works that demonstrate coordinated full-body compliant responses are restricted to single motion imitation [4] or command the lower body only with base velocity and height [5]. Alternatively, other works perform general motion tracking but restrict compliant responses to the upper-body [6, 7]. These approaches jointly train motion tracking and compliance within the same policy, requiring the agent to simultaneously follow the commanded motion, maintain balance, infer external wrenches, and learn to respond compliantly. Consequently, single-stage training poses significant challenges with long training times, many infeasible force events, and sensitive reward tuning. Our key insight is that we can achieve both competitive generality and compliance in a single policy by exploiting the capabilities of pretrained general motion trackers and introducing compliance through a residual adapter conditioned on a proprioception history.

We introduce Compliant GMT (C-GMT), the first framework for general motion tracking with unified full-body compliant responses. Rather than asking the motion tracking policy itself to learn both tracking and compliance, we formulate compliance as a reference adaptation problem. This decomposition separates the two objectives: a force-robust GMT based on [3] is responsible for faithfully executing the commanded motion and maintaining balance under disturbances, while a learned residual adapter modifies the reference motion to realize the desired compliance. To generate compliant reference motions for the downstream GMT, we construct an analytical teacher that observes the applied external force and uses a spring law and an inverse-kinematics (IK) solver to compute compliant adaptations. We can use the teacher and pretrained GMT to tune the desired response and verify its feasibility before training the adapter. To learn to estimate force and react appropriately at deployment time, we distill the compliant behavior into a residual adapter conditioned on proprioception that provides compliant references to the GMT. Our contributions are twofold:

1. We introduce Compliant GMT, a modular framework that unifies general motion tracking with adjustable whole-body compliance through residual reference adaptation. We propose a proprioceptive residual adapter distilled from a force-privileged teacher to generate compliant references.

2. Through simulation and real world experiments on the Unitree G1, we show that C-GMT matches both the compliance adherence of previous compliant single-motion tracking policies [4] and maintains tracking performance comparable to state-of-the-art GMTs. We further demonstrate C-GMT’s novel advantages of compliance during highly dynamic whole-body motions and coordinated whole-body compliant responses.

title: CF-Splat: Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors
authors: Yixin Fang,Liang Zhao
abstract:
Splatting-based radiance-field representations have recently gained popularity in robotic perception, enabling high-quality novel-view synthesis (NVS) through explicit scene primitives. However, existing splatting methods typically rely on iterative nonlinear optimization that jointly optimizes millions of coupled primitive parameters, resulting in substantial computation time, peak GPU memory consumption, and susceptibility to local minima. In this paper, we propose CF-Splat, a novel closed-form triangle-splatting framework for efficient scene appearance estimation over a known mesh either pre-existing or provided by upstream mapping or reconstruction pipelines. Our key insight is that, by properly formulating the problem over the given mesh geometry and calibrated cameras, the rendered pixel colors can be expressed linearly with respect to the per-vertex spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients, allowing multi-view scene appearance estimation to be formulated as a global linear least-squares (LLS) problem without the need of iterative nonlinear optimization. To guarantee a well-posed solution under uneven multi-view observation coverage, we introduce adaptive SH regularization that constrains insufficiently supported high-order SH coefficients and yields a unique global minimizer. To ensure the scalability to large-scale scenes, we develop a triangle-structured matrix-free preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver that avoids explicitly constructing the large sparse normal system while producing the same LLS solution. Experiments on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate that CF-Splat achieves competitive or superior NVS quality compared with state-of-the-art splatting methods. While, CF-Splat requires approximately 27.5×\times–378.0×\times less computation time and 1.8×\times lower peak GPU memory on average than 3DGS across scenes of different scales on a consumer-grade laptop.
Interactive live demos are available on an anonymous website11

introduction:
Radiance-field representations have become increasingly important in robotic perception, including augmented reality [1], photorealistic simulation [2], and autonomous navigation [3]. In these settings, an effective scene representation should capture reliable geometry while efficiently modeling appearance, enabling high-quality novel-view synthesis (NVS) with low computational overhead for downstream robotic tasks. Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) [4] methods represent scenes as continuous volumetric functions parameterized by multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and have demonstrated remarkable NVS quality, but typically require hours of per-scene optimization. Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [5] has achieved rendering quality comparable to NeRF while substantially reducing optimization time and enabling real-time rendering. It explicitly represents a scene as a set of anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives and employs a differentiable tile-based rasterizer. However, 3DGS still faces four major bottlenecks: (1) its nonlinear optimization is susceptible to local minima, causing the solution to depend on initialization and optimization settings; (2) the optimized Gaussians do not accurately conform to the underlying scene surfaces; (3) per-scene optimization requires tens of thousands of iterations, making it still computationally expensive; and (4) the training process typically needs substantial GPU memory overhead.

These limitations of 3DGS primarily lie in its training pipeline, which jointly optimizes millions of coupled Gaussian parameters, including geometry parameters such as positions, opacities, and covariances, as well as appearance parameters represented by spherical harmonics (SH), through iterative gradient-based optimization on the Adam optimizer [6]. During this nonlinear optimization shown in Fig. 1, additional Gaussians are progressively introduced, moved, reshaped, and recolored to better fit the appearance with photometric-only residual at each per-view iteration. This inevitably increases optimization time and GPU memory overhead, while potentially trapping the optimization in view-specific appearance overfitting and degrading the underlying geometric structure.

Existing methods have attempted to alleviate these limitations from different perspectives. Multi-view regularization-based methods [10] introduce cross-view constraints to improve global consistency. Geometry-aware representations [11, 12] employ more compact primitives and surface-aligned constraints to better conform to the underlying geometric structure. Triangle-integrated approaches [13, 14, 15]
incorporate mesh constraints or directly adopt triangle-based representations to achieve a better balance between geometry and appearance fitting. More recently, efficiency-oriented
methods [16, 17, 18] regulate Gaussian densification and pruning to suppress redundant primitives, thereby reducing computational and memory costs. In parallel, numerical optimization methods [19, 20] explore LM-based and matrix-free solvers to efficiently compute parameter updates within iterative nonlinear optimization. Despite these advances, they do not fundamentally alter the iterative nonlinear optimization framework of 3DGS, leaving its inherent bottlenecks unresolved. Therefore, a clear gap remains toward a closed-form splatting formulation for more efficient appearance estimation.

To this end, we propose CF-Splat, a novel triangle-splatting framework that leverages a mesh prior to enable closed-form scene appearance estimation. In many real-world robotic systems, this scene geometry prior is readily available such as pre-operative CT scans in surgical robotics or CAD models for object manipulation, or can be obtained from upstream mapping or reconstruction pipelines, such as SLAM systems [21, 22, 23, 24] and SDF-based reconstruction methods [25, 26, 8]. Rather than re-optimizing geometry together with appearance, by properly formulating view-dependent appearance over the given mesh and calibrated cameras, we can establish a linear relationship between rendered pixel colors and per-vertex spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. Based on this, scene appearance estimation can be formulated as a global linear least-squares (LLS) problem and a closed-form solution can be obtained without any iteration. To further ensure a unique global minimizer, we introduce adaptive SH regularization for uneven observation coverage to make the LLS problem well posed. The proposed LLS formulation also results in a block-sparse structure corresponding to mesh topology that leads us to develop an efficient triangle-structured matrix-free preconditioned conjugate-gradient (PCG) solver, extending its scalability across different scene sizes. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of CF-Splat.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose CF-Splat, a novel closed-form triangle-splatting framework for
efficient scene appearance estimation over a known mesh.

We propose CF-Splat, a novel closed-form triangle-splatting framework for
efficient scene appearance estimation over a known mesh.

We derive a global LLS formulation for scene appearance estimation by exploiting the linear dependence of rendered pixel colors on per-vertex SH coefficients, thereby eliminating iterative nonlinear optimization and substantially reducing computation cost.

We introduce adaptive SH regularization to address uneven multi-view
observation coverage, resulting in a well-posed LLS problem with a unique
global minimizer and improved cross-view stability of the solution.

We develop a triangle-structured matrix-free PCG solver that avoids
explicitly constructing the global normal system, reducing GPU memory consumption and enabling the proposed LLS formulation to large-scale scenes.

We extensively evaluate CF-Splat on diverse real-world datasets against state-of-the-art splatting methods. CF-Splat achieves competitive or even superior NVS quality while maintaining high computational efficiency on a consumer-grade laptop. The source code will be released upon the acceptance of this paper.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section II reviews related works. Section III presents our proposed closed-form scene appearance estimation.
Section IV presents the triangle-structured matrix-free PCG solver.
Section V presents the comprehensive experiments.
Finally, Section VI concludes the paper with
its limitations and future directions.

title: Onboard Lightweight LLM Reasoning for Human-Aware Safe UAV Navigation
authors: Siwei Cai,Yuwei Wu,Vijay Kumar,Lifeng Zhou
comment: HEAI -- IROS 2026 Workshop
abstract:
Aerial robots operating near people must treat a pedestrian, a parked car, and a wall differently, yet conventional perception–planning stacks reduce all of them to occupied geometry—a human-aware safety gap in which category-specific clearance is unavailable to the planner and temporary occlusions remove pedestrian-specific constraints from its map.
We present a modular, fully onboard pipeline that closes this gap by turning visual observations into context-dependent safety constraints for real-time UAV navigation.
A shared BLIP encoder drives scene captioning and text-conditioned segmentation, which is fused with depth to localize obstacles in 3D.
Obstacle-specific risk is inferred by a lightweight LLM (Qwen-2.5-0.5B) stabilized with retrieval-augmented generation and grammar-constrained decoding that restricts its output to a planner-compatible JSON schema.
The LLM reasons once per object category rather than per frame: its verdicts are cached per class, so previously seen categories are resolved without inference and new ones trigger a fresh retrieval-grounded query; detections are additionally given persistent identities and held in the map across occlusions.
The perception pipeline runs at 10 Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, while fallback LLM queries take approximately 0.8 s and remain off the control-critical path.
In Gazebo, low-altitude urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles shows a roughly 3×3\times reduction in collision events over a geometric planner, and semantics-aware landing among moving actors raises success from 34% to 96%.
The 224-pixel encoder input limits reliable small-object perception at range; conservative pedestrian margins and short-term persistence mitigate this limitation during navigation.
introduction:
UAVs are increasingly deployed for delivery, inspection, and monitoring in environments shared with people [1, 2, 3].
Such environments are not only dynamic but semantically heterogeneous: a pedestrian, a moving truck, a parked car, and a hedge all constrain the feasible trajectory, yet they imply very different risk and should not receive identical avoidance behavior.
Conventional pipelines optimize trajectories well when the environment is accurately modeled [4, 5], but they treat obstacles as geometry: occupancy maps and detections say where an object is, not how it should modify clearance, priority, or motion response [6].

We call the resulting deficiency the human-aware safety gap: a geometric planner assigns a person and a lamp post the same clearance, and its map carries no notion of who or what is being avoided.
Human-aware planning should instead maintain larger, category-dependent clearance around people and preserve short-term awareness of them through temporary occlusions.
Our goal is therefore not to model people merely as dynamic obstacles, but to preserve category-specific safety semantics when planning around them: closing the gap means producing context-dependent safety constraints—clearance, dynamism, and persistence that depend on the object’s category and the operating context—and delivering them to the planner in real time, onboard.

Large language models (LLMs) offer the abstraction needed to produce such constraints [7, 8], and LLM-based monitoring and planning has begun to appear in robotics [9, 10, 11].
Sinha et al. [9] pair a fast embedding classifier with a slow generative fallback, but the vehicle must wait while the large model reasons; contact-aware planners [11] model interaction physics rather than grounding live observations.
Prior landing methods [12, 13] focus on cooperative targets and typically assume obstacle-free landing zones.
We ask instead: how can language-based reasoning run onboard an aerial robot so that its understanding of the people and vehicles around it becomes spatially grounded, real-time planner constraints?

Three system-level obstacles stand in the way.
(i) LLMs cannot consume raw imagery or 3D geometry, and end-to-end vision-language models (VLMs) are too heavy for Size, Weight and Power (SWaP)-limited platforms [14]; we therefore decouple a light vision-language encoder (VLE) [15] from a text-only LLM and ground its output with depth.
(ii) Lightweight LLMs that fit onboard hallucinate [16]; we stabilize them with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [17] over a safety knowledge base and constrain decoding to a JSON grammar.
(iii) Semantic guidance must not break real-time control; the LLM never commands the vehicle but adjusts planner-level constraints (unsafe regions and margins) consumed by a model-based planner and controller.
A fourth obstacle emerged only after closed-loop deployment among pedestrians: with a 2 s map decay, a brief occlusion removes a person’s constraint from the map before they reappear, so the pipeline needs object persistence in addition to semantics.

This paper contributes:
(1) a semantic-to-spatial grounding pipeline that turns RGB-D observations into obstacle-specific risk and 3D safety constraints;
(2) a RAG-stabilized, grammar-constrained lightweight LLM reasoning module, whose per-class verdicts are cached so that the LLM reasons once per category rather than per frame, with a cache-miss reasoning pathway for categories outside a fixed semantic policy;
(3) persistent obstacle identities with occlusion-aware holding in the planner map; and
(4) an onboard feasibility study on Jetson-class hardware together with closed-loop Gazebo experiments in urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles and in autonomous landing, with an analysis of perception under the limited input resolution that onboard compute imposes.

title: CBF-Based Control Allocation for Omnidirectional Tiltrotor Aerial Robots
authors: Seobeom Lee,Hyondong Oh
abstract: Actively tilting aerial robots can generate six-dimensional wrenches, but slow servo response can make a desired wrench infeasible during reconfiguration. This paper develops a control barrier function (CBF) allocator that preserves wrench feasibility under bounded servo-configuration mismatch. An exact equivalent-wrench identity connects the thrust required at nominal and actual configurations. For a nonsingular six-channel allocation map, inverse allocation reduces robust wrench containment to twelve thrust margins tightened by an ellipsoidal reserve. Their complete derivatives yield a six-variable servo-rate quadratic program, followed by differential thrust allocation for tracking. A conditional forward-invariance result establishes actual-configuration feasibility under reserve coverage, feasible initialization, and admissible CBF inputs. A complementary MuJoCo study evaluates a measured-angle implementation against geometric, augmented differential, and normalized differential allocation in circular and cartwheel maneuvers, with and without disturbances. The proposed implementation achieves lower position error in all four recorded scenarios, with an attitude tradeoff in circular tracking. During the disturbed cartwheel, the desired wrench is feasible at all 1751 stored samples of continuous rotation; baseline violation rates range from 60.8% to 100%. These comparisons evaluate sampled feasibility; validation of the nominal-trajectory certificate requires nominal-state and reserve-coverage records.
introduction:
Omnidirectional aerial robots can regulate position and attitude independently, enabling contact inspection, tool alignment, and six-dimensional physical interaction [1, 2, 3]. Fixed tilted-rotor designs obtain this capability through their geometry [4, 5], whereas actively tilting platforms can reorient their thrust directions during flight [6, 7]. In the latter case, control allocation must coordinate fast thrust changes with slower servo motion.

Servo transients can make a desired wrench infeasible even when the target pose is kinematically admissible. A force and moment achievable after reorientation may lie outside the thrust-limited set at the current tilt angles. Aggressive motion therefore requires an allocator that preserves wrench authority while both the request and the actuation geometry evolve.

Wrench tracking and instantaneous feasibility are distinct objectives. Tracking reduces the difference between the desired and generated wrench; feasibility requires an admissible thrust vector at the current rotor directions. Servo motion changes the attainable wrench set. We constrain that motion to retain the requested wrench together with a neighborhood accounting for nominal-to-actual configuration mismatch.

Geometric and differential allocators provide direct actuator setpoints, coordinated reconfiguration, and limit handling [8, 7, 9]. Augmented and normalized differential allocation further connect wrench controllers to actuator-rate commands and account for heterogeneous limits [10]. The remaining question addressed here is how to constrain servo reconfiguration so that a specified wrench request remains inside the instantaneous thrust-limited set despite configuration mismatch.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) express this objective as constraints on servo motion [11, 12]. For a nonsingular six-channel configuration, inverse allocation gives six lower and six upper thrust margins. An ellipsoidal wrench reserve tightens them against nominal-to-actual configuration mismatch. Their complete derivatives, including the changing reserve, define a servo-rate quadratic program (QP); a downstream differential allocator commands thrust rates for tracking.

The contributions are threefold:

An exact nominal-to-actual required-thrust identity and a support-based reduction of configuration-robust wrench containment to twelve scalar margins.

An explicit servo-rate CBF-QP and a conditional invariance proof connecting nominal margins to desired-wrench feasibility at the actual servo angles, without assuming identical commanded and actual servo velocities.

A telemetry-based comparison of a measured-angle CBF variant with geometric allocation (GA), augmented differential allocation (ADA), and normalized differential allocation (NDA) across four scenarios. Recorded force-space views and six-dimensional margins relate tracking performance to instantaneous wrench feasibility.

Sections III–IV establish the model and baseline allocators. Sections V–VI develop the CBF formulation and guarantee. Sections VII–IX present the simulation comparison, design implications, and conclusions.

title: Plans Are Not Executions: Adapting Frozen World-Model Planners to Controller-Induced Execution Shift
authors: Danqi Zhao,Keyu Chen,Wenchao Sun,Minglei Huang,Jianhe Zhang,Yan Zhu,Hao Cheng,Zifan Cao,Sifa Zheng
abstract:
World-model planners evaluate candidate trajectories by predicting their future consequences, implicitly relying on the plan-to-motion relationship learned during training. At deployment, a different downstream controller may execute the same planned trajectory differently, creating a planning–execution gap between the frozen model’s imagined future and actual execution.
A natural remedy is to replace the planned trajectory with its predicted or observed execution. However, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily yield better decisions:
directly substituting predicted execution trajectories yields only a 0.048 PDMS improvement across 10 unseen controller configurations, far smaller than the gain from our proposed adaptation.
This suggests a semantic mismatch between a planned trajectory, which serves as a reference for downstream control, and an executed trajectory, which already describes the resulting post-controller motion.
introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving [1, 2] has evolved from directly predicting a
single planning output [3, 4, 5]
toward generating and evaluating multiple candidate
trajectories [6, 7].
As illustrated in Fig. 1, existing planning paradigms can be
broadly divided into model-free and model-based approaches.
Model-free planners predict or score trajectories primarily from the current
scene representation, without explicitly reasoning about their downstream
consequences.
In contrast, model-based planners use a learned world model to imagine the
future induced by each candidate before selecting a
trajectory [8, 9, 10, 11].
Such models represent future states in image, occupancy, BEV, or latent spaces,
enabling the planner to ask a seemingly simple but powerful question:
what will happen if this trajectory is executed?

The answer, however, depends not only on the planned trajectory, but also on
how it is executed by the downstream controller.
World-model-based evaluation implicitly relies on the plan-to-motion
relationship learned during training.
At deployment, changes in feedback controllers, control gains, actuation
constraints, or vehicle dynamics can cause the same planned trajectory to
produce different ego motion [12, 13, 14].
A frozen world model may therefore predict a future that is consistent
with its implicit training-time plan-to-motion mapping, yet inconsistent with
the execution actually encountered by the deployed vehicle.
We refer to this discrepancy as the planning–execution gap.

A natural remedy is to predict how the deployment controller will execute each
candidate trajectory and use the resulting executed trajectory in place of the
original plan.
Surprisingly, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily
translate into better planning decisions.
Even when the executed trajectory is known exactly in simulation, direct
substitution yields only limited improvements in candidate ranking and
downstream planning quality.

We attribute this failure to a semantic mismatch between planned and executed
trajectories.
Although both are represented as trajectories, they play fundamentally
different roles.
During training, the world model is conditioned on a planned trajectory
and implicitly learns how such an input relates to ego motion and subsequent
scene evolution.
An executed trajectory, in contrast, already describes the motion
resulting after downstream control.
Substituting it as the trajectory condition therefore asks the frozen world
model to reinterpret post-controller motion through its implicit
plan-to-motion mapping.
As a result, a geometrically more accurate execution does not necessarily
produce a more accurate imagined consequence or a better candidate ranking.

This observation suggests a different adaptation principle:
execution information should adapt how the future is imagined, rather than
replace the planned trajectory itself.
As illustrated in Fig. 2, we retain the original planned
trajectory as the conditioning input and use controller-specific execution
evidence to adapt the future representation.

Based on this principle, we propose ExecutionBridge, a lightweight
adaptation framework for frozen world-model planners.
Given a support set of paired planned and executed trajectories from the
deployment controller, ExecutionBridge infers a compact controller
representation that captures persistent execution characteristics.
For each candidate, the frozen world model first produces its native latent
rollout from the original planned trajectory, after which ExecutionBridge
adapts the ego-related latent using the inferred controller representation.
The planner, world model, and reward head remain frozen, enabling
controller-conditioned candidate evaluation without replacing the planned
trajectory with post-controller motion.

Our contributions are threefold:

We identify controller-induced execution shift as a source of the
planning–execution gap in frozen world-model planning.
Through a diagnostic study, we show that even exact post-controller execution
provides only limited benefit when directly substituted for the planned
trajectory, demonstrating that execution fidelity does not necessarily imply
decision fidelity.

We introduce ExecutionBridge, which infers controller-specific
execution characteristics from a set of paired planned and executed
trajectories and uses them to adapt the native ego latent rollout while
retaining the original planned trajectory and all pretrained planning
components unchanged.

We evaluate ExecutionBridge under a strict controller-disjoint protocol
and across multiple frozen world-model planners.
ExecutionBridge consistently improves planning across ten unseen controller
configurations, with substantially larger gains in challenging driving scenes
where execution shift has a greater impact on candidate evaluation and
selection.

title: DemoStream: Batched Task-and-Motion-Plan Optimization for Automated Learning from Demonstration
authors: Caelan Garrett,Neel Jawale,Fabio Ramos
abstract:
Learning from demonstration is an effective strategy for endowing robots with manipulation capabilities
but requires training on datasets comprised of massive amounts of demonstrations.
Existing demonstration collection approaches either require constant human involvement, for example, via teleoperation or are
specialized for a single task.
Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems are able to autonomously solve and therefore generate demonstrations for general-purpose tasks; however, learning from their demonstrations has proven difficult due to multi-modality in their solutions.
In this work, we build on recent work leveraging GPU acceleration for TAMP and propose DemoStream, a TAMP system that optimizes demonstration quality in order to improve behavior cloning success rates.
First, we introduce batched TAMP sampling operations
along with a new TAMP algorithm that correspondingly performs batched constraint satisfaction in order to explore many solutions in parallel.
We conduct simulation experiments ablating different action spaces, cost functions, and batch sizes to analyze the effect of these choices on downstream policy success rates.
Finally, we show that we can leverage the safety guarantees of TAMP to directly collect real-world demonstrations at an average rate of 66 demos per hour.
See our website for policy rollout videos: demostream.github.io.

title: VP-EVT: Active Visibility Preservation for Embodied Visual Tracking
authors: Yanci Wen,Tianle Zeng,Jianwei Peng,Weixi Situ,Hanjing Ye,Hong Zhang
abstract:
Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) is an essential capability for intelligent robots in human–robot collaboration, requiring an agent to follow a designated target person in dynamic environments relying solely on egocentric visual perception. However, persistent pedestrian occlusions in dynamic scenes pose critical challenges to existing EVT methods. Lacking proactive visibility preservation, reactive tracking methods frequently experience prolonged target loss under severe occlusions. Therefore, we propose VP-EVT, a framework that treats target visibility as an explicit objective of motion control rather than a by-product of following. Acting on this objective requires understanding both what obstructs the target and how robot motion can change that obstruction. VP-EVT therefore uses language-guided perception to extract separate target and pedestrian observations. When occlusion makes current observations incomplete, VP-EVT combines visual history with ego-motion to maintain estimates of their relative positions and motion. Using these estimates and the current following waypoints, VP-EVT predicts whether continued following will sustain the obstruction. When the predicted risk is low, the original following motion is retained; otherwise, a recurrent controller combines updated estimates with maneuver context from preceding decisions to coordinate viewpoint adjustment and the return to stable following.
Moreover, we introduce OccEVT-Bench for closed-loop evaluation of persistent occlusion and collect expert demonstrations for training. On its Risk split, VP-EVT improves success rate by 121.4% relative to a competitive baseline and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%, respectively.
introduction:
Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) requires an agent to follow a designated moving target using egocentric visual observations [1, 2, 3, 4]. However, when target visibility is treated as a by-product of following rather than an explicit motion objective, the agent may continue following without addressing an obstructed view. As illustrated in Fig. 1, a robot in a dynamic pedestrian scene can maintain the desired following distance and avoid collisions while remaining behind a pedestrian that blocks the target. Continuing along the same following motion can sustain this obstruction, leading to prolonged target loss and eventual tracking failure even when a viewpoint change could improve visibility. The challenge is therefore to anticipate when following motion will prolong pedestrian occlusion and actively adjust the viewpoint while continuing to follow the target.

Robust target estimation and effective recovery do not by themselves prevent persistent physical occlusion. Recognition, localization, and temporal memory preserve target information under degraded observations [5, 6, 7, 8], but even an accurate target estimate does not specify how the robot should move to avoid remaining behind an occluding pedestrian. Recovery mechanisms intervene when tracking becomes unreliable [9, 10, 11], responding to degraded visibility rather than explicitly predicting whether continued following will prolong the obstruction. The missing decision is therefore whether the current following motion will sustain the blockage and should be changed. These limitations motivate treating target visibility as an explicit objective of motion control, so that the robot can adjust its following motion to prevent avoidable occlusion from persisting.

We propose VP-EVT, an active visibility-preserving framework. To understand which pedestrian may obstruct the target, VP-EVT first uses language-conditioned grounding to extract their visual evidence separately. As occlusion makes this evidence incomplete, we integrate successive observations with ego-motion into target–pedestrian temporal beliefs, maintaining uncertainty-aware spatial and motion estimates even when direct observations are unavailable. Because persistent occlusion also depends on the agent’s future motion, VP-EVT evaluates these beliefs along the current following waypoints to determine whether intervention is needed. VP-EVT selectively adjusts its motion to preserve target visibility and restore stable following. Evaluating this capability requires distinguishing reduced persistent occlusion from eventual target recovery. Aggregate success and tracking scores [4] alone cannot distinguish these outcomes or reveal whether reduced physical occlusion comes at the cost of out-of-view target loss.

To bridge this evaluation gap, we introduce OccEVT-Bench, a dedicated closed-loop benchmark for occlusion-aware embodied visual tracking that comprehensively quantifies visibility loss alongside tracking safety. Complemented by this platform, we contribute OccEVT-Expert, an expert demonstration dataset containing 20,000 dynamic-occlusion episodes for training proactive visibility-preserving policies.

title: VeriVLA: Adaptive Test-Time Verification for Flow-Based VLAs with Latent World Models
authors: Xueli Sun,Yuxiang Lu,Yantong Liu,Xianzhe Fan,Xi Chen,Zhe Liu,Hengshuang Zhao
abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are inherently stochastic: different noise seeds can produce action chunks of varying quality from the same observation. At test time, however, the policy typically commits to a single sample without an explicit estimate of its quality. In fine-grained manipulation, executing a suboptimal action can irreversibly disrupt task progress and lead to failure. To exploit policy stochasticity, we introduce a training-free two-axis trigger that uses two initial samples to measure within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance, detecting the critical states. Once triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latent states and the corresponding changes in task progress. By operating in latent space, the verifier avoids pixel reconstruction and enables efficient and more accurate ranking. Across three real-world tasks (i.e., pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement), our method raises the average completion score from 50.8% to 65.5%, while adding 326 ms for sampling and verification per triggered decision on a single RTX 4090. Consistent gains are also observed in simulation, where the average success rate rises from 66.4% to 73.6% in the clean setting of RoboTwin 2.0, from 62.8% to 69.6% in its randomized setting, and from 96.9% to 97.6% on LIBERO. Project page: https://shirley430316.github.io/projects/verivla/.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm towards general robotic control [6, 22, 4]. In the pretraining stage, the field has evolved from VLMs autoregressively generating over discretized action tokens [54, 22, 38] to more recent flow-matching action experts coupled with pretrained VLMs [36, 4, 19], enabling scalable learning from diverse action trajectories. The paradigm shift was foreshadowed by diffusion-based visuomotor policies [10], which established iterative denoising as an effective means of learning multi-modal (i.e., multi-peaked) action distributions. However, the stochasticity that benefits learning also introduces a unique challenge at deployment.

Given the same observation and instruction, different noise seeds yield samples of different quality during inference. However, the flow-based VLA model cannot distinguish which action chunk is most likely to succeed. During execution, a robot must commit to one sampled action chunk, which may irreversibly change the physical world. A good action chunk advances the task, while a poor one could directly lead to failure or accumulate errors that drift the trajectory out of distribution [40, 30, 31]. We empirically show that the policy variance is non-uniform along the task, and failures tend to happen in high-variance segments of the action trajectory, as in Figure 1(a). What if we could detect these critical moments before committing to an irreversible action, and briefly “rewind” the decision by spending additional computation? This calls for two components: a trigger that decides when the states are critical and additional computation is worthwhile, and a verifier that determines which sampled action should be executed.

To answer the first question, we start with the policy’s uncertainty. As shown in Figure 1(a), when the end-effector is close to a contact-rich interaction region, the trajectory follows a more complex motion [37], and internally, the policy uncertainty increases. We therefore combine temporal action variation and cross-sample uncertainty into a training-free two-axis trigger. Computed with two sampled action chunks, the trigger closely tracks the contact information from the environment and aligns well with the policy’s intrinsic uncertainty, as shown in Figure 1(b). We therefore use the trigger to activate repeated sampling and verification at critical decision steps.

Once repeated sampling is activated, the second question arises: how should candidate actions be evaluated? We argue that latent world models are a natural fit. The verifier evaluates the quality of action chunk samples by predicting the progress or relative ranking [23, 11]. Therefore, the model must understand world dynamics and represent the future states resulting from executing the action chunk.
In addition, verification is a low-dimensional problem: how much an action chunk advances the task is a scalar judgment, and most camera pixels are irrelevant to it. As a result, pixel-level world models have two pitfalls: (1) the image or video generation incurs substantial latency, making it difficult to deploy at real-time control frequencies; and (2) they solve the harder pixel generation before the easier progress estimation, making the quality of downstream verification unnecessarily dependent on generation fidelity. We compare these paradigms in Figure 2. This motivates verification in a latent space, which compresses the pixel observation into compact and dynamic-rich features, where we can jointly predict the latent states and task progress.

Building on these observations, we recast action randomness not as a hazard to be suppressed but as a resource to select from, with the latent world model as a verifier. Specifically, we claim the following contributions:

A latent world model as a verifier. We exploit the action-conditioned latent representation produced by a pretrained latent world model to estimate the progress of candidate action chunks.

A latent world model as a verifier. We exploit the action-conditioned latent representation produced by a pretrained latent world model to estimate the progress of candidate action chunks.

An empirical characterization of policy stochasticity in flow-based VLAs and the two-axis trigger. We characterize policy stochasticity. Leveraging the temporal action variation and the cross-sampling variance, we propose a two-axis trigger that is action-based and training-free. It detects the critical states and reduces inference costs while preserving the benefits of test-time selection.

A simple training, evaluation, and real-robot deployment pipeline. On real-world manipulation tasks, each triggered round of repeated sampling and verification adds 326 ms of latency. Our method improves the average completion score by 14.7 percentage points over the base policy, outperforming baselines, including VLM-based verifiers and pixel-level world model verifiers.

title: GRID-Planner: Graph-Structured Relational Reward Shaping for Diffusion Planning
authors: Zhao Yang,Zezhong Qian,Yinan Shi,Longjun Liu,Yawei Jueluo
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Autonomous driving planning requires selecting trajectories that remain safe, rule-compliant, and comfortable under complex multi-agent interactions, yet robust closed-loop decision making in planning-critical scenes remains challenging. Existing diffusion- and RL-based planners often rely on generic rewards and use relational structure mainly for representation, limiting how planning-critical rollouts shape policy improvement. We present GRID-Planner, a graph–reward integrated diffusion planning framework that aligns generative planning with structured relational signals. Specifically, GRID-Planner combines graph-aware importance weighting, a time-indexed relational reward surrogate, and an advantage-weighted diffusion objective with on-policy self-distillation, forming a rollout-return-advantage-update loop without explicit likelihoods. Experiments on nuPlan and interPlan show that, compared with the diffusion-only baseline, GRID-Planner reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8%, 60.8%, and 27.4%, respectively, and improves the planning score by 3.4%. Project website: https://github.com/yangzhaojason/GRID-Planner.
introduction:
Autonomous driving planning requires selecting ego trajectories that are safe, rule-compliant, and comfortable under complex multi-agent interactions (Caesar et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023; Dauner et al., 2023; Jia et al., 2023a; Jia et al., 2024). Despite rapid progress in learning-based planning, robust closed-loop decision making in dense urban scenes remains challenging (Caesar et al., 2021; Dauner et al., 2023; Jia et al., 2024). A core challenge is that planning performance depends not only on average-case trajectory realism but on learning from a small set of planning-critical trajectories—those arising in highly interactive, safety-sensitive, and rule-constrained scenarios such as merging, yielding, and intersection conflicts (Caesar et al., 2021; Dauner et al., 2023; Jia et al., 2024). In practice, however, most training trajectories are semantically flat, weakly constrained, and low-conflict, contributing limited signals to the decision boundaries that matter most for planning (Dauner et al., 2023). This long-tail structure makes pure imitation learning insufficient, since abundant easy trajectories dominate supervision, while naive reinforcement learning is also inadequate because generic rewards are difficult to design stably for complex multi-agent interactions. These challenges motivate graph-structured relational modeling to prioritize planning-critical trajectories and support planning-oriented policy improvement.

Existing methods improve planning from different angles, but the core issue remains unresolved. Strong imitation-based planners, such as UrbanDriver (Scheel et al., 2022), PlanTF (Cheng et al., 2023), and PLUTO (Cheng et al., 2024), optimize similarity to expert behavior, allowing abundant easy trajectories to dominate training and under-emphasizing safety-critical and rule-sensitive cases. Interaction-centric methods, such as GameFormer (Huang et al., 2023b), improve multi-agent relation modeling, but mainly at the representation level, without explicitly using relational structure to determine trajectory value or optimization priority. Diffusion-based planners, such as Diffusion Planner (Zheng et al., 2025), provide flexible multi-modal trajectory generation, while reward-guided variants such as Diffusion-ES (Yang et al., 2024) demonstrate the promise of reward-driven optimization. However, existing approaches still rely either on behavior cloning objectives, which suffer from compounding errors and exposure bias in closed-loop inference, or on generic reward-driven optimization, which does not explicitly encode planning-oriented relational semantics. This leaves open how relational semantics should shape both the training distribution and the optimization objective, rather than serving only as scene representations or sampling-time guidance.

To address this gap, we propose GRID-Planner, a Graph-Reward Integrated Diffusion planner that uses graph-structured scene semantics to directly shape the optimization signal of generative planning. Rather than treating graph structure as just an input representation, we use it to define both trajectory importance and planning-oriented return. Our framework answers three questions left open by prior planners: which trajectories should matter more during training, how their quality should be evaluated for planning, and how relational signals should reshape diffusion-based policy learning. Specifically, our framework contains three tightly coupled components: ❶ Graph-Aware Importance Weighting, which upweights trajectories from complex, high-risk scenes using scene-interaction centrality and collision-risk cues; ❷ Relational Reward Surrogate (RRS), which evaluates candidate rollouts through time-indexed ego-centric scene graphs, producing a dense trajectory-level signal with smooth bounded penalties over safety, lane/route consistency, and comfort; and ❸ Graph-Reward Integrated Diffusion Objective, which incorporates structured returns into a low-variance advantage-weighted diffusion objective, coupled with an advantage-gated on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) mechanism. The resulting advantage reweights diffusion denoising and gates OPSD teacher selection and updates, forming a rollout–return–advantage–update loop in which graph-reward signals directly drive policy improvement.

The main contributions of this work are:

We propose GRID-Planner, a unified graph-reward integrated diffusion framework that redefines how scene graphs are used in autonomous driving planning: rather than serving only as input representations, they directly shape optimization priority and trajectory value for closed-loop decision making.

We introduce a planning-oriented relational learning mechanism, instantiated by Graph-Aware Importance Weighting and a Relational Reward Surrogate, which together focus training on planning-critical trajectories and score candidate rollouts using safety, lane/route consistency, and comfort criteria.

We develop a unified on-policy diffusion objective that combines advantage-weighted diffusion with advantage-gated self-distillation to support stable on-policy refinement and consolidate high-return behaviors, yielding consistent gains over strong baselines on nuPlan and interPlan.

1. We propose GRID-Planner, a unified graph-reward integrated diffusion framework that redefines how scene graphs are used in autonomous driving planning: rather than serving only as input representations, they directly shape optimization priority and trajectory value for closed-loop decision making.

2. We introduce a planning-oriented relational learning mechanism, instantiated by Graph-Aware Importance Weighting and a Relational Reward Surrogate, which together focus training on planning-critical trajectories and score candidate rollouts using safety, lane/route consistency, and comfort criteria.

3. We develop a unified on-policy diffusion objective that combines advantage-weighted diffusion with advantage-gated self-distillation to support stable on-policy refinement and consolidate high-return behaviors, yielding consistent gains over strong baselines on nuPlan and interPlan.

title: Towards bio-inspired visual navigation: a neuromorphic navigation paradigm for MAVs
authors: Junjie Jiang,Ankang Zhou,Zheng Fang
abstract:
Biological visual navigation achieves remarkable robustness at extremely low power, whereas frame-based robotic systems relying on artificial neural networks remain limited in both respects, particularly for energy-constrained micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) operating in complex environments.
Inspired by the event-driven, sparse, and asynchronous principles of biological visual systems, neuromorphic sensing and computation provide a promising alternative for robust and energy-efficient navigation.
In this paper, we propose the first end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic paradigm for MAV visual navigation in complex environments by integrating neuromorphic vision, spiking neural networks, and neuromorphic processors.
The proposed method first extracts the environmental representation from event streams using a spiking perceptual representation module.
This representation is fed into a spiking navigation module, where guidance learning and population coding enable efficient policy learning with few time steps.
The navigation module then outputs a waypoint converted into executable trajectory points.
Experiments show that the proposed neuromorphic method achieves navigation performance comparable to ANN-based methods while markedly reducing power consumption.
The spiking perceptual module consumes only 19.57% of the power of its ANN counterpart, while the spiking navigation module deployed on Intel Loihi consumes only 12.37% of that required by its ANN counterpart running on NVIDIA Orin NX.
Beyond prior neuromorphic systems focused mainly on relatively simple navigation subtasks, we demonstrate a complete neuromorphic visual navigation system spanning simulation and real-world deployment.
Our results establish the feasibility of the neuromorphic paradigm for autonomous navigation and provide a bio-inspired pathway toward robust and low-power MAV navigation.

title: Perceptual Comparisons of Viscoelastic Renderings: Fractional- vs Integer-Order Models
authors: Gorkem Gemalmaz,Harun Tolasa,Volkan Patoglu
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Haptics for possible publication.
abstract: Realistic haptic rendering of viscoelastic materials requires reproducing time-dependent behaviors such as creep and stress relaxation, which arise from the material’s inherent memory effects. Fractional-order viscoelastic models have been shown to capture these dynamics accurately and compactly, but it remains unclear whether their increased fidelity translates into perceptual benefits during haptic interaction. In this work, we investigate whether users perceive fractional-order models as more realistic than conventional integer-order models while rendering viscoelastic materials. We compare the fractional-order standard linear solid (FO-SLS) model with two integer-order alternatives: the 3-parameter SLS model and the 5-parameter generalized Maxwell model. We consider two complementary approaches to optimal parameter selection to evaluate rendering realism from both objective and perceptual perspectives: In the first approach, we determine the model parameters via least-squares based system identification of physical viscoelastic reference materials to establish evaluation baselines. In the second approach, we determine population-level perceptually optimal parameters using a qualitative-feedback-based human-in-the-loop optimization and aggregation method. This method establishes model parameters that maximize perceived realism of viscoelastic behaviors through qualitative evaluations. Human-subject experiments indicate that the FO-SLS model is perceived as significantly more realistic than both integer-order alternatives under both parameter selection approaches. Overall, this study provides experimental evidence that fractional-order viscoelastic models are not only theoretically well-motivated, but also perceptually relevant for realistic haptic rendering of creep- and relaxation-dominated behaviors of viscoelastic materials.
introduction:
Viscoelastic materials, including biological tissues and polymers, show inherently time-dependent mechanical behavior. In particular, these materials exhibit phenomena such as creep and stress relaxation, which arise from the dependence of the response on the deformation and loading history. Accurately capturing these behaviors is important for applications involving physical interaction with soft materials, particularly in haptic medical and surgical training simulators [1]. For instance, palpation can detect changes in tissue viscoelasticity associated with abnormalities such as tumors, and haptic medical simulators may assist in training for diagnosing such tumors [2, 3, 4]. Therefore, realistic rendering of viscoelastic tissue behavior is essential for applications involving physical interaction with soft biological materials.

Selecting an appropriate model for viscoelastic haptic rendering requires considering both how accurately the model captures the physical material response and how realistic the resulting interaction is perceived by users. Classical compliance models based on integer-order (IO) spring-damper networks, including the standard linear solid (SLS) model and the generalized Maxwell (GM) model, approximate these behaviors, but fail to represent long-term memory effects and frequency-dependent dynamics accurately [3]. Fractional-order (FO) viscoelastic models provide an appealing alternative, as non-integer derivatives naturally encode memory-dependent dynamics and can represent complex viscoelastic responses with relatively few model parameters [5, 6, 7].

Despite these modeling advantages, it remains unclear whether the improved descriptive performance of FO models necessarily translates into perceptually more realistic haptic rendering. Model accuracy is commonly evaluated through physical characterization, by assessing how well a model fits measured response in a least-squares sense. On the other hand, during haptic rendering, an accurate physical description of the reference does not necessarily correspond to the most realistic percept during physical interactions [8, 9].

This distinction is particularly relevant for viscoelastic rendering, where the perceived response depends on the combined perception of stiffness, damping, and the interaction history provided by the haptic interface. Consequently, comparing viscoelastic rendering models only through system-identification error or model complexity is insufficient to determine which model provides the most realistic haptic experience. A fair comparison among viscoelastic rendering models requires not only determining optimal parameters for each model to capture the same physical reference material, but also evaluating whether users perceive the resulting renderings as realistic.

Determination of optimal parameters can be achieved through system identification or human-in-the-loop (HiL) optimization of perceived realism [10, 11, 12]. While tuning the model parameters through HiL optimization, different model structures introduce different trade-offs. A lower-dimensional IO model is relatively easier to tune and interpret, whereas a higher-dimensional IO model can represent richer dynamics at the cost of a larger parameter space. An FO model can capture memory-dependent behavior more compactly with fewer parameters, but the coupling among its parameters makes their individual perceptual effects harder to predict.

In this study, we investigate whether the modeling differences and trade-offs between FO and IO viscoelastic models are also reflected in their perceived realism during haptic rendering.
In particular, we evaluate whether the compact representation of memory-dependent behavior provided by the FO-SLS model results in higher perceived realism than its IO counterparts, and whether increasing the number of parameters in an IO model provides sufficient improvement in perceived realism to compensate for the added complexity.

Accordingly, we compare the rendering performance of the 4-parameter FO-SLS model with two integer-order alternatives of different model complexities: the 3-parameter IO-SLS model and the 5-parameter IO-GM model. We perform such comparisons under two complementary optimal parameter-selection approaches. First, we compare model parameters identified through physical characterization of the reference viscoelastic materials. Second, we compare population-level perceptually optimal parameters determined from participants’ qualitative feedback through HiL optimization experiments conducted according to [12]. This way, we evaluate the effects of model structure and complexity on perceived realism under both physically and perceptually optimized parameter sets.

The main contribution of this paper is a human-subject comparison of FO and IO viscoelastic rendering models under various optimal parameter selection settings. By comparing the FO model with IO models of increasing complexity, using qualitative participant evaluations, we provide experimental evidence indicating that rendering viscoelasticity with FO-SLS models results in perceptually more realistic interactions than conventional IO alternatives. Overall, this study shows that FO models are not only theoretically more suitable for describing viscoelastic materials but also that users perceive these modeling advantages while rendering viscoelasticity.
