introduction:
In-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing (ISAM) could support structures
whose dimensions are not constrained by a single launch-vehicle fairing and
could allow spacecraft to be repaired or upgraded in orbit
[1, 2]. Realising either depends on a
capability that remains largely unqualified for flight: permanent, load-bearing
metal joining. Mechanical fasteners and adhesives cover part of the design space,
but neither restores parent-metal continuity in a pressure boundary or a primary
structural member, and both introduce additional mass. Ground demonstrators have
examined high-degree-of-freedom
robotic assembly of structures too large for single-launch deployment
[3].

Figure 1 illustrates the representative on-orbit joining
scenario considered in this study.

Fusion welding is one candidate and has been tested in space. The Skylab M551
experiment produced electron-beam melts on 304 stainless steel, 2219-T87
aluminium and commercially pure tantalum in 1973, providing a rare in-space
fusion-welding dataset on structural alloys
[5]. Soviet
work established that an arc can be sustained in vacuum, while also documenting
its instabilities [6]. Recent campaigns have
investigated laser beam welding in parabolic-flight and thermal-vacuum
demonstrations on AISI 316L
[7, 8].
Taken together, these studies do not report a qualified welding procedure or a
validated operating envelope spanning the gravity and pressure conditions
relevant to a mission.

Establishing that envelope experimentally is resource intensive. Reduced-gravity
access is limited to short parabolic-flight intervals, thermal-vacuum testing is
costly, and each run covers only a small part of the parameter space. The
coupled process physics therefore make exhaustive empirical mapping impractical.

A physics-based computational model can screen this operating space before
hardware tests, but a three-dimensional weld-pool calculation requires minutes
of computation per operating point. This cost prevents direct use at robotic
control rates and makes dense exploration of a five-dimensional design space
impractical. A faster surrogate model is therefore required.

This paper develops a reduced thermal weld-pool model parameterised by the CMT
operating condition and effective local-pressure parameter, compares Gaussian-process
and neural-network surrogates, and couples the GP surrogate to a
six-degree-of-freedom manipulator simulation. Gravity is sampled to check numerical
invariance and enters a separate hydrostatic-to-capillary pressure ratio, but is
absent from the implemented thermal energy equation. The
contributions are:

A finite-volume thermal model applied here to 1 mm 316L
stainless-steel sheet, with explicit numerical convergence and
field-quality criteria; extension to the 2 mm coupon configuration is
not evaluated in this paper.

A finite-volume thermal model applied here to 1 mm 316L
stainless-steel sheet, with explicit numerical convergence and
field-quality criteria; extension to the 2 mm coupon configuration is
not evaluated in this paper.

GP and neural-network surrogates evaluated by repeated cross-validation
and deterministic boundary cases, with empirical interval coverage and
measured inference latency.

A model-based closed-loop study in which a controller adjusts the
synergic power-source setting in response to a trajectory-imposed change
in travel speed.

A sensitivity analysis that separates conclusions supported within the
reduced model from gravity-dependent free-surface and metal-transfer
mechanisms that still require experiments and higher-fidelity models.

Verification concerns the numerical solution of the governing equations,
whereas validation assesses agreement with physical observations.
This paper reports
numerical quality-control criteria, quantified
surrogate fidelity to the finite-volume model, and literature-informed parameter
priors. A formal grid-convergence study is still required before discretisation
uncertainty can be quantified. The paper does not claim
experimental validation: the targeted literature review identified no bead-
geometry dataset for 1–2 mm 316L in the relevant travel-speed range, and
validation against the ISPARK coupons is unavailable in this study.

Section 2 sets out the framework architecture and its latency
budget. Section 3 gives the weld-pool formulation, and
Section 4 its convergence and numerical-quality criteria.
Section 5 describes literature-informed parameter priors.
Section 6 reports surrogate fidelity and speed-up, and
Section 7 the model-based closed-loop study.

title: TS-WAM: Temporal Latent Actions and World-Action Coupling for Vision-Language Robot Control
authors: Menghao Yin,Jiaju Yin,Xiyue Dong,Lixin Xu,Zhenhui Zhang,Ke Zhang,Yating Feng,Renjing Xu
abstract:
Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot
demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual
states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can
encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization
and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action
Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal
learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from
heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human
videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained
external teacher. By coupling vlm-jepa with delta-lwm, TS-WAM learns to
predict latent actions from the current observation and instruction and uses
them to predict future visual features that guide action generation at
inference. A unified end-to-end training architecture jointly optimizes
temporal representation learning, visual dynamics, and robot control without
a separate latent-action or world-model pretraining stage. The EMA target
branch is removed at inference, keeping the deployed policy lightweight.
Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world
manipulation experiments on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate
that TS-WAM achieves strong manipulation performance, generalization, and
robustness.
introduction:
A robot must convert a language instruction and a changing visual scene into a
temporally coherent sequence of actions. Recent vision-language-action (VLA)
systems use a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) as a semantic backbone
and attach a diffusion or flow-matching action decoder
[1, 2, 3, 4].
This recipe gives strong instruction following, but
the action interface is commonly learned directly from robot trajectories. The
resulting hidden state need not represent the short-horizon visual change that
an action is intended to cause. Consequently, the policy has no explicit
internal prediction of what its action will do before it is executed.

At the same time, large video collections contain abundant information about
how objects and hands move, but generally do not provide robot actions. Latent
action models (LAMs) address this gap by compressing temporal changes into a
compact code [5]. Existing systems, however, often pretrain a
LAM or a latent world model separately and subsequently adapt it to a robot
policy. This multi-stage procedure introduces an additional checkpoint and
optimization boundary, and it does not guarantee that the learned latent is
useful to the final action decoder.

We propose TS-WAM (Teacher-Student World-Action Model), a task-adaptation
architecture that makes temporal prediction the central interface of a VLA
policy without requiring a separately pretrained latent-action model. The
model uses an asymmetric pair of VLM branches.

The online XX-VLM
receives only the current observation and language instruction. It produces
latent-XX tokens that a small transformer predictor maps to a predicted latent
action. The EMA YY-VLM receives the current and future observations and reads
the corresponding target latent action. This temporal information asymmetry
turns future visual evidence into a training-only teacher signal while keeping
the deployed policy causal.

The latent action is coupled to visual dynamics and control. A frozen DINO
encoder represents the current and future images as spatial feature grids. A
newly initialized latent world decoder predicts the feature displacement
Δ​Ft=Ft+1−Ft\Delta F_{t}=F_{t+1}-F_{t} conditioned on the current feature and latent action.
The predicted future feature Ft+Δ​F^tF_{t}+\widehat{\Delta F}_{t} is passed to a
conditional flow-matching action head together with VLM context and robot
state. The policy therefore follows an explicit chain: infer a latent intent,
predict its visual consequence, and ground that consequence into an action
chunk.

The same training procedure can mix robot demonstrations and action-free human
videos. Human clips contribute current–future visual pairs to the teacher and
world-model objectives, whereas robot clips additionally provide state and
action supervision for the flow head. Thus, action-free data expands temporal
supervision without providing embodiment-specific action labels. The
task-specific world decoder is initialized from scratch and co-adapts with the
VLM and policy.

This joint objective keeps temporal prediction aligned with the downstream
control interface throughout task adaptation. At deployment, the resulting
policy uses only the current observation while retaining visual anticipation
learned from both data sources.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce vlm-jepa, a self-supervised framework for learning
temporal latent-action representations from robot demonstrations and
action-free human videos.

We propose TS-WAM, a lightweight world-action model that unifies
temporal representation learning, visual prediction, and action generation
through end-to-end training. It anticipates action consequences to guide
control, without separate latent-action or world-model pretraining.

Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with
real-world evaluations on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate
TS-WAM’s strong manipulation performance.

1. We introduce vlm-jepa, a self-supervised framework for learning
temporal latent-action representations from robot demonstrations and
action-free human videos.

2. We propose TS-WAM, a lightweight world-action model that unifies
temporal representation learning, visual prediction, and action generation
through end-to-end training. It anticipates action consequences to guide
control, without separate latent-action or world-model pretraining.

3. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with
real-world evaluations on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate
TS-WAM’s strong manipulation performance.

title: What Should Robot Policies Learn to Predict? Rethinking Supervision Targets in Vision-Language-Action Learning
authors: Haitao Shen,Hanyu Liu,Yihan Lin,Huiping Liu,Junbo Cui,Daoheng Li,Yang Li,Jing Zhang,Wenxin Li,Yuan Yao
comment: . Haitao Shen and Hanyu Liu contributed equally
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are typically trained with action
prediction as the primary supervision signal, since robots ultimately execute
actions. Auxiliary objectives such as latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV)
prediction are often added to improve policy learning, yet they compete with
action prediction for the same training budget. We ask whether, under a fixed
budget, allocating a substantial share of training samples to such objectives,
rather than to further action prediction, can improve policy learning. We build
a unified VLA framework that couples a two-stream multimodal diffusion
transformer (MMDiT) with a sample-level router, which assigns each training
sample to either action prediction or an auxiliary objective and thus makes
supervision allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA
targets based on LAPA and its DINO-feature variants, and three FV targets based

introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for robot learning, achieving strong performance across many manipulation tasks (Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025a). Beyond direct action supervision, recent studies increasingly introduce additional learning objectives into VLA training, including geometric representation alignment and spatial or 3D structure prediction (Li et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2025). Among these, latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV) prediction have become two representative forms of supervision. Latent action abstracts visual transitions into compact tokens that characterize how the scene changes over time (Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026), whereas future vision encourages the policy to predict future representations, providing supervision about how the scene is expected to evolve (Wu et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025).

Because executable actions are the ultimate outputs of robot policies, direct action prediction is typically treated as the dominant training objective, while LA and FV prediction are introduced as auxiliary supervision. Prior studies have examined latent-action formulations and integration strategies (Lin et al., 2026; Bu et al., 2026), showing that such supervision can benefit downstream policy learning. More importantly, LA and FV are not merely auxiliary in effect: by providing learning signals about state changes and task structure, they directly shape the same policy during optimization. Yet, showing that an additional target is useful does not establish that direct action prediction is itself the most effective supervision. We therefore ask (Figure 1): under a fixed training budget, what should robot policies learn to predict, and can assigning LA or FV prediction an equal or larger share of training samples than direct action prediction improve action execution?

To investigate this question, we build a unified VLA framework that places a two-stream MMDiT on top of a pretrained VLM, with separate action and auxiliary experts interacting through joint self-attention. We further introduce a sample-level router that assigns each training sample to either action or auxiliary supervision under a fixed training budget, making their relative training allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets and three FV targets: LA predicts discrete latent tokens extracted by different encoders, whereas FV predicts future features in different visual representation spaces. This unified setup enables a controlled comparison of how different supervision targets shape policy learning, with source-matched controls that change only routing for each FV target; FV prediction still conditions on demonstrated actions.

We evaluate our framework on two simulation benchmarks (LIBERO and CALVIN) and four real-robot manipulation tasks, and obtain three main findings. First, suitable LA and FV supervision can outperform action-only training under the same training budget, even when direct action prediction receives only half or fewer of the training samples. Second, FV generally performs better than LA across both simulation and real-robot tasks, while the strongest LA configuration remains competitive on CALVIN. Third, our analyses suggest that LA and FV shape policy learning in different ways: DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets better capture absolute position and task identity, and both can alter policy attention toward task-relevant regions.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) We revisit the dominant role of direct action prediction in VLA training and investigate how allocating supervision to LA and FV affects policy learning. (2) We introduce a unified VLA training framework with a sample-level training router that explicitly controls the allocation of action and auxiliary supervision under a fixed training budget, enabling controlled comparisons across multiple LA and FV targets. (3) We conduct extensive experiments on LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot manipulation tasks, together with representation and attention analyses, and derive systematic findings on action-supervision allocation, the performance differences between LA and FV, and their representation characteristics.

title: Sub-Millisecond Reflexes for Continuous Physical Human-Robot Interaction
authors: Jon Škerlj,Sami Haddadin
comment: Submitted to IEEE, source code available at:this https URL
abstract: Continuous physical human-robot interaction requires robots to rapidly adapt their control behaviour without interrupting task execution. However, existing ROS 2 control architectures rely on stop-to-switch mechanisms that introduce substantial delays and interrupt execution. We present an open-source, sub-millisecond reflex engine based on an enhanced ROS 2-compatible multimode controller that enables deterministic switching between control modalities and integrates reflex behaviours for mitigating contact hazards and kinematic limit violations. Experiments on a Franka Robotics manipulator demonstrate switching delays below 0.1​ms0.1\>\text{ms}, more than four orders of magnitude faster than conventional ros2_control, while maintaining continuous operation during safety-critical events. In a multi-stage manipulation task, the proposed framework reduced execution time by 3.5%3.5\% and peak trajectory jerk by more than threefold. By eliminating runtime middleware overhead, controller transitions are implemented as lock-free pointer operations, enabling reflex-level responsiveness within an open-source robotics framework.
introduction:
The deployment of service robots in domestic and home environments creates a need for physical human-robot interaction (pHRI) that is inherently safe and robust [1, 2]. Unlike a structured lab environment or an industrial cell, a home is a dynamic and unpredictable setting. While future humanoid service robots are expected to operate with human-level capabilities to execute complex, contact-rich manipulation tasks [3, 4], there is still work to be done, with current state-of-the-art systems primarily serving as research platforms [5, 6, 7, 8, 9].

During operation in such surroundings around humans, unforeseen collisions become inevitable [10]. Actively mitigating the severity of injuries during these collisions requires torque-controlled systems capable of rapid, low-latency reactions [11, 12]. While safety standards specify the high-rate measuring frequencies, such as 1 kHz (ISO 10218 [13], ISO 13482 [14]), for collision detection, a major gap remains in translating advanced safety and interaction algorithms to modular, open-source architectures [10].

In addition, the selected range of diverse domestic tasks, e.g., surface cleaning, folding clothes, or close-proximity physical assistance, directly dictates the requirements of the system’s real-time control architecture. Different phases of these tasks often impose conflicting control objectives, such as accurate free-space motion, compliant interaction, force regulation, or safety-oriented recovery behaviours [15]. While unified control formulations can address several of these objectives at once [16, 17], no single control strategy is universally optimal for all phases of service robotic tasks. Different approaches may prioritize accuracy, compliance, force regulation, or rapid safety reactions, requiring distinct control characteristics and tuning objectives. Hence, enabling service humanoids to execute these multifaceted routines successfully requires the capability to dynamically and instantaneously switch their control behaviour according to task demands and environmental conditions [16, 15, 18].

Nowadays, the prevalent state-of-the-art open-source middleware like Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) [19] and its hardware-agnostic control framework ros2_control are constrained by their reliance on lifecycle node state transitions with a conservative “stop-to-switch” implementation [20]. This introduces timing inconsistencies and additional communication overhead [21], which fails to fulfill the real-time requirement and introduces time delays for long-horizon tasks. Consequently, conventional safety mechanisms may completely halt the robot’s motion upon safety-critical events. By doing so, these approaches sacrifice fluid physical manipulation and system autonomy for functional safety [10].

Having established the need for multi-modal control, safety requirements of low-latency interactions, and the limitations of the middleware “stop-to-switch” bottleneck, as visualized in Fig. 1, the novel contributions of our work are:

A real-time, sub-millisecond controller switching architecture for smooth continuous task execution compatible with existing ROS 2 ecosystems.

A reflex engine built upon the proposed switching architecture, enabling rapid reactions to contact hazards, joint limits, and excessive velocities before manufacturer safety stops are triggered.

Continuous execution of multistage manipulation tasks through seamless transitions between control behaviours, eliminating the traditional stop-to-switch interruption.

Empirical validation on a physical Franka Robotics manipulator, demonstrating switching latencies below 0.1​ms0.1\>\text{ms}, successful hazard mitigation, and uninterrupted task execution.

1. A real-time, sub-millisecond controller switching architecture for smooth continuous task execution compatible with existing ROS 2 ecosystems.

2. A reflex engine built upon the proposed switching architecture, enabling rapid reactions to contact hazards, joint limits, and excessive velocities before manufacturer safety stops are triggered.

3. Continuous execution of multistage manipulation tasks through seamless transitions between control behaviours, eliminating the traditional stop-to-switch interruption.

4. Empirical validation on a physical Franka Robotics manipulator, demonstrating switching latencies below 0.1​ms0.1\>\text{ms}, successful hazard mitigation, and uninterrupted task execution.

title: MAGMA: Multiplier-Augmented Geometric Motion Algorithm
authors: César E. Ramos Chuquiure,Vansh Thakur,Challen Enninful Adu,Ram Vasudevan
abstract:
Solving optimal control problems for high-dimensional mechanical systems subject to constraints remains challenging due to nonlinear dynamics and non-convex feasible sets.
This paper introduces MAGMA(Multiplier–Augmented Geometric Motion Algorithm), an Affine Geometric Heat Flow (AGHF)–based trajectory optimizer that incorporates an augmented Lagrangian framework solved via a primal–dual flow.
A theoretical characterization of the primal-dual AGHF is provided, establishing that MAGMA is a gradient flow on an appropriately defined energy.
MAGMA is validated across a variety of challenging trajectory generation problems with obstacles, state limits, and actuation limits.
Comparative evaluations against state-of-the-art solvers demonstrate that MAGMA achieves high quality solutions with significantly reduced tuning effort on the hardest problems.
introduction:
For practical deployment, an optimal control algorithm must satisfy several requirements: (1) computational efficiency for online or near real-time planning, (2) scalability to high-dimensional systems, (3) compatibility with nonlinear constraints, and (4) reliable convergence from a wide range of initializations.
Existing optimal control methods struggle to simultaneously satisfy these criteria.

Existing methods can be grouped into Dynamic Programming (DP) and Variational methods.
DP-based approaches leverage Bellman’s Principle to compute optimal policies.
Global approaches that solve the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) PDE provide strong optimality guarantees, but require discretizing the entire state space, rendering them intractable beyond moderate dimensions [1].
Local variants such as Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) [2] improve scalability, but suffer from poor convergence when initialized far from the optimum and require careful treatment of inequality constraints.
Variational methods provide an alternative route.
Direct methods such as collocation-based nonlinear programming [3, 4] can incorporate complex constraints, but incur high computation times and exhibit sensitivity to discretization and initialization.
Parameterized approaches such as [5] improve robustness and speed, but still struggle with convergence.

One can also perform trajectory optimization by computing the solution to the Affine Geometric Heat Flow (AGHF) PDE [6].
AGHF evolves an initial, potentially infeasible trajectory toward dynamic feasibility by minimizing control effort over a two-dimensional domain, enabling scalability beyond HJB-based approaches.
More recent implementations  [7, 8] demonstrate that AGHF-based solvers can rapidly produce trajectories for high-dimensional systems.
However, these methods rely on penalty and barrier formulations to enforce constraints, leading to two key limitations: (i) hyperparameter tuning to balance task costs and feasibility and (ii) degraded convergence when constraints compete with the objective.
A recent formulation of the AGHF [9] casts the problem as a primal-dual flow by introducing Lagrange multipliers associated with the equality constraints.
This remedies the shortcomings of penalty and barrier functions while enforcing constraints.
However, this formulation has only been demonstrated for kinematic constraints and while considering just a single type of cost function.

The key observation underlying our approach is that the AGHF can be identified as a gradient flow in an appropriate function space.
This identification allows classical augmented Lagrangian primal-dual schemes to be lifted directly to the AGHF setting.
Building on this idea, this paper introduces the Multiplier-Augmented Geometric Motion Algorithm (MAGMA), a new AGHF-based trajectory optimization framework that incorporates an augmented Lagrangian structure solved via an augmented primal–dual geometric flow.
Unlike penalty-driven AGHF variants, MAGMA automatically balances constraint satisfaction and optimality by evolving primal and dual variables.
In contrast to Kim and Park [9], MAGMA considers arbitrary nonlinear constraints and cost functions.

The primary contributions of this paper are: (i) a theoretical connection between gradient flows and the AGHF, and (ii) a formulation (MAGMA) of an augmented primal-dual flow based on the AGHF  for nonlinear constraints. 
All code is made available at https://github.com/roahmlab/MAGMA.

title: Time-Optimal Ergodic Retrieval
authors: Christian Sulana,Christian Hughes,Ian Abraham
abstract:
Retrieval tasks are a form of search task where a robot must explore, find an object, and return with it as quickly as possible.
Recent work in ergodic control has demonstrated time-optimal path planning for search tasks where visitation is proportionally matched, within some tolerance, to a given target distribution.
However, these planners minimize the duration of a full deterministic search, while retrieval missions end their search at an unknown point in the trajectory and must return to a given base.
In this work, we propose a new formulation of the time-optimal ergodic search problem that models detection as a Poisson process and minimizes total mission time by including the return phase in the objective.
Experimental results show that time-optimal ergodic retrieval (TOER) achieves up to 19%19\% shorter mission durations relative to ergodic baselines and that this advantage grows as the return phase becomes more costly.
Simulation and hardware implementations validate TOER’s compatibility with environments of non-convex geometry as well as both 2D and 3D search domains.
introduction:
Retrieval tasks are common in search-and-rescue, logistics, and inspection tasks, where a robot must locate an object and bring it to a given destination [1, 2, 3].
Such missions do not end when the object is found, but rather when it is delivered back to base.
Because detection is uncertain, the point of transition from search to return is a random variable unknown at the time of planning.
A planner that optimizes only up to the moment of detection therefore optimizes a fraction of the total mission which is smallest when the object is hardest to find.
In this work, we address the question: How should a robot order its search when the cost of completing the mission depends on where the search ends?

Ergodic search methods plan single-shot trajectories whose time-averaged visitation is proportional to a given target distribution on the domain [4, 5].
Kernel-based formulations have extended these guarantees to non-Euclidean domains via the Maximum Mean Discrepancy metric [6], while time-optimal ergodic search methods (TOES) invert the classical objective to minimize terminal time subject to an ergodic inequality constraint to produce the fastest trajectory that still covers the domain to a chosen tolerance [7].

However, these formulations do not currently represent that the search outcome is stochastic.
The optimized horizon is the duration of the full planned search, while retrieval missions end at a random point in the path where the target is detected.
Since the robot rarely executes the entire plan, minimizing the terminal search time generally optimizes an incorrect duration.
In addition, while current time-optimal formulations define a terminal boundary constraint to force the trajectory to end at a base, this hard constraint fixes the final pose even when detection occurs at an earlier segment.

In this paper, we propose time-optimal ergodic retrieval (TOER), which minimizes the expected duration of the full search-and-return mission subject to an ergodic constraint.
We model detection along a trajectory as an inhomogeneous Poisson process whose rate is set by the sensor’s response to a given target distribution such that the probability that the robot is still searching decays with accumulated detection pressure.
The objective sums the expected search time with an expected return time charged from the node at which detection occurs.
We retain ergodicity as a constraint to preserve the coverage guarantees of time-optimal ergodic search and eliminate the degenerate solution of immediately abandoning the search.

We show that the return may be modeled by any lower bound on the return cost, including a straight-line estimate that ignores obstacles, and that the resulting plan carries a computable certificate of ε\varepsilon-optimality.
Constraining the survival probability at the horizon certifies that the target is detected with at least the given probability.
We prove that ergodic coverage guarantees transfer unchanged, and that the value of return-awareness scales predictably with the difficulty of the return toward a computable ceiling fixed by domain geometry, coverage tolerance, and the target distribution.

In summary, the contributions of this work are:

A novel formulation of ergodic retrieval that minimizes the expected duration of a search-and-return mission by charging the return from an unknown detection point;

Derived guarantees that any admissible lower bound on the return yields a certifiably ε\varepsilon-optimal plan, that ergodic coverage guarantees hold in this formulation, and that return-awareness’ advantage grows with return discrepancy toward a fixed ceiling;

Validation in 2D and 3D domains in simulation and on hardware, including isolation of the return term against a search-only reference.

1. A novel formulation of ergodic retrieval that minimizes the expected duration of a search-and-return mission by charging the return from an unknown detection point;

2. Derived guarantees that any admissible lower bound on the return yields a certifiably ε\varepsilon-optimal plan, that ergodic coverage guarantees hold in this formulation, and that return-awareness’ advantage grows with return discrepancy toward a fixed ceiling;

3. Validation in 2D and 3D domains in simulation and on hardware, including isolation of the return term against a search-only reference.

title: Cross-Embodiment Causal Transfer from Human Videos to Robot Manipulation
authors: Xingyu Zhang,Yingchao Li,Peizheng Guo,Jie Hu,Changwen Zheng,Wenwen Qiang
abstract: Scaling robot manipulation models requires large amounts of interaction data, yet collecting diverse real-robot experience remains costly. Human manipulation videos, in contrast, provide abundant and diverse task experience that could potentially benefit robot learning. However, differences in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms make human motions unsuitable as direct supervision for robot actions, raising a scientific question: what knowledge in human videos should be transferred across embodiments to robot manipulation? To address this question, we analyze subtask transfer through the lens of causal beams, focusing on which contextual conditions and interaction dependencies should be retained to support local task effects. Based on this perspective, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST). CBST learns manipulation-related representations from human videos and grounds them in task-level semantic variables using robot demonstrations. Within a predefined manipulation model, causal-beam constraints guide contextual information selection by requiring retained assignments to sustain local mechanism outputs while preserving nontrivial responsiveness to retained inputs. The selected semantic information conditions a world-action model, allowing the robot to generate actions from its own observations without requiring human–robot motion correspondence. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show improvements in task success over the corresponding world-action model baselines.
introduction:
Recent robot manipulation models are evolving toward World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly model future scene evolution and robot behavior, enabling predictions of interaction outcomes (Kim et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). However, scaling real-world robot data requires dedicated hardware, human operation, and physical deployment, making broad coverage of tasks, objects, and scenes expensive. In contrast, human manipulation videos are abundant and capture diverse task processes and object interactions, making them an attractive source of additional experience for robot learning (Khazatsky et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2023). Yet humans and robots differ substantially in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms, so concrete human actions cannot be directly reused as robot supervision (Bahl et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025a). This leads to the central question of this work: what knowledge in human manipulation videos should be transferred across embodiment differences to robot manipulation?

A complete human manipulation sequence contains two types of information: object-interaction relations that support task progress, and concrete motion realizations that are closely tied to the human embodiment. For long-horizon manipulation tasks, we first organize continuous execution into local task processes using temporally extended subtasks, thereby avoiding the requirement that the robot reproduce human motion step by step. However, defining a subtask only specifies the local scope within which transfer takes place; it does not further determine which information within that scope should be preserved together with the task experience. Retaining only the task intention or boundary states of a subtask may discard the conditions and interaction relations that determine how a local effect is realized, whereas retaining the complete human execution trajectory reintroduces substantial embodiment-specific motion details.

We study this selective information-preservation problem through the lens of causal beams (Pearl, 2009). Given a structural model and a specific context, a causal beam allows part of the inputs to be projected out in a context-dependent manner, while requiring the actual values of the retained variables to sustain the actual outcome of the current mechanism and the projected mechanism to retain nontrivial responsiveness to its retained inputs. This perspective motivates separating task-level abstraction from contextual information selection. Task-level variables provide an abstraction of execution, while causal-beam conditions constrain which semantic dependencies are retained within a specified model.

Based on this, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST). CBST first learns manipulation-related temporal representations through human-video pretraining and grounds them, under robot demonstration supervision, into a candidate SCM instantiated from shared manipulation templates. A contextual subtask-conditioning module then selects a contextual causal beam from the candidate SCM according to the current execution context, producing the local task effect, relevant conditions, and their effect-relevant dependencies. This structural information conditions the target robot WAM, while concrete actions are still generated from the robot’s current state and its own action space. CBST therefore combines human-video representation transfer with causal-beam-constrained selection of contextual subtask information for robot execution.

Our contributions are summarized as: (1) We study human-to-robot learning from the perspective of cross-embodiment transfer, focusing on which task-progress structures should remain transferable after embodiment-specific motion is discarded; (2) We propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST), which combines a shared candidate manipulation SCM with learned contextual causal beams to preserve effect-relevant conditions and dependencies for conditioning robot WAMs; (3) We systematically evaluate CBST on WAMs including LingBot-VA and Cosmos Policy, examining the contributions of human video pretraining, context-specific causal selection, and their effects on robot control.

title: Trajectory-based Diffusion from One-shot Human Video for Generalizable Manipulation
authors: Guoping Pan,Xinmiao Yu,Wannan Cao,Jincheng Li,Baolin Jiang,Yizhe Li,Yi Cheng,Houde Liu
abstract: Imitation learning enables robots to perform complex tasks by leveraging human-collected demonstrations. However, most existing approaches require labor-intensive data collection with additional teleoperation systems, which hinders scalability. Human videos represent a natural source of data that implicitly contain knowledge of manipulation behaviors. However, transferring them to robots remains challenging due to the visual domain gap and the absence of explicit action labels. In this work, we introduce TDV, a trajectory-based framework that leverages data generation to enable generalizable manipulation. TDV focuses on task-relevant objects by leveraging plug-and-play 6D pose estimation techniques to extract object trajectories from human videos, thereby mitigating the impact of irrelevant backgrounds and varying viewpoints. As a modality-agnostic intermediate representation, trajectories are inherently independent of the visual domains and different embodiments, enabling efficient data generation. Our method outperforms previous approaches on RLBench simulation tasks, achieving near 100% success rates across seven tasks. In real-world experiments, TDV enables cross-embodiment generalization manipulation from one-shot human demonstrations by leveraging efficient trajectory generation techniques.
introduction:
Imitation learning enables robots to perform complex tasks without the need for manually configured heuristic rules. Most existing imitation learning approaches rely on proprioceptive states and visual data collected directly from the robot system, typically obtained through additional teleoperation systems operated by humans [1, 2, 3]. However, this approach is inefficient and presents significant challenges in scaling up data collection. In addition to images and text, there is a vast amount of human demonstration videos available on the internet, which inherently encode procedural knowledge for performing various manipulation tasks. Nevertheless, extracting meaningful perceptual information and actions from these videos for robot manipulation remains a non-trivial challenge.

This problem involves two main aspects: the significant gap in visual domains and the lack of robot action information. To address the visual domain gap, the most straightforward approach is to leverage image editing techniques, replacing the human with a robot in the images or erasing the human entirely [4, 5]. However, this method heavily depends on the editing quality, and there is currently a lack of studies that ensure both good consistency and compliance with physical laws. Some studies utilize flow as an intermediate representation [6, 7, 8, 9], which captures the motion trends of task-relevant objects and exhibits robustness to visual discrepancies introduced by different embodiments. However, these methods require the camera viewpoint during deployment to be consistent with the one used during data acquisition, which limits their scalability in practical applications [10]. For manipulation tasks, the primary focus is on the state changes of task-relevant objects, rather than the agent executing the actions, thereby enabling cross-embodiment deployment. We find that object-centric representations, such as 6D object pose [11, 12, 13], can effectively capture the real-time state of the object while mitigating the effects of irrelevant background and different viewpoints. A trajectory composed of a sequence of 6D object poses encapsulates the state transitions during the manipulation process. The previous method [12] requires pre-generated grasp poses for the object and fails to fully exploit the advantages of trajectory representations in scaling datasets [14], which is crucial for enhancing the generalization of manipulation.

To overcome these shortcomings, we propose a trajectory-based diffusion framework, TDV, which enables generalizable manipulation across different embodiments from one-shot human demonstrations, as shown in Fig. . Our framework is structured into three stages.
First, we parse human videos to extract motion trajectories relevant to the manipulation task. The full trajectory is then divided into multiple subtask segments according to changes in the moving entity or the reference object. Based on the type of moving entity, we categorize each subtask segment into two types, as illustrated in Fig. 2: hand tasks, where the motion is dominated by the hand itself, and object tasks, where the motion corresponds to manipulated objects. For example, in the pouring task, grasping the kettle is treated as a hand task, while the subsequent pouring action is treated as an object task. In hand tasks, we employ a hand pose estimation model [15] to reconstruct human hand trajectories. For object tasks, we adopt a plug-and-play 6D pose estimation model [16] to extract object trajectories. To eliminate the influence of viewpoint changes, we represent trajectories relative to the reference object frame. Then, the resulting trajectories provide a modality-agnostic intermediate representation, enabling efficient data augmentation through simple trajectory scaling and interpolation. Finally, we then use the augmented dataset to train a trajectory-based diffusion policy, which achieves robust generalization across diverse manipulation tasks and supports multi-procedure execution conditioned on high-level task descriptions. During deployment, the pose of the moving entity is detected in real time and fed into the history sequence of the diffusion policy, enabling closed-loop execution.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We propose a trajectory-based diffusion framework (TDV) that learns manipulation policies solely from human videos, significantly improving data collection efficiency and enabling scalable policy learning across diverse tasks.

We leverage an object-centric intermediate representation based on trajectories to enable effective learning and cross-embodiment generalization.

Our experiments demonstrate that TDV achieves strong spatial generalization and remains robust under complex backgrounds and diverse camera viewpoints.

title: Comfortably Stuck: Evaluation Pitfalls in Bench2Drive's Closed-Loop Protocol
authors: Thomas Schwarzfischer,Emad Aghajanzadeh,Moritz Thoma,Nael Fasfous,Manoj Rohit Vemparala,Pierpaolo Mori,Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder,Ulf Schlichtmann
abstract: Closed-loop evaluation is widely regarded as a more faithful way to assess end-to-end (E2E) driving models than open-loop evaluation, and Bench2Drive, built on the CARLA simulator, has become the dominant benchmark for it. We show that its evaluation protocol itself contains pitfalls that can misrepresent the models scored on it. Bench2Drive’s comfort metric, adapted from nuPlan, has several implementation errors and a segmentation scheme that rewards standing still, so it mostly measures how long a vehicle stays stationary, correlating with stationary time at r=0.97r=0.97 across eight models. We propose a corrected, distance-based metric that cuts that correlation to r=0.06r=0.06. Under it, the strong driving-score/comfort tradeoff the original metric reports is no longer detectable once models are compared at matched driving speed, which suggests that comfort trades against how fast a model drives rather than against how well it drives. We also uncover two pitfalls in how the harness supplies navigation signals: the default controller can replace a model’s own steering with an angle toward the route target point, and the target point supplied at evaluation time can differ substantially from what a model saw in training. We demonstrate both on UniAD and VAD, where their effects differ sharply, and argue that future closed-loop evaluations should check for them. We will release all fixes as standalone code, so corrected comfort scores can be obtained from logged trajectories without re-running closed-loop simulation.
introduction:
End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models have recently attracted substantial attention, and as the space grows, reliable evaluation becomes essential for directing research and comparing models fairly [1, 2]. Closed-loop evaluation, in which a model reacts to the consequences of its own past decisions rather than replaying a fixed expert trajectory, is a more faithful proxy of real-world driving quality than open-loop evaluation [3, 2]. CARLA [4] is the most widely used platform for closed-loop testing, and Bench2Drive [2] builds on it with a curated set of edge-case routes to standardize closed-loop evaluation across the field. We show that the Bench2Drive protocol itself contains issues that can lead to large misinterpretations of E2E models along two axes: driving comfort and driving behavior.

Comfort: Bench2Drive adapts nuPlan’s comfort check [5], which tests six kinematic quantities, among them lateral and longitudinal acceleration, jerk and yaw rate, against thresholds calibrated on human driving logged at 10​Hz10\,\mathrm{Hz} with angles in radians. Ported to CARLA’s 20​Hz20\,\mathrm{Hz} logs, the implementation gets the sampling rate, the smoothing window, the angular units and the yaw derivative wrong, and together these errors inflate the measured jerk and yaw terms enough that segments in which the vehicle is genuinely driving fail thresholds a human driver would pass. Worse, comfort is scored over fixed one-second chunks rather than distance travelled, so a vehicle that simply stops satisfies every threshold for free and keeps banking comfortable segments for as long as it stands there. The resulting score measures how long a model stands still rather than how smoothly it drives, correlating with stationary time at r=0.97r=0.97 across eight models and ranking the models that most often get stuck as the most comfortable. Fixing the implementation alone does not help, because time-based segmentation rewards standing still by construction. We therefore propose a distance-based metric that scores comfort per meter driven, which cuts that correlation to r=0.06r=0.06 and moves VAD and SimLingo sharply down the comfort ranking. Measured this way, the strong tradeoff between driving score and comfort that prior evaluations report is no longer detectable once models are compared at matched driving speed, so comfort trades against how fast a model drives rather than against how well it drives.

Navigation signals: E2E models rely on a high-level navigation signal, a discrete command or a continuous target point, to know where the route leads. Prior work studies how best to integrate that signal into the architecture [6, 7]; we instead study how the harness supplies it, and find two issues. First, Bench2Drive’s default controller replaces the model’s own predicted steering with an angle toward the route target point, a behavior we call steering overruling (SO), in more than half of all frames in some scenarios. This masks whether a model can correct its own drift or react to a sudden obstacle, and it affects models so unevenly that scores obtained under the default controller are not comparable across models. Second, the target point supplied at evaluation time can differ substantially in density and distance from what a model saw during training, pushing it toward out-of-distribution inputs. We propose fixes for both: a controller that never overwrites the model’s steering, and a route planner whose target-point sampling matches the training distribution.

Our contributions are as follows:

We show that Bench2Drive’s comfort metric is dominated by a bias toward standing still, and propose a corrected, distance-based metric that removes it while staying faithful to nuPlan’s thresholds.

We uncover two protocol-level pitfalls in how Bench2Drive supplies navigation signals, a controller that overwrites the model’s steering and a train-deployment mismatch in the target point, and propose fixes for both.

We re-benchmark comfort across eight recent E2E models under the corrected metric and demonstrate the navigation fixes on UniAD and VAD. We will release all fixes as standalone code, so corrected comfort scores can be obtained from existing logs without re-running closed-loop simulation.

title: Uni-PNP: Unified Prehensile and Non-prehensile Policy Learning for Generalizable Object Pose Reaching
authors: Wenxuan Zhu,Yuze Wang,Jiangran Lyu,Jiayi Chen,Yixin Zheng,Mi Yan,Li Yi,Zhizheng Zhang,He Wang
abstract: Object manipulation often requires combining non-prehensile actions with grasping. However, existing approaches typically develop these capabilities separately and integrate them by sequencing distinct primitives through prescribed intermediate objectives, limiting the coordination of contact motions and grasping. Their integration also remains sensitive to object and gripper geometry and depends on particular environmental supports, complicating real-world deployment. We present Uni-PNP, a unified policy that jointly learns prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation for object pose reaching across diverse objects and grippers. To achieve this, we first pretrain a geometry encoder to predict contact-induced object motion using a contact-dynamics dataset constructed from simulated interactions between diverse objects and grippers. We then train the policy in a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum from graspable objects to ungraspable peers, encouraging the discovery of non-prehensile interactions and their integration with grasping. Experiments show 76.39% success on hundreds of seen objects with grippers, and 57.91% on unseen peers, outperforming the strongest pose-reaching baseline by 20.52 and 17.79 percentage points, respectively. We also analyze emergent behaviors, including nonprehensile and prehensile repositioning, grasp acquisition that requires grasping after tipping, and table-assisted reorientation while grasping, and transfer to the real-world scenario. Project page available at lgswdn.github.io/Uni-PNP.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation can be broadly divided into prehensile and nonprehensile modes. Prehensile manipulation moves an object while holding it in a stable grasp. Nonprehensile manipulation moves an object without grasping, through actions such as pushing or tipping. We often combine these skills in everyday activities. For instance, a phone lying flat on a table leaves little clearance for a direct grasp. We slide and tilt the phone while closing our fingers, creating room to secure and lift it. Nonprehensile contact creates access for grasping, while a secure grasp enables controlled lifting and repositioning. However, prior work typically develops prehensile and non-prehensile capabilities separately, and combines them either by preparing objects for a grasp using non-prehensile manipulation [1, 2], or by planning sequences of prehensile and non-prehensile primitives [3, 4, 5]. Treating the two modes as separate skills limits their ability to learn unified manipulation behaviors.

Moreover, prior methods depend strongly on the geometry of the environment, object, and gripper. Several grasp-preparation strategies exploit environmental features such as edges and walls to obtain extrinsic dexterity [6, 1, 7], requiring suitable environmental supports. GOMP [2] uses a learned graspability field to guide non-prehensile manipulation toward configurations suitable for subsequent grasp execution. Furthermore, these methods are constrained to the gripper geometry seen in training, which is inconvenient for real-world deployment. Cross-gripper policies learn grasp poses from grasp synthesis  [8, 9]. However, geometry influences manipulation beyond grasp pose selection: it also determines the contact interactions and resulting object motions. These geometry-dependent effects motivate jointly learning prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation across diverse objects and grippers.

We present Uni-PNP, a unified policy for prehensile and non-prehensile (PNP) object manipulation. Our policy reaches target object poses across diverse objects and grippers. To achieve this, we first construct a contact-dynamics dataset by sampling object–gripper contact configurations and recording the resulting object motions under gripper actions. We then pretrain a compact geometry encoder to predict these motions, learning a representation of geometry-dependent contact dynamics for the policy. Finally, we train the policy on these features through a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum. The policy first learns grasping and repositioning with smaller, readily graspable objects. Training then continues on an object set whose initial configurations are challenging for direct grasping, encouraging the policy to discover non-prehensile interactions and combine them with grasping.

We evaluate Uni-PNP in simulation on 1,218 objects from this challenging set and 249 unseen objects from a different distribution, using grippers drawn from a training catalog of 200 geometries and the unseen Panda gripper. Uni-PNP achieves 76.39% pose-reaching success on training objects and grippers, and 57.91% on unseen objects with the unseen Panda gripper, outperforming the pose-reaching baselines across all settings. We complement these benchmarks with real-world experiments and an analysis of emergent manipulation skills, including tip-assisted grasping and table-assisted reorientation.

Our contributions are:

We introduce Uni-PNP, a unified policy that learns prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation jointly for object pose reaching.

We construct a contact-dynamics dataset and propose motion-prediction pretraining to learn a compact geometry representation across varied objects and grippers.

We demonstrate effective object pose reaching and generalization to unseen objects and grippers in simulation and real-world experiments.

1. We introduce Uni-PNP, a unified policy that learns prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation jointly for object pose reaching.

2. We construct a contact-dynamics dataset and propose motion-prediction pretraining to learn a compact geometry representation across varied objects and grippers.

3. We demonstrate effective object pose reaching and generalization to unseen objects and grippers in simulation and real-world experiments.

title: MAIA: Anticipating Interaction Anomalies in Contact-Rich Manipulation via Multimodal World Models
authors: Yi Qiao,Maolin Zheng,Haoran Sun,Lujia Dong,Wenzhao Lian
abstract:
Reliable contact-rich manipulation requires detecting execution deviations early enough for corrective action. Yet most monitoring methods are reactive, identifying anomalies only after they become observable. Anticipating such anomalies is challenging because visual observations only partially reveal physical interaction, while planned actions describe intended motion rather than their actual physical consequences.
We address this problem with MAIA, a multimodal framework for anomaly anticipation. Its vision–action–force world model learns nominal interaction dynamics and predicts the visual and force responses of planned actions, while a lightweight anomaly head predicts impending interaction anomalies.
To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset of 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution.
Experiments on both seen and novel tasks show that MAIA achieves more accurate anomaly discrimination than representative baselines while providing earlier warnings, with bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 and median anticipation lead times of 28.0 and 25.1 steps, respectively. Moreover, using these predictions for anomaly-aware action selection improves end-to-end task success from 52.6% to 61.5% without retraining the underlying manipulation policy.
These results highlight the value of modeling future physical consequences for proactive anomaly anticipation.
View our project in https://joringell.github.io/MAIA/
introduction:
Modern robot manipulation policies can plan and execute increasingly complex behaviors, yet even strong policies cannot eliminate execution uncertainty during physical interaction [1, 2, 3].
While policy-generated actions appear reasonable, perception errors, imperfect alignment, object constraints, and environmental variations can cause the resulting interaction to deviate from the intended trajectory.
This uncertainty is especially pronounced in contact-rich manipulation, where similar actions can lead to substantially different physical outcomes depending on how the interaction unfolds [4, 5].
Reliable execution therefore requires monitoring the evolving robot–environment interaction and responding to deviations before they escalate and compromise task progress.

Existing approaches to robot execution monitoring predominantly focus on reactive detection of failures and anomalies [6, 7]. By identifying deviations only after observable evidence emerges, they leave little window for intervention. This is particularly limiting for anomalous interactions, which may emerge locally and evolve without producing clear task-level failure signals.
Modern manipulation policies, however, often generate action sequences over a future horizon, enabling evaluation of their potential consequences in advance [1, 2, 8].
This motivates anomaly anticipation, which assesses whether planned actions are likely to induce anomalous interactions before they occur, thereby providing an early warning for intervention or replanning, as illustrated in Fig. MAIA: Anticipating Interaction Anomalies in Contact-Rich Manipulation via Multimodal World Models.

A central challenge in predicting anomalous interactions stems from the partial observability of underlying physical dynamics.
While visual observations provide valuable geometric context and task progress, they offer only indirect evidence of contact forces, friction effects, resistance, and mechanical constraints.
Planned actions specify the robot’s intended motion, yet do not reveal how the environment will physically respond.
Thus, similar visual states and actions can lead to substantially different interaction outcomes.
Force–torque feedback reduces this ambiguity by providing direct measurements of physical responses.
This calls for modeling future multimodal physical responses under planned actions to anticipate anomalous interactions.

Driven by these insights, we formulate contact-rich anomaly anticipation as prospective action evaluation: predicting whether planned actions will cause the robot–environment interaction that deviates from its expected dynamics.
We instantiate this formulation in MAIA, a framework for Multimodal Anticipation of Interaction Anomalies.
At its core, the vision–action–force world model learns expected interaction dynamics from nominal executions and predicts future visual and force responses under planned actions. A lightweight anomaly head then integrates the resulting predictive representations to estimate whether an anomaly will occur and its temporal prevalence over the future horizon.

However, evaluating anomaly anticipation requires temporally localized supervision indicating when an anomaly begins and how it evolves, which is not provided by conventional failure-oriented datasets. Thus, we introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset for Contact-Rich Interaction Anomaly anticipation. CRIA comprises 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, covering nominal and anomalous executions. It provides temporally aligned visual, action, and force/torque signals with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution.

Built on this data, MAIA learns interaction dynamics rather than task-specific failure templates. This interaction-centric representation captures shared dynamics across diverse contact regimes while remaining sensitive to task-specific deviations, supporting transfer to novel tasks with limited adaptation.
Additionally, because model predictions are conditioned on planned actions, MAIA can evaluate candidate action sequences before execution, extending anomaly anticipation from passive monitoring to proactive action selection.

Our key contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate contact-rich anomaly anticipation as prospective action evaluation and introduce MAIA, a vision–action–force framework for anticipating anomalous interactions.

We introduce CRIA, a real-world aligned visuo-action-force dataset for contact-rich manipulation, comprising 2,852 trajectories across 18 tasks with fine-grained temporal anomaly annotations.

We demonstrate that MAIA learns transferable predictive interaction representations across diverse contact regimes, achieving bACC of 0.765 on seen tasks and 0.710 on novel tasks. MAIA further enables anomaly-aware action selection, improving real-robot success from 52.6% to 61.5% without policy retraining.

1. We formulate contact-rich anomaly anticipation as prospective action evaluation and introduce MAIA, a vision–action–force framework for anticipating anomalous interactions.

2. We introduce CRIA, a real-world aligned visuo-action-force dataset for contact-rich manipulation, comprising 2,852 trajectories across 18 tasks with fine-grained temporal anomaly annotations.

3. We demonstrate that MAIA learns transferable predictive interaction representations across diverse contact regimes, achieving bACC of 0.765 on seen tasks and 0.710 on novel tasks. MAIA further enables anomaly-aware action selection, improving real-robot success from 52.6% to 61.5% without policy retraining.

title: Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering: Improving Imitation Learning Policy Robustness through Expert Hidden-State Geometry
authors: KwangBin Lee
abstract:
Small observation or action errors can compound during closed-loop execution and disrupt a trained imitation learning policy.
We study whether the original expert demonstrations can improve robustness through test-time hidden-state steering without additional demonstrations or policy retraining.
Our analysis of a trained policy finds that expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in relatively few dimensions, while the directions capturing this variation differ across regions.
Motivated by this geometry, we propose Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states obtained by replaying the demonstrations through the frozen policy.
DHS attenuates coordinates with low expert variance more strongly than those with high variance, then maps the modified coordinates back to hidden-state space.
This allows steering directions to vary with the current hidden state while retaining every coordinate.
Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over the unmodified Transformer policies.
Controlled comparisons yield higher mean success with learned nonlinear coordinates than with linear coordinates under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling.
Combining DHS with action smoothing improves mean success rate under observation noise in certain tasks compared with action smoothing alone.
introduction:
Imitation learning (IL) trains robot policies from expert demonstrations, but the observations encountered during execution also depend on the policy’s own actions.
Observation noise or action errors can therefore take the policy into conditions poorly represented in the demonstrations, where further errors can compound and disrupt task execution.
DAgger addresses this distribution mismatch by obtaining expert actions on learner-visited states, while DART collects demonstrations that include recovery from disturbances [1, 2].
Online reinforcement learning can also improve pretrained robot policies by updating their parameters using reward feedback from interaction [3].
These approaches all require information beyond the original demonstration set, such as new expert labels, additional demonstrations, or reward feedback from interaction.
This motivates a complementary question: whether the original demonstrations alone can improve the closed-loop robustness of a trained IL policy without additional demonstrations or policy retraining.

A neural IL policy processes observations into hidden states, which its later layers use to generate actions.
Replaying the original demonstrations through the frozen policy exposes the hidden states associated with expert behavior, providing a policy-specific reference that can be reused during deployment without additional supervision.
Intermediate hidden states therefore provide a natural intervention point: modifying one during execution can change the action while leaving the policy parameters fixed. We refer to this operation as test-time hidden-state steering.
Prior work learns hidden-state correction modules jointly with the task network [4], or steers trained robot policies using conceptors fitted to successful and failed roll-out activations [5].
In our demonstration-only setting, the steering reference instead consists solely of expert hidden states collected from the original demonstrations.
The resulting challenge is how to use the structure of these expert hidden states to suppress undesirable deviations while preserving the variation needed for action generation.

Our empirical analysis finds that expert hidden states vary predominantly within relatively few dimensions, while linear subspaces fitted to different clusters of expert hidden states differ in orientation (Section IV-A).
These observations motivate viewing the expert distribution as concentrated near a low-dimensional manifold, with broad variation along local tangent subspaces and narrow variation along local normal subspaces.
Variation along this structure can reflect differences between demonstrated situations that require different actions.
The steering problem can therefore be viewed as reducing departures from the structure while limiting changes to the variation needed for action generation.

One way to pursue this goal is to attenuate components along directions with low expert variance more strongly than those along directions with high variance.
A linear filter can implement this rule using globally fitted directions and attenuation factors [6].
Under the manifold view, however, local tangent and normal subspaces can change orientation with location.
A fixed linear filter may therefore attenuate tangential expert variation as well as normal deviations, motivating steering directions that adapt to the local geometry.

Our key idea is to use nonlinear expert coordinates for selective attenuation, limiting changes to high-variance coordinates while attenuating low-variance coordinates more strongly.
We implement this idea with Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns a diffeomorphic coordinate map, or chart, from expert hidden states.
DHS builds on score-based pullback Riemannian geometry (SPRG) [7] to learn the chart and an anisotropic Gaussian model of expert variation in its coordinates.
Under the manifold view, high and low-variance coordinates serve as proxies for tangential variation and normal deviations, respectively.
The inverse chart provides location-dependent coordinate directions for selective attenuation in hidden-state space.
At test time, DHS maps the current hidden state to chart coordinates, rescales them according to their fitted expert variances, and maps the result back before the remaining policy layers generate an action (Fig. 1).

Our contributions are as follows:

We characterize expert hidden-state geometry in a trained IL policy, observing concentrated variation and differences in the orientation of linear subspaces fitted to different clusters of expert hidden states.

We introduce DHS, a full-rank nonlinear steering operator that uses expert hidden-state geometry to attenuate low-variance chart coordinates while limiting changes to high-variance coordinates in a frozen IL policy.

We demonstrate that DHS achieves higher mean success than the unmodified policy under observation noise across four simulated manipulation tasks.
Also, learned nonlinear coordinates yield higher mean success than linear coordinates from principal component analysis (PCA) under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling.

1. We characterize expert hidden-state geometry in a trained IL policy, observing concentrated variation and differences in the orientation of linear subspaces fitted to different clusters of expert hidden states.

2. We introduce DHS, a full-rank nonlinear steering operator that uses expert hidden-state geometry to attenuate low-variance chart coordinates while limiting changes to high-variance coordinates in a frozen IL policy.

3. We demonstrate that DHS achieves higher mean success than the unmodified policy under observation noise across four simulated manipulation tasks.
Also, learned nonlinear coordinates yield higher mean success than linear coordinates from principal component analysis (PCA) under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling.

title: SPEAR: Selective Preference Elicitation with Adaptive Rewards for VLM-Guided Robotic Manipulation
authors: Zewen Wu,Ruizhe Liu,Pei Zhou,Feng Chen,Yanchao Yang
comment: . Accepted at IROS 2026. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
enable automated preference labeling
for robotic manipulation,
yet their deployment
remains impractical since each query incurs
substantial inference cost,
while VLMs frequently abstain on visually challenging comparisons.
We propose SPEAR,
a framework that transforms
VLMs into efficient preference oracles
via two synergistic mechanisms.
First, we design distinguishability-aware query selection to reduce abstention rates by targeting only informative and distinguishable comparisons.
Second, we deploy an adaptive reward transition that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized guidance before preference-based refinement.
Experiments on the manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that SPEAR achieves 88.9% average success, outperforming baselines by 23.3 percentage points, while significantly reducing abstention and wall-clock training time on contact-rich tasks.
SPEAR learns three Mobile ALOHA manipulation tasks fully online on real hardware, demonstrating end-to-end real-world applicability.
By addressing query efficiency
and exploration challenges, SPEAR establishes VLMs
as practical preference oracles
for scalable robot learning without manual reward engineering. Project page:
https://zevinwu.github.io/spear-project.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL)
offers a principled way to
acquire robotic manipulation skills in demonstration-scarce settings, yet practical deployment remains constrained by reward specification.
Preference-based Reinforcement Learning (PbRL)
addresses this by learning from pairwise trajectory comparisons rather than numerical rewards [1, 2].
However, the scalability of PbRL is constrained by the need for frequent human-in-the-loop preference queries.
Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
present an appealing solution:
modern VLMs can naturally serve as automated preference oracles [3]
due to their encoding of extensive world knowledge and robust visual-language grounding.
This enables automated robot learning from online interaction and language goals,
without relying on demonstrations, manually designed rewards, or ongoing human labeling.

However,
VLMs introduce a notable computational constraint –
each preference query incurs a significant inference cost.
This makes query efficiency critical,
yet existing VLM-guided PbRL methods waste considerable budgets due to two fundamental inefficiencies.
First,
VLMs are frequently incapable of providing valid preferences for visually similar or indistinguishable trajectories, i.e., returning abstention.
Naive query selection
could misuse a significant portion
of expensive queries
on comparisons that yield zero learning signal.
Across backbones, higher visual distinguishability leads to both lower abstention and higher preference accuracy, motivating abstention-aware acquisition as a core design target.
Second,
meaningful preferences
require behaviorally task-related trajectories,
yet initial random policies produce only aimless motions.
This creates a bootstrapping paradox:
generating task-related behaviors requires rewards that need to be learned from comparing task-related behaviors.
Together, these dilemmas make VLM-guided preference learning inefficient for automated learning.

We present SPEAR (Selective Preference Elicitation with Adaptive Rewards),
a framework that addresses both challenges with two synergistic mechanisms designed specifically for VLM-based preference learning under computational constraints.
To overcome the query efficiency challenge,
we develop Distinguishability-Aware Query Selection
that predicts VLM response likelihood before querying.
Our approach combines global semantic embeddings with local spatial patterns,
and further trains a calibrated distinguishability prediction model.
By weighting information gain with predicted distinguishability,
we ensure computational resources target only answerable and informative comparisons, while enhancing learning efficiency.
To resolve
the exploration bootstrapping challenge,
we introduce Adaptive Reward Transition that leverages VLM-synthesized rewards to jumpstart exploration before transitioning to refined preference-based learning.
While VLM-synthesized rewards lack precision for task completion,
they successfully guide initial exploration toward semantically task-relevant regions.
Combined with relay exploration that maintains distributional coverage,
this mechanism ensures continuous generation of diverse yet task-relevant trajectories that are necessary for meaningful preference comparisons.

We evaluate our approach on six diverse manipulation tasks from Meta-World [4].
SPEAR achieves an 88.9% average success rate, surpassing the strongest VLM-based baseline by 23.3 percentage points, with substantially fewer wasted oracle queries and reduced wall-clock training time.
Beyond simulation, we further validate SPEAR on a real Mobile ALOHA robot by running the full online pipeline directly in the real world, demonstrating VLM-guided preference learning can bootstrap manipulation skills from scratch under realistic sensing and actuation constraints.
The ablation studies confirm that both mechanisms are essential for efficient online PbRL. Our contributions are threefold:

First, we propose a distinguishability-aware query selection mechanism that predicts VLM answerability through multi-scale visual features and online-adapted modeling, effectively reducing wasted queries.

Second, we introduce an adaptive reward transition strategy
that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized reward before transitioning to preference-based learning, ensuring the collection of informative trajectories.

Third, we demonstrate substantial improvements across diverse manipulation tasks and on a real robot,
validating that addressing query efficiency and exploration bootstrapping enables practical VLM-guided preference learning under realistic computational constraints.

1. First, we propose a distinguishability-aware query selection mechanism that predicts VLM answerability through multi-scale visual features and online-adapted modeling, effectively reducing wasted queries.

2. Second, we introduce an adaptive reward transition strategy
that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized reward before transitioning to preference-based learning, ensuring the collection of informative trajectories.

3. Third, we demonstrate substantial improvements across diverse manipulation tasks and on a real robot,
validating that addressing query efficiency and exploration bootstrapping enables practical VLM-guided preference learning under realistic computational constraints.
