title: Training-Free Target-Aware Refinement of 3D Gaussian Language Map
authors: Sibaek Lee,Kyeongsu Kang,Seongbo Ha,Yewon Jeon,Joonyeol Choi,Daegeol Ko,Jaehyuk Hur,Taemin Choi,Minsu Kim,Hyungjoo Ahn,Wonsok Yoo,Hyeonwoo Yu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Distilling vision-language features into 3D Gaussian Splatting yields a language map that can be queried with arbitrary text. In deployment, however, a small set of user-specified targets must be reliably located, which current distilled maps often miss, while open-vocabulary queryability for other words must remain intact. We propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Guided by a text-promptable segmenter, the visual embedding inside each detected target region is blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient sets the amount of injected prior, while non-target regions are left untouched. Injecting too much overwrites appearance cues and general queryability, so we seek, for each target, the smallest coefficient that still lets it win, and we obtain every coefficient in closed form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. We further identify a failure mode of injection in language-goal localization. Text embeddings share a common component, and injecting them makes the standard cosine read-out query-agnostic, which a centering step in the read-out removes. Across three benchmarks, the refinement consistently improves open-vocabulary segmentation, roughly doubling the base mIoU on Replica, and localizes language goals more reliably than the base map. It also transfers as a plug-in to off-the-shelf field-based and object-level language maps and supports a real-world demonstration in which a legged robot navigates to natural-language goals.
Project page and code: https://lab-of-ai-and-robotics.github.io/target-aware-langmap/
introduction:
A reliable spatial representation is central to robotic autonomy, since a robot must understand its environment before it can act within it across tasks such as localization, navigation, and manipulation. The recent emergence of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [21] and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [12] has made photorealistic spatial representation possible. Moreover, by combining these representations with vision language models [25], a scene is no longer restricted to a fixed set of semantic labels, and open-vocabulary NeRF and 3DGS representations [13, 37, 24] have become possible, allowing the space to be queried with arbitrary natural language.

However, existing methods for building such language maps tend to fall toward one of two ends of a spectrum, and we instead pursue the practical middle ground, precise localization of user-specified targets without giving up open-vocabulary generality. Closed-set methods are trained per scene with semantic supervision [18, 38] and are accurate on their predefined labels, but cannot be queried with any word outside that set. Open-vocabulary methods instead distill vision-language features and respond to arbitrary text [13, 24, 37]. Yet because the distillation blends surrounding context into each feature, the resulting relevancy can be spatially diffuse, so a query often yields a plausible heatmap whose peak is not always precise enough to serve directly as a navigation goal. We first tried to sharpen such maps with a training-free post-processing, but found that the limitation is already present in the 2D features themselves, whose top-ranked retrieval is often wrong before any lifting to 3D. Purely post-hoc processing is therefore insufficient, which motivates injecting the target text directly into the features.

To this end, we propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Given a small set of user-specified target words, we localize each target in every training view with a text-promptable segmenter, retain the open-vocabulary base from a class-agnostic segmenter, and encode both with a vision-language model. Within each target region the visual embedding is then blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient decides how much prior is injected, while non-target regions are left untouched. Such coefficients are conventionally treated as hyperparameters, swept over a grid or set by heuristics. Injecting too much overwrites the region’s visual embedding and erodes the appearance cues and general queryability that make the map open-vocabulary. We therefore formulate the problem as finding the smallest coefficient that still lets each target win, and we solve it in closed form. Each detection yields this minimum as a flip point, and the per-target strength is read off the knee of the capture curve that the flip points form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. This minimal injection, together with the untouched non-target regions, is what keeps the refined map open-vocabulary.

Because the refinement acts only on the 2D features before distillation, it is pipeline-agnostic and drops into different language maps as a plug-in module, from dense feature fields to object-level maps. It also carries over to language-goal localization, where the map must turn a query word into a 3D goal position. We observe a failure mode rooted in the geometry of contrastive vision-language embeddings [19, 22]. Text embeddings cluster around a shared direction, so injecting them plants this common component in the map, and under the standard cosine read-out every query then retrieves the same dominant regions. A centering step in the read-out removes this common mode. Notably, centering barely changes the base map but is decisive on the refined one, after which the refined map localizes goals more reliably than the base across Replica [30], ScanNet [3], and HM3D-Semantics [35]. We summarize our contributions as follows:

A training-free, target-aware refinement that makes user-specified targets reliably retrievable while keeping the map open-vocabulary, with each target’s injection strength obtained in closed form instead of tuned.

A centered read-out that identifies and removes the query-agnostic bias of injection, turning the refined map into a reliable source of language-goal locations.

Consistent gains in segmentation and localization on three benchmarks, plug-in transfer to field-based and object-level maps, and a real-world demonstration on a legged robot.

1. A training-free, target-aware refinement that makes user-specified targets reliably retrievable while keeping the map open-vocabulary, with each target’s injection strength obtained in closed form instead of tuned.

2. A centered read-out that identifies and removes the query-agnostic bias of injection, turning the refined map into a reliable source of language-goal locations.

3. Consistent gains in segmentation and localization on three benchmarks, plug-in transfer to field-based and object-level maps, and a real-world demonstration on a legged robot.

title: A Flow-Theoretic Multimodal Control Framework Fusing Mental and Physical Engagement for Upper-Limb Rehabilitation
authors: Jun Leng,Pengcheng Li,Hanze Wang,Shuxiang Guo,Junlin Jiang
abstract: While Assist-as-Needed (AAN) control aims to maximize user participation in robot-assisted training, existing methods relying solely on physical metrics cannot distinguish muscular inability from mental disengagement, leading to suboptimal interventions. To address this ambiguity, a Flow-theoretic multimodal AAN framework is proposed, fusing EEG-based mental engagement and sEMG-based physical engagement into an adaptive impedance control strategy. A four-quadrant fuzzy decision engine translates these dual physiological metrics into continuous control policies. This enables the upper-limb exoskeleton to inject feedforward assistance during intent-execution mismatch (e.g., motor output attenuation despite mental focus) and escalate guiding stiffness to penalize mental distraction. The framework was validated with healthy participants against a state-of-practice sEMG-only AAN baseline. Kinematically and mechanically, the proposed framework reduced robotic energy expenditure by 71.9% while maintaining precise trajectory tracking, confirming it elicited greater voluntary human effort. Physiologically, the system increased the time spent in the neuroplasticity zone (Flow State Ratio) from 4.6% to 42.8%. These results validate that decoupling and jointly regulating mental and physical states enhances the selectivity of robotic assistance, mitigating user passivity and sustaining the engagement crucial for motor learning.
introduction:
Upper limb movement dysfunction caused by neurological injuries, such as stroke, severely impairs an individual’s ability to perform Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) and significantly reduces quality of life [1]. Modern neurorehabilitation relies on promoting patients’ active participation in high-intensity, repetitive training to stimulate neuroplasticity and facilitate functional recovery [2]. To address these rigorous demands, robot-assisted therapy provides consistent, quantifiable training that directly complements traditional therapist-led methods [3, 4]. These systems offer precise physical guidance while reducing the labor burden on clinicians, making them essential for delivering the high-dosage therapy required for motor learning.

To maximize therapeutic outcomes, the field has widely adopted the “Assist-as-Needed” (AAN) paradigm. The core principle of AAN is to minimize robotic intervention, providing assistance only when the user cannot complete the movement independently. This approach aims to ensure maximal active effort [5]. However, accurately inferring the user’s true “need” remains a critical challenge. Traditional AAN strategies rely heavily on physical performance metrics, such as kinematic error or interaction force. For instance, Han et al. [6] proposed an adaptive control method that infers movement intention by decomposing real-time interaction forces. The system then adjusts the robot’s impedance parameters to promote active participation. More recently, researchers have integrated surface Electromyography (sEMG) to incorporate physiological effort into the control loop. Xu et al. [7], for example, developed a framework that adapts training trajectories and robotic assistance based on sEMG-derived muscle activation. This system encourages patient participation by modulating feedback gains. However, while such approaches successfully measure mechanical or muscular execution, they still fail to capture user’s mental focus. Although high-amplitude sEMG quantifies physical exertion, it cannot differentiate genuine task engagement from pathological co-contraction or abnormal compensatory synergies. Execution-level metrics alone fall short in revealing the user’s mental intent. Without monitoring mental focus, purely physical assistance strategies often fail to maintain an optimal training challenge, eventually leading to user passivity.

To resolve this ambiguity, integrating electroencephalography (EEG) into the control loop is essential for providing a direct measure of task-related attentional focus [8]. While EEG is widely applied in robotic rehabilitation, current paradigms mostly use it within Motor Imagery-based Brain-Computer Interfaces (MI-BCI) to decode discrete movement intentions [9], [10].

This paper introduces an adaptive control framework grounded in Flow Theory to map these multidimensional physiological signals into actionable robotic interventions. Classic Flow Theory defines an optimal mental state as a balance between external task challenge and intrinsic user skill [11, 12]. The modern four-quadrant extension categorizes user experience into Flow, Anxiety, Boredom, and Apathy based on these misalignments [13]. In robot-assisted training, keeping users within this flow state mitigates both task-induced anxiety and under-stimulated boredom [14, 15]. This equilibrium sustains intrinsic motivation and facilitates motor learning [16].

Most existing flow-aware systems rely on predefined task difficulties or intermittent self-reporting, limiting their real-time adaptability. Directly quantifying the abstract Challenge and Skill axes in real-time is also highly impractical during dynamic robot-assisted training, as the user’s motor capabilities fluctuate continuously due to fatigue and varying physical demands. To address this gap, the proposed framework bypasses the direct measurement of classic Flow coordinates. It instead establishes a two-dimensional physiological diagnostic space using mental engagement (sme∗s^{*}_{\text{me}}, via EEG) and physical engagement (spe∗s^{*}_{\text{pe}}, via sEMG) as continuous proxies. By continuously monitoring the congruence or mismatch between cognitive intent and motor execution, the system inversely infers the user’s psychological state. This diagnostic mapping directly drives the real-time, closed-loop interventions. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

A multimodal, mental-physical aware exoskeleton system is developed to fuse real-time EEG and sEMG signals, enabling the continuous monitoring of the user’s mental and physical engagement during robot-assisted training.

A multimodal, mental-physical aware exoskeleton system is developed to fuse real-time EEG and sEMG signals, enabling the continuous monitoring of the user’s mental and physical engagement during robot-assisted training.

A Flow-grounded fuzzy decision engine, coupled with a sensorless variable impedance controller, is proposed. By estimating the user’s Flow state, the system dynamically adjusts guiding stiffness and feedforward assistance to mitigate physical passivity, address the mismatch between mental intent and physical execution, and optimize the AAN interaction.

title: AVALON: Zero-Shot Indoor Navigation with Human-Seeded Topological Memory
authors: Jing Xia,Changyan Li,Yuduo Wang,Guiyin Tian,Bo Wang,Yifan Liao,Mingjun Li,Shiyan Hu
abstract:
Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts and task constraints are already familiar to users. We address this human-familiar, robot-unseen setting with AVALON, a topological navigation framework organized around human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and task-triggered, evidence-gated human–robot memory co-updating.
The robot has no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training. Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment.
Visual depth point-goal navigation leverages verified node arrivals to perform translational re-anchoring, without requiring a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human–robot memory co-updating fuses complementary sources of information. Human operators specify task constraints that are unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, whereas the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation. Task relevance governs whether human-reported environmental changes undergo robot validation during the active mission. Field-collected perceptual evidence gates memory updates, maintaining an explicit separation between human-specified permissions and robot-observed traversability. Our experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/55/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/54/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.
introduction:
Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts, routes, and closures are already familiar to users. This human-familiar, robot-unseen setting offers a remarkable opportunity for rapid deployment of robots. Users can supply a floor plan and delivery instructions before the first mission (Fig. 1). The robot must turn these priors into executable navigation memory and detect disagreements with observations.

Dedicated pre-mapping and online topological exploration [1, 2, 3] both require robot data collection that may delay service. Existing CAD, BIM [4], and user knowledge offer alternative spatial priors, but these must be grounded in observations and updated as conditions change.

In this paper, we propose AVALON (Asymmetric Visual-Architectural Layered Online Navigation), built around seed, execute, and co-update. A spatial memory framework is constructed based on floor-plan topological skeletons with visibility-aware constrained traversal hops, and paired with editable task memory that shares unified node and edge identifiers. Multi-modal contextual clues, including casual imagery, linguistic descriptions, and RoadBook annotations, are explicitly associated with these topological primitives. The topological skeleton provides global route planning priors for the robot, while the attached multi-modal clues serve as verification signatures to validate the arrival at target topological nodes. Local point-goal control governs the robot’s inter-node navigation, and node arrival is rigorously validated via fused visual-semantic observations and odometry measurements.

Successful arrival confirmation enables translational re-anchoring and progressive route execution. In case of visual observation mismatch with the expected node template, the robot adaptively refines its localization hypothesis. For object search tasks, real-time perceptual inference is deployed to verify object presence within the corresponding spatial regions, and the collected perceptual evidence is archived to support subsequent downstream missions. Robot onboard observations continuously record environmental physical states, whereas human operators supplement task-specific constraints and update unobserved environmental variations. Benefiting from the initialized prior memory seed, the system can execute initial missions without standalone dedicated mapping procedures. Furthermore, human-robot collaborative memory updating maintains the timeliness and accuracy of the memory bank, accommodating dynamic changes in workspace layouts and task specifications.

AVALON replaces globally precise localization with human-seeded, task-sufficient spatial grounding. Topology specifies where to go, sparse semantic anchors re-ground route progress, and terminal perception confirms what the task seeks. AVALON turns human-held spatial knowledge into executable memory for a robot’s first mission by coupling a human-seeded structural prior, node-verified local execution, and task-triggered evidence acquisition through stable graph IDs. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows.

Human-Seeded Layered Spatial Memory. We propose to decouple a floor-plan skeleton from editable task memory, and use shared node-edge identifiers to associate human-provided clues, task constraints, and robot sensory evidence. This design eliminates the requirement for a dedicated pre-mapping traversal prior to deployment.

Node-Verified Topological Execution. The robot navigates along human-seeded routes via local graph transitions. Node-associated visual and textual clues validate arrival and re-anchor execution progress. Mismatches between real observations and expected node signatures trigger incremental revision of the localization hypothesis.

Task-Triggered, Evidence-Gated Human-Robot Memory Co-Updating. Graph identifiers are shared across execution and memory maintenance modules. Human permissions remain authoritative, while change notifications invoke on-site physical validation only when relevant to the active task. Physical world states are updated exclusively using spatially localized robot evidence, and verified execution outcomes refresh the spatial memory graph to support subsequent missions.

Experimental Validation. We validate our proposed closed-loop pipeline on a Dining-to-Meeting-Room navigation scenario involving a human-reported cart at the entryway. On a Unitree Go2, AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/55/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 [5] (78.5 s, 4/54/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. In the five AVALON + X-NavDP Dining-to-Meeting-Room trials reported in Table II, user reports of environmental changes trigger on-site robot verification before the entrance node condition is updated. AVALON successfully completes the report–verification–update sequence and subsequently reaches the meeting room in all five trials. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.

title: Attribution-Gated Joint Estimation of Intention and Capability for Assist-as-Needed Upper-Limb Robots
authors: Pengcheng Li,Shuxiang Guo,Hanze Wang,Jun Leng,Bin Wang,Mingchao Ding
abstract:
Assist-as-needed (AAN) control must distinguish between changes in intended motion and changes in effective voluntary torque capability, even though both can produce similar kinematic and interaction responses. A dual-measurand multimodal MHE–MPC architecture is developed as the base framework, in which the intended trajectory and the task-dependent effective voluntary torque capability are estimated online as distinct quantities, and both estimates are used to adapt robotic assistance. Building on this architecture, the ambiguity between the two update channels is formulated as a continuous credit-assignment problem and resolved by an attribution gate. A trajectory-change indicator is obtained from persistent corrective interaction, whereas a capability-change indicator is derived from the residual between normalized muscle activation and dynamics-reconstructed voluntary torque.
Nine healthy participants completed factorial target-height–load trials and a pre–post fatigue cup-transport task. Without target-height input, the gated method generated correctly ordered Low–Middle–High references under every load: target changes were preferentially assigned to trajectory adaptation, whereas added load shifted adaptation toward the capability channel. It achieved the lowest RMSE in all nine conditions (0.017 rad versus 0.041 rad for ungated dual estimation and 0.127 rad for fixed-reference error-based AAN). Post-fatigue capability estimates decreased and assistance increased at all heights, supporting functional feasibility.
introduction:
Upper-limb motor impairment creates demand for intensive and task-specific rehabilitation training [1, 2]. Repeatable movement practice can be delivered and human–robot interaction can be quantified by rehabilitation robots during training [2]. Robot-mediated rehabilitation can be further extended by wearable platforms toward functional tasks and less structured environments [3, 4, 5, 6].

Task completion can be facilitated by assist-as-needed (AAN) control while the user’s voluntary contribution is preserved. This balance is particularly difficult in wearable systems, which operate in continuous physical interaction with users whose movement goals, effort, fatigue, and physical limitations may vary across repetitions [7, 8]. A reference trajectory that is inconsistent with the user’s intended movement can produce tracking error and interaction torque, but similar responses can also arise when voluntary capability is insufficient for the required motion. Active participation may be suppressed by excessive assistance, whereas task completion may be compromised or interaction load may be increased by insufficient assistance. Effective AAN control must therefore address both trajectory compatibility and assistance demand.

Trajectory compatibility has been addressed by one line of research through human-intention estimation and reference adaptation. sEMG, kinematics, and interaction torque are combined with model-based or data-driven inference by multimodal methods [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]; the reference is further adapted by iterative learning and optimization [15, 11, 12]. Motion intention and arm stiffness have also been estimated simultaneously for variable-impedance interaction [10]. However, stiffness is an interaction property rather than the voluntary torque effectively available for the current task. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, intended trajectory and task-dependent effective voluntary torque capability have not been jointly estimated as distinct online measurands for AAN. Moreover, trajectory-adaptation signals depend on whether the user can execute the intended movement.

Assistance is modulated by error-based AAN schemes from kinematic deviation [16, 17, 18, 19], whereas voluntary torque, stiffness, or strength are estimated by capability-centered methods to compensate for an inferred deficit [20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. Physiological effort information is provided by direct sEMG-based assistance, although signal variability and session-specific calibration remain practical considerations [23, 24]. How much assistance should be provided is determined by these approaches, but tracking and effort deviations may also reflect a purposeful change in the desired trajectory.

Trajectory adaptation and capability-based assistance consequently cannot be treated as unrelated estimation problems. The task demand is modified by a change in intention, while the effective voluntary contribution available in the current task context is modified by fatigue, activation–torque inconsistency, and unmodeled external demand. These effects can occur during the same movement and appear in the same motion, interaction, and effort observations. If the two states are updated from overlapping residuals without explicit credit assignment, capability- or demand-related signals can be absorbed into trajectory adaptation, while intention-related signals can be absorbed into assistance.

To address this problem, a dual-estimation architecture is established and then extended by automatic attribution. The contributions are as follows:

(1) An ungated dual-measurand MHE–MPC architecture is developed to estimate intended-trajectory deformation and task-dependent effective voluntary torque capability online, and both estimates are used for AAN.

(2) An attribution gate is introduced to compensate cross-sensitivity by allocating shared observations through a gating variable α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] and its complement 1−α1-\alpha, thereby limiting leakage between intention and capability estimates.

(3) The two layers are evaluated separately: dual estimation is tested by comparison with error-based AAN, whereas credit assignment is tested by gated–ungated comparison.

title: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Lichao Ni,Yuhan Liu,Pengfei Li,Guanghuan Fang
comment: . Includes supplementary material
abstract: Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4–9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7–18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2–4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions. Generalist policies such as OpenVLA, π0\pi_{0}, and π0.5\pi_{0.5} provide a foundation for learning diverse manipulation skills [14, 2, 26]. Further specialization can improve individual domains, leaving useful capabilities distributed across separate policies. Multi-teacher consolidation seeks to transfer these capabilities into one student whose learned parameters are shared across domains. Across LIBERO, Meta-World, and CALVIN, the student must accommodate distinct observation and native action interfaces while integrating specialist supervision through the same learned parameters.

Teacher-generated data provide a direct route to capability transfer [34, 32]. During deployment, however, the student may encounter observations that differ from the teachers’ demonstrations: a missed grasp changes both the next observation and the recovery action required. On-policy distillation (OPD) obtains teacher guidance at inputs induced by the student, following the principle of interactive imitation learning [28, 1, 38]. For flow-based policies, the choice of supervision also extends inside action generation. A teacher can supply a final action chunk or local velocity predictions at intermediate states along the student’s noise-to-action trajectory.

Flow-based VLA consolidation therefore involves two evolving input distributions. The student’s executed actions determine which environment observations it encounters, while its velocity field determines which intermediate states it traverses during action generation. Guidance on teacher demonstrations can leave both distributions mismatched to the deployed student. Recent work develops student-trajectory supervision for continuous generators and robot policies [8, 25, 20]. For cross-domain consolidation, the central design question is how to couple teacher guidance to the shared student’s behavior at both levels as its capabilities evolve.

We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework for consolidating domain-specialized flow-based VLAs into a shared student. The framework couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories, aligning supervision with the evolving student at both the environment and action-generation levels. Each frozen specialist supplies local velocity targets in its domain. We aggregate weighted domain-loss gradients to update the student once, then use the updated policy to collect new environment experience and action-flow trajectories. The student shares learned parameters while retaining the preprocessing, normalization, and action decoding required by each domain interface. Teachers are used only during training.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce a two-level on-policy framework that consolidates domain-specialized flow-based VLAs through teacher supervision on student-induced environment and action-generation states.

We demonstrate cross-domain capability consolidation in a shared π0.5\pi_{0.5} student. It outperforms the SFT initialization, Action Loss OPD, and Teacher-rollout SFT on all aggregate metrics across LIBERO, Meta-World, and CALVIN.

We characterize the roles of supervision targets and joint input sources through matched comparisons. Learning curves establish persistent advantages over endpoint matching, while suite-level results and domain-weight comparisons identify how transferred capabilities are distributed across tasks.

1. We introduce a two-level on-policy framework that consolidates domain-specialized flow-based VLAs through teacher supervision on student-induced environment and action-generation states.

2. We demonstrate cross-domain capability consolidation in a shared π0.5\pi_{0.5} student. It outperforms the SFT initialization, Action Loss OPD, and Teacher-rollout SFT on all aggregate metrics across LIBERO, Meta-World, and CALVIN.

3. We characterize the roles of supervision targets and joint input sources through matched comparisons. Learning curves establish persistent advantages over endpoint matching, while suite-level results and domain-weight comparisons identify how transferred capabilities are distributed across tasks.

title: TRACE: Typed Reference-Aware Conversational Editing for Humanoid Motion Diffusion
authors: Zejian Kang,Yifu Luo,Boyang Shen,Jingxuan Li,Zekai Chen,Zekun Shi,Yongxue Xu,Zhenyu Hou,Bingqian Wu,Shaolei Zhang,Wentao Yang,Xiangru Huang
abstract:
Language-conditioned humanoid motion generation enables users to create
and refine robot movements through natural language. The central challenge
is to connect an underspecified request to concrete motion structure that
can subsequently be revised relative to an accepted reference. We present
TRACE, a generation and editing framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid
robot built around typed, measurable kinematic quantities. Our insight is
to ground generation conditions in paired training motions and editing
goals in the current motion. A language model learns to predict support,
root, and hand events from motion-derived supervision; their time-aligned
encodings complement the original text in a diffusion generator.
Gravity-referenced states and trajectory–contact objectives improve
kinematic consistency. For editing, typed requests define body–time scopes
and source-relative goals. A separate reference-conditioned diffusion editor
uses these goals and revised events to realize changes, while sampling-time
projection preserves protected state coordinates. Quantitative evaluation
and human assessment show improved semantic alignment and motion quality
over the compared methods. Controlled ablations support the value of
motion-grounded conditioning and kinematic consistency, while multi-turn
editing evaluations demonstrate more reliable execution of successive
relative requests under shared preservation constraints. Together, these
results support typed kinematic structure as a common basis for motion
generation and reference-aware revision.
introduction:
Language-conditioned humanoid motion generation maps a natural-language
instruction to a sequence of root poses and joint configurations. It lets
users specify behavior such as walking, dancing, or jumping without
authoring each pose. The resulting trajectory can serve as an animation
or a reference for a downstream robot controller. In interactive use,
generation also provides a starting point for refinement: after seeing a
motion, a user may ask for a higher jump or a different hand position while
expecting the accepted parts of the sequence to remain recognizable.

Existing text-to-motion models learn mappings from captions to continuous
trajectories or discrete motion codes (Tevet et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023a; Jiang et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2024).
Structured approaches expose body-part or temporal conditions
(Zhang et al., 2023b; Yazdian et al., 2025), and language-model planning decomposes
instructions into detailed descriptions (Ouyang et al., 2026). These intermediate
conditions provide a way to specify motion structure, but a caption alone
rarely determines exactly when a foot supports the body or how high a hand
rises. A plan inferred solely from that caption can describe a valid
realization different from its paired training motion. Grounding the plan
in measurable properties of the demonstration gives supervision a direct
connection to the trajectory the generator learns to reconstruct.

Editing makes this connection to a particular motion equally important.
Source-conditioned methods learn revisions from language and an existing
sequence (Athanasiou et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026). A relative request such as
“raise the hand” must be interpreted against the current pose and
trajectory, while the rest of the motion supplies a reference to preserve.
An interactive system therefore needs both an explicit description of the
requested change and a mechanism that restricts its effect to the selected
body region and time interval.

The key challenge is to turn underspecified language into a coherent
motion reference whose intended properties can be revised selectively.
Figure 1 illustrates this requirement. An initial instruction
produces a jumping jack; the follow-up “Jump higher, rest unchanged” refers
to that particular motion. The edited example crouches deeper and jumps
higher, requiring coordinated changes in preparation and take-off while
retaining the overall action. A useful intermediate description should
therefore expose quantities such as support and height over time.
Our insight is that these measurable quantities can connect both stages:
the paired demonstration determines the event targets used to train
generation, and the current reference determines the baseline and protected
coordinates for editing.

We introduce Typed Reference-Aware Conversational Editing (TRACE)
for the Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Typed refers to explicit categories
for support, root, and hand events and for requested changes.
Reference-aware means that the current motion defines both the baseline
for a relative change and the coordinates to preserve. For generation, we
extract event targets from training motions through forward kinematics and
supervise an LLM to predict duration and event intervals from text.
The predicted Plan is converted into numerical conditions aligned with
motion patches. A diffusion Transformer combines these conditions with
the original caption, retaining language information beyond the compact
event vocabulary. A gravity-referenced state directly represents height
and tilt, while integrated-trajectory and support-selective contact
objectives constrain motion consistency.

For editing, a language request is parsed into a typed change and compiled
into a body–time scope and a source-relative goal. A separately trained
diffusion editor receives the current motion, its revised events, and the
compiled goal. At every sampling step, reference projection restores
protected coordinates, allowing the selected region to change while
retaining the rest of the encoded motion. Each output supplies the reference
for the next request. Generation and editing thus share a motion
representation and a kinematic vocabulary, with separate models for their
respective conditioning tasks.

Experiments on BONES-SEED (Bones Studio, n.d.) evaluate generation, kinematic
consistency, and successive request execution. TRACE leads the compared
methods in retrieval, MM-Dist, FID, and human ratings
(Section 4.2). Matched controls establish the
value of event conditioning and motion-derived auxiliary supervision,
while representation and objective ablations measure their effects on

title: Location-Based Safety Management with Wearable Seamless Indoor-Outdoor Positioning
authors: Anh-Van Vu,Seungwoo Chae,Changmin Sung,Van-Tuan Nguyen,Dongsoo Han
abstract: Reliable worker localization is essential for real-time industrial safety management, but seamless outdoor–indoor positioning remains challenging. GNSS performs well outdoors yet degrades near buildings and fails indoors, while many indoor systems require costly infrastructure or extensive calibration. This paper presents a practical safety-oriented positioning system that uses resource-constrained wearable tags and a device–cloud split architecture for continuous outdoor–indoor worker tracking. The tag integrates GNSS, IMU, barometric sensing, LTE Cat-M communication, and performs lightweight sensor fusion, while the cloud server executes map-aware fusion for continuous tracking. Developed as an operational platform, the system also includes a database, a map tool, and a dashboard that provide real-time monitoring, geofencing-based access alerts, and safety and productivity analysis. Experiments with multiple participants, each walking an approximately 1400 m outdoor–indoor route, using LTE Cat-M communication, achieve mean errors of 1.32 m indoors and 3.30 m outdoors, while maintaining low positioning latency and efficient power consumption. These results demonstrate the feasibility of wearable-based seamless positioning for scalable real-time safety management.
introduction:
In industrial worksites and large-scale facilities, worker localization is a fundamental requirement for safety management. Real-time location information allows managers to monitor worker distribution, detect entry into hazardous or restricted zones, support emergency response, and analyze mobility patterns for safer and more efficient operations [1, 2, 3]. However, seamless pedestrian positioning across outdoor and indoor spaces remains challenging. GNSS offers broad outdoor coverage but degrades near buildings and often becomes unavailable indoors. Meanwhile, many indoor positioning systems depend on BLE[4, 5], UWB[6, 7], or RFID[1] infrastructure, which can be costly to deploy and maintain, especially in dynamic workplaces, temporary sites, and large facilities with frequently changing layouts.

A practical safety-management system therefore needs an infrastructure-light, scalable, and continuously available positioning solution that works across outdoor and indoor spaces. Wearable sensing is a promising direction because each worker can wear a compact device that collects inertial, barometric, and GNSS measurements without dense localization infrastructure. However, wearable tags are constrained by size, power, computation, memory, and communication bandwidth. Running complex map-aware fusion entirely on the device can exceed these limits, while streaming raw sensor data to a remote server increases energy consumption, latency, and network load. Practical wearable positioning thus requires a careful split between local device and server-side processing.

This paper presents a wearable seamless pedestrian positioning system for location-based safety management (LBSM). The system applies a distributed architecture in which the wearable tag performs sensing and lightweight local processing to produce motion summaries, while a cloud server fuses these summaries with GNSS, barometric pressure, and indoor occupancy maps using an event-driven map-aware particle filter. The system further integrates map management, real-time monitoring, geofencing, and safety analytics to support practical LBSM deployment. This system demonstrates how resource-aware wearable sensing and server-side intelligence can jointly support scalable, real-time positioning for practical safety management.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We develop an end-to-end, infrastructure-light seamless pedestrian positioning system using resource-constrained wearable tags and a device–cloud split architecture, enabling reliable and scalable LBSM. The system integrates custom LTE Cat-M wearable tags, a positioning server, operational and map databases, a map tool, and a real-time dashboard.

We develop the operational LBSM functions built upon the positioning system, including real-time worker and device monitoring, geofencing-based access alerts, and location-based safety and productivity analytics.

We validate the complete system with multiple participants, each traversing an approximately 1400 m outdoor–indoor route, and evaluate its positioning accuracy, communication latency under different IoT protocols and connectivity conditions, wearable power consumption, and geofencing-based alert performance.

The system integrates custom LTE Cat-M wearable tags, a positioning server, operational and map databases, a map tool, and a real-time dashboard.

2. We develop the operational LBSM functions built upon the positioning system, including real-time worker and device monitoring, geofencing-based access alerts, and location-based safety and productivity analytics.

3. We validate the complete system with multiple participants, each traversing an approximately 1400 m outdoor–indoor route, and evaluate its positioning accuracy, communication latency under different IoT protocols and connectivity conditions, wearable power consumption, and geofencing-based alert performance.

title: A 2D Image Feedback-Based Autonomous Endovascular Navigation Method: A Perception and Control Framework
authors: Sheng Cao,Shuxiang Guo,Yonggan Yan,Jian Guo,Chunying Li,Bin Wang,Mingchao Ding,Yongxin Zhang,Yongwei Zhang,Pengfei Yang,Jianmin Liu
abstract: In endovascular interventions, physicians rely on planar DSA and X-ray fluoroscopy to interpret vessel anatomy and device motion, yet converting these images into feedback for autonomous navigation remains difficult. A perception and control method is formulated for two-dimensional image feedback. Vessel masks are converted into a labeled centerline graph, and device-tip estimates are projected onto a planned path to obtain progress, deviation, and direction. A rule-based controller uses these quantities for delivery, branch selection, probing, rollback, and recovery. The method was evaluated on a physical dual-device robotic platform in 65 closed-loop runs using simulator-rendered planar images across three paths. All runs reached at least 0.95 maximum observed guidewire progress; two runs (3.1%) met the prespecified failure rule of three or more autonomous stop events. The results establish route-level performance on the tested platform; clinical image sequences and broader anatomy remain to be evaluated.
introduction:
Endovascular intervention is a sequential decision problem observed through a planar projection. The clinical need for reliable vascular intervention has motivated robotic assistance across vascular and neuroendovascular procedures [1, 2, 3, 4]. Recent studies have also examined autonomous endovascular systems and embodied intelligence for image-guided intervention [5, 6]. During DSA or X-ray fluoroscopy, vessel anatomy, device–vessel contact, and depth are represented only indirectly in the image. Each device command changes the configuration that produces the next image, so autonomous navigation requires a state that remains useful under incomplete and changing observations.

Local image cues do not uniquely determine route-level intent. Existing fluoroscopic methods have addressed catheter segmentation and guidewire-pose tracking, but these measurements do not by themselves specify the intended route or the next action [7, 8]. A guidewire tip and its local tangent can be consistent with more than one branch, while projection overlap, occlusion, and segmentation jitter can change the apparent direction. A useful state must therefore preserve branch identity and progress along the selected route while suppressing pixel-level variation that is irrelevant to the next decision.

The path-relative representation used here provides this task-oriented abstraction. A vessel centerline is represented as a labeled topology graph, and the operator-selected route is parameterized by arc length. Projection of the guidewire and catheter tips onto the route yields progress, transverse deviation, directional consistency, and inter-device lag. The graph supplies discrete branch structure; arc length supplies continuous progress; and the residuals indicate whether the observation remains compatible with the intended motion. Static vessel topology is initialized and locked, whereas device measurements remain frame dependent. This factorization converts image observations into a state that can be inspected at every control transition.

Image-guided navigation studies have used local directional cues, learned policies, and short-horizon visual feedback [9, 10, 11]. Route progress, branch identity, and recovery conditions are not always explicit in these control states. A deterministic policy based on path-relative variables makes the cause of each advancement, probe, rollback, or recovery transition observable and allows run-level failures to be traced to image-derived conditions.

The formulation targets the macroscopic layer of endovascular autonomy: delivery along a selected route, simple branch choice, deviation correction, and recovery. The physical dual-device robot builds on prior multi-manipulator, autonomous-delivery, remote-control, and multi-device intervention platforms [12, 13, 14, 15]. Force-related sensing, multimodal feedback, haptic interfaces, and steerable-catheter mechanisms provide complementary directions for extending the control state [16, 17, 18, 19]. The Mentice platform provides repeatable planar projections for controlled validation. Two segmentation models, skeleton-based tip and direction estimation, topology-constrained route construction, and a deterministic state machine form the closed loop. At a junction, an alternating rotation scan is followed by a bounded advancement trial; the next image determines acceptance or rollback. Direct force measurement and three-dimensional reconstruction are not required for this route-level formulation.

The central contribution is a topology-constrained, path-relative state abstraction that converts planar device and vessel observations into interpretable progress and branch-decision variables for physical-robot navigation. Route-level behavior is evaluated over 65 runs on three paths, with explicit stop-based failure accounting and image-derived measurements reported throughout the control loop.

title: CarryOn: A Dual-Loop Harness for Personalized and Reliable Robot Assistance
authors: Zixuan Wang,Yuqi Liu,Yuxin Chen,Sengqiao Yang,Jinhui Ye,Pengguang Chen,Changsheng Lu,Shu Liu,Bei Yu,Jiaya Jia
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract:
While generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models have enabled diverse open-world manipulation, real-world robotic assistance requires two critical capabilities they currently lack: personalization and reliable execution. First, executing an instruction like ‘make me a sandwich’ requires grounding subtask decomposition in persistent user preferences rather than relying on a single generic solution. Second, reliable deployment demands explainable safety assurance that proactively prevents hazards and gracefully recovers from occasional physical failures.
To address these gaps, we present CarryOn, a dual-loop harness designed to augment a frozen VLA policy. The planning loop maintains persistent user-level and scene-level context that is continually grounded against new observations and revised through interaction, enabling personalized task selection and execution grounding across conversations and changing scenes. The execution loop actively supervises policy rollouts, shielding actions from predicted hazardous contact. When execution fails, the system invokes reusable control-based recovery skills that restore task progress and are refined through reflection on earlier failures. On a real robot and in simulation, CarryOn dispatches preference-consistent subtasks across users and scenes, reduces the violation rate of an already safety-finetuned VLA from 52.6% to 6.1%, and increases recovery success from 13% to 80% when refined skills are reused.
introduction:
Robot assistance ultimately aims to serve people in their everyday lives. Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced this goal by learning to execute diverse manipulation instructions across tasks and environments [1, 2, 3]. Large-scale robot datasets further support learning across tasks and embodiments [4, 5, 6]. However, progress in instruction-conditioned manipulation alone does not bridge the gap to everyday assistance. A robot must know both what to do to meet the user’s needs in the current environment and how to carry it out reliably as physical conditions change. Bridging this gap requires a system that connects context-sensitive task decisions with reliable execution.

A harness is the system surrounding a base model that orchestrates execution and decides how the model plans, perceives and manages context, stores artifacts, and evaluates results [7]. Language-agent systems illustrate how memory and reflection can support decisions across interactions [8, 9]. In the field of robotics, hierarchical VLA systems connect high-level requests to manipulation instructions [10]. Recent concurrent works on embodied harnesses use memory to steer frozen VLAs and coordinate heterogeneous policies [11, 12], or evolve runtime critics and recovery skills from execution experience [13]. These works mainly focus on how to improve VLA models’ performance in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. However, for everyday assistance, reliable execution must also be coupled with deciding what is appropriate for the user in the current situation.

We study this connection through personalized robot assistance, which exposes two challenges. First, task decisions must remain aligned with the user’s needs as interactions and scenes change, and the same request can require different actions. Learning preferences or identifying personal objects [14, 15] provides context, while in reality the context can be dynamically changed and thus requires revision in stored memory. Second, the resulting plan must be supported by reliable physical execution: impending hazardous contact calls for intervention [16] to ensure safety, while a failure that has already occurred calls for repair [17] to ensure robustness. The harness must connect these responses to the intended task and retain failure experience to improve later recovery.

Consider a user who asks a robot to “serve me food” (Fig. 1). The robot should respect an earlier vegetarian preference without requiring it to be repeated in the query. It may look beneath a remembered cover for a carrot, but finding meat instead must change its original plan. Even when the ingredient is suitable, an obstacle or a lost grasp can interrupt delivery to the bowl. The harness must preserve the user’s dietary requirement when observations change the plan, restore progress when a grasp fails, and use that failure to improve later recovery.

We present CarryOn, a dual-loop harness that connects adaptive task decisions with reliable execution for personalized robot assistance. Its central design makes task context and recovery behavior persistent, revisable parts of the runtime around a frozen VLA. The planning loop determines what to do for the user and scene, and the execution loop protects and repairs the active subtask. Visual feedback connects them, informing plan revision and determining whether execution should advance or invoke recovery while retaining the task goal.

The planning loop supports contextual adaptation through memories. User context expresses needs and preferences, while scene context helps determine where and how they can be fulfilled. The planner combines both with the current multimodal request and available observations to select an endpoint and supported subtasks. Dialogue revises user context, and observations trigger explicit scene-memory updates before subsequent plans proceed. Memory thus participates in a feedback loop: it guides action, while the resulting evidence updates what later plans can rely on.

The execution loop supports physical reliability through fast proactive shielding and slower reactive recovery. A fast proactive shield predicts gripper and carried-object motion and filters commands against geometric contact constraints. After a failure, slower, event-triggered recovery skills repair the physical state so the interrupted task can continue. Offline reflection then uses failures of the current recovery version to revise its parameters and strategies, retaining successive versions in a skill library for later attempts. Immediate protection and reactive repair operate within an episode, and accumulated experience changes recovery behavior across attempts. This design keeps the VLA fixed while allowing the recovery pathway to improve through repeated reflection.

Contributions. In this paper, we present a dual-loop harness, called CarryOn, with the features of personalization and reliable execution. The planning loop of the harness connects persistent user and scene contexts with observation-driven revision, supporting personalized task decisions across interactions, scenes, and query modalities, while the execution loop combines proactive geometric shielding with reusable and iteratively refined recovery skills. Real-world studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our harness in planning preference-oriented tasks across diverse users and scenes. Notably, our method strongly increases recovery success rates from 13% to 80% using refined skills, and reduces the constraint-violation rate from 52.6% to 6.1%.

title: X-Fly: Learning to Reach and Stop in Full-Chunk Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
authors: Ruibin Ju,Ruifeng Cai,Min Xu,Lin Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) agents built on large vision-language models are expensive to query. Executing a complete predicted action chunk before replanning amortizes this cost, reducing model inference from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint for our policy. It also moves the states at which the policy is queried away from expert demonstrations, which supervise neither recovery from these states nor termination at the learner’s own arrival. On OpenFly test-seen, no-stop failures account for 47.78% of full-chunk behavior cloning (BC) outcomes. We present X-Fly, a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial VLN. Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited decision states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in-region state. Flow-GRPO then jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from same-task closed-loop outcomes, supplemented by outcome-verified stopping supervision. With eight controls per decision, X-Fly reaches 74.18% SR on test-seen and 51.73% on test-unseen, compared with 16.45% and 18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04% and 29.46% for DreamFly.
introduction:
Aerial VLN asks an embodied agent to follow a free-form instruction through a large urban environment and terminate within a target radius [19, 11]. Compared with indoor graph navigation [1, 6], the agent must produce continuous translation and rotation, cope with large viewpoint changes, and recover from control errors that alter every subsequent observation. Success therefore depends on two coupled abilities: flying to the described goal, and deciding when the goal has been reached.

Recent aerial agents condition on large vision-language models (VLMs), which makes every policy query expensive [9, 35]. Action-chunk policies predict several future controls per query [34, 8], yet aerial VLN agents such as DreamFly execute only the first control and query again [9]. Executing the complete chunk amortizes policy inference across its controls: for our fast–slow policy, executing all eight cuts model inference from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint (Sec. 4.1).

Full-chunk execution also changes where the policy is queried. The aircraft moves through eight controls before new visual feedback can correct it, so the states at which the policy is next queried, its decision anchors, drift away from the expert trajectories it was trained on. Expert-only data cover these learner-visited anchors poorly in two ways: they contain no chunk that starts at an off-route learner pose and returns it to the route, and their positive STOP labels are confined to expert terminal windows, leaving the anchors where the learner itself arrives poorly represented. We call this the full-chunk support gap. On test-seen, switching BC from single-step to full-chunk execution drops SR from 46.57% to 16.45% (Fig. 1), although navigation failures barely change (28.02% vs. 30.77%); no-stop failures account for 47.78% of the full-chunk outcomes (Sec. 4.3). Reaching the goal is not the same as stopping there.

X-Fly addresses both sides of the gap with two training stages applied after multi-domain BC (Fig. 2). Recovery DAgger [24] runs the learner with the deployed full-chunk executor and labels every visited anchor with a smooth chunk that decays the learner’s offset and reconnects to the future expert segment; the first anchor inside the success region receives a positive STOP label. Recovery reduces navigation and no-stop failures, while premature stopping remains common. Flow-GRPO [18] then compares closed-loop attempts of the same task and updates the chunked flow controller and a separate Bernoulli STOP policy from their outcomes. With eight controls per decision, X-Fly reaches 74.18% SR on test-seen and 51.73% on test-unseen, all from explicit in-region STOP.

Our contributions are:

We study full-chunk execution in aerial VLN and characterize the support gap it creates at learner-visited decision anchors, with separate effects on goal reaching and termination.

We present X-Fly, a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial navigation that combines multi-domain BC, recovery supervision at learner-visited anchors, and closed-loop outcome optimization of chunked control and STOP.

We demonstrate improved full-chunk navigation on OpenFly and characterize distinct stage-level gains: recovery improves goal-region reachability and reduces no-stop failures, while outcome post-training further reduces premature termination.

1. We study full-chunk execution in aerial VLN and characterize the support gap it creates at learner-visited decision anchors, with separate effects on goal reaching and termination.

2. We present X-Fly, a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial navigation that combines multi-domain BC, recovery supervision at learner-visited anchors, and closed-loop outcome optimization of chunked control and STOP.

3. We demonstrate improved full-chunk navigation on OpenFly and characterize distinct stage-level gains: recovery improves goal-region reachability and reduces no-stop failures, while outcome post-training further reduces premature termination.

title: Policy-Aligned Predictive Verification for Adaptive VLA Action-Chunk Execution
authors: Minkyu Kim,Junhoo Lee,Seungyeon Kim,Suhyun Jeon,Baekseung Kim,Donghoon Han,Nojun Kwak
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate action sequences that reduce repeated inference, but deciding how much of each sequence to execute is critical to task success. Existing adaptive methods make this decision using generation stability or prediction agreement, yet these signals do not establish whether executing a candidate prefix preserves the ability to complete the task. We introduce a policy-aligned predictive verifier (PAV) that anticipates the consequences of candidate action prefixes and evaluates their compatibility with successful continuation before execution. Rather than using future prediction to generate actions, our method evaluates existing proposals in the VLA’s internal task-conditioned representation space. To learn local judgments from terminal task outcomes, we combine trajectory-level survival supervision with a localization prior that preserves useful behavior within failed rollouts. The resulting validity scores guide execution-horizon selection. Evaluations with π0\pi_{0} and π0.5\pi_{0.5} across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation show improved success–query trade-offs. These findings point toward a different role for future prediction in robotics, using it to assess how far to trust a policy’s proposed actions rather than to generate new ones.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong performance in generating robot actions from visual observations and language instructions (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Miao et al., 2026). Yet querying a large VLA policy at every control step is costly, while robot behavior requires coordinated motion over multiple steps. Action chunking addresses both demands by generating a sequence of future actions in one query, supporting temporal coherence with fewer policy calls. However, executing an entire chunk without new observations limits responsiveness to environmental changes and allows execution errors to accumulate. Many systems therefore use a shorter execution horizon to execute only an initial prefix of each chunk before replanning from new observations. Adapting this horizon is thus central to retaining the efficiency of action chunking while remaining responsive to feedback.

Adaptive execution seeks the longest prefix of each action chunk that still allows the policy to complete the task successfully. Identifying this prefix requires anticipating how the proposed actions will affect the policy’s ability to complete the remaining task. Because the effects of a candidate prefix on task success are not directly observable before execution, existing approaches rely on indirect signals to guide execution. Some methods use generation stability as this indirect signal, drawing on internal policy information to select an execution horizon (Wang et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). Others use prediction agreement, comparing action-conditioned predictions with incoming observations to guide correction or replanning during execution (Pan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Generation stability and prediction agreement alone, however, do not establish whether a candidate prefix preserves compatibility with successful task completion. As illustrated in Figure 1, an action proposal can be consistently generated and its consequences accurately predicted, yet executing it can still lead to a missed grasp and task failure.

To assess this compatibility directly, we introduce proposal validity, which estimates the probability that the policy can successfully complete the task after executing a candidate prefix. This probability depends on the state reached after executing the prefix, because the policy must complete the remaining task from that state. We therefore predict this future state to evaluate whether it supports successful continuation under the policy. World models and World Action Models have demonstrated this capability, building on pretrained visual representations or video models to predict future observations or latent states for planning and action generation (Seo et al., 2022; Du et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). However, because VLA policies already generate effective action proposals, we use this predictive capability to evaluate those proposals rather than to generate new actions. To ground this evaluation in the same information used for action generation, we predict the effects of each prefix in the VLA’s task-conditioned representation space, which integrates visual observations and language instructions.

We therefore propose a policy-aligned predictive verifier (PAV) that assesses each action extension’s compatibility with successful continuation from predicted VLA representations. These extension-level assessments provide local validity estimates used to select execution horizons. To learn these local judgments, however, we must rely on rollouts that provide only terminal task outcomes. These outcomes do not reveal the validity of individual extensions, since even a failed rollout may contain valid action prefixes. We therefore treat extension-level validity as latent and supervise its accumulated product using the terminal outcome. However, the model can fit a failed rollout by slightly lowering validity scores across the rollout, including those of valid extensions. We therefore introduce a localization prior that encourages the model to concentrate these reductions in fewer extensions. At inference time, we combine the local validity scores to evaluate each candidate prefix, accounting for its length. We use these prefix-level scores to decide how many actions to execute before obtaining a new observation and querying the policy again.

Our experiments with π0\pi_{0} and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks assess whether proposal validity selects execution horizons that improve success with fewer policy queries. To examine the basis for these decisions, prediction tests assess action sensitivity, while ablations examine future prediction, policy alignment, and the contributions of individual loss terms. Predicting future VLA representations achieves higher success with fewer queries than direct verification or prediction in generic visual features.

title: MuSTMM: Learning Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation across Multiple Scenes
authors: Hao Ju,Feng Yan,Zhihao Zhong,Heng Yang,Shaofei Huang,Zhedong Zheng
abstract:
Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (STMM) requires robots to respond to sound events by navigating to the associated objects and performing appropriate physical interactions.
Existing STMM evaluations primarily vary object layouts within limited architectural structures, leaving challenges to unseen scenes insufficiently explored.
We introduce Multi-scene Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (MuSTMM), a dataset that combines spatial audio rendering and physical interaction across 31 scenes with diverse architectures and object layouts.
MuSTMM contains 14.36 million precomputed binaural Room Impulse Responses (RIRs) and a scene-disjoint split for evaluating single-event and multi-event settings in unseen scenes.
We further augment the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory that complements acoustic cues with observed geometry.
Specifically, we accumulate pose-aligned depth observations in a shared coordinate frame and project this memory into an egocentric Bird’s-Eye View (BEV) occupancy map.
Fusing map features with sound context produces a goal descriptor that provides both target-location and scene-structure priors, guiding navigation to the target region required for subsequent physical interaction. This policy achieves a 3.81% success rate boost over existing methods, while component ablations further support the effectiveness of spatial memory.
MuSTMM and the navigation policy provide a testbed for the new challenge of studying sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes.
The code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.
introduction:
Sound events provide a natural trigger for robots to perceive their surroundings and interact with physical objects.
Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (STMM) (Ju et al., 2026) studies this capability by requiring a robot to respond to sound events, navigate to the associated objects, and perform appropriate physical interactions.
These interactions include relocating sounding rigid objects and changing the states of articulated objects, either for a single event or sequentially for multiple events.
Existing benchmarks provide only partial challenges of different scene structures and object layouts.
Audio-visual navigation benchmarks, such as SoundSpaces (Chen et al., 2020a) and SAVi (Chen et al., 2021), support sound rendering across multiple scenes but do not include the physical interactions required by STMM.
Conversely, mobile manipulation benchmarks, such as Habitat-M3 (Gu et al., 2023) and ManiSkill-Hab (Shukla et al., 2025), support physical interaction in a limited structure variation without sound rendering.
STMM (Ju et al., 2026) brings these capabilities together, but evaluates object-layout variation within limited scene structures.
Although varying object placements brings partial layout variation, it does not evaluate whether agents can perceive and respond to sound events in unseen structures.
This motivates a benchmark that combines structural diversity with both sound rendering and physical interaction.

To address this gap, we introduce MuSTMM, a multi-scene benchmark that supports sound rendering and physical interaction across 31 scenes from HSSD (Khanna et al., 2024) (see Figure 1).
MuSTMM expands variation at two complementary levels.
Structure variation covers differences in scene architecture, including room geometry and spatial connectivity.
Layout variation combines episode-specific placements of sounding targets and silent source-capable distractors with scene-specific arrangements of non-source background furniture.
To support sound rendering across these scenes, we leverage SoundSpaces (Chen et al., 2022) to densely precompute 14.36 million binaural Room Impulse Responses (RIRs), providing scene-specific sound rendering.
A scene-disjoint split, with 23 training scenes and 8 held-out test scenes, enables evaluation of both single-event and multi-event tasks in unseen scenes.
The accompanying configurable simulator and data-generation pipeline also supports extensions with additional scenes, assets, and task configurations.

We study MuSTMM with a hierarchical framework in which a Sound-triggered Task Planner uses the initial RGB and audio observations to predict an ordered skill chain, which is executed by the corresponding skill-specific policy models.
Among the low-level policy models, sound navigation policy brings the robot to the target region required for subsequent interaction, providing the spatial precondition for executing the next skill.
This cross-scene setting motivates a closer examination of how navigation policies estimate and represent sound-source goals.
Binaural sound supplies directional cues about the source but contains limited geometry information of the observed scene.
Instead, vision observations contain rich geometry priors.
However, this geometric context is distributed across observations acquired at different viewpoints and time steps.
Previous methods encode vision and sound observations into temporal memories (Zeng et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2021). But the geometry information of the scene may misalign across different time steps in this way.
To this end, we augment memory-based goal estimation with explicit spatial memory.
Rather than relying on compressed observation history alone to represent observed geometry, we accumulate depth observations in a shared coordinate frame, and project them into an egocentric BEV occupancy map.
The map records occupancy and exploration status, while its features are fused with acoustic and temporal context to form a goal descriptor.
In this way, the explicit spatial memory contains both goal-related cues and observed scene structure, providing priors for the navigation policy.

We evaluate MuSTMM under a scene-disjoint protocol in single-event and multi-event settings.
Results identify navigation as a major execution bottleneck in held-out scenes, even when ground-truth skill chains are provided.
Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory achieves a navigation success rate of 75.28%, outperforming existing methods.
Memory ablations further show that combining explicit spatial memory with compressed spatio-temporal memory outperforms either component alone, highlighting their complementary roles in across-scene sound navigation.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce MuSTMM, a multi-scene benchmark that combines spatial audio rendering and physical interaction with architectural structure variation and object layout variation. MuSTMM consists of 30.11k episodes. The scene-disjoint evaluation protocol and configurable data-generation pipeline support the study of sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes.

We augment the Goal Descriptor Branch of the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory accumulated from depth observations. By integrating observed geometry with sound context, the resulting goal descriptor provides target-related and structural priors for the navigation policy model and ensures subsequent interaction.

We systematically evaluate baselines in held-out scenes under both single-event and multi-event settings. Navigation comparisons and memory ablations show that explicit spatial memory complements compressed observation history to improve sound-source navigation. Despite these gains, results of the Oracle baseline identify navigation as a major bottleneck in unseen scenes, highlighting a key direction for future research.

MuSTMM consists of 30.11k episodes. The scene-disjoint evaluation protocol and configurable data-generation pipeline support the study of sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes.

2. We augment the Goal Descriptor Branch of the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory accumulated from depth observations. By integrating observed geometry with sound context, the resulting goal descriptor provides target-related and structural priors for the navigation policy model and ensures subsequent interaction.
