title: Modular Inverse Dynamics and Wrench Recovery for Closed-Chain Mechanisms Using Path Assembly
authors: Mohammad Dastranj,Jouni Mattila
abstract:
Rigid closed chains can admit indeterminate internal reactions
even when their motion is fully specified. This paper develops
a modular inverse-dynamics workflow that combines path-based
motion reconstruction with recovery of uniquely determined
actuator and joint-wrench outputs. Analytical second-order
differentiation of assembled transformation paths supplies
passive velocities and accelerations on a regular closure branch.
Spatial Newton–Euler balances are then assembled over the
physical body-and-joint graph. Established nullspace and dual
criteria identify and recover unique outputs, while balance,
ideal-joint admissibility and affine-family diagnostics assess
nonunique reference reactions. Evaluation against Simscape
Multibody uses prescribed motion of a seven-degree-of-freedom
heavy-duty hybrid serial–parallel manipulator under common
rigid-body, ideal-joint assumptions. The results show close agreement with the reference for passive positions, actuator efforts and uniquely recoverable constraint-wrench components. Reaction diagnostics support compatibility with the admissible numerical load family.
introduction:
Modular modeling supports the reuse of submechanism descriptions
while preserving their kinematic and dynamic coupling.
Systematic treatments of closed chains include modular dynamics
for parallel manipulators with hybrid limbs [1]
and constraint embedding for recursive dynamics with local
loops [2].
Virtual Decomposition Control (VDC) likewise requires compatible
motion and wrench quantities for its virtual-power-flow
analysis [3];
applications include heavy-duty hydraulic
manipulators [4, 5]
and, more recently, hydraulic
robot legs with triangular closed chains [6].
These developments motivate reusable motion and load descriptions
for closed-chain modules.

Closure-consistent motion, however, does not imply that every
joint load is uniquely determined. Redundant rigid constraints
can admit multiple reaction distributions while selected
components remain unique [7].
Free-body-diagram [8]
and constraint-matrix [9] approaches have been
developed for analyzing reaction and driving-force uniqueness,
with subsequent
developments within the divide-and-conquer
framework [10].
Consequently, load recovery requires identifying which requested
outputs are invariant across the admissible solutions of the
balance equations.

Path-Assembled Closure Differential Mapping (PACDM) provides
closure resolution and local active-to-passive mappings from
ordered transformation paths [11].
This representation has also been connected to actuator-port
mappings, acceleration reduction, and reduced inverse and forward
dynamics [12]. However, integrating reaction-uniqueness analysis into PACDM-based inverse dynamics for physical actuator and joint-wrench recovery remains to be demonstrated.
Building on these developments and established body-balance and
reaction-uniqueness formulations [8, 9, 13],
the present work develops a path-assembly workflow for motion
reconstruction and recovery of uniquely determined actuator and
joint-wrench outputs in the presence of indeterminate internal
reactions. Here, modularity refers to module-local closure reconstruction and assembly of body-level balance equations; the coupled load-recovery problem is solved globally.

The workflow extends the inherited kinematics through analytical
second-order path differentiation, reconstructing passive
velocities and accelerations on a regular closure branch.
Spatial Newton–Euler balances are assembled over an explicitly
specified physical body-and-joint graph, with each body’s
inertia included once. The established nullspace criterion
and its dual formulation recover each determined output,
subject to numerical consistency and rank checks.
Reference reactions that are nonunique are assessed through
body balance, ideal-joint admissibility and distance to the
normalized affine solution family.
Together, these elements retain the modular path description
while separating uniquely recoverable loads from indeterminate
reaction distributions.

The formulation is evaluated against Simscape Multibody under
prescribed motion of a 7-degree-of-freedom heavy-duty
hybrid serial–parallel manipulator with two closed-chain modules.
Simulation provides reference constraint forces and torques that
are difficult to measure comprehensively in
hardware [13].
The common rigid-body, ideal-joint setting isolates reconstruction
and load recovery from measurement noise and unmodeled physical
disturbances.

title: Fast-VLA: You Only Think Once for Robot Manipulation
authors: Kehong Gong,Guanli Hou,Xiaoxu Zheng,Qi Wang,Mingxi Xu,Anbang Zhai,Xiaoyu He,Mingyuan Zhang,Michael Bi Mi
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Vision–language–action (VLA) policies commonly place a multi-billion-parameter
model inside the feedback loop, repeatedly recomputing task context whenever
they predict a new action chunk. Yet task understanding changes far more slowly
than the robot state. We introduce Fast-VLA, which invokes a frozen 4B
VLM once per episode to contextualize the instruction and
initial views as fixed, multi-layer key–value task memory. During execution, a
lightweight online actor fuses learned time- and arm-indexed queries with
current visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries retrieve task
context from the fixed memory and predict action chunks without re-running the
foundation model. Fast-VLA achieves 92.46% and 92.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0
Clean and Randomized, and 95.95% and 79.11% on LIBERO and
LIBERO-Plus evaluation. Against three continually conditioned baselines on the
same hardware, it reduces RoboTwin amortized policy inference time by
10.9–17.1×\times and requires 1.22 GiB of post-prefill online resident
memory. Task-memory swaps further show that the actor relies on episode-matched task
memory. These results show that task context can be established once while
closed-loop control remains responsive throughout execution.
Project page: https://garfield-kh.github.io/FastVLA.
introduction:
VLA models bring the semantic knowledge of large
pretrained VLMs into robot control, enabling a single policy
to follow diverse instructions across objects and scenes
(Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026). This capability, however, is commonly coupled to
repeated backbone execution: each action chunk re-encodes the current images
and language instruction with a large model. The robot must continuously
observe the environment and revise its actions, but the instruction and overall
task remain largely unchanged. Must the large VLM backbone also be
re-run at every control decision?

When manipulating objects, people typically work out the goal and identify the
relevant objects before acting. As they reach, grasp, and place, they adjust
their movements from what they see and feel without reinterpreting the whole
task before every small action. This suggests two timescales: task
understanding can remain stable, while control must respond continuously to
changes in the scene. This motivates a policy that establishes task context once and then stays
responsive to live observations throughout execution.

Prior work reduces VLA inference cost by changing action representations or
generation procedures (Pertsch et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026). These improvements leave a
separate question: must a large model recompute task context for every action
chunk? Can a VLA think once about the task and still manipulate effectively as
the scene changes throughout an episode?

A fixed memory cannot represent the current world state: objects and arms
move, and the visible scene changes during execution. The central challenge
is to use live observations to query fixed task context at every control
decision. We address this with Fast-VLA—You Only Think Once. A frozen
4B VLM encodes the instruction and initial multi-camera
views into layer-wise key–value task memory at the start of an episode, then
leaves the repeated control loop.

The online actor continually processes current camera views and
proprioception, with short visual history in the RoboTwin configuration.
Query fusion combines learned time- and arm-indexed queries with current arm
state and wrist-view features to form action queries. The action decoder uses
these queries to read visual tokens and task memory, and an action head
predicts an action chunk in one forward pass. The memory remains fixed, but the observations and predicted
actions change at every control decision. The policy therefore remains
closed-loop even though its task memory is fixed.

We evaluate Fast-VLA on RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025), LIBERO
(Liu et al., 2023), and LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025). On RoboTwin 2.0, it reaches
92.46% success in the Clean setting and 92.40% under domain randomization. Fast-VLA obtains 95.95% on standard LIBERO and 79.11% on the
LIBERO-Plus protocol. On RoboTwin, same-hardware measurements against
Faster-WAM (HUST), DM0.5, and Fast-WAM show a 10.9–17.1×\times
reduction in amortized policy inference time after including its one-time
initial call, and its post-prefill online resident memory is 1.22 GiB.
Task-memory swaps cause large performance drops, showing that the actor
depends on episode-matched memory in our evaluation.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce an episode-level VLA architecture that represents
one-time task understanding as fixed, multi-layer memory, moving a frozen
4B VLM outside the repeated control loop.

We develop an online actor that fuses learned queries with live
visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries

title: From Optical Flow to Safety: Visual Safety Certification via Scale-Free Relative Motion
authors: Bazeela Banday,Jishnu Keshavan
abstract:
Safe autonomous navigation using monocular vision remains challenging
because explicit obstacle states are not directly observable. This
letter introduces a visual safety-certification paradigm that uses
scale-free, depth-normalized relative motion encoded by monocular
optical flow as the representation for collision-risk certification,
without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or a
metric world model. Unlike conventional optical-flow-based navigation approaches that rely on image motion to shape avoidance behavior, the proposed framework directly encodes collision-cone geometry and safety constraints in this relative-motion representation. An online Concurrent
Learning observer estimates the normalized relative velocity and
provides a computable estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is
propagated into the collision cone through angular inflation and a
monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding a Robust Vision-Based
Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C3BF). An optimal-decay
CBF quadratic program minimally modifies the nominal control input to
enforce the resulting robust safety constraint under the stated
assumptions. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments on a TurtleBot3 in cluttered environments with static and dynamic obstacles demonstrate collision avoidance using
only monocular vision and onboard proprioception, with the estimation-error bound containing the measured error in 98.3%98.3\% of simulation samples and the robot achieving collision-free navigation in 9393 of 100100 real-world trials.
introduction:
Safe autonomous navigation in dynamic and unstructured environments
requires robots to reason about collision risk despite incomplete
knowledge of their surroundings. Monocular cameras offer a lightweight
sensing modality for mobile robots but do not directly provide metric
depth or explicit obstacle states. Optical flow, however, encodes
scene motion relative to the camera without requiring explicit
three-dimensional reconstruction [1].
This raises a fundamental question: can collision risk be formally
certified directly from optical flow, without reconstructing a metric
representation of the environment?

Optical flow has long been used to guide collision-avoidance
behavior in autonomous systems
[2, 3]. However, its use as a
representation for formal safety certification remains largely
unexplored. Existing optical-flow-based methods primarily use image
motion to generate or condition avoidance actions, rather than to
construct explicit safety constraints. This work addresses this gap by
introducing a visual safety-certification paradigm that bypasses
obstacle-state reconstruction and constructs collision geometry and
robust safety constraints directly from the scale-free relative motion
encoded by optical flow.

Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provide a formal framework for
enforcing safety through optimization-based control filters
[4]. Collision Cone Control Barrier Functions
(C3BFs) characterize collision risk through relative-motion
direction [5], but typically rely on explicit
obstacle states or geometric information. Recent vision-based CBF
approaches use RGB-D sensing [6], dense point clouds
[7], vision-language models [8],
or learned multi-camera perception [9].
Measurement-robust CBFs account for perception uncertainty
[10, 11], but require uncertainty
bounds defined over an explicit measurement representation. Thus, existing approaches either rely on explicit geometric models or use image motion without formal safety certification.

The key insight is that collision-cone reasoning fundamentally depends
on relative-motion direction rather than metric obstacle state. Under
perspective projection, translational optical flow is directly related
to depth-normalized relative velocity, preserving its relative-motion
direction while eliminating metric scale. Together with the
line-of-sight direction, these quantities provide the information
required to construct collision-cone geometry. Thus, monocular optical
flow, combined with onboard proprioception, provides a scale-free
representation in which collision risk can be certified directly,
without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or
a metric world model. Rather than treating optical flow merely as a cue for
avoidance behavior, we use it as the underlying representation for
formal collision-risk certification.

Building on this representation, we develop the estimation and safety
machinery required to make the certification robust to visual estimation
errors. An online Concurrent Learning (CL) observer estimates the
depth-normalized relative velocity and provides a computable
estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is propagated into the
collision-cone geometry through angular inflation and combined with a
monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding the Robust Vision-Based
Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C3BF). An optimal-decay
CBF quadratic program (QP) [12] then enforces the
resulting robust safety constraint while minimally modifying the nominal
control input. The complete framework is implemented onboard a TurtleBot3
and validated in cluttered environments containing both static and
dynamic obstacles.

The main contributions are:

A visual safety-certification paradigm showing that
scale-free relative motion, naturally encoded by monocular optical
flow, is sufficient for collision-cone safety certification without
explicit obstacle-state or geometric world-model reconstruction.

An online Concurrent Learning observer that relies on a finite-time excitation condition to estimate the
depth-normalized relative velocity in this representation and
provide a computable estimation-error bound.

The RV-C3BF that propagates representation uncertainty and a
monocular robot-footprint margin into the collision-cone constraint
for robust safety enforcement.

Extensive simulation and real-world validation on a TurtleBot3 navigating cluttered environments populated with static and dynamic obstacles using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception.

1. A visual safety-certification paradigm showing that
scale-free relative motion, naturally encoded by monocular optical
flow, is sufficient for collision-cone safety certification without
explicit obstacle-state or geometric world-model reconstruction.

2. An online Concurrent Learning observer that relies on a finite-time excitation condition to estimate the
depth-normalized relative velocity in this representation and
provide a computable estimation-error bound.

3. The RV-C3BF that propagates representation uncertainty and a
monocular robot-footprint margin into the collision-cone constraint
for robust safety enforcement.

4. Extensive simulation and real-world validation on a TurtleBot3 navigating cluttered environments populated with static and dynamic obstacles using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception.

title: LTM: Latent Transition Based In-Context Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Qixin Sun,WenLong Gao,Xiansheng Chen,Zhongyuan Wang,Si Liu,Pengwei Wang
comment: Dataset & Code:this https URL

introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained visual and linguistic representations with action generation to follow diverse manipulation instructions (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). Yet the current observation may omit information needed for the next action. A robot placing three objects into a bag must remember completed transfers; one tracking an occluded object must retain the effects of earlier interactions. Similar scenes can therefore require different actions depending on the preceding history, motivating explicit memory for robotic control (Dai et al., 2026; Chung et al., 2026).

Existing memory designs retain visual observations, summarize experience in language, or update a recurrent state (Shi et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2026; Torne et al., 2026; Cherepanov et al., 2026). Dense visual histories consume substantial context, whereas sparse sampling can omit intermediate interactions. Language summaries abstract away visual detail but may miss fine-grained motion. Recurrent representations support compact updates but must continually decide what to preserve in a bounded state.

These trade-offs raise a representational question: what should a VLA remember about its past interactions?

For many manipulation tasks, the relevant history is the sequence of changes induced by robot–environment interactions. Latent action models encode an observation pair into a compact code from which the later observation can be reconstructed conditioned on the earlier one (Bruce et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024). This objective encourages the code to capture temporal changes. While latent actions have been used for policy pretraining and world-model control (Ye et al., 2024; Bu et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026a), we study their use as an ordered episodic memory for action generation.

We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which encodes consecutive observations with a frozen latent action model and projects each code into one memory token. The policy receives a delayed transition prefix alongside the instruction and current observation. Each code depends only on an adjacent observation pair, allowing encoding to overlap action execution. We instantiate LTM on π0.5\pi_{0.5} as LTM-π\pi, with a lightweight adapter and causal attention that permits persistent KV caching. Sparse initial-frame anchors provide visual grounding for video-conditioned tasks. The policy and adapter learn from robot demonstrations without memory-specific semantic annotations. At inference, the frozen encoder supplies transition codes directly to the policy, without an external reasoning model or intermediate language generation.

We evaluate LTM-π\pi with two frozen latent encoders, CD-LAM and DreamDojo, on RoboMME and LIBERO-Mem. With the original benchmark data, the DreamDojo variant reaches 58.54% average success on RoboMME, compared with 17.93% for the reported memory-free π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline, and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem, compared with 42.5% for the strongest baseline included in our comparison. We then isolate the effects of memory content and inference lag. Replacing observation-dependent latent transitions with fixed random representations reduces RoboMME success from 57.67% to 44.50%, supporting the contribution of transition-specific content beyond temporal-progress cues. Using a five-step lag reduces estimated latent-encoder blocking from 114.25 ms to 9.47 ms relative to zero lag, with a small change in success (57.88% to 57.67%).

We next test how LTM benefits from broader demonstration coverage. We expand RoboMME from 100 to 1,000 episodes per task family and increase training from 40K to 120K steps. With the same encoder and policy architecture, success rises from 57.67% to 87.50% (Figure 1). All four tracks improve; Reference, the weakest base-data track, gains 47.50 percentage points. Extending training to 120K steps on the original data alone yields no appreciable gain, supporting the benefit of broader demonstration coverage. LTM-π\pi exceeds the reported PonderPounce result with 9×9\times data by 11.96 points overall, under different data budgets and supervision assumptions.

Scaling does not fully resolve the challenge of composing local transitions into persistent object states: VideoUnmaskSwap and ButtonUnmaskSwap reach 74% and 62%, versus 100% for their non-swap counterparts. In a Cup Swap diagnostic, process supervision achieves 97.93% final-state recovery from latent transitions, compared with 2.40% under final-state-only supervision. These results demonstrate that latent transitions preserve recoverable multi-step interaction information and highlight the importance of intermediate supervision, motivating language-guided reasoning and process supervision to address remaining temporal-composition challenges.

To bound execution-memory growth, we merge the most similar adjacent projected tokens under the same quota during training and inference. On RoboMME-10x, a 200-token budget retains 84.00% success versus 87.50% uncompressed and reduces mean transition-token count by at least 38.26% on profiled training queries.

Finally, we evaluate LTM-π\pi on a Galbot G1 robot in a real-world repeated pick-and-place counting task. LTM-π\pi improves average success from 11.25% for the memory-free π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline to 82.50%, demonstrating that transition memory also helps track completed interactions during physical manipulation.

Our contributions are threefold:

We propose Latent Transition Memory (LTM), a memory representation that uses compact latent transitions between consecutive observations as historical context instead of retaining the full visual history. This focuses memory on interaction-induced changes and enables the policy to use past experience without external reasoning-model calls or memory-specific semantic annotations.

We develop LTM-π\pi, integrating transition memory into π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s inference context through a lightweight adapter. Causal attention, persistent KV caching, and asynchronous transition encoding support efficient online control. Experiments on RoboMME and LIBERO-Mem demonstrate strong memory-dependent manipulation performance, with a measured policy inference time of 66.71 ms on an H100.

We characterize transition-memory information, data scaling, and context-budget trade-offs. Ablations distinguish transition content from temporal cues; tenfold RoboMME data expansion raises success from 57.67% to 87.50%; process-supervised Cup Swap decoding recovers final states with 97.93% accuracy; and a 200-token budget retains 84.00% success. Finally, real-robot counting experiments improve success from 11.25% to 82.50%.

title: Hierarchical Building-Floo-Room Framework for Privacy-Preserving Autonomous Delivery in Large-Scale Buildings
authors: Xu Xiaoji,Luo Rui,Chen Jinhua,Xiang Changying,Zhang Leihan,Liao Zhongyuan
comment: under review
abstract: Autonomous delivery in large-scale buildings requires coordinated planning across multiple spatial levels, including building, floor, and room, while ensuring scheduling efficiency. Existing methods often focus solely on algorithmic development, neglecting integration with physical robotic platforms, and rarely validate performance in real-world scenarios. Many approaches also overlook hierarchical building structures and room-level privacy constraints, limiting practical applicability. To address these challenges, this paper presents a hierarchical delivery framework based on a Building–Floor–Room abstraction, which decomposes the problem across multiple levels to significantly reduce optimization complexity. We formulate a building-aware extension of the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) that explicitly models inter-building and inter-floor connectivity, room-level access constraints, and privacy-sensitive areas, enabling globally feasible and privacy-compliant task assignment and routing. Based on this hierarchical model, the framework can evaluate delivery efficiency across different building layouts and optimize depot placement for specific configurations. At the execution level, we introduce a novel hardware design for non-interactive, privacy-preserving delivery, supported by reachability-aware distances and a closed-loop mapping, localization, and navigation system, ensuring consistency between planned routes and physical navigation. The proposed framework is validated on a real multi-sensor robotic platform, demonstrating reliable multi-floor delivery with improved path rationality and overall efficiency.
introduction:
The increasing demand for last-mile delivery in building complexes, campuses, and large residential communities necessitates mobile robots capable of executing multi-goal delivery tasks in real-world indoor environments [34]. Unlike conventional indoor navigation, which often focuses on a single floor or building, real-world facilities exhibit a three-level hierarchical structure—building, floor, and room—each posing distinct operational challenges [24]:
(1) Building-level, where physical separation and sparse inter-building connections make inter-building travel costly and planning-sensitive;
(2) Floor-level, where vertical mobility relies on elevators with vertical transfer cost and nontrivial waiting times, creating significant scheduling constraints;
(3) Room-level, where each floor features complex 2D topologies, branched corridors, diverse room layouts, and privacy-restricted zones, complicating local path planning and reachability.

Such hierarchical structures pose fundamental challenges to classical Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) formulations. VRP typically relies on ideal Euclidean distances and metric properties (e.g., symmetry and triangle inequality), assumptions fundamentally violated by non-Euclidean path distances, elevator access costs, and time-varying vertical transfers. Furthermore, while the base Capacitated VRP (CVRP) is already known to be NP-hard [1], constructing a unified graph spanning all building, floor, and room levels exacerbates this complexity. This unified modeling leads to a combinatorial explosion of the state space, rendering the global hierarchical routing problem intractable for real-time operation and preventing timely responses to dynamic delivery requests [7].

Beyond structural complexity, reliable multi-goal delivery in real-world deployments is further hindered by three key practical challenges.

(1) Lack of effective large-scale cross-building optimization models.
Most existing approaches focus on single-building or small-scale routing problems, and do not scale to delivery scenarios involving multiple buildings and heterogeneous inter-building distances. As a result, cross-building delivery decisions are often handled by ad hoc heuristics, leading to suboptimal capacity utilization and excessive depot returns.

(2) Dynamic environments and sensing limitations.
Real-world indoor environments are highly dynamic, with moving pedestrians and time-varying layouts that disrupt stable perception and localization. These factors introduce uncertainty into navigation and execution, necessitating robust odometry and sensor fusion methods to maintain reliable operation [40].

(3) Plan–execution mismatch in decoupled systems.
Global VRP solutions are typically computed on idealized maps and assume perfect execution. In practice, however, discrepancies between planned routes and feasible robot trajectories frequently arise. Moreover, mapping, localization, scheduling, and navigation modules are often designed and optimized independently, preventing closed-loop coordination and resulting in inconsistent end-to-end performance.

Moreover, with the increasing adoption of autonomous delivery systems and the rising cost of manual labor, delivery efficiency has become an important consideration in residential building design. In many communities, building layout and depot placement directly affect the feasibility and performance of unmanned delivery. Therefore, it is also essential to use quantitative models to guide building layout design toward better support for autonomous delivery.

To address these challenges, a hierarchical autonomous delivery system tailored to the Building–Floor–Room structure is proposed. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A hierarchical Building–Floor–Room model and a building-aware CVRP formulation are introduced, accounting for inter-building and inter-floor connectivity, room-level access, and privacy-sensitive areas, which reduces optimization complexity while enabling globally feasible and privacy-compliant routing.

A hierarchical Building–Floor–Room model and a building-aware CVRP formulation are introduced, accounting for inter-building and inter-floor connectivity, room-level access, and privacy-sensitive areas, which reduces optimization complexity while enabling globally feasible and privacy-compliant routing.

A unified mapping and autonomous navigation system integrated with a non-interactive, privacy-preserving robot design is developed, ensuring consistency between hierarchical planning and real-world execution.

A layout evaluation and depot optimization method is proposed, allowing quantitative assessment of delivery efficiency across different building configurations and optimal depot placement.

2. A unified mapping and autonomous navigation system integrated with a non-interactive, privacy-preserving robot design is developed, ensuring consistency between hierarchical planning and real-world execution.

3. A layout evaluation and depot optimization method is proposed, allowing quantitative assessment of delivery efficiency across different building configurations and optimal depot placement.

title: A Black-Box Positioning Solution for Effortless Integration in Wearable Navigation
authors: Anh-Van Vu,Changmin Sung,Dongsoo Han
abstract: Accurate localization is critical for a wide range of applications, including navigation, augmented reality, safety management, and healthcare. However, achieving accurate positioning remains challenging, especially in GPS-degraded environments. Pedestrian Dead Reckoning (PDR), which estimates position based on inertial sensor data, offers a promising alternative but typically demands substantial effort in algorithm design and system integration. This complexity often leads to prolonged development timelines and elevated costs. To address these challenges, we present the PDR Sensor (PDRS), a plug-and-play, black-box PDR module optimized for seamless integration into wearable and IoT platforms. PDRS integrates a microprocessor and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) within a compact, low-power module. It executes real-time sensor fusion onboard, providing position updates via standard interfaces (I²C, SPI, UART). Experimental evaluations demonstrate its high robustness, achieving a step detection error of just 0.16% over 1250 steps and a traveled distance error of 1.87% under diverse conditions. The system further exhibits low latency (2.5 ms) and modest power consumption (52.35 mA). Unlike conventional studies, the PDRS leverages a holistic co-design of hardware and software to enhance performance and integration aspects, simplifying adoption without requiring deep expertise. By lowering technical barriers, PDRS enables developers and researchers to prioritize innovation in IoT and wearable technologies, accelerating prototyping, reducing development time, and advancing industry progress. Future work aims to enhance accuracy, reduce power usage and module size, and integrate AI-driven techniques to better mitigate drift.
introduction:
Indoor positioning, crucial for diverse applications ranging from navigation in complex environments (e.g., airports, shopping malls) to augmented reality and healthcare [1, 2, 3], relies heavily on PDR. Its infrastructure-free nature, utilizing only inertial sensors (accelerometers and gyroscopes) to track user movement, offers a significant advantage where satellite or RF methods are ineffective [4, 5]. This autonomy, achievable with compact IMUs integrated into modern smartphones and wearables [6, 7], has fueled extensive research resulting in numerous PDR algorithms and system designs [8, 6, 7, 9, 10]. Therefore, it is now an essential component of most indoor localization systems[11, 4, 12, 13, 14].

Despite significant advancements, deploying practical PDR systems remains challenging. PDR is a relative positioning method prone to cumulative drift errors over time [15, 8, 6, 16], where even minor sensor biases or step length inaccuracies compound, causing trajectory divergence. Consequently, standalone PDR is unsuitable for long-term tracking, necessitating fusion with external references or additional sensors (e.g., magnetometers, barometers, UWB, map constraints) to mitigate drift [16, 11, 4, 12, 13, 14]. However, such multi-sensor fusion increases system complexity, power consumption, and cost, undermining PDR’s inherent simplicity. Practical indoor positioning demands ease of implementation, affordability, and minimal computational complexity [17], criteria often unmet by research prototypes requiring specialized hardware or extensive calibration.

Another key challenge involves the significant expertise and development effort required to create robust PDR solutions. Building a PDR system necessitates real-time coordination of numerous components on resource-constrained hardware: sensor data acquisition, signal processing (step detection, orientation and distance estimation), and error correction. As Nilsson et al. observe, although “dead reckoning is not rocket science,” the number of hardware/software components that must work in harmony is large, and achieving a well-performing embedded implementation is far from trivial [18]. Careful selection of an embedded processor with sufficient processing power and algorithmic optimization for low latency and energy consumption is crucial.

Further complexities arise from the need for small form factors and mechanical reliability (for wearable or mobile applications), with few readily available modular, reusable hardware-algorithm solutions [18]. Commercial solutions, such as Bosch Sensortec’s BHI160B and BHI260AP, can fulfill these requirements but require specialized PDR-enabled firmware, which is often publicly unavailable [19]. This necessitates significant custom integration, increasing development time and costs for solutions seeking to utilize PDR. Therefore, despite the ubiquity of low-cost MEMS sensors, the barrier to entry for deploying PDR systems remains high. This gap between algorithmic research and deployable products, highlighted in recent literature [17], emphasizes that accuracy alone is insufficient; stability, real-time capability, energy efficiency, and easy integration are equally critical for widespread adoption.

This paper addresses the challenges of deploying PDR systems by introducing the PDR Sensor (PDRS), a compact, low-power hardware module integrating a microcontroller unit (MCU), an inertial measurement unit (IMU), and an onboard adapted PDR algorithm. Designed as a plug-and-play solution, the PDRS encapsulates complex sensor fusion and computation logic, providing real-time position updates via standard interfaces (I²C, SPI, UART). Our module can be treated as an off-the-shelf component – effectively a “black box” PDR unit – that researchers, and system designers can drop into their prototypes or products with minimal effort. This hardware-software co-design contrasts with previous research primarily focused on algorithmic accuracy within high-end processing environments [9, 8, 6, 16]. By offloading computational complexity and sensor management, the PDRS enables developers to obtain accurate step counts, heading, and displacement estimates without specialized signal processing or inertial navigation expertise. Utilizing inexpensive, commercially available, reproducible components, the PDRS achieves competitive accuracy (0.16% step detection error, 1.87% travel distance estimation error) with low latency (milliseconds) and power consumption (tens of milliamps), suitable for numerous real-time positioning applications. This simplified PDR integration significantly lowers the barrier to entry for indoor localization, accelerating adoption in applications ranging from IoT devices to assistive wearables, where a self-contained inertial positioning module unlocks new functionality without added cost or complexity.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section III details the hardware and software co-design of the PDRS. Section IV describes the adapted PDR algorithm and bias mitigation technique. Section V presents evaluations of positioning accuracy in different environments, real-time latency, power consumption, and thermal characteristics. Finally, Section VI concludes and outlines future works.

title: CQDC-Warp: GPU-Accelerated Differentiable Quasi-Dynamic Simulation for Contact-Rich Manipulation
authors: Yanchen Ding,Jiayi Chen,Jianfeng Xu,Wei Zhao,Li Yi,He Wang
abstract:
Efficient synthesis of contact-rich manipulation trajectories is essential for
downstream robot learning. Gradient-based planning offers a promising approach,
but jointly optimizing motion and contact decisions remains challenging.
Meanwhile, many existing planners run on CPUs with limited throughput.
We present CQDC-Warp, a GPU-accelerated differentiable quasi-dynamic
simulator for batched model predictive control (MPC). We use it to study
contact-guided trajectory optimization, in which intended robot–object
contacts are specified before planning and encouraged through soft costs,
while the simulated dynamics
determine contact geometry and frictional response without a prescribed
contact-mode schedule. Across
17,40817{,}408 trials on the 1717-object Allegro in-hand rotation benchmark, our
framework achieves 79.8%79.8\% success, compared with 73.7%73.7\% for CFree and
65.2%65.2\% for IMPACT, and reduces mean trajectory-generation time by
factors of 27.027.0 and 50.250.2, respectively. On a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with
2,0482{,}048 parallel worlds, forward and backward throughput reach
2.06×1052.06\times 10^{5} and 2.25×1052.25\times 10^{5} world-steps per second, respectively.
Further experiments cover manipulation with LEAP and Shadow hands,
environmental contact exploitation, bimanual manipulation, whole-body control,
and real-world trajectory replay on a Sharpa hand.
introduction:
Contact-rich dexterous manipulation is a central capability for
general-purpose embodied intelligence. Modern robot learning increasingly
relies on large, diverse, and high-quality datasets of robot
behavior [14]. Collecting such data for dexterous hands is
particularly challenging due to the high cost and complexity of teleoperation,
as well as differences between human and robot
embodiments [15, 16]. Scalable generation of
physically plausible dexterous trajectories could therefore support both
task execution and demonstration collection for downstream robot learning.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated impressive dexterous manipulation
behaviors [17, 18, 19] covering a broad range of objects [20, 21, 22]. However, acquiring these behaviors with
model-free RL typically requires extensive trial and error guided by
task-specific rewards. The underlying dynamics are treated as a black box:
policy updates rely on sampled experience rather than derivatives of the
physical dynamics. Moreover, learned policies remain sensitive to their
training distributions, which can limit their reuse across contact-rich
tasks and scenes.

Gradient-based planning provides another route, exploiting dynamics
derivatives to efficiently refine action
sequences [23, 24]. Within this paradigm,
contact-implicit trajectory optimization is an active and promising research
direction: it jointly optimizes state and control trajectories and contact
interactions without prescribing intended contact in advance [25, 26, 27, 28, 29].
However, this generality also introduces strong coupling between motion and
contact decisions, resulting in large, nonconvex optimization problems that
can be difficult to solve reliably. Yet, from a practical standpoint, an even
more basic question remains open: given a suitable initialization and intended
contacts specified in advance, can existing tools reliably optimize action
sequences across diverse robot platforms and contact-rich tasks? Here, intended contacts
specify which robot link should touch the object, rather than prescribing a complete
contact-mode schedule; their exact geometry and frictional response are still determined
by the simulated dynamics. This assumption is practical in many manipulation settings,
where intended contacts can be inferred from task structure, grasp or trajectory initialization,
or human demonstrations with tactile gloves.

Differentiable simulation supports such local optimization by providing
gradients through simulated rollouts. Existing differentiable contact
simulators, however, face several limitations. Some methods introduce
force-at-a-distance through smoothing [5] or neglect coupling
between contact constraints [8]. Many implementations run on CPUs
or optimize only one trajectory at a time [8, 30, 29], limiting throughput. GPU-based differentiable simulators are
available [9, 12, 13],
but their published evaluations typically cover only one or two robot
embodiments and a limited set of tasks. Efficient trajectory generation across
diverse robot platforms and contact-rich tasks remains less explored.

In this work, we propose CQDC-Warp, a GPU-accelerated differentiable
simulator that extends the Convex Quasi-Dynamic Contact (CQDC) model in three
respects. First, we introduce compliant frictional contact to regularize the
contact solve and revise the inertial model to retain coupling between
actuated and unactuated coordinates. Second, we provide implicit derivatives
of the contact dynamics and sampled surrogate derivatives of contact geometry.
Third, we develop an efficient GPU implementation built on MuJoCo-Warp’s
batched pipeline [31], enabling parallel model predictive
control (MPC) across independent simulation worlds. Experiments demonstrate
in-hand manipulation, environmental contact exploitation, bimanual
manipulation, and whole-body control across dexterous hands, quadrupeds, and
humanoids, as well as a trajectory replay in the real world.

Our main contributions are:

CQDC-Warp, a GPU-accelerated differentiable quasi-dynamic contact simulator,
integrated into a batched MPC framework.

A contact-guided trajectory optimization setting in which intended
contacts are specified before planning, while the exact contact realization
remains implicit.

Experimental validation across diverse robots and
contact-rich tasks, including simulation benchmarks and
real-world trajectory replay.

1. CQDC-Warp, a GPU-accelerated differentiable quasi-dynamic contact simulator,
integrated into a batched MPC framework.

2. A contact-guided trajectory optimization setting in which intended
contacts are specified before planning, while the exact contact realization
remains implicit.

3. Experimental validation across diverse robots and
contact-rich tasks, including simulation benchmarks and
real-world trajectory replay.

title: MR-MPCC: Model Predictive Contouring Control for Robotic Manipulator Tracking under Moving Reference Frames
authors: Chonghao Cheng,Tiancheng Li,Jonathan Woolfrey,Liang Zhao,Shoudong Huang
comment: Accepted by The IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems 2026 (IROS 2026)
abstract: Maintaining small path-tracking errors under moving reference frames is essential for robotic manipulation tasks with tight execution tolerances, such as machining and surgical automation. Conventional time-indexed controllers, including tracking Model Predictive Control (MPC), rely on a fixed temporal correspondence with the reference trajectory and may therefore accumulate path-relative error under abrupt reference-frame motion or timing mismatch. This paper presents MR-MPCC, a Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) framework for velocity-controlled robotic manipulators with 6-DoF end-effector pose regulation under Moving-Reference disturbances. A hierarchical control architecture is adopted, in which an upper-level MPCC optimizes path progress while penalizing contouring and orientation errors, and a constrained resolved motion rate control (RMRC) layer maps the commanded Cartesian twist to feasible joint velocities under joint-level and safety constraints. MR-MPCC is implemented in a ROS2–MuJoCo pipeline and validated on a UR5e platform under moving-reference disturbances, where the path frame is perturbed and tracked by electromagnetic sensors. Compared with PI control and time-indexed tracking MPC under matched disturbance, MR-MPCC achieves lower geometric path-following error and smaller deviations in the moving path frame, demonstrating improved path-following performance under reference-frame motion.
introduction:
Accurate end-effector motion control is fundamental to robotic
manipulation in industrial assembly, surgical automation, and machining [1, 2].
In such tasks, performance is usually determined by geometric fidelity to a prescribed path rather than by strict adherence to a preassigned timing law [3]. The control objective is therefore to minimize spatial deviation
from the path in the presence of disturbances and modeling uncertainty.

Conventional controllers such as proportional–integral–derivative (PID) control provide intuitive and computationally efficient solutions [4], but do not explicitly predict future system evolution or systematically handle state and input constraints.
Model Predictive Control (MPC) addresses these issues by optimizing
future control actions over a finite horizon [5, 6].
However, standard MPC formulations are time-indexed and rely on a fixed
time parameterization of the reference [7]. Under disturbances that induce
timing mismatch or abrupt motion of the reference frame, time-indexed
tracking can accumulate geometric error, leading to degraded robustness,
especially when simultaneous position and orientation regulation is
required.

Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) offers an alternative by reformulating tracking relative to the reference path [8]. It decomposes the tracking deviation into a contouring component orthogonal to the path and a lag component along the path, allowing geometric path-following accuracy and path progress to be regulated separately.
Despite these advantages, its application to robotic manipulators remains in its infancy, with only a small number of recent works beginning to explore this domain [9].

Extending MPCC to robotic manipulators is challenging because nonlinear kinematics, and joint-level constraints complicate real-time task-space control [10]. The challenge increases when the reference frame moves abruptly, since stable joint-level control does not necessarily ensure small path-relative errors. In applications such as surgical milling and high-accuracy assembly, these errors can affect task quality and safety. This motivates direct regulation of path-relative error under reference motion and joint constraints.

This paper presents MR-MPCC, a task-space MPCC framework for velocity-controlled manipulators with full 6-DoF end-effector pose regulation. The method combines MPCC with constrained RMRC to generate feasible joint-velocity commands in real time. It is implemented in a ROS2–MuJoCo pipeline (Fig. 1) and validated on a physical UR5e, where reference-frame motion is measured using electromagnetic tracking and the controller operates at 500 Hz. Under matched paths and disturbance, MR-MPCC achieves lower contouring error than PI control and time-indexed tracking MPC in both simulation and physical experiments.

The main contributions are:
(i) a task-space MPCC formulation for full 6-DoF manipulator path following under moving reference frames;
(ii) a unified simulation and physical evaluation pipeline for reference-frame disturbances; and
(iii) a comparison with PI control and time-indexed tracking MPC of contouring, lag, and rotational tracking errors.

title: LICOA: Learning Instruction-Conditioned Optical Actions for Mobile Spatial Augmented Reality
authors: Yuchen Deng,Shunkai Zhou,Ruixuan Zhu,Haibin Ling,Bingyao Huang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Spatial augmented reality (SAR) augments physical environments with projected content, but most systems assume that the projector pose, target region, or motion path has been fixed or specified. We instead make projected light an embodied action: given a language instruction and current visual observations, a system must decide how to move and where and at what scale to place the projection. We introduce LICOA to realize this capability. Its differential-drive chassis provides room-scale approach and repositioning, while a steerable mirror with two degrees of freedom (2DoF) and projection scale provide rapid local control of the beam. A shared interface maps synchronized external and onboard RGB cameras with robot control state to physical optical actions across pretrained action models. Because instruction-conditioned optical action lacks dedicated training data and a common evaluation protocol, we construct a matched simulation embodiment and a corpus with 150150 tasks and 7,5007{,}500 rendered episodes, then evaluate models trained only on this corpus in previously unseen real-world environments. Across 480480 complete closed-loop real-world execution trials (rollouts) on 1212 tasks, the best adapted action model achieves a 57.50%57.50\% success rate and 40.64%40.64\% success weighted by path length, compared with 8.33%8.33\% and 5.15%5.15\% for the same architecture trained from scratch. A further 150150 real-world ablation rollouts support the need for both camera views and coordinated control of the chassis and mirror. These results establish a physical platform, shared perception and optical action interface, corpus, and real-world evaluation protocol for treating projected light as an embodied action.
introduction:
Spatial augmented reality (SAR) overlays digital visual content directly onto physical environments using projectors [2, 22, 35]. Unlike head-mounted or handheld displays, projection requires no worn or held device, supports shared viewing, and presents spatial cues for navigation, object localization, and collaborative work [47, 49, 24, 69]. Yet useful projection also requires placing light at the intended location,
direction, and scale. Most existing SAR systems rely on fixed projector setups and predefined projection regions. Such configurations provide geometric calibration [62, 32, 14] and support diverse projection mapping applications [54, 1, 30, 31, 17, 18, 45, 12], but restrict the workspace to surfaces visible from a predetermined projector pose. Mobile and steerable systems expand the reachable workspace, but their targets, paths, or control rules are commonly predefined [53, 42, 64, 19, 63, 24, 69, 57]. They therefore do not address a general case in which a system enters an unfamiliar environment, interprets a language instruction, and decides both how to move and where to place light. Achieving this capability requires treating the placement of projected light as part of the system’s physical action. A language instruction such as “project onto the bear” specifies a desired physical effect rather than a target robot pose or a preselected display surface. The system must identify the referenced region, approach a feasible projection pose, redirect the beam, adjust its scale, and determine when placement is complete.

We call this task instruction-conditioned optical action. Throughout, physical describes tangible entities and actuator-level quantities, such as scene objects, the platform, and its actions, whereas real-world denotes the non-simulated deployment and evaluation domain. Realizing this capability introduces three practical challenges.
First, room-scale coverage and local beam placement require different controls. Moving the projector offers broad reach but is slow and changes the sensing viewpoint, whereas beam steering is fast but locally bounded. Multi-projector installations provide coverage at the cost of fixed infrastructure and calibration [11, 56, 36], while arm-mounted systems provide local pose flexibility with a more complex mechanism and a workspace bounded by the arm [47, 7, 49]. A mobile SAR
platform must therefore combine broad repositioning with fast local optical control in one action space.
Second, pretrained action models target embodiments such as manipulators and grippers, with different camera inputs, state dimensions, action outputs, and training objectives [6, 51, 21, 41, 4, 3]. Training from scratch must learn both general vision-language grounding and optical action semantics from task-specific data. We therefore ask whether pretrained models can retain their grounding and action-generation knowledge while learning optical action from task-specific demonstrations [5, 51, 3].
Third, pretraining does not remove the need for task-specific data and evaluation. No existing corpus pairs spatial instructions and external and onboard RGB images with coordinated commands for the differential-drive chassis, a steerable mirror with two degrees of freedom (2DoF), and projection scale, plus episode termination outputs, and no common evaluation protocol assesses their physical outcomes. This absence is the underlying data problem; simulation is our means of addressing it. A useful real-world evaluation protocol must match the physical embodiment and sensing roles and test whether models trained without real-world demonstrations can act in unseen real-world settings.

To address these challenges, we introduce LICOA (Learning Instruction-Conditioned Optical Actions), a mobile SAR system that makes projected light an embodied action, as summarized in \creffig:teaser. First, its differential-drive chassis provides coarse room-scale approach and repositioning, whereas its 2DoF steerable mirror provides rapid local beam redirection and projection scale controls the footprint. The resulting action components jointly determine where light is placed. Second, LICOA combines timestamp-synchronized external and onboard RGB images with the robot control state in a shared perception and optical action interface. This interface maps the observations and action output of different pretrained action models [3, 52, 68] to the same physical embodiment. Third, we reproduce the embodiment in simulation [20, 59] and construct 150150 spatial placement tasks with 7,5007{,}500 rendered episodes. Models are fine-tuned only on this corpus and evaluated through real-world rollouts with new scenes, targets, instructions, and initial configurations.
Experiments evaluate three action-generation paradigms, isolate pretraining with a scratch version of π0.5\pi_{0.5} [3], and ablate the camera views and action components. Across 480480 complete closed-loop real-world executions (rollouts), adapted π0.5\pi_{0.5} achieves 57.50%57.50\% success and 40.64%40.64\% success weighted by path length, compared with 8.33%8.33\% and 5.15%5.15\% for the scratch control; another 150150 rollouts support the ablations.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We formulate projected light as an instruction-conditioned optical action and realize it with a mobile optical platform whose differential-drive chassis, 2DoF steerable mirror, projection scale, and episode termination output form a coupled physical action space.

We define a shared perception and optical action interface comprising external and onboard RGB images, the robot control state, action chunks, and physical action components, and instantiate it with pretrained action models based on continuous action generation, autoregressive action tokenization, and world-action modeling.

We establish a matched simulation corpus and real-world evaluation protocol for this new task, including 150150 spatial placement tasks, 7,5007{,}500 rendered episodes, fine-tuning only in simulation, a real-world evaluation task set of 1212 previously unseen real-world tasks with 480480 real-world evaluation rollouts, and 150150 ablation rollouts that test the sensing and hardware design.

1. We formulate projected light as an instruction-conditioned optical action and realize it with a mobile optical platform whose differential-drive chassis, 2DoF steerable mirror, projection scale, and episode termination output form a coupled physical action space.

2. We define a shared perception and optical action interface comprising external and onboard RGB images, the robot control state, action chunks, and physical action components, and instantiate it with pretrained action models based on continuous action generation, autoregressive action tokenization, and world-action modeling.

We establish a matched simulation corpus and real-world evaluation protocol for this new task, including 150150 spatial placement tasks, 7,5007{,}500 rendered episodes, fine-tuning only in simulation, a real-world evaluation task set of 1212 previously unseen real-world tasks with 480480 real-world evaluation rollouts, and 150150 ablation rollouts that test the sensing and hardware design.

title: CLIS-MPPI: Closed-Loop Model Predictive Path Integral Control With Initial-State Sampling Under Execution Delay
authors: Zidong Liu,Xu Chen
comment: 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026)
abstract:
Sampling-based motion planning such as Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control has become attractive for robotics due to its ability to handle nonlinear dynamics and non-smooth objectives without gradient information, while leveraging parallel rollout computation for real-time performance. However, in real-world robotic systems, the optimized control input is often applied after a non-negligible planning delay, causing a mismatch between the state used in forward simulation and the actual state at control execution, which can significantly degrade planning accuracy and may even lead to unsafe behavior such as collisions. This paper proposes Closed-Loop MPPI with Initial-State Sampling (CLIS-MPPI), which explicitly addresses execution-time state mismatch by modeling planning delay as a distribution over plausible execution-time initial states, performing rollout optimization from sampled initial states, and applying a rollout-based local feedback correction during control execution.
The proposed method is validated through real-world experiments on a 6-DoF UR5e manipulator in a narrow-passage task involving obstacle avoidance and end-effector target reaching.
Across 5 real-world runs of the same task, standard MPPI collided in 2 runs, whereas CLIS-MPPI remained collision-free in all 5 runs. Averaged over all collision-free runs for each method (3 for MPPI and 5 for CLIS-MPPI), CLIS-MPPI reduced the average task completion time from 25.4 s to 24.4 s and the average end-effector path length from 0.456 m to 0.425 m. It also reduced the overall joint-position and joint-velocity root mean square errors (RMSEs) from 0.100 rad and 0.108 rad/s to 0.017 rad and 0.011 rad/s, respectively. These results demonstrate improved safety, planning-execution consistency, and motion smoothness.
introduction:
With the rapid growth of computing hardware, sampling-based motion planning methods [1, 2], especially Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control [3], have emerged as a powerful framework for real-time robotic motion planning and control. MPPI repeatedly samples stochastic control rollouts, performs forward simulation, evaluates trajectory costs, and refines the control sequence through a path-integral weighted update over a receding horizon. Compared with traditional gradient-based model predictive control (MPC) [4], MPPI does not require differentiable cost functions, making it particularly suitable for robotic systems with nonlinear dynamics, obstacle-rich environments, and complex non-smooth objectives [5]. Furthermore, unlike learning-based methods such as reinforcement learning [6], which typically depend on large-scale offline training, MPPI is a fully online planning method and can leverage GPU-parallelized rollout computation [7] to enable real-time decision-making.

Despite these advantages, the performance of MPPI in real-world robotic systems can be significantly degraded by execution-time delay. In particular, the quality of MPPI critically depends on the accuracy of its forward simulation and cost evaluation, since both are used to determine the control update at each planning cycle. However, forward simulation is typically the most computationally expensive step in MPPI, and the resulting planning latency can introduce a substantial mismatch between the state used for optimization and the state at which the optimized control is actually applied. As illustrated in Fig. 1, at planning time tiplant_{i}^{\mathrm{plan}}, MPPI starts forward simulation from the measured robot state xirefx_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}, and the rollout costs are evaluated based on this state. During the planning interval τi\tau_{i}, however, the robot continues executing the previous control command ui−1u_{i-1}. Consequently, when the newly optimized control uiu_{i} becomes effective at tisendt_{i}^{\mathrm{send}}, the actual robot state has already evolved to xiapply≠xirefx_{i}^{\mathrm{apply}}\neq x_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}. As a result, the control command uiu_{i} is no longer applied to the state on which it was optimized, leading to a delay-induced state mismatch. This issue becomes particularly critical in high-frequency control settings or when the robot operates with large control actions, where even a small planning delay may produce a significant state deviation. In safety-critical tasks such as obstacle avoidance in narrow spaces, such mismatch can cause severe performance degradation and even collisions, despite the fact that the planned rollouts themselves are collision-free during forward simulation.

To address the delay-induced state mismatch, we propose closed-loop MPPI with initial-state sampling (CLIS-MPPI), as illustrated in Fig. 2. The key idea is to explicitly convert execution delay into an initial-state uncertainty at each planning cycle, and to compensate for the resulting mismatch through a closed-loop control update. Instead of assuming that the control optimization starts from a single measured state, CLIS-MPPI samples a distribution of perturbed initial states around the currently measured state to represent the possible system evolution during the planning interval. For each sampled initial state, perturbed control sequences are generated and parallel forward simulations are performed to obtain rollout trajectories and their associated costs. Based on the weighted rollout distribution, a nominal state-control trajectory is constructed, from which a local feedback gain is further extracted in a rollout-based manner. The final control input is then computed as a closed-loop combination of the MPPI feedforward update and a state-feedback correction term. In this way, the proposed method enables the applied control command to better match the actual robot state at execution time, thereby improving consistency between planning and execution, motion smoothness, and safety in delay-sensitive real-world tasks.

In contrast to standard MPPI, which assumes immediate actuation after planning and samples only control perturbations from a single planning state, CLIS-MPPI replaces this assumption with a distribution over plausible execution-time initial states, jointly samples both initial-state and control perturbations, and augments the control update with rollout-based feedback correction.

MPPI was originally introduced for aggressive autonomous driving tasks, where its sampling-based formulation demonstrated strong capability in handling high-speed, nonlinear systems under complex objectives [3]. Since then, MPPI has been extended to a wide variety of robotic platforms, including robotic manipulators [5, 8, 9], aerial robots [10], and legged systems [11]. In robotic manipulation, STORM [5] and RAMP [8] showed that GPU-accelerated MPPI can achieve real-time obstacle avoidance and goal-reaching on 6–7 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) manipulators in cluttered environments. For dynamic environments, Zhou et al. [9] proposed a parallel MPPI framework for manipulators that improves computational efficiency and incorporates a gradient-velocity modulated signed distance field cost for dynamic obstacle avoidance. Zhai et al. [10] developed a perception-aware MPPI method for quadrotor navigation in unknown environments, where perception-driven objectives are integrated into the planning process to promote exploration and path recovery under occlusion.

Delay-induced state mismatch causes the optimized control input to be applied to a state that is no longer consistent with the one used during planning, which may lead to degraded performance and even unsafe behavior. To improve the safety of MPPI, several works have combined MPPI with control barrier functions (CBFs) [12, 13, 14]. Tao et al. [12] proposed SCBF-MPPI, which constrains the sampling distribution using stochastic control barrier function conditions to improve probabilistic safety and sample efficiency. Parwana et al. [13] combined an MPPI planner with a CBF-based safety filter so that MPPI handles task planning while the CBF layer enforces safe execution. Rabiee and Hoagg [14] proposed GS-MPPI, which incorporates a composite CBF into the system dynamics and enables MPPI to optimize only over guaranteed-safe trajectories. In a different direction, Belvedere et al. [15] proposed Feedback-MPPI, which augments MPPI with local feedback gains extracted from rollout sensitivity analysis to improve closed-loop responsiveness. However, these methods mainly focus on safety filtering or high-frequency feedback enhancement, and do not explicitly address the execution-time state mismatch caused by planning delay.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

We propose CLIS-MPPI, a novel MPPI formulation that explicitly compensates for execution-time state mismatch. Unlike standard MPPI, which implicitly assumes immediate actuation after the planning stage, CLIS-MPPI models planning delay as a distribution over plausible execution-time initial states, jointly samples both initial-state and control perturbations, and computes the applied control input using a closed-loop combination of the MPPI feedforward update and a rollout-based local feedback correction.

We validate CLIS-MPPI through real-world experiments on a UR5e manipulator in a narrow-passage task involving both obstacle avoidance and end-effector target reaching. Across 5 real-world runs of the same task, standard MPPI collides with the environment in 2 runs, whereas CLIS-MPPI remains collision-free in all trials. Averaged over all collision-free runs for each method (3 for MPPI and 5 for CLIS-MPPI), CLIS-MPPI reduced the average task completion time from 25.4 s to 24.4 s and shortened the average end-effector path length from 0.456 m to 0.425 m. In addition, the overall joint-position and joint-velocity root mean square errors (RMSEs) were reduced from 0.100 rad and 0.108 rad/s under MPPI to 0.017 rad and 0.011 rad/s under CLIS-MPPI, corresponding to reductions by factors of approximately 5.9 and 9.7, respectively.

title: An Agentic Framework for Proactive Robots with Procedural Assistance Memory
authors: Dohyun Lee,Minho Park,Jeonghoon Park,Dongyoon Hwang,Junha Hyung,Sungwon Hwang,Byungkun Lee,Jaegul Choo
comment: Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Proactive robots should anticipate user needs and provide assistance before being explicitly asked. A straightforward approach is to infer human intentions from commonsense knowledge, but the same observed behavior can imply different needs across users, potentially leading to unwanted assistance.
We observe that everyday routines in the real world exhibit recurring patterns, so learning these patterns can reduce ambiguity in proactive decisions.
Based on this, we propose a memory-based agentic framework in which a VLM task predictor
reads a Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation
to decide when to assist and what task to perform, and a VLA executor performs the predicted task.
PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance
rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day’s
interaction trace without weight updates or retraining.
In our 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, memory-free baselines remain conservative, with limited recall on proactive tasks.
Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest
precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds
on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5.
Our approach also adapts to changes in the user’s routine through continued memory reflection, recovering from memory–routine misalignment after a single memory update.
The project page is available at https://DAVIAN-Robotics.github.io/PAM.
introduction:
A truly useful assistant in everyday life does not only respond to requests, but also anticipates when help would be valuable.
This may involve handing over an object at the right moment, putting away an item after it has been used, or preparing something that will be needed in the next step.
By contrast, robot assistants are still commonly evaluated as systems that execute explicit user commands [1, 2].
For robots to play the role of capable assistants in household, and home-office settings, they must move beyond waiting for instructions and learn to recognize when intervention would be helpful.
This has motivated growing interest in proactive robot assistance: robots that infer when help may be useful and act in advance of explicit commands.

One line of work in proactive robot assistance predicts task progress in structured sequential tasks [3, 4, 5]. However, these approaches are largely confined to robots that perform a single task by following a fixed protocol (e.g., chair assembly), and are ill-suited to generalist robots tasked with open-ended housekeeping. Recently emerging generalist Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) [1, 6, 7, 2] may appear to offer an alternative, but robotics datasets remain scarce across the diverse scenarios such settings demand. As a result, end-to-end models that map perception directly to action face clear limitations even when equipped with reasoning, and proactive tasks, where intent is often underspecified, have received little attention.
In response, recent work has adopted a System 1–2 design [8] that explicitly separates a high-level reasoning module from a VLA that executes atomic tasks [9, 10, 11, 12].
This separation simplifies learning, since the VLM decides when and what to help with while the VLA need only carry out the prescribed action. We adopt this structure, which in turn places the burden of proactivity squarely on the high-level VLM.

The central challenge, then, is accurately predicting human intention at the high level [13], and recent approaches leverage pretrained, large-scale VLMs to do so in open-ended settings [14, 15, 16].
Yet zero-shot prediction remains unreliable when the same observable behavior corresponds to different desired outcomes across users: one person setting out a mug wants coffee, another wants hot water for tea (Figure 1).
A fixed, pretrained predictor cannot resolve such ambiguity, because the missing information is not in the scene but in the individual user’s habits.

Crucially, this missing information can be learned during deployment. In housekeeping settings, an individual’s behavior is highly repetitive, so even a handful of past interactions reveal stable preferences, and corrective feedback gathered once can be reused whenever a similar situation recurs. This suggests that a proactive robot should not treat each deployment as zero-shot, but should accumulate experience about its specific user over time. We therefore investigate a test-time learning approach for the high-level VLM, building a robot that personalizes quickly from few interactions, continues adapting after deployment, and carries user feedback forward into future behavior.

To this end, we introduce Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM), a continually updated deployment-time memory that records when assistance is needed and what assistive task should be issued for a particular user.
PAM structures this memory as a finite-state machine over the user’s activity, where states represent activity phases, transitions represent progress between phases, and per-state assistance entries store the assistive opportunities associated with each phase.
In our five-day scenario, the user repeatedly performs a daily activity; PAM is updated across these days so that the robot can provide increasingly appropriate assistance. Our contributions are threefold:

We propose a memory-based agentic framework for proactive robot assistance.
By conditioning the high-level VLM on user-specific routine context, it decides both when to assist and what task to issue without explicit user requests.

We propose a memory-based agentic framework for proactive robot assistance.
By conditioning the high-level VLM on user-specific routine context, it decides both when to assist and what task to issue without explicit user requests.

We propose Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM), a memory following a finite-state-machine structure with activity phases, transitions, and per-state assistance entries.
It uses user and activity context to reduce ambiguity in assistance needs.

We develop a self-evolving memory loop whose reflector revises PAM offline after each day using observed behavior and user feedback.
This enables the robot to learn the user’s routine, adapt to changes, and incorporate user feedback without retraining.
