title: LIN-SLAM: Lightweight LiDAR--Inertial Neural SLAM for Real-Time Onboard Navigation
authors: Shiqi Che,Yijie Liu,Shuo Wang,Wenxin Liu
comment: submitted to Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
abstract:
Geometric light detection and ranging (LiDAR)–inertial simultaneous
localization and mapping (SLAM) provides efficient state estimation but lacks the continuous map representation and global
refinement capabilities of neural implicit SLAM, while neural implicit methods remain computationally expensive. We propose Lightweight LiDAR–Inertial Neural SLAM (LIN-SLAM), a hybrid method that couples
high-rate geometric LiDAR–inertial estimation with neural implicit
tracking, continual mapping, and global refinement for accurate real-time
onboard SLAM. Experiments on twelve representative sequences from three datasets spanning 32-, 64-, and 128-channel LiDAR configurations show that LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest overall mean absolute trajectory error (ATE) among the evaluated state-of-the-art geometric and neural implicit methods, while substantially reducing runtime compared with existing neural implicit SLAM methods. On a Unitree Go2 equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and a 16-channel LiDAR, LIN-SLAM sustains real-time localization and neural mapping over a 1.47-km indoor trajectory through challenging repetitive corridor environments, with an endpoint closure error of only 0.141 m.
To the best of our knowledge, LIN-SLAM is the first LiDAR–inertial SLAM system with a neural implicit backend to achieve real-time online operation on a mobile robotic platform while maintaining state-of-the-art localization accuracy. The code will be released upon acceptance.
introduction:
Mobile robots require real-time state estimation and globally
consistent mapping within limited onboard computational and memory
budgets.
Geometric LiDAR–inertial odometry (LIO)
provides efficient local
motion estimation through point registration and inertial
fusion [1, 2, 3]. However, its local motion
constraints provide limited correction of accumulated drift and
inconsistencies across revisited locations, motivating map-level
refinement.
Neural implicit SLAM integrates
continuous surface representations with
map-based tracking, continual reconstruction, and global map
refinement [4, 5]. However, these capabilities
require repeated signed distance field (SDF) queries, gradient
evaluation, and online optimization, introducing substantial computational
and memory overhead. Sustaining this workload alongside responsive
state estimation is particularly challenging on resource-constrained
onboard platforms. Achieving the accuracy and map consistency of
neural implicit SLAM while maintaining low computational cost within
onboard resource constraints therefore remains an open challenge.

We present LIN-SLAM, a hybrid framework that combines the best of both worlds: the computational efficiency of traditional geometric methods with the map consistency and high accuracy of neural implicit approaches.
LIN-SLAM consists of three complementary components.
The geometric frontend provides responsive motion estimates and
posterior-consistent scans. The keyframe interface transfers geometry,
motion, and uncertainty to the neural implicit backend. The neural implicit backend refines
poses, continually learns a continuous map, and maintains global
consistency, while asynchronous operation supports real-time
onboard execution.

The geometric frontend further improves neural implicit tracking and
mapping by providing posterior-conditioned geometry, relative motion,
and uncertainty. These outputs provide better-aligned observations and
reliable initialization for the neural implicit backend, reducing
trajectory estimation error and improving map reconstruction quality.
In return, the accepted global map revisions correct the high-rate frontend tracking through the map-to-odometry transform without interrupting the local estimator.
We evaluate our hybrid framework on twelve public sequences from Newer College Stereo-Cam, Newer College Multi-Cam, and M2DGR, spanning 32-, 64-, and 128-channel LiDAR configurations. The results show that LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest overall mean ATE among all evaluated geometric and neural implicit methods.

We further optimize our hybrid approach for computational efficiency, enabling real-time performance on resource-constrained edge computing platforms.
We successfully deploy LIN-SLAM on a Unitree Go2 equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and a Hesai 16-channel LiDAR, demonstrating real-time localization and neural mapping over kilometer-scale trajectories in challenging indoor environments with low endpoint closure error. In contrast, the evaluated geometric baselines accumulate substantial drift or diverge on the challenging onboard trajectories, while the evaluated neural implicit baselines cannot execute the complete SLAM pipeline under the same onboard resource constraints. To the best of our knowledge, LIN-SLAM is the first LiDAR–inertial SLAM system with a neural implicit backend to achieve real-time online operation on a resource-constrained mobile robotic
platform.

Our contributions are threefold:

A hybrid framework for LiDAR–inertial neural implicit SLAM.
We integrate high-rate geometric LiDAR–inertial estimation with neural
tracking, mapping, and global refinement through bidirectional
frontend–backend information exchange. LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest
overall mean ATE across the evaluated public sequences and endpoint closure errors below 0.15 m over two real-time onboard trajectories.

A hybrid framework for LiDAR–inertial neural implicit SLAM.
We integrate high-rate geometric LiDAR–inertial estimation with neural
tracking, mapping, and global refinement through bidirectional
frontend–backend information exchange. LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest
overall mean ATE across the evaluated public sequences and endpoint closure errors below 0.15 m over two real-time onboard trajectories.

Lightweight optimization for real-time onboard deployment.
We decouple geometric estimation and neural implicit processing into asynchronous threads to preserve estimation accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. Selective neural-backend processing together with an optimized implementation in C++ and CUDA substantially reduces complete-system processing cost, enabling real-time onboard operation.

An open-source implementation of LIN-SLAM.
We will release LIN-SLAM as open-source software to facilitate reproducibility, real-world deployment, and further research on lightweight neural implicit SLAM.

2. Lightweight optimization for real-time onboard deployment.

Selective neural-backend processing together with an optimized implementation in C++ and CUDA substantially reduces complete-system processing cost, enabling real-time onboard operation.

title: Evo-DexBench: Benchmarking Generalization across Related Tasks for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Bing Cheng,Yiran Mao,Zewei Ye,Yifan Jin,Xinyi Chen,Ruifeng Tu,Shuhuai Wang,Tao Lin,Zhimu Zhou,Yuxin Du,Fangwei Zhong,Junchi Yan,Bo Zhao
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
General dexterous manipulation requires policies to learn shared manipulation patterns from existing tasks and transfer functional interactions to new tasks with only a few demonstrations [9, 27]. Recent progress in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [20, 16, 43, 38] and World Action Models (WAMs) [36, 11, 13] makes it possible to learn reusable functional interactions from multi-task demonstrations. Many tasks use different objects and scenes but share the same functional interaction. For example, turning a knob, opening a bottle cap, and twisting a tool all require a stable grasp and proper contact. Success should not come from memorizing specific objects, trajectories, or instructions. Instead, a policy should learn reusable object-use behaviors.

A key test of general dexterous manipulation is whether a policy can transfer interaction knowledge from related tasks to new ones, yet existing evaluations struggle to measure this ability. Dexterous hands have many degrees of freedom and require coordinated finger movements. Task success therefore depends not only on the end-effector trajectory, but also on finger configurations and contact relationships [42, 30]. When the target object changes, the policy must preserve the functional interaction requirements while adapting its finger and arm motions. Collecting many demonstrations for every new task is costly. Transferring interaction knowledge from related tasks is therefore essential for scaling to a broader range of everyday manipulation skills [1, 12]. However, current evaluations [14, 35] often make this ability difficult to assess: Too many target-task demonstrations may allow a model to rely on task memorization. If the source and target tasks differ too much, it is difficult to determine whether performance differences result from functional interaction transfer or other factors.

To address these issues, we propose Evo-DexBench, a benchmark for evaluating generalization across related tasks, in addition to robustness to scene variations. Given source tasks that share functional interaction requirements with a target task, Evo-DexBench changes the object instances and scene conditions and gives the policy only a few target demonstrations. By controlling how much the target task is directly exposed, we test whether the policy learns reusable knowledge from related source tasks and whether experience with more related tasks leads to better performance.

Our contributions can be summarized as:

We introduce Evo-DexBench, which evaluates the generalization of dexterous policies across related tasks. It follows the Core-Gen design principle: each evaluation unit is a core-task-set–gen-task pair with shared functional interaction. We provide only a few target demonstrations and measure how well a policy transfers interaction knowledge to new tasks.

We build an integrated simulation environment and a VR teleoperation data collection pipeline. For each task, we create three everyday scenes. We also equip simulated Shadow Hands with 123 taxels per hand and collect 1,248 multimodal demonstrations. These resources provide the data needed for evaluation.

We systematically evaluate representative models on Evo-DexBench. We compare few-shot adaptation strategies, Core sources of different relatedness and breadth, and the effect of tactile input. The best mean success rate is only 38.5%, and functionally matched Core data tends to yield larger gains than mismatched data. These results show that current methods still struggle to extract and reuse functional interaction knowledge.

title: When to Ask for Help: A Decision-Theoretic Account and Measurement Standard for Slow-Module Scheduling in Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Shilin Zhang(North China University of Technology)
comment: . Preprint
abstract:
Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency
fast policy with a slow, more expensive module, and differ both in
how the module intervenes (latent refreshing, value-guided
resampling, action-suffix reuse) and in when it is invoked.
The invocation question has just begun to be mechanized by trigger
mechanisms, but these come with no shared objective, no measured
costs, and no evaluation standard that separates schedule quality
from slow-module quality. We provide the missing account. We
formalize invocation as a calibrated decision problem under a query
budget, show that fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated
scheduling are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of
Intervention (VoI), and prove a renewal baseline that locates the
economics: under state-independent collapse the optimal schedule is
periodic, and the gain of any adaptive trigger is governed by the
cost ratio ρ=cslow/cfast\rho=c_{\text{slow}}/c_{\text{fast}} and the temporal
dispersion of collapse. Published systems span an order of magnitude
on ρ\rho; measuring FiS-VLA on one RTX 4090
places it at the low end, one slow refresh costing 5252 ms, about
one fast action (5555 ms) or 3.83.8 denoising steps, which explains
why its hand-tuned 1:41{:}4 cadence is reasonable and bounds what any
trigger can gain there. A direct test confirms the prediction: on a
controlled testbed the calibrated advantage over the fixed cadence
vanishes under homogeneous collapse and grows monotonically with
collapse heterogeneity. A calibrated router instantiates the account:
on a synthetic testbed with matched budgets it Pareto-dominates all
three baseline families (0.825±0.0020.825\pm 0.002 vs. 0.762±0.0020.762\pm 0.002 success
at a 0.250.25 query rate), and we characterize its boundary, not only
its wins: the advantage is insensitive to estimator variance but
vanishes once the estimator loses validity on most steps, the
requirement any trigger mechanism must meet to pay. Finally, we
contribute a four-measure protocol with an explicit leak-free rule;
on 929 deployment traces from RoboICL the rule is load-bearing,
cutting the apparent early-warning AUC of schedule statistics from
0.930.93 post hoc to 0.620.62 (p=0.010p=0.010), and failure attribution
reverses across task categories, so no single fixed ratio can exploit
the signal. A detection-limited frontier theorem converts such
early-warning AUC into a schedulability statement: rescoring
33,44333{,}443 RoboICL decision points leak-free, a threshold router
reaches the deployed reuse gate’s 3333–48%48\% call-reduction regime
at an explicit missed-failure price, and the release’s reported API
costs anchor the continuum’s high-asymmetry end at ρ≈103\rho\approx 10^{3}, three orders of magnitude above FiS. We close the loop on
the released system itself:
fine-tuning FiS-VLA on RLBench, we measure the freshness value
function of the slow latent directly and find it nonpositive over
ages up to eight fast steps while amortized latency falls
2.1×2.1\times; the latent drifts with the δ\sqrt{\delta} law of a
Wiener process, yet the action map is locally insensitive to it; and
a negative closed-loop result, realized under two fine-tuning
regimes, isolates the failure mechanism and yields a
competence-conditioned criterion for when success-level scheduling
comparisons are informative at all. A compilation loop completes the
account: on controlled task families the per-task period compiled
from the measured value function tracks the closed-loop oracle
within 2.4%2.4\%, and the released checkpoint compiles to the boundary
its nonpositive value function dictates. Closed-loop arms on LIBERO
instantiate the account where the economics are contested
(ρ=1.53\rho=1.53): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly
as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel
cannot convert them into success on either of two task suites,
while a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only
intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and
LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to
forty-two points. Together these results turn slow-module
invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) systems increasingly adopt a dual-system
architecture: a fast policy executes at control frequency, while a
slower, more expensive module intervenes occasionally to correct or
re-plan. This pattern appears in trained systems, where the slow layer
is a large VLM conditioned on the fast policy’s latents
(Fast-in-Slow (Chen et al., 2025)) or performs value-guided best-of-NN
resampling (Hume (Song et al., 2025)), and in zero-training systems built
on frozen LLMs, where a gate decides when to reuse predicted action
suffixes (RoboICL (Liu et al., 2026)).

These systems differ in how the slow module acts. Our starting
observation is that they also differ in when it acts, and that
this second choice has just begun to be mechanized: OneTwoVLA learns a
decision token that toggles between reasoning and acting; the
concurrent TUD trigger invokes the generalist on high predictive
uncertainty (Yang et al., 2026); System Switch
defers to a reasoning model on low
confidence (Bailo, 2026). What these mechanisms lack
is an account of the problem they solve: no shared objective, no
measured costs, no evaluation standard that separates schedule
quality from slow-module quality, and no prediction for when
adaptivity beats a hand-tuned fixed ratio at all.

We give that account
(Figure 1). We model slow-module invocation as a
calibrated decision problem under a query budget; show that existing
fixed schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value
of Intervention (VoI); and locate the economics of the problem on a
cost-asymmetry continuum ρ=cslow/cfast\rho=c_{\text{slow}}/c_{\text{fast}}
that spans three orders of magnitude across published systems and
that we measure at both ends (ρ=0.95\rho=0.95 on FiS-VLA hardware,
∼103{\sim}10^{3} from the RoboICL deployment’s reported API costs). This
yields four contributions.

A decision-theoretic account with a cost baseline. We
define VoI as the expected quality gap between the slow-corrected and
fast-only actions, weighted by the probability that the fast policy
collapses in state ss (Section 3). Fixed-ratio,
fixed-budget, and history-gated scheduling are degenerate cases of VoI
routing (Propositions 1–3). A renewal
baseline (Proposition 4) then locates the regimes:
under state-independent collapse the optimal schedule is periodic with
interval 2​cslow/(wfail​π)\sqrt{2c_{\text{slow}}/(w_{\text{fail}}\pi)}, so fixed
ratios are hard to beat at low ρ\rho and low collapse heterogeneity,
while adaptivity pays as either grows. This explains why hand-tuned
cadences are reasonable on embedded-latent systems and why triggered
invocation concentrates on separate-VLM systems.

A decision-theoretic account with a cost baseline. We
define VoI as the expected quality gap between the slow-corrected and
fast-only actions, weighted by the probability that the fast policy
collapses in state ss (Section 3). Fixed-ratio,
fixed-budget, and history-gated scheduling are degenerate cases of VoI
routing (Propositions 1–3). A renewal

under state-independent collapse the optimal schedule is periodic with
interval 2​cslow/(wfail​π)\sqrt{2c_{\text{slow}}/(w_{\text{fail}}\pi)}, so fixed
ratios are hard to beat at low ρ\rho and low collapse heterogeneity,
while adaptivity pays as either grows. This explains why hand-tuned
cadences are reasonable on embedded-latent systems and why triggered
invocation concentrates on separate-VLM systems.

A calibrated router with its boundary characterized. A
lightweight router estimates VoI online and queries the slow module
only when the estimate exceeds the query cost. We characterize where
this construction breaks, not only where it works: the advantage is
insensitive to estimator variance but vanishes when the estimator
loses validity on most steps, which is the requirement any trigger
mechanism must meet to pay (Sections 5.2–5.3).

A leak-free measurement standard. We contribute
staleness curves, routing frontiers, failure attribution, and
calibration reliability as a four-measure battery for slow-query
policies (Section 4), with an explicit leak-free
rule. On 929 deployment traces from the RoboICL release the rule is not decoration:
the same features reach AUC 0.930.93 post hoc but 0.620.62 (p=0.010p=0.010)
leak-free, so without it the early-warning capability of schedule
statistics would be overstated by roughly 1.5×1.5\times. The traces
also fix the precision of frontier claims themselves: skip decisions
cluster by episode at design effects of 88–1818, so a frontier
estimate over 16,00016{,}000 decision points carries the information of
about one thousand episodes
(Proposition 8).

Schedule compilation. The measured quantities are not
only diagnostic. A renewal compiler turns a task’s measured staleness
value function into a per-task refresh period; on controlled task
families the compiled period tracks the closed-loop oracle at a cost
gap of at most 2.4%2.4\%, the compilation is a sample-average
approximation whose optimality gap admits a statistical
certificate (Mak et al., 1999), and the underlying trade-off inherits
the cost flatness of the Harris–Wilson order-quantity
problem (Harris, 1913), so moderate cost-estimate errors degrade
the achieved schedule only at second order; and the validation
budget itself has an optimal allocation, concentrated on the
near-ties of the cost bowl, which roughly doubles the probability
of recovering the oracle period at a fixed budget
(Remark 4). On the FiS backbone the
compiler sends every task to the boundary its measured (nonpositive)
value function dictates (Section 5.9). Adaptive
triggers, fixed periods, and compiled schedules become commensurable
as different amounts of measurement invested in the same cost
functional.

On a synthetic testbed with matched query budgets, calibrated routing
dominates the Pareto frontier of the fixed-ratio, always-query, and
reuse-gate baselines
(Section 5.1). On real systems, we apply the
protocol to all 929 deployment traces released by RoboICL
(Section 5.4): failed episodes query the slow module
25%25\% less densely and run with greater staleness, and the effect is
category-dependent, so no single fixed ratio can exploit it. On
hardware we instantiate the cost side of the continuum with
FiS-VLA: one slow refresh costs 5252 ms, about one fast action
(5555 ms), or 3.83.8 denoising steps, on a single RTX 4090
(Section 5.6), placing embedded-latent dual
systems at the ρ≈1\rho\approx 1 end, opposite the separate-VLM
systems at ρ\rho of 1010–2020 that trigger-based invocation
targets, and the frozen-LLM API systems at ρ≈103\rho\approx 10^{3}
measured from the same release’s reported costs
(Section 5.5): three orders of magnitude with both
ends anchored on hardware measurement or audited cost reports
(Table 5). A closed-loop dual system placed at the
continuum’s middle (ρ=1.53\rho=1.53: OpenVLA-7B as the fast policy and
Qwen2.5-VL-7B as the slow module on LIBERO-Spatial) then tests the
account where the economics are contested. Fourteen closed-loop arms
at matched seeds, initial states and budgets, eleven on LIBERO-Spatial
and a three-arm replication on LIBERO-Goal with an LLM slow endpoint,
sweep the two layers the
account separates: the adaptive trigger allocates its queries
exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet a subgoal-rewrite
channel cannot convert them into success, and neither can the
screened, faster or slower variants of that channel, whose pooled
rate sits at 43%43\% against fast-only’s 58%58\% with no dose axis in
sight. The failure is the channel’s, not the schedule’s: replacing
the language channel with action ranking, or adding an actuator that
undoes an unhelpful rewrite, changes the outcome’s risk profile
rather than its mean, and the revert arm produces the table’s only
direction-consistent positive contrast (1515 vs. 44 discordant
pairs, nominal p=0.019p=0.019, null under family correction), landing
on exactly the tasks the risk coordinate predicts. The cross-suite
replication keeps the ordering: the rewrite channel’s deficit
deepens to 4242 points on the second suite while the revert arm
tracks fast-only exactly (48/10048/100 against 48/10048/100). The operating
point is thus a boundary case in which the deployment, not the
module, sets the value of asking
(Section 5.10).

This is a methodology contribution: a decision-theoretic account, a
constructive router with characterized boundaries, and a measurement
standard. Third-party systems enter only as measurement subjects:
they anchor the continuum’s two ends and stress-test the standard;
no contribution depends on their internals or on access beyond
public artifacts. The account’s low-ρ\rho prediction is tested directly: on
the testbed, the calibrated advantage vanishes under homogeneous
collapse and grows monotonically with collapse heterogeneity, exactly
as the renewal baseline predicts
(Section 5.7). Fine-tuning the open checkpoint
on four consumer GPUs and measuring its staleness frontier directly
confirms the prediction’s transfer to the deployed FiS system
(Section 5.8).

title: KODA: Kinematics--Observation Data Alignment for Humanoid Learning from Human Egocentric Demonstration
authors: Zibo Zhou,Yueru Chen,Junsong Wu,Weiji Xie,Qingyao Xu,Sheng Yin,Shiqing Wang,Jiyuan Shi,Siheng Chen,Chenjia Bai,Xuelong Li
abstract:
Training humanoid whole-body vision–language–action (VLA) policies requires
costly robot demonstrations with aligned robot-view observations and
controller-compatible whole-body state–action labels. Egocentric human
demonstrations offer scalable supervision but have misaligned views and
sparse motion cues. Existing approaches either pretrain policies that still
require robot data for adaptation or generate controller-specific commands
that limit reuse. Conversion also requires robot-view observations aligned
with the generated whole-body motion. We present KODA
(Kinematics–Observation Data Alignment), which converts egocentric RGB
demonstrations into whole-body VLA training data using a reusable canonical
trajectory to guide robot-view synthesis and generate controller-specific
whole-body state–action supervision. KODA first generates a
simulator-checked whole-body trajectory using a sparse tracker with
sampling-based command optimization. This generated trajectory directly
determines the onboard camera poses used to synthesize corresponding
robot-view observations. The motion, observations, and task instruction form
a canonical record. For each deployment controller, KODA optimizes commands
to track the stored motion and records the corresponding action labels and
proprioceptive states. When switching controllers, KODA retains this
canonical record and regenerates whole-body state–action supervision for
co-training with matching robot demonstrations. We evaluate KODA on four
Unitree G1 loco-manipulation tasks using two whole-body controllers, SONIC
and HEFT. With robot data held fixed, macro-average success on conditions
covered by human demonstrations but absent from robot data improves by
45.0 and 46.25 percentage points, respectively. Under both controllers, this
metric shows an upward trend across the evaluated human-data budgets,
suggesting potential for further scaling.

title: Manifold Generative Annealing for Contact Constraint-aware Impedance Control with Reinforcement Learning Prior
authors: Zhilin He,Guoquan Qi,Changliu Liu
abstract: Contact-rich robotic tasks require coordinated motion and impedance under uncertain interaction dynamics and physical constraints. While recent methods on learned policies provide useful interaction strategies, they may fail when contact conditions differ from those encountered during training. Model-based generative methods show promising receding-horizon trajectories optimization results, but often lack structured behavioral guidance and refinement that jointly accounts for constraint geometry and actual contact responses. To this end, we propose Manifold Generative Annealing (MGA), a joint model-free and model-based generative framework for motion–impedance optimization. MGA first organizes pretrained reinforcement learning policies into structured sequence proposals, retaining task-specific interaction strategies without committing to their execution. It then evaluates these proposals alongside exploratory samples through model-based rollouts for refinement or separate execution selection. Crucially, realization-aware manifold refinement aligns updates from the refinement bank with both task constraints and locally achievable physical responses, allowing learned experience to guide online adaptation under changing contact conditions. Experiments cover surface scanning, peg insertion, and humanoid pushing, with improved safety success rate of impedance control under nominal and sensing-shift conditions. Code: https://github.com/hhhhzl/genedynamics
introduction:
Contact-rich tasks such as surface scanning, peg insertion, and whole-body pushing require robots to coordinate motion with compliant interaction while respecting physical constraints. Impedance learning and control provide an interface for regulating the relationship between motion and interaction forces (Hogan, 1984; Buchli et al., 2011; Martín-Martín et al., 2019). Selecting these commands remains challenging due to multimodal interaction behaviors, uncertain physical responses, and safety-critical execution, requiring their joint optimization to sustain task progress under changing contact conditions (Abu-Dakka and Saveriano, 2020; Tsuji et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a).

Safe Reinforcement Learning (RL) combines learned task policies with stiffness adaptation, recovery mechanisms, or action safeguards (Zhao et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024), providing behavioral structure for contact-rich decisions. Beyond individual policy outputs, the same learned experience can define distributions over candidate behaviors. Model-free diffusion planners provide this generative extension by representing multimodal trajectory distributions, while constrained variants incorporate model-based projections and primal–dual sampling to enforce deployment-time constraints (Römer et al., 2025; Christopher et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Blanke et al., 2026). These learned distributions can therefore supply task-informed candidates that reduce unguided search. However, they remain proposals rather than reliable plans because their relevance is inherited from the training distribution and may deteriorate as task or contact conditions change.

Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) (Pan et al., 2024) offers a way to revise sequences through their predicted consequences: it casts trajectory generation as optimization using objective-weighted dynamics rollouts without a learned denoising score. Constrained extensions (He et al., 2026b; He et al., 2026a) improve feasibility through Control Barrier Function (CBF) (Ames et al., 2019) or Convex Feasible Set (CFS) (Liu et al., 2018) with adaptive scheduling. Building on this trajectory-optimization view, DIAL-MPC brings diffusion-style annealing to short-horizon model predictive control for online refinement (Xue et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). With a limited rollout budget, learned proposals can focus this search on useful contact strategies, and model-based evaluation can reassess them under current conditions. However, weighting promising candidates does not ensure that their combined sequence preserves nonlinear task relationships. Evaluation therefore leaves a second problem: how to correct the update it produces.

Constraint geometry provides local information for correcting such updates. ATACOM constructs safe actions in the tangent space of constraint manifolds (Liu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2025), while geometry-aware generative optimization uses active constraints to shape refinement and exploration (He et al., 2026c). Geometric impedance control further exploits SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) structure in learned variable-impedance policies for contact-rich manipulation (Seo et al., 2023). Under compliant contact, jamming, or switching, however, displacement commands may produce deformation or force, and stiffness changes the local response. Refinement must therefore account for measured tracking and contact responses when defining the task residual. Shaping the update can reduce the normal response it introduces, but residuals already present or left after a finite step require a further correction. These two operations connect model-based reassessment to continued contact execution.

We propose Manifold Generative Annealing (MGA), a short-horizon controller that organizes learned behavioral structure, model-based reassessment, and feedback-conditioned geometric correction in the same motion–impedance sequence space. Rollout weighting determines which candidates inform the update. Geometry shaping adjusts its direction. Local residual correction then revises the updated sequence. The proposal and evaluation stages supply task-informed candidates for refinement or separate execution selection. Our Contributions are three-fold:

C1: We organize model-free learned action policies into structured short-horizon motion–impedance proposals, supplying task-specific interaction behaviors alongside Gaussian exploration in a common sequence space.

C2: We integrate these candidates with model-based generative annealing (online optimization) through common closed-loop evaluation, reassessing their relevance under current task and contact conditions through bank weighting or separate expert selection.

C3: We develop realization-aware manifold refinement that adjusts update directions and corrects remaining task residuals. Contact feedback updates the task references, while response reliability controls the refinement strength. We analyze how the normalized core suppresses encoded normal responses and reduces local residuals.

title: Slip-Induced Fall Suppression During Cornering for a Remotely Operated Motorcycle with a Rear-Wheel-Swing Mechanism
authors: Tadashi Sumioka,Kazushi Akimoto,Takuya Tsujimura,Sho Takayanagi,Kineo Tomura
comment: Journal papaer
abstract: Slip-induced falls when riding motorcycles are difficult to avoid even for expert riders and represent a major cause of single-vehicle accidents. Despite their prevalence, no practical solution has yet been proposed to suppress this phenomenon. We previously introduced a motorcycle model applicable to systems with both front- and rear- wheel steering. In this paper, we extend that model and formulate the suppression of slip-induced falls as an optimization problem that distributes assistive control inputs according to vehicle speed and road surface conditions. To evaluate the proposed method, we developed a remotely operated motorcycle and conducted experiments under two scenarios: slalom driving on a low-friction surface at 5.5 m/s, and turning maneuvers on synthetic ice to simulate driving over manholes on rainy days. The results demonstrate that our approach successfully suppresses falls under these challenging conditions.
introduction:
Motorcycles are attractive vehicles because they are small, highly maneuverable, and environmentally friendly.
However, when a motorcycle falls over, it can cause serious injury to the rider.
A lot of research has thus been conducted on the dynamic performance of motorcycles (e.g., [1], [2], [3]), particularly on the suppression of falls.

The causes of motorcycle falls can be divided into two categories depending on the vehicle speed. When a motorcycle is stopped or moving at an extremely low speed,
falls are due to the fundamental lack of stability of motorcycles. Many methods have thus been developed to improve stability, such as those that add flywheels or movable axles (e.g.,[4], [5], [6], [7], [8]).
Although there are still issues to be addressed, such as the coordination between the rider and fall suppression control and implementation costs, progress has been made in terms of fall prevention.
When a motorcycle is moving at a normal speed, falls are often caused by a loss of traction.

Falls that occur at normal speeds can be further divided into falls that occur while going straight and falls that occur while turning.
Technologies for suppressing slippage and falls while going straight include an anti-lock
braking system[9], which prevents the wheels from locking during braking, and a traction control system[10], which prevents the rear wheels from spinning due to an excessive driving force.
These two technologies, which are used in many mass-produced motorcycles, detect the longitudinal slip ratio of each wheel and control the braking and driving force such that the slip ratio does not become excessive.
In contrast, there is little research on preventing motorcycle slips and falls while turning.
A slip and fall avoidance method developed by Bosch [11] uses gas injection to generate a restoring moment; however, this makes the method difficult to use in mixed traffic situations involving cars, motorcycles, and pedestrians.
The present study proposes an extension of a previously developed front- and rear-wheel steering control method [8] to achieve slip-induced fall suppression while preserving the fundamental characteristics of the motorcycle structure.

Considering rider safety, it is difficult to test a motorcycle in terms of slipping and falling while turning.
Furthermore, although tire–road interaction modeling has been investigated in works such as [2], the behavior in limit conditions—e.g., rollover—does not match real vehicle dynamics, making simulation-based verification difficult.
To overcome the above problems, experiments can be conducted using a remotely operated motorcycle.
Riderless motorcycles have been investigated mostly using simulations; few studies have verified their effectiveness using actual vehicles (e.g., [12] –[16]).
BMW [17] and Yamaha [18] have developed actual autonomous motorcycles, but neither has published a related study.
Miyagishi et al. [19] used an actual autonomous motorcycle in their study. Their stabilization control method outputs a front-wheel steering angle that makes the roll angle track the target roll angle, as done in self-driving bicycles [20]. However, there are no reports on the behavior when slippage occurs.

Although autonomous bicycles using gyroscopes—such as those described in [21]—have been proposed, this approach is not practical for slip‑induced rollover avoidance in motorcycles operating in normal speed ranges. This is because a significantly larger restoring roll moment is required, and the associated actuator output and power demand become impractically high.

In this study, we propose a method for suppressing slips and falls while turning and verify it using a remotely operable motorcycle, shown in Fig. 1.

Based on a previously developed vehicle [8], we propose an optimal front- and rear-wheel assist method that takes into account vehicle speed and the road surface friction coefficient for driving speeds that range from extremely low to 5.5 m/s while maintaining the divergent component of motion (DCM) feedback control, which is the best regulator in terms of stabilization.
In order to establish a fall‑prevention method safely, rider-on-board experiments are beyond our present scope. However, when a rider is on board, assist control is expected to require additional rider–machine cooperative control methods, as suggested in [8]. Therefore, future work will extend this approach toward systems capable of interacting with a rider.

title: MoCaP: Mobile Code-as-Policies for Zero-Shot Mobile Manipulation from Passive Human Videos
authors: Yiyang Cai,Tatsuya Kamijo,Ninghao Lu,Zijin Hu,Sherry Yang
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Passive human videos of everyday activity offer robots access to a massive amount of human experience without requiring a demonstration for each task. However, using this experience requires recovering knowledge from unstructured video recordings and adapting it to a different body (i.e., the robot). To overcome these challenges, we present mobile code-as-policy (MoCaP), an agentic framework that turns passive human video recordings into guidance for an end-to-end mobile manipulation policy. MoCaP extracts spatial memory and cues of how people prepare to interact with objects, which inform navigation and the search for a manipulation-ready configuration. Guided by passive human experience and current observations, MoCaP uses a closed-loop code-as-policy to coordinate planning and tool use primitives to solve motions under the robot’s geometry and kinematic constraints.
On a real mobile manipulator, MoCaP achieves 80% success on each of two mobile manipulation tasks in an indoor environment whereas existing approaches cannot succeed at the task. Video-derived spatial memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, and human approach prior raises the rate of finding a reachable base pose from 0% to 100% at an unfavorable start location.
Videos and code are available on the project website.
introduction:
Household robots should be able to assist different users in a wide range of homes, responding to everyday requests without requiring users to specify every action. Open-vocabulary mobile manipulation moves toward this goal by enabling robots to act on natural-language instructions involving diverse objects and environments [1]. To fulfill a request such as “bring the cup back,” a robot must determine which objects and places are relevant, locate them, and decide how to act. Supporting this ability across homes and users motivates learning from experience beyond the robot’s own interactions.

Passive recordings of human activity offer a potentially abundant source of such experience. Wearable cameras can capture how people interact with objects and their surroundings during everyday life, without requiring robot teleoperation or prescribed demonstrations [2]. We investigate how robots can draw on this accumulated human experience for open-vocabulary mobile manipulation. We consider the setting where a collection of human activity videos is passively recorded through people’s daily lives capturing diverse activities that may be requested of a robot. Rather than reproducing a particular demonstration, the robot must use relevant experience from the collection to guide its actions in its current environment.

However, passive recordings of egocentric human data do not directly provide the information a robot needs to act. Specifically, using passive human experience for robots presents three challenges.

First, the recorded experience lacks explicit spatial structure. A video supplies neither object coordinates nor labeled places and traversable connections. Relevant observations are distributed over time, with objects and regions reappearing from different viewpoints. Searching beyond the current view requires connecting objects to their spatial context.

Second, human and robot sensing and morphology differ. Camera height and viewing angle change the visible scene, while different cameras introduce further differences in intrinsics, field of view, resolution, and color response. These visual discrepancies complicate matching recorded experience to the robot’s current observations. Body dimensions, joint structure, and available motions also determine which actions can be executed: a person can turn sideways through a narrow passage or manipulate an object with a dexterous hand, whereas a mobile manipulator has a different footprint and gripper. Transferring experience therefore requires interpreting observations across cameras and viewpoints and grounding actions in the robot’s own geometry and kinematics.

Third, navigation and manipulation are not explicitly separated in human activity. People naturally adjust their approach and position as they get ready to interact, without marking when navigation ends and manipulation begins. For a robot, reaching the vicinity of an object does not ensure that it can manipulate it. The recording does not explicitly reveal which movements simply bring a person closer and which make the subsequent interaction possible.

To overcome these challenges, we present MoCaP, which turns passive human video into guidance for mobile navigation and manipulation (Fig. 1). MoCaP extracts spatial memory about a place together with records of where people stood when they reached for objects. During task execution, the spatial memory helps locate the requested object, and the human approach prior guides the robot to approach the object in the right way. A code agent uses this guidance together with current observations to coordinate navigation and manipulation primitives. The primitives solve and check motions for the robot’s embodiment, returning execution feedback that lets the agent revise subsequent actions.

Our contributions are:

A unified Code-as-Policy system for mobile manipulation. MoCaP flexibly coordinates navigation and manipulation through executable code, without a predefined division into navigation and manipulation stages. The agent selects and revises actions using prior human experience, live observations, and feedback from robot-grounded primitives.

Reusable spatial memory from passive human video. We develop a fine-grained spatial memory pipeline that draws on the abundance of everyday human activity recordings to extract object relations, landmarks, and place connectivity for subsequent robot search and navigation. This video is task-independent and can be reused to different tasks.

Human-guided base placement for manipulation. We infer the direction to approach object from how a person positioned themselves before manipulation in passive human videos, then search nearby base poses under the robot’s own reachability and collision constraints. A poor arrival side can leave no feasible pose within reach of local adjustment, and this guidance is designed to turn such arrivals into graspable configurations, using only video that accumulates from everyday activity.

We evaluate MoCaP on a real mobile manipulator in an indoor environment through an object-navigation task and two mobile manipulation tasks. MoCaP achieves 80% success on each manipulation task, whereas existing methods [3] cannot succeed at the task. To examine the contributions of video-derived guidance, we separately evaluate spatial memory for object search and human approach priors for base placement. Spatial memory increases navigation success from 70% to 100%, while controlled comparisons suggest that human approach priors improve manipulation readiness from unfavorable initial base configurations.
Base placement guided by the human prior found a reachable pose in 5 of 5 trials whereas a naive proximity-based docking failed in all five.
Together, these results suggest that passive human video can help robots complete mobile manipulation tasks by guiding both object search and the approach to manipulation.

title: When a robot can trust reversing wind to find an odour source
authors: Junlong Shen,Shunsuke Shigaki
abstract:
A wind-derived heading can guide a robot towards an odour source even after the wind reverses, but its reliability depends on the plume’s transport history.
On a quadruped initially facing the source, holding the initial heading reached it in every reversing-wind trial, whereas comparison controllers never settled there. An exact geometric condition links heading correctness to net odour transport, and simulations separate sensing error from departures from nominal flow.
Where the alternating wind directions are too close for reversal alone to produce wrong-side headings, the wrong-side rate rises from 1.0% under uniform transport to 4.7% in a stochastic flow. Re-acquiring headings from new odour contact improves simulated search when contact is intermittent.
These results identify distinct requirements for wind-guided search: a heading supported by the transport geometry and sufficient intermittent contact to replace it.
introduction:
A robot searching for a gas leak detects intermittent filaments of odour, thin strands separated
by clean air [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].
Many search strategies follow an insect-inspired rule: surge upwind during contact and cast
crosswind after contact is lost [8, 9, 10].
Robotic implementations include underwater plume tracers [11, 12]
and time-varying moth strategies [13]. These strategies use the current wind
as a cue to the source direction. A reversal can invalidate that cue while previously released
odour is still arriving.

Holding an earlier heading can protect a searcher from this error. On a Unitree Go1 quadruped
searching for ethanol between alternating fan banks, a held heading reached the source while
the comparison controllers failed to settle there (Fig. 1). However, the robot
started facing the source, so its initial upwind heading was favourable. The demonstration
motivates a separate question: under what conditions does a wind-derived heading point toward
an unknown source?

The answer starts with transport. A packet detected now has accumulated displacement under the
wind along its path. The source lies back along that displacement, whereas a wind sensor reports
only the local wind now. Their agreement depends on the packet’s history and on how the plume
departs from the nominal flow. We call storing a world-frame heading from the sensed wind a
commitment. Its sign is correct when the heading lies within a right angle of the true
source bearing. Correct sign is weaker than accurate alignment or eventual arrival.

We separate these requirements using physical trials and controlled simulations. The robot
tests whether a held heading survives real reversals and sensor limitations. Simulations expose
packet release times and transport, and allow plume models to change while retaining the same
robot and sensing parameters. WindReacquire (WR-G in Methods and the Supplementary Information) supplies the test
controller: it stores an upwind heading on odour contact, rejects conflicting wind readings, and replaces
the heading after odour contact is lost. The contribution is a diagnosis of when these rules
work. Three findings carry the argument:

A held heading reaches the source through real wind reversals from a favourable start
(§2.1).

Transport geometry gives an exact sign condition; controlled plume comparisons identify
errors that nominal wind histories alone miss (§2.3–§2.6).

Re-acquisition improves simulated search when odour contact is intermittent
(§2.8).

title: SOMA: Stack-of-Objects Manipulation using a Quadruped Robot
authors: Stergios E. Bachoumas,Panagiotis Artemiadis
abstract: Executing heavy-duty physical manipulation in unpredictable environments remains a major challenge for quadrupedal robots lacking dedicated manipulators. This paper presents SOMA, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for whole-body non-prehensile manipulation of multi-object stacks using a quadruped robot. Unlike traditional methods restricted to two-dimensional planar pushing, SOMA integrates explicit robot base-height control, unlocking full three-dimensional pushing strategies. This capability enables the quadruped to manipulate complex payload stacks as a unified system while preventing relative sliding or tipping of upper layers. The architecture factorizes control into a high-level manipulation policy using a Simplified Structured State Space Sequence (S5) encoder to reason over long-horizon temporal history and predict bounded target tracking commands via Beta distributions, and a low-level locomotion policy that dynamically adapts leg stance configurations. In extensive simulation benchmarks, SOMA achieves a 90.3%90.3\% success rate for single-object reposing and up to 90.1%90.1\% for dynamic two-box stacks under stringent error margins (0.05​ m0.05\text{ m} position error, 1​°1\degree orientation error). Finally, we validate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot across diverse payload masses and geometries, demonstrating active base-height adjustments to maintain traction and balance during heavy pushing tasks.
introduction:
Recent work on quadrupedal locomotion has enabled significant maneuverability across diverse and complex terrains [11, 13], and has also enabled gymnastic-style maneuvers such as a running backflip [15]. However, these platforms still exhibit limitations when executing tasks that require close physical interaction with the environment. Truly autonomous robotic systems must physically interact with their environment and thus act as mobile manipulators [23]. Recently, the robotics community has increased efforts in this direction, with promising work combining locomotion and manipulation for quadruped robots, commonly referred to as loco-manipulation.

Unlike bipeds, quadrupedal platforms inherently lack dedicated end-effectors for physical interaction.
Nevertheless, in [33, 4, 16, 2], the authors used pedipulation, i.e., manipulation using the legs of a quadruped as an on-demand manipulator, to accomplish tasks such as opening spring-loaded doors, pushing lightweight objects out of the way, doing laundry, pushing switches, and even collecting rock samples in the wild. While these strategies prove effective for versatile manipulation, most prior work [4, 2] strictly constrains the robot’s mobility by prioritizing base static stability, with the notable exceptions of [16, 33].

To overcome this limitation, a prominent body of work has successfully integrated robotic manipulators onto quadruped bases, achieving significant progress in mobile prehensile loco-manipulation [7, 20, 6, 8, 17, 22, 31, 33].
Despite these advancements, dedicated manipulator-base systems face severe physical constraints when deployed in complex environments. The increased spatial footprint and payload capacity limits of mounted arms hinder operation in tightly confined spaces and restrict the maximum load the system can manipulate. This gap becomes particularly critical in search-and-rescue operations, where robots must navigate narrow passages and interact with heavy, unstable debris under shifting dynamic loads. Consequently, achieving heavy-duty physical manipulation within highly constrained, unpredictable, and hazardous environments remains an open challenge.

Quadrupedal robots can manipulate objects without dedicated arms either by deploying individual limbs or by leveraging their entire body for pushing interactions. While limb-based manipulation enables fine control over lightweight objects, whole-body pushing provides a compelling mechanism for transporting heavy or bulky payloads. Although non-prehensile pushing was historically underexplored [14], foundational work by Mason established the underlying mechanics and motion planning challenges of contact-driven manipulation [19]. Modern optimization-based techniques have since made this problem more tractable by formulating pushing as a multi-contact planning problem [9]. Recently, these optimization frameworks have been extended to quadrupedal platforms to enable body-pushing behaviors [24, 29]. However, planning through contact remains inherently difficult [19], and current optimization methods rely heavily on pre-specified environmental models and fixed robot parameters. As a result, existing controllers struggle to generalize across diverse or unpredictable environments, leaving generalizable, whole-body pushing locomanipulation an open challenge.

To address these limitations, we leverage learning-based paradigms [1, 12] and propose SOMA, a novel framework designed for whole-body object-stack manipulation on quadrupedal platforms (see Fig. 1). Built upon a hierarchical reinforcement learning architecture [10, 12], SOMA decouples control into a high-level manipulation planner that commands a low-level locomotion policy. We extend prior work by incorporating explicit control over the robot’s base height, unlocking full three-dimensional pushing strategies. This vertical degrees-of-freedom integration enables the quadruped to intelligently manipulate and reconfigure complex stacks of objects from arbitrary initial states to target poses.

The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows:

A learning-based framework for quadruped whole-body manipulation of a stack of objects. Our approach incorporates direct robot base height commands, enabling full 3D pushing strategies—a crucial component missing from previous methods that restrict the robot to a predefined height and, consequently, to 2D planar pushing strategies.

A learning-based framework for quadruped whole-body manipulation of a stack of objects. Our approach incorporates direct robot base height commands, enabling full 3D pushing strategies—a crucial component missing from previous methods that restrict the robot to a predefined height and, consequently, to 2D planar pushing strategies.

The proposed policy successfully reasons about latent physical parameters of the stack—such as object mass, geometry, inter-object friction, and ground-surface friction—thereby enabling robust generalization across diverse problem instances.

title: Line-Augmented cuVSLAM: Robust Visual Odometry in Low-Texture Environments
authors: Dara Molloy,Terry Wu,Wonju Lee,Abhilash Nand Kumar,David Adley,Conor Ferguson,Hesam Rabeti
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) in warehouses and production facilities operate in
precisely the environments that defeat point-feature visual odometry: featureless
aisles, uniform walls, repetitive racking and specular floors. Such environments are,
however, rich in straight-edge structure: rack uprights, door frames, wall
junctions and cabinet outlines present high-contrast linear edges stable across wide
viewpoint changes. A line-feature extension to cuVSLAM [1],
a CUDA-accelerated visual-SLAM system, is presented that recovers this
signal. Lines are parameterised as Plücker coordinates for geometric transport
and as the minimal 4-DOF orthonormal representation of Bartoli and Sturm [2]
for optimisation; a Cauchy-robust point-to-line residual with analytic Jacobians is
folded directly into cuVSLAM’s per-frame Gauss–Newton pose solve, and the same line
state is jointly refined in the Schur-complement sliding-window bundle adjustment. An
adaptive information weight causes lines to assume more of the estimation burden exactly
as point features become scarce, and the extension adds residual blocks to existing
solvers rather than introducing a second estimator, reducing exactly to the unmodified
point pipeline when disabled. Evaluated in RGB-D mode under SE(3) Umeyama alignment with
no scale correction, line features reduce mean absolute trajectory error by
38.5% over the 22 sequences of the TUM RGB-D freiburg3 collection and by
30.1% over the 8 Replica room and office sequences, where median
translation error falls by 38.9% and median rotation error by
66.4%, with zero tracking failures in any configuration tested.
introduction:
Cameras are inexpensive, compact and information-dense, making visual odometry an
attractive alternative to LIDAR-based localisation for autonomous mobile robots,
provided it can match LIDAR’s robustness in the industrial
environments where point-feature tracking degrades.
cuVSLAM [1] represents a modern, state-of-the-art
visual-SLAM system: CUDA-accelerated, supporting up to 32 cameras across RGB,
depth and stereo-inertial pipelines, and running in real time on NVIDIA Jetson
edge hardware.
As in ORB-SLAM3 [3], VINS-Mono [4] and other
deployed visual or visual-inertial odometry (VIO) systems, its front end tracks sparse
point features: corners and textured patches carried across frames by descriptor
matching or optical-flow tracking. cuVSLAM’s own point path uses the latter: GFTT
corner detection followed by GPU Lucas–Kanade optical-flow tracking with
normalised-cross-correlation validation, not descriptor re-matching.

Point features are precisely the primitive that indoor structured environments lack. A
warehouse aisle or production facility presents long stretches of uniformly painted wall,
repetitive shelving, specular flooring and low-contrast or distant ceiling structure. Corner
detectors yield few correspondences in these conditions, and the surviving matches are
often poorly conditioned or attached to moving inventory.

These environments are, however, rich in straight-edge structure. Rack uprights, door
frames, wall–floor junctions, pallet edges and cabinet outlines are abundant,
high-contrast and stable across wide viewpoint changes. A line is also a
better-conditioned measurement than a point in these scenes, as it aggregates gradient
evidence along its full length, which increases robustness to noise, motion blur and
partial occlusion relative to a small tracked point patch. The point-line VIO
literature converges on this observation, reporting that line features yield the
largest gains in degenerate, low-texture and structured
scenes [5, 6, 7].

This paper carries the point-line VIO formulation established by
PL-VINS [5] and its lineage into cuVSLAM’s CUDA-accelerated pose
solve and bundle adjustment, and extends it with five departures aimed at the
industrial degradation regime above. The extension augments rather than replaces the
point pipeline and preserves the low-latency front end/back end separation that makes
cuVSLAM deployable on edge hardware. The contributions are:

A persistent, cross-window line landmark registry
that keeps a landmark alive after its originating frame
leaves the bundle-adjustment sliding window, so an early, wide-baseline observation
can still be paired against a much later one for triangulation, in place of
PL-VINS’s window-scoped landmarks, which are deleted outright once their originating
frame marginalises out.

A persistent, cross-window line landmark registry
that keeps a landmark alive after its originating frame
leaves the bundle-adjustment sliding window, so an early, wide-baseline observation
can still be paired against a much later one for triangulation, in place of
PL-VINS’s window-scoped landmarks, which are deleted outright once their originating
frame marginalises out.

A trimmed-mean multi-view line fusion that
ranks each landmark’s recently triangulated endpoint pairs by mutual agreement and
discards a fixed worst-agreeing fraction before averaging, in place of PL-VINS’s
landmark state, which is otherwise a free variable updated only by the joint bundle
adjustment, with no separate fusion step.

An adaptive, clamped point/line weight that scales inversely with
surviving point observations and saturates at fixed floor/ceiling bounds, in
place of PL-VINS’s single fixed information matrix
shared unweighted between points and lines.

A cuVSLAM integration of point-to-line residuals into both the
per-frame front end pose solve, with a Cauchy robust loss, and the windowed back end
bundle adjustment, with a Student’s-tt robust loss.

An evaluation on two public benchmarks, TUM RGB-D and Replica,
under strict SE(3) alignment with no scale
correction, paired with an analysis of
which scene properties predict benefit.

title: Adaptive Prescribed Performance Trajectory Tracking for Uncertain Autonomous Underwater Vehicles With Input Saturation
authors: Athanasios K. Gkesoulis,Christos Vlachos,George K. Fourlas,Charalampos P. Bechlioulis,George C. Karras
comment: . Supplementary video included as ancillary material
abstract: Accurate trajectory tracking is essential for autonomous underwater vehicles operating with uncertain hydrodynamics and limited thruster authority. This paper develops a low-complexity adaptive prescribed performance controller for uncertain underwater vehicle dynamics with coupled and saturated inputs. The proposed method adapts the performance functions directly through the mismatch between the requested and saturated control inputs, enlarging the performance funnels only when the available actuation cannot meet the nominal specifications. A coupled invariant-set analysis establishes boundedness of all closed-loop signals, prescribed bounds on the filtered tracking errors, and explicit feasibility conditions. Comparative simulations on a BlueROV2 underwater vehicle show that the adaptive design maintains prescribed performance during a figure-eight maneuver, whereas conventional prescribed performance control loses feasibility under input limits. A real-time pool experiment further demonstrates stable trajectory tracking and the practical implementation of the proposed method on an underwater robotic platform.
introduction:
Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are increasingly expected to execute inspection, mapping, intervention, and environmental monitoring missions under limited actuation authority. In these operations, trajectory tracking accuracy is a robotic mission requirement: large transient deviations may compromise sensor coverage, vehicle safety, or the quality of collected data. Underwater vehicles also operate with uncertain hydrodynamics, restoring forces, disturbances, and hard thruster limits whose effects propagate through control allocation and coupled body motion. Experimental prescribed performance tracking of underwater robots [1] and open-water funnel control under input saturation [2] reinforce the need to jointly address tracking performance and actuation limits.

Prescribed performance control (PPC) imposes transient and steady state tracking specifications through designer-selected performance envelopes [3], while funnel control achieves the same following a different design [4]. Barrier-like transformations of normalized errors can enforce convergence rate, overshoot, and residual error requirements without exact model identification. Actuator saturation, however, creates a feasibility conflict whenever a fixed performance envelope demands more control authority than the vehicle can deliver, particularly during aggressive maneuvers or in the presence of strong currents and other disturbances.

Input constraints have been studied through adaptive, robust, neuroadaptive, finite-time, and sliding-mode control [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Saturation-aware PPC and funnel designs include adaptive-gain and MIMO funnel controllers [10, 11, 12], bang-bang designs [13, 14], disturbance-regularity and bounded-gain methods [15, 16, 17], and approximation-free constrained PPC [18]. Flexible envelopes, switching mechanisms, auxiliary dynamics, observers, and neural or fuzzy approximators have also been employed [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. Recent underwater-vehicle work combines prescribed performance with dynamic compensation, neural approximation, filtering, and velocity observation to handle saturation and uncertainty [25]. Although effective, the use of such structures increases implementation complexity on robotic platforms that usually operate with limited computational capabilities.

Among low-complexity alternatives, an adjustable outer funnel is employed in [26], adaptive performance bounds are adopted in [21, 27], and desired-motion modification is considered in [28, 29] to recover feasibility. The MIMO adaptive performance design of [21] exploits the available control authority across the input channels. However, its adaptation mechanism contains the saturation mismatch divided by the normalized error |ξi|<1|\xi_{i}|<1, together with user-selected cross-channel coupling parameters. Consequently, its saturation-induced relaxation contains a term of order 𝒪⁡(|Δ​τi|/|ξi|)\mathcal{O}(|\Delta\tau_{i}|/|\xi_{i}|), where Δ​τi\Delta\tau_{i} denotes the mismatch between the saturated and required unsaturated input. The scalar design of [27] instead adapts the performance envelope directly through |Δ​τi||\Delta\tau_{i}|, avoids divisions by the normalized error, and yields an 𝒪⁡(|Δ​τi|)\mathcal{O}(|\Delta\tau_{i}|) degradation bound, but it does not address coupled MIMO dynamics. Reference modification methods preserve the nominal performance funnel by altering the commanded motion. In particular, [30] treats uncertain MIMO systems with coupled and constrained inputs and obtains a mismatch-dependent tracking bound through reference adaptation rather than performance adaptation. In contrast, [28] does not consider the state-dependent cross-channel input coupling induced by the inverse inertia matrix. Therefore, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, no low-complexity adaptive performance result has yet considered direct mismatch-proportional adaptation of the performance bounds and an explicit treatment of the coupled input action of uncertain Euler–Lagrange underwater vehicles. This combination is challenging because the inverse inertia matrix maps each saturated generalized input into multiple acceleration channels. Saturation in one channel can thus affect all filtered errors, invalidating the decoupled invariant-set arguments employed in the scalar case [27].

Motivated by the aforementioned discussion, we develop an adaptive PPC framework for uncertain AUV Euler–Lagrange dynamics with coupled and saturated inputs. Each performance function is driven directly by the corresponding saturation mismatch and recovers its prescribed form exponentially when saturation is inactive, while the desired trajectory remains unchanged. To overcome the coupling challenge, we construct a coupled invariant set and a saturation-aware auxiliary Lyapunov function whose cancellation structure exploits the positive definite symmetric part of the inverse inertia matrix. This establishes boundedness of all closed-loop signals, explicit feasibility conditions, and a tracking degradation bound that is linear in the saturation mismatch, without the normalized-error denominator appearing in [21].

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose a low-complexity adaptive prescribed performance trajectory tracking controller for uncertain AUV Euler–Lagrange dynamics with saturated generalized inputs and coupled error channels, without reference modification, dedicated controller-side observers, regressors, neural networks, or fuzzy approximators.

We establish boundedness and adaptive prescribed performance through a coupled invariant-set argument and an auxiliary Lyapunov function tailored to the saturation mismatch.

We derive explicit sufficient feasibility conditions linking the required saturation levels to the performance envelopes, controller gains, uncertain dynamics, and the positive definite symmetric part of the inverse inertia matrix, together with a mismatch-dependent tracking degradation bound.

We validate the design through comparative BlueROV2 simulations and a real-time pool experiment.

The analysis explicitly accommodates coupled MIMO dynamics and constrained generalized inputs while retaining the commanded trajectory and adapting only the performance functions.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II states the AUV model, assumptions, and control objective. Section III presents the adaptive PPC design and the stability and performance analysis. Section IV reports comparative simulations and experimental validation, and Section V concludes the paper.

1. We propose a low-complexity adaptive prescribed performance trajectory tracking controller for uncertain AUV Euler–Lagrange dynamics with saturated generalized inputs and coupled error channels, without reference modification, dedicated controller-side observers, regressors, neural networks, or fuzzy approximators.

2. We establish boundedness and adaptive prescribed performance through a coupled invariant-set argument and an auxiliary Lyapunov function tailored to the saturation mismatch.

3. We derive explicit sufficient feasibility conditions linking the required saturation levels to the performance envelopes, controller gains, uncertain dynamics, and the positive definite symmetric part of the inverse inertia matrix, together with a mismatch-dependent tracking degradation bound.

4. We validate the design through comparative BlueROV2 simulations and a real-time pool experiment.

5. The analysis explicitly accommodates coupled MIMO dynamics and constrained generalized inputs while retaining the commanded trajectory and adapting only the performance functions.

title: LEAP: Gradient Flow Augmented Lagrangian Trajectory Optimization for Contact Constrained Robots
authors: César E. Ramos Chuquiure,Ryan Tsai,Yutong Zhou,Zihang Huang,Vansh Thakur,Akshunn Trivedi,Zachary Lin,Pearl Lin,Ruikai Yang,Challen Enninful Adu,Ram Vasudevan
abstract:
Generating dynamically feasible motions for legged and manipulating robots requires solving a large, nonlinear, non-convex optimal control problem (OCP) in which contact wrenches must satisfy friction-cone constraints throughout the motion, not only at isolated instants.
Existing solvers are sensitive to the initial guess and scale poorly with the number of joints.
This paper introduces LEAP, which transcribes the OCP with pseudospectral collocation and, instead of a Newton or SQP solve, integrates a primal–dual gradient flow of a Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar augmented Lagrangian to compute a solution.
Because the flow is stiff, this paper designs a linearly implicit integrator with a Gauss–Newton metric, momentum, and a merit-based step controller that keeps the augmented Lagrangian monotone.
Across locomotion benchmarks on five robot platforms, from planar hoppers to 32-joint humanoids, LEAP is the only method to solve every tested problem, achieves substantial speedups over Crocoddyl and Aligator on several benchmarks, and reaches trackable references at smaller compute budgets.
The resulting trajectories are validated by tracking them in a high-fidelity simulator and on hardware.
We will make the code public upon final acceptance of this paper.
introduction:
Robots interact with the world through contact: a humanoid walks by planting and lifting its feet, a manipulator pushes, grasps and releases objects, and a quadruped climbs by loading and unloading its limbs.
Planning such motions means choosing joint torques and contact forces that respect the robot’s dynamics, its actuation limits, and the physics of contact, which requires the contact wrench to stay inside a friction cone at every instant.
Trajectory optimization formalizes this as an Optimal Control Problem (OCP) over hybrid dynamics: minimize a cost, subject to the equations of motion in each contact mode, and the constraints above.

Solving this OCP is difficult for three reasons.
The dynamics are nonlinear and change discontinuously across contact modes.
The constraints, in particular the friction cones and the dynamics themselves, are nonlinear and non-convex, and any solver must decide how to enforce them and where in time.
And the resulting problem is non-convex in the decision variables, so the outcome depends on the initial guess, and a good one is often unavailable for a new behavior or a new robot.
We refer to these as the dynamics, constraint, and initialization challenges.

State-of-the-art solvers exploit the temporal structure of the dynamics to make each iteration cheap.
Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) methods such as Crocoddyl [17] and Aligator [11] combine quadratic approximations of the value function with multiple shooting, and direct methods such as acados [24, 26] transcribe the OCP into a nonlinear program (NLP) with banded structure.
In both families each iteration is a Newton-type step, and this is what makes the constraint and initialization challenges persist.
A Newton step is only meaningful near a solution, so these solvers rely on a good warm start and on line-search or trust-region globalization whose parameters must be tuned per problem.
Constraints are handled by penalties, by projection onto a box, or by an augmented Lagrangian inside the Riccati recursion, and they are enforced only at discrete knots, so the friction cone can be violated between them. In Section V illustrates that, on the contact-constrained problems, these solvers scale poorly with the number of joints and their performance depends strongly on hyper-parameters.

Gradient flows (GF) offer a different way to handle the initialization challenge.
Instead of taking Newton steps, the trajectory is deformed continuously in a pseudo-time until it becomes stationary for an action functional.
Every step of the flow is a descent step that is well defined anywhere, not only near a solution, so the method tolerates poor initial guesses and admits continuation naturally.
[15] and [14] introduced the Affine Geometric Heat Flow (AGHF), whose steady state solves the OCP, and [6], [16] and [7] extended it to free boundary conditions and to low-dimensional legged systems.
[1] and [2] improved the numerics to reach higher-dimensional systems, and [13]extends the idea to extended Lagrangians.
What these methods gain on initialization they give back on the other two challenges.
Constraints enter as quadratic penalties, so they are never satisfied exactly, and raising the penalty to reduce the violation makes the flow stiffer.
The stiff flow is then integrated with general-purpose solvers whose error control is unaware of the optimization structure, so the dynamics challenge reappears as a numerical one.

This paper introduces LEAP, a gradient-flow trajectory optimizer for robots in contact under a prescribed contact sequence, together with a numerical scheme designed for that flow.
It keeps the robustness to initialization of gradient flows while resolving the aforementioned constraint and stiffness problems.
Our contributions are four-fold:
First, we utilize a Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar (PHR) augmented Lagrangian formulation and derive a two-time-scale primal–dual flow to enable exact constraint handling (Section III).
Second, we describe how to extend this approach to hybrid dynamical systems and illustrate how to ensure that wrench feasibility is satisfied for all timein Lemma 2.
Third, we develop a linearly implicit solver to ensure that the augmented Lagrangian monotonically decreases along the numerical solution to the primal-dual flow (Section IV).

Finally, we compare LEAP against Crocoddyl and Aligator on solve time and terminal tracking accuracy under a time budget across two tasks and five robots with two to thirty-two joints with solution quality judged by a whole-body tracking controller in a high-fidelity simulator (Section V).

A hopscotch trajectory is executed on a Unitree Go2 quadruped (Section VI).
