title: Planning to Learn: Real-Time Robust Adaptive Control on the GPU with Guaranteed Future Learning
authors: Anutam Srinivasan,Siddhant Panse,Glen Chou
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.
introduction:
Robots operating in unstructured environments must act safely despite uncertainty in their dynamics and surroundings. Robust control is one approach to achieve this, providing worst-case guarantees by treating uncertainty as persistently adversarial, propagating reachable tubes over admissible uncertainty, and tightening constraints accordingly. While this is appropriate for irreducible aleatoric uncertainty, it can be overly conservative for epistemic uncertainty arising from unknown but learnable physical parameters such as mass, friction, wind, or motor damage. Because this structured uncertainty can be reduced through interaction, robust adaptive control can become less conservative as parameter estimates improve online. As data is collected and parameter uncertainty shrinks, controllers can safely exploit the reduced uncertainty to improve performance. Moreover, because the rate of learning depends on how informative the chosen trajectory is, control actions can directly influence future parameter uncertainty, creating a tradeoff between performance, robustness, and information gathering.

However, designing robust adaptive controllers for robotics remains an open problem, with two central challenges. First, synthesizing adaptive controllers while jointly reasoning about estimation error, aleatoric uncertainty, and parametric uncertainty is computationally expensive for long-horizon, high-dimensional nonlinear systems, yet practical robotic systems require real-time learning, verification, and controller adaptation. Second, many existing methods update parameter estimates online but plan using the current parameter uncertainty set, incorporating newly learned information only reactively after measurements are collected. As a result, they cannot exploit guaranteed future uncertainty reduction during planning and may produce unnecessarily large reachable tubes even along informative trajectories. For example, a drone traversing an uncertain but learnable wind field should be able to plan knowing that it can measure, estimate, and compensate for the wind during execution. Ignoring this future learning can degrade performance or prevent task completion, while also leading to myopic planning that fails to seek informative trajectories that accelerate uncertainty reduction. Addressing these challenges requires jointly modeling the state and parameter-estimate dynamics while efficiently forecasting the worst-case learning guaranteed under all admissible uncertainties.

In this work, we close these gaps with A-SLS, a scalable robust adaptive policy optimization framework that explicitly accounts for future learning during planning. Building on system-level synthesis (SLS) [1], we augment the physical state with the online parameter estimate so that estimator evolution becomes part of the closed-loop dynamics. We propagate bounded parameter uncertainty and parameter-estimate shifts over the planning horizon, while adaptive SLS responses preserve correlations among process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tighter reachable tubes. Crucially, this enables assured future learning: for each candidate trajectory, we forecast the parameter uncertainty guaranteed to remain after future observations, allowing the optimizer to exploit worst-case future tube contraction without assuming favorable measurements. Because informativeness depends on the trajectory, the same formulation can also favor motions that accelerate uncertainty reduction. Finally, the structured SLS policy class admits efficient parallel reachability and robust constraint tightening, enabling GPU-parallel optimization for long-horizon, high-dimensional nonlinear systems. Our contributions are:

We formulate learning-aware robust adaptive control as an SLS problem that augments the state with the online parameter estimate, returning policies that adapt to online data while remaining robust to residual uncertainty.

We derive reachable sets that preserve correlations between disturbances, parameter error, and estimate shifts, enabling tightened robust tubes that account for and guarantee future learning. These information-sensitive tubes also enable planning that favors informative trajectories that reduce uncertainty and improve performance.

We develop a GPU-parallel solver that enables real-time long-horizon control on high-DoF nonlinear systems.

We evaluate safety, tube tightness, parameter learning, active information gathering, and scalability on high-dimensional nonlinear robotic systems and hardware.

1. We formulate learning-aware robust adaptive control as an SLS problem that augments the state with the online parameter estimate, returning policies that adapt to online data while remaining robust to residual uncertainty.

2. We derive reachable sets that preserve correlations between disturbances, parameter error, and estimate shifts, enabling tightened robust tubes that account for and guarantee future learning. These information-sensitive tubes also enable planning that favors informative trajectories that reduce uncertainty and improve performance.

3. We develop a GPU-parallel solver that enables real-time long-horizon control on high-DoF nonlinear systems.

4. We evaluate safety, tube tightness, parameter learning, active information gathering, and scalability on high-dimensional nonlinear robotic systems and hardware.

title: EgoJEPA: Beyond Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Videos
authors: Meng Cao,Can Zhao,Jinjie Wei,Haonan Zhao,Yulong Zhang,Duo Han,Xiaofan Li,Ziwu Song,Rongtao Xu,Ruyi Gan,Hao Wang,Qian Wang,Daolin Ma,Ian Reid,Xiaodan Liang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Egocentric human videos offer a scalable alternative to costly robot demonstrations, yet transferring their manipulation priors to robot control remains challenging. The commonly adopted retargeting-based approaches convert human wrist and finger poses into embodiment-specific action commands through hand-crafted geometric mappings. However, such mappings require meticulous recalibration across different embodiments and risk propagating hand-tracking errors into downstream robot control pipelines. To this end, we propose EgoJEPA, a three-stage framework that learns embodiment-agnostic representations from egocentric human videos without rule-based human-to-robot retargeting: 1) Human-action pre-training learns effect-aware latent actions through JEPA-style visual prediction conditioned on hand-motion differences; 2) Latent-action-based world modeling jointly predicts future visual dynamics and latent actions, which decouples human prior pre-training from robot-specific control parameterizations; 3) Embodiment-specific tuning adapts the pretrained model to diverse robots through lightweight action adapters. Experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of EgoJEPA. It achieves a 74% average success rate under the out-of-domain evaluation, compared with 65% for the retargeting baseline, while reducing cumulative cross-embodiment wall-clock cost by 47.2%, from 743.2 to 392.7 hours.
introduction:
Despite recent advances in robotic manipulation policies (Chi et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024), scaling such systems remains constrained by their reliance on task-specific robot demonstrations, typically obtained through teleoperation or specialized capture systems (Zhao et al., 2023; Khazatsky et al., 2024; Chi et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). Collecting these demonstrations is costly, labor-intensive, and time-consuming, posing a significant bottleneck to scalable robot learning. In contrast, egocentric human videos provide a scalable supervision source for transferring manipulation skills from human hand-object interactions to robotic systems (Ma et al., 2026b; Feng et al., 2026).

Earlier action-free methods operate without explicit hand-pose annotations, instead learning latent action representations directly from inter-frame visual dynamics (Ye et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; Bjorck et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024). However, the resulting representations may capture generic visual variations rather than action-induced physical effects, limiting their interpretability and transferability to robot control. To move beyond learning solely from visual supervision, recent approaches explicitly leverage human hand-pose annotations and adopt a retargeting-based pipeline (Kareer et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026c). Specifically, human hand motions, such as wrist and finger poses, are captured using specialized devices (e.g., Leap Motion (Weichert et al., 2013) or Aria glasses (Engel et al., 2023)) and subsequently mapped to a target robot action space through hand-crafted rules for policy pre-training or human-robot co-training.

Despite the intuitive formulation, the retargeting pipeline suffers from two key limitations: 1) Embodiment-specific mapping. Retargeting relies on low-level geometric or kinematic mappings tailored to a particular robot embodiment, rather than learning transferable action semantics. Consequently, such mappings are tightly coupled to the robot morphology and typically require meticulous recalibration whenever either changes. As shown in Figure 1 (a), human–robot calibration alone takes 52.1 hours, accounting for 25.2% of the total pipeline time. Figure 1 (b) shows that this cost compounds when scaling to multiple robots, i.e., retargeting must repeat the embodiment-specific human-robot calibration and pre-training whenever the robot morphology changes, which causes the cumulative wall-clock time to grow rapidly. 2) Noise propagation. Retargeting is highly sensitive to errors in estimated human motion. Hand-pose estimation noise caused by occlusions, viewpoint variations, or temporal jitter can propagate through the retargeting process, resulting in physically infeasible robot actions. As a concrete stress test, we inject Gaussian noise into human action annotations while keeping robot training unchanged. As shown in Figure 6 (a), under a mild per-axis position noise of σ=10\sigma=10 mm, the retargeting pipeline on the task of bottle cap unscrewing drops drastically from 60% to 30% success rate, showing that annotation errors are directly amplified into downstream robot control failures.

To this end, we propose EgoJEPA, an Egocentric instantiation of the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (Assran et al., 2023) that learns embodiment-agnostic latent action representations from human videos. As shown in Figure 1, EgoJEPA comprises three stages: 1) Human-action pre-training learns generic effect-aware latent actions through human-motion-conditioned visual prediction; 2) Latent-action-based world modeling jointly predicts future visual dynamics and the latent actions learned in Stage 1 via joint flow matching, rather than embodiment-specific robot commands; and 3) Embodiment-specific tuning adapts the pre-trained world model to robot action spaces through lightweight adapters. Evaluated on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments (two dexterous hands and a gripper), EgoJEPA achieves the highest average success rate of 74% under the out-of-domain evaluation, outperforming the action-free method LAPA (Ye et al., 2025), the retargeting pipeline, and the prior egocentric human-video method DexWild (Tao et al., 2025). In addition, EgoJEPA significantly reduces the cost of scaling across robot embodiments. By reusing Stage 1–2 models and adapting only Stage 3 for each new robot, EgoJEPA reduces cumulative wall-clock cost from 743.2 to 392.7 hours over retargeting (c.f. Figure 1 (b)).

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose EgoJEPA, a JEPA-style framework that eliminates the need for rule-based human-to-robot retargeting by learning embodiment-agnostic representations from human videos.

We introduce effect-aware latent actions as a transferable interface between human motion priors and robot control, enabling efficient policy adaptation across diverse embodiments via lightweight action adapters.

Extensive experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments demonstrate the effectiveness and cross-embodiment scalability of EgoJEPA.

1. We propose EgoJEPA, a JEPA-style framework that eliminates the need for rule-based human-to-robot retargeting by learning embodiment-agnostic representations from human videos.

2. We introduce effect-aware latent actions as a transferable interface between human motion priors and robot control, enabling efficient policy adaptation across diverse embodiments via lightweight action adapters.

3. Extensive experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments demonstrate the effectiveness and cross-embodiment scalability of EgoJEPA.

title: TGrasp6D: Task-Informed Vision-Language Priors and Pose Refinement enable Zero-Shot Task-Oriented 6DoF Grasping
authors: Manav Kulshrestha,Apoorva Vashisth,Damon Conover,Aniket Bera
abstract:
Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) has emerged as an important skill for purposeful robotic manipulation.
Given the task of using a knife to “slice bread,” a robot must choose to grasp from the handle, whereas for “hand[ing] the knife over,” it is preferable for the handle to remain unobstructed for safe handoff.
Current approaches for TOG either focus on 2D planar grasping, remain limited by their reliance on task-agnostic grasp generators, or are constrained by reliance on finite, manually-annotated, task-specific grasp datasets that cannot cover all possible grasp-task pairs. To that end, we present TGrasp6D, a vision-language based approach for generating task-oriented 6DoF grasps in a zero-shot manner.
Given a task and a single RGB-D image of an associated object, TGrasp6D reasons about the appropriate semantic affordance for the given task and object geometry to produce an initial task-informed prior.
This generated prior is further refined via 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art success rate of 94% on the TaskGrasp dataset, with the best baseline at 74%.
We also deploy our approach on a Franka Research 3 robot to demonstrate zero-shot generalization to real world objects.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation, and specifically robotic grasping, is a fundamental capability for enabling robots to physically interact with, and operate, in the real world [23, 12].
Recent methods have significantly advanced this field [11, 1, 10] by prediction of stable grasps for diverse objects.
However, a stable grasp solves half the problem: it does not consider whether the resulting hand-object configuration will support the intended task.
Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) captures this coupling between grasp and intent, requiring joint reasoning over object affordances and task semantics, rather than treating grasp selection as a purely geometric problem.
This matters wherever robots operate around humans or chain manipulation steps together – an assistive robot handing over a tool, or an industrial arm that must re-grasp a part differently depending on whether it’s inserting or fastening.

Various methods have been proposed for TOG.
Training-based approaches [20, 19, 4, 14] rely on large human-annotated datasets of object-task-grasps labels [14].
However, due to the boundedness of these datasets in the space of valid grasps and possible tasks, even large annotation efforts [4] yield sparse coverage.
Hence, their performance [20, 19, 4, 14] is capped by the dataset size, and generalization to novel task-object combinations remains limited.
Many approaches [20, 19, 5, 8, 22] attempt to bypass the generative aspect of grasp synthesis by coupling with a task-free generator [18, 26, 6] and then scoring the resulting grasps for the given task, essentially reducing the problem to that of score regression.
By injecting task semantics onto task-agnostic grasp priors, these methods are bottlenecked by the coverage of the upstream generator: if no candidate near the task-relevant region was proposed, no downstream semantic reasoning can recover it.
Finally, planar-grasp methods [24, 7, 21, 13] restrict prediction to the image plane, discarding a broad class of feasible grasps with out-of-plane approach directions.

In contrast, large vision-language models offer a different foundation for TOG.
Pretrained on internet scale image-text corpora, they encode priors over object semantics and functional affordances without requiring the exhaustive supervision that prior TOG methods depend on.
These priors, however, are expressed in the image and text modalities that the models were trained on.
Extending their reasoning requires situating the model in the three-dimensional, geometric space where manipulation actually occurs.

Hence, we present TGrasp6D, a framework that leverages VLMs to synthesize 6DoF task-oriented grasps in a zero-shot manner, requiring no task-specific training or fine-tuning.
Given a single RGB-D observation of an object and a natural language task instruction, TGrasp6D first reasons jointly over the object’s geometry and semantics to identify the task-relevant grasp affordance, then localizes this affordance within the image.
To bridge the resulting image-space localization into 3D, we lift it into a plane consistent with the camera’s projective geometry, yielding a task-informed grasp prior around the localized affordance.
Candidate grasps sampled within this prior are then refined through pose optimization that trades off collision avoidance against consistency with the task-relevant region, yielding grasps that are simultaneously geometrically feasible and appropriate to the task at hand.
In summary, we make the following four contributions:

We introduce TGrasp6D, a zero-shot framework for task-oriented 6DoF grasping from a single RGB-D observation and natural-language task instruction.

Our VLM-guided grasp synthesis pipeline grounds task-relevant affordances in image space, lifting them into 3D task-informed grasp priors, and refining candidate grasps through collision-aware pose optimization.

TGrasp6D achieves a 94% success rate on the TaskGrasp benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline by ∼𝟐𝟎%\mathbf{\sim 20\%}.

We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to real-world manipulation on a Franka Research 3 robot across novel objects and task instructions.

1. We introduce TGrasp6D, a zero-shot framework for task-oriented 6DoF grasping from a single RGB-D observation and natural-language task instruction.

2. Our VLM-guided grasp synthesis pipeline grounds task-relevant affordances in image space, lifting them into 3D task-informed grasp priors, and refining candidate grasps through collision-aware pose optimization.

3. TGrasp6D achieves a 94% success rate on the TaskGrasp benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline by ∼𝟐𝟎%\mathbf{\sim 20\%}.

4. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to real-world manipulation on a Franka Research 3 robot across novel objects and task instructions.

title: BubbleCBF: Constructive Safety for Second-Order Systems and Application to Autonomous Robot Navigation in Unknown Environments
authors: Mani Amani,Mohammed Alyaseen,Zhirui Dai,Ki Myung Brian Lee,Nikolay Atanasov,Jorge Cortes
abstract:
Satisfying safety constraints for systems with second-order dynamics is challenging because a position constraint may require infeasible deceleration. Higher-order control barrier functions (CBFs) provide an approach for expressing safety conditions for such systems but feasibility depends on the system dynamics and available control authority. We develop a constructive approach for designing feasible safety constraints for second-order control-affine systems. Starting from a signed distance function (SDF), we construct collision-free spheres, i.e., bubbles, in position space, and use their quadratic geometry and overlap to construct a velocity-dependent safety constraint. The associated safe set is represented as a union of intersections and enforced through a quadratic-program safety filter. Under mild assumptions on the dynamics, bubble overlap, and design parameters, we prove that the quadratic-program-based controller is well defined, continuous in the system state, and renders the set forward invariant. We also derive sufficient conditions for feasibility under bounded inputs. We demonstrate that our BubbleCBF, applied to a differential-drive robot, achieves safe autonomous navigation in unknown environments. Videos and results are available at:
https://existentialrobotics.org/bubblecbf/.
introduction:
Autonomous navigation in unknown environments requires a robot to simultaneously build a map of its surroundings and execute actions that avoid collisions.
Beyond representing obstacle-free space, robots with second-order dynamics must ensure that feasible actions exist to enforce safety constraints. Since actuation enters at the acceleration level, a robot may remain positionally safe while approaching the boundary too quickly for any admissible input to prevent escape.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) [1] provide a principled approach for safe control design. A CBF limits how quickly the safe set boundary may be approached with rate dependent on the barrier value.
Far from the boundary, the barrier value may decrease more quickly, while near the boundary, the permitted decrease becomes increasingly restrictive. Signed distance functions (SDFs) are natural CBF candidates because they encode free space using the distance to the nearest boundary [2]. SDF models of the environment can be estimated from point-cloud observations using data-driven and probabilistic approaches, including neural implicit methods [3] and Gaussian-process methods [4]. However, for second-order systems, a position-dependent safety constraint has relative degree two and cannot be enforced by formulating CBF constraints directly from SDF values. Higher-order CBFs (HOCBFs) [5] formulate safety constraints for high-relative-degree systems but do not by themselves guarantee the existence of feasible control inputs. A key challenge in safe control synthesis for second-order systems is therefore to construct valid safe sets in the joint position-velocity space whose invariance can be enforced with admissible inputs.

To address this challenge, we develop BubbleCBF, a safe control method for second-order control-affine systems. Starting from an SDF representation of the obstacles, we derive a velocity-dependent safe set from overlapping collision-free spheres, i.e., bubbles, illustrated in Fig. 1. Our design extends the union-of-intersections CBF approach of [6] to quadratic constraints and guarantees forward-invariance of the safe set and feasibility under input constraints. Our contributions are summarized as follows.

We develop BubbleCBF, a safe control method for second-order control-affine systems that constructs velocity-dependent CBFs from position-space bubbles.

We develop BubbleCBF, a safe control method for second-order control-affine systems that constructs velocity-dependent CBFs from position-space bubbles.

Under mild assumptions on the system dynamics, bubble overlap, and input constraints, we prove that the quadratic program (QP) for BubbleCBF is feasible over the safe set, and renders the set forward invariant.

BubbleCBF enables safe autonomous navigation with a Clearpath Jackal robot in real-world environments, achieving a 100% success rate, compared to 50% for an SDF-CBF baseline, while increasing average obstacle clearance by 4.8%.

1. We develop BubbleCBF, a safe control method for second-order control-affine systems that constructs velocity-dependent CBFs from position-space bubbles.

2. Under mild assumptions on the system dynamics, bubble overlap, and input constraints, we prove that the quadratic program (QP) for BubbleCBF is feasible over the safe set, and renders the set forward invariant.

3. BubbleCBF enables safe autonomous navigation with a Clearpath Jackal robot in real-world environments, achieving a 100% success rate, compared to 50% for an SDF-CBF baseline, while increasing average obstacle clearance by 4.8%.

title: Optimally Trading Energy for Information through Speed Trajectory Optimization of Sustainably Powered Mobile Robots
authors: Kavin M. Govindarajan,Dimitra Panagou,Chris Vermillion
abstract: Sustainably powered mobile robots enable long-duration observational missions by harvesting energy from the environment. However, effective autonomy requires the robots to make decisions as to how to allocate this energy to maximize information quality over time. In this paper, we study a persistent (infinite-horizon) speed trajectory optimization problem that is posed as a periodic optimal control problem in which a robot repeatedly traverses a fixed closed path, coupling a super-linear propulsion cost with dynamic information gain and decay. Using the information-theoretic quantity of clarity as an information metric, we first derive the necessary conditions for optimal control. We then derive a number of specialized follow-on properties, which characterize (i) the nature of the optimal control when points on the path are of varying importance and when they are of equal importance, along with (ii) a high-speed information limit that is approached when energy reserves approach infinity. We illustrate the information-optimal speed trajectories on a simple example in order to showcase key trends that are followed under the optimized speed profile. This is followed by a simulation study based on the persistent characterization of salinity in the Chesapeake Bay, illustrating the practical merit of applying the results from this work.

title: Race to Recovery: Designing Advanced Safety Systems for Autonomous Driving via Learning Autonomous Racing
authors: Teodor Ilie,Kleber Cabral,Sidney Givigi
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Vehicles
abstract: Vehicles that lose control at the handling limit through icing, hydroplaning, or an abrupt evasive maneuver fall outside the operating envelope of production safety systems such as electronic stability control, which focus on preventing instability rather than recovering from it. Expert drivers regain authority in these conditions by drifting. Existing autonomous recovery approaches are validated on idealized scenarios, define “recovered” states empirically and inconsistently, or rely on offline-planned trajectories rather than acting online. We address these gaps by first training a racing policy with reinforcement learning that learns drifting as a time-optimal maneuver, then adapting it to recovery through continued training with a minimum-time reward. We define recovery relative to a phase-plane-grounded stable equilibrium and introduce Gym-Khana for controller training and evaluation. Across 294 initial loss-of-control states, the transferred policy improves recovery by 186.8%186.8\% over a Stanley path tracker and outperforms both a nonlinear model predictive controller and a recovery-only policy trained from scratch, while also recovering faster on states the baseline can already handle. An ablation shows that racing pretraining, rather than broader initial-state exposure alone, drives this gain. Deployed on a physical 1:10-scale F1TENTH vehicle using system identification, actuator-lag modelling, and domain randomization, the transferred policy outperforms Stanley on every tested loss-of-control state, including recovering 50%50\% of the time from a hard state the baseline never recovers from.
introduction:
Usually, driving takes place in the linear tire regime, where manual inputs or conventional controllers perform well. Controlling a vehicle safely at the limit of handling remains an open challenge. Events that could cause loss of control, such as driving on ice, high-speed hydroplaning, or a sudden evasive maneuver, are rare but dangerous, and excessive speed alone is a factor in roughly a third of all traffic fatalities [1]. They are also the events an advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) is least able to help with. Production systems such as electronic stability control (ESC) are designed to keep the vehicle inside a conservative, linear-tire handling envelope, braking individual wheels to suppress the onset of tire saturation. That design is well suited to preventing a loss of control, but not to act once one has occurred: beyond this stable envelope, suppressing instability is no longer the same problem as recovering from it.

Expert rally and drift drivers, by contrast, routinely operate at the limit by “drifting”, where they intentionally saturate the tires to sustain large sideslip angles. Saturation decouples the direction the vehicle points from the direction it travels, giving the driver direct lateral control through two inputs, steering and throttle, rather than one, enabling more agile vehicle control [2]. This is the authority an expert exploits when control is lost, while current production safety systems cannot. Recent research has begun to reproduce this capability autonomously in the service of active safety, using drift-based control to regain control of the vehicle in scenarios where conventional safety systems fall short [3, 4]. We call this task recovery: returning an out-of-control vehicle to a stable driving state while keeping it on its intended path. We aim to develop a controller that recovers from the broadest possible set of loss-of-control states and recovers in the least time while remaining within the track. Our motivation is to endow an ADAS with the recovery skill of an expert driver.

Existing autonomous approaches to recovery, however, leave three elements unresolved. Each addresses a single narrow, idealized scenario from a fixed initial condition, so nothing is established about the range of loss-of-control states from which a controller can recover [5, 6]. Each defines the “recovered” state empirically, and differently, so no two results are comparable. And the one method validated on a real vehicle relies on a trajectory planned offline in advance [3], whereas an intervention must act online, from whatever state the vehicle is in.

A recovery controller that closes these gaps must therefore act online, without a precomputed plan, across a broad domain of loss-of-control states in the saturated-tire regime. That is the regime of racing and drifting at the limit of handling, where reinforcement learning (RL) has been shown to outperform state-of-the-art model predictive control (MPC) [7, 8].
We therefore derive the controller with RL, focusing on the control task in particular, assuming knowledge of the vehicle state, and leave perception, state estimation, and planning out of our scope. The open question is how to set up training.

Our central insight is that the answer lies in racing. The recovery task has much in common with drifting: both are defined primarily by a large sideslip angle and yaw rate, but where a racing driver produces the drift state intentionally, a loss of control is an unwanted drift that can lead to a collision. A policy that has learned to race by drifting has, in the process, learned to manage saturated tires and large sideslip angles across the whole regime, which is precisely the competency that recovery requires. We therefore investigate the following hypothesis: a policy first trained to race with drifting, and then adapted to recovery, recovers control more reliably than a policy trained on recovery alone, and more reliably than classical control baselines. To test it, we train a racing policy in Gym-Khana, a simulator we built for prototyping vehicle control at the limit, adapt it to recovery by continuing training under a minimum-time recovery reward, and deploy the result on a 1:10-scale F1TENTH vehicle [9].

In summary, our contributions are:

A racing-to-recovery transfer learning method, which builds a recovery controller by pretraining a policy to race with drifting and then adapting it to recovery. Over a grid of 294294 initial states spanning conditions more extreme than any seen in training, the transferred policy recovers 186.8%186.8\% more than a Stanley path tracker, and outperforms both a model predictive controller and a recovery-only policy trained from scratch.
Additionally, we demonstrate that even non-specialized racing policies recover competently with no recovery-specific training (Sections IV-C and V-C).

Gym-Khana, a simulator for prototyping vehicle control at the limit of handling, built around the drift-capable single-track model used here, on which both the racing and recovery policies are trained (Section IV). It is released open-source, with online documentation.11

Validation on a physical F1TENTH vehicle, enabled by a sim-to-real pipeline of system identification, actuator-lag modelling, and domain randomization. title: Clarity-Driven Adaptive Mission Planning for a Solar-Powered Autonomous Surface Vessel
authors: Kavin M. Govindarajan,Kaleb Ben Naveed,David Li,Devansh R. Agrawal,Mary Maceda,Matthew Bryant,Dimitra Panagou,Chris Vermillion
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive methodology, backed by simulation and experimental results, for an adaptive mission planning strategy that is mathematically grounded in the maximization of the information-driven quantity of clarity. In particular, the methodology introduced in this work addresses the use of sustainably powered autonomous surface vessels (ASVs) to perform scientific missions that prioritize locations of maximum interest. Because these locations of maximum interest are not known a priori but are rather identified based on in-situ measurements, online adaptation is essential for mission planning. Furthermore, the reliance on a limited-power renewable resource requires an adaptation strategy that maximizes information gathering subject to mobility restrictions imposed by the renewable resource. Our approach addresses these challenges through a clarity-driven ergodic search, where clarity represents a mathematical quantity that has been rigorously linked to differential (information) entropy. In our approach, a target clarity map is adapted online to reflect the prioritization of certain areas based on in-situ measurements, and an ergodic path planner continually re-plans based on the target clarity map and ASV speed limitations (driven by the renewable propulsion source). Focusing on a solar-powered ASV, we present simulations and experiments conducted at Jordan Lake, North Carolina, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
introduction:
The collection of spatiotemporally varying data is critical for many environmental and engineering applications: characterizing wind and ocean currents enables the identification of energy-harvesting sites [1], surface temperature data supports improved weather forecasting [2], and salinity data enhances understanding of climate-driven processes [3]. While fixed platforms (e.g., moored sensor arrays [4] and high-frequency radar [5]) enable data acquisition over extended periods, there has been recent emphasis on using mobile observational platforms that can adjust their physical locations to target areas of interest, which are often unknown a priori and can change over time. Mobile observation can be accomplished through vessels equipped with finite amounts of energy (e.g., diesel-powered research vessels [6] and undersea gliders [7, 8]) or through renewably powered platforms (e.g., sailing drones, wave gliders, or solar-powered autonomous surface vessels (ASVs)) that enable longer-term missions. Example applications include tracking plumes of pollutant or contaminant dispersion [9, 10], adaptive front-following for estimating transport and mixing processes [11, 12], and resource measurement (e.g., wind or ocean current) for siting energy-harvesting devices [13, 14].

Regardless of the motivation for adaptation or whether the mobile observational platform at hand is powered by a finite or renewable resource, the basic objective is the same: maximize the collection of useful scientific information under a limited energy resource. In the case of a finite energy resource, the limitations map to a restricted range that is influenced by the device’s velocity profile. In the case of a renewable energy resource, the total range is not limited, but the achievable velocity profile is constrained by the available power. In either case, both the energy and information resources evolve over time. Notably, the information known about the scientific resource at any given location can increase due to sensor measurements but can also decay if that point goes unvisited for a long time. Ultimately, therefore, a unified framework for adaptive mission planning should satisfy three features:

Rigorous consideration of an evolving information field (where information is gained through observation but will also decay over time at points that go unvisited), based on observations taken;

Explicit consideration of an evolving battery state of charge, based on the environmental (solar) energy input and energy used for mobility;

Real-time adaptation based on in-situ scientific measurements.

Information-driven planning has been heavily popularized (see [15, 16]), with efforts often tying information measures to statistical quantities like entropy. To capture complex spatial fields, recent robotic information gathering frameworks employ nonstationary spatiotemporal models for autonomous surface vehicles [17]. However, energy constraints in such formulations are typically imposed as simplistic “budgets” [18] (e.g., total distance, time, or control effort as a surrogate [19]) without accounting for vehicle power dynamics or state of charge (SOC) [20]. Furthermore, standard IPP formulations generally assume non-decaying information, optimizing over truncated horizons for one-off coverage. Consequently, these approaches are prone to local extrema and struggle to sustain long-term tracking of dynamic scientific resources where unvisited locations decay in certainty over time.

A notable exception addressing this limitation is the information-theoretic quantity clarity [21], derived from differential entropy [22], which explicitly models time-varying certainty decay. A natural planning strategy for clarity is ergodic search [23]. By matching the Fourier coefficients of the vehicle’s trajectory statistics to a target spatial distribution (TSD), ergodic control inherently balances exploration and exploitation over long horizons without heuristic switching. Recent efforts have begun incorporating energy awareness into ergodic control: Seewald et al. [24] integrated battery models for multi-agent coverage, while Naveed et al. [25] introduced clarity-driven ergodic search under SOC constraints. However, existing energy-aware ergodic methods rely on static target distributions defined offline, or achieve persistence through multi-agent duty cycling to fixed charging stations rather than optimizing trajectory-level energy dynamics for continuous operation of a single sustainably powered vehicle. In contrast, our work enables real-time, online adaptation of the target clarity map based on in-situ scientific measurements, allowing the planner to dynamically re-prioritize informative regions while explicitly controlling speed to satisfy energy constraints.

The present work extends the framework of [25] by (i) enabling online adaptation according to in-situ measurements, (ii) augmenting the ergodic adaptive mission planner with energy-informed speed control, and (iii) validating the integrated framework experimentally. In particular, we utilize a spatiotemporal Gaussian Process Kalman Filter (STGPKF) to maintain real-time estimates of the prediction means and variances of the scientific quantity of interest, based on real-time, in-situ measurements. From the prediction mean and variance models, we generate both an actual clarity map and a target clarity map. These maps jointly define the ergodic objective, allowing the controller to prioritize scientifically meaningful regions as the environment evolves. Additionally, following our earlier work [26] that established the optimality of piecewise constant speeds when the battery state of charge did not satisfy tightened saturation limits at equality, this speed control approach is incorporated into the ergodic planning problem.

To ground the problem in a real deployment scenario, we focus on a solar-powered ASV, namely the SeaTrac SP-48 (shown in Fig. 1). Both simulation and field trials consider a mission domain in Jordan Lake, North Carolina, where the scientific objective is to characterize the evolving wind resource. Motivated by wind turbine siting studies, wherein regions with wind speeds close to a rated value are of primary interest, we construct the target clarity map from the STGPKF wind speed estimates and their deviation from the rated speed.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are as follows:

We develop an energy-aware, adaptive clarity-driven ergodic control framework that unifies a statistically rigorous information metric with energy-aware speed control.

We introduce an STGPKF-based method that generates real-time actual and target clarity maps from online measurements, enabling fully adaptive, science-aware planning.

We validate the complete framework using both simulations and field experiments on the SeaTrac SP-48 ASV at Jordan Lake, demonstrating that the system actively targets informative regions while respecting energy and speed constraints.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the information (clarity) and energy models used throughout this work. Section III presents the problem formulation and proposed control framework. Section IV evaluates performance in simulation. Section V presents field results from a wind characterization mission on the SeaTrac ASV. Section VI concludes and outlines future research directions.

title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Mozes Jacobs,Aiden Swann,Mathilde Papillon,Siddharth Boppana,Fenil R. Doshi,Usha Bhalla,Thomas Icard,Matt Feiszli,Thomas McGrath,Vasudev Shyam,Demba Ba,Leon Bergen,Nina Miolane,Owen Lewis,Jack Merullo,Ekdeep Singh Lubana,Atticus Geiger,Matthew Kowal,Thomas Fel
comment: pages of main text, 8 main text figures
abstract:
Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it?
Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional.
Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models.
We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp.
The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation.
We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes.
Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept’s shape carries as much importance as its readability.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric. Robotic systems operate in three-dimensional space through articulated kinematic structures, while the objects they manipulate and the tasks they perform have their own geometric organization, including symmetries, constraints, and phases of interaction. Any general manipulation policy must contend with this structure, and vision-language-action (VLA) models have become the dominant paradigm for building such policies (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025b; Lee et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026; Deshpande et al., 2026).
VLAs inherit visual and semantic priors from backbones pretrained on internet-scale data, including vision encoders (Radford et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2024; Zhai et al., 2023), language models (Touvron et al., 2023; Gemma Team et al., 2024), and full vision-language models (Driess et al., 2023; Beyer et al., 2024; Deitke et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024).
This data has grown by orders of magnitude in volume and diversity (O’Neill et al., 2024; Walke et al., 2023; Bu et al., 2025; Deshpande et al., 2026; Bjorck et al., 2025), with generalization improving along power-law-like trends (Lin et al., 2025).
The resulting systems are increasingly capable, general, and even deployed in the real world (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025b; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025a; Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025; Figure AI, 2026; Gemini Robotics Team, 2026; Figure AI, 2025b; Figure AI, 2025a).

How such competence is reflected in the representations of these VLAs is the subject of a nascent literature (Qi et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2026; Swann et al., 2026; Buurmeijer et al., 2026; Häon et al., 2025; Bhardwaj et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2025; Molinari et al., 2025; Khan et al., 2025; Grant et al., 2026; Goyal, 2026; Yang and Mokalla, 2026; Shi et al., 2026).
In particular, one line of work uses probes, testing whether a quantity of interest can be read out from the model’s activations (Joseph et al., 2026; Buurmeijer et al., 2026; Bhardwaj et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2025; Molinari et al., 2025; Grant et al., 2026; Yang and Mokalla, 2026).
A second trains sparse autoencoders (SAEs) (Cunningham et al., 2024; Bussmann et al., 2024; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024b; Fel et al., 2025; Costa et al., 2025; Hindupur et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Bricken et al., 2023; Lubana et al., 2026; Bhalla et al., 2026b; Templeton et al., 2024; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024a; Lieberum et al., 2024; Thasarathan et al., 2025; Makhzani and Frey, 2014) to discover concepts without supervision (Swann et al., 2026; Khan et al., 2025; Grant et al., 2026), and the discovered features even provide control over the policy via steering Joseph et al. (2025).

Both lines of work share a limitation. A probe can ensure that a variable is decodable, yet says nothing about the structure through which the model “realizes” it, and an SAE inherits the linear representation hypothesis (LRH) (Park et al., 2024; Costa et al., 2025), which casts each concept as a single direction in activation space and therefore fixes that structure in advance.
Interpretability for language and vision models, conscious of this limitation, has moved beyond the single direction to multi-dimensional features and curved geometry (Modell et al., 2025; Feucht et al., 2026; Wurgaft et al., 2026; Bhalla et al., 2026a; Fel et al., 2026b; Fel et al., 2026a; Engels et al., 2025; Lubana et al., 2026; Karkada et al., 2026; Dooms and Gauderis, 2025; Kantamneni and Tegmark, 2025; Gurnee et al., 2026; Yocum et al., 2025; Park et al., 2025a; Sarfati et al., 2026; Costa et al., 2025; Pearce et al., 2025; Diego-Simón et al., 2024; Chung et al., 2018; Cohen et al., 2020; Hosseini et al., 2026; Dhimoila et al., 2026; Fel et al., 2025; Gorton, 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Tvetkova et al., 2025; Park et al., 2025b; Park et al., 2026), a line of work now gathered under the name of Neural Geometry (Geiger et al., 2026).

Do VLAs realize their variables through similarly rich geometry? Two facts suggest they might.
First, vision models, including the backbones VLAs inherit, already carry colors, shadows, and position as multi-dimensional features rather than single directions (Fel et al., 2026b; Fel et al., 2026a; Pach et al., 2026; Uselis et al., 2026).
Second, representations tend to inherit the symmetries of their training data, so that cyclic concepts, for example, come to be arranged on circles (Karkada et al., 2026).
The variables a manipulation policy must track, such as poses, distances, contacts, and task phase, are geometric objects with symmetries of their own before the network ever represents them.

We take up this question and make the following contributions:

Realized geometry as a lens for VLA interpretability. We formalize the distinction between concept realization—the capacity to extract information about a concept under a given readout—and its realized geometry—the structure activations trace as the concept varies. Linear readability establishes only that a concept is present, while its realized geometry determines how its values are structured and whether they can be manipulated.

Realized geometry as a lens for VLA interpretability. We formalize the distinction between concept realization—the capacity to extract information about a concept under a given readout—and its realized geometry—the structure activations trace as the concept varies. Linear readability establishes only that a concept is present, while its realized geometry determines how its values are structured and whether they can be manipulated.

A taxonomy of realized geometry in MolmoBot. Combining controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we chart the realized geometry of seven control concepts: gripper state, end-effector position, distance to the target, target object position, contact, task phase, and wrist orientation. We find this geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts: joint limits leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, while the numerical precision of the embedding splits distance into orthogonal coarse (meter-scale) and fine (centimeter-scale) rulers.

Real-world transfer. We reproduce these geometries in π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025b) and MolmoAct2 (Fang et al., 2026) on the real-world DROID dataset (Khazatsky et al., 2024), indicating they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation.

title: Persistent Profile-Guided Reset-Free Recovery Improves Final Gait Selection after Irreversible Leg Damage
authors: Minjoong Kim
abstract: Damage-recovery algorithms often rank gaits from short trials, yet a gait that performs well briefly may not remain effective during continued execution. In reset-free recovery, each trial also changes the physical state inherited by the next. We introduce persistent profile-guided reset-free recovery (PGRR), which predicts multiple outcomes over repeated gait execution and uses conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot. Across 108 matched MuJoCo tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock, PGRR improves final quality by 0.106 and slot-averaged recovery quality (SRQ) by 0.044 relative to an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline, while reducing low-quality failures by 27.8 percentage points. Final-quality gains occur in all three damage classes. Against no adaptation, PGRR also improves final quality and reduces low-quality failures, whereas the aggregate SRQ difference is inconclusive. Development ablations identify conservative uncertainty handling as the clearest supported contributor to the observed gains. These results show that PGRR can identify stronger post-damage gaits under continuous physical state and that final-gait quality and recovery-summary performance provide complementary evidence for evaluating reset-free recovery.
introduction:
Robots enable monitoring and inspection in environments that are difficult or hazardous for people to access. Deployments in nuclear facilities and underwater survey and inspection illustrate the value of performing these tasks remotely or autonomously [1, 2]. As missions extend from individual inspections to repeated operation over days or weeks, maintaining mobility with limited human intervention becomes increasingly important [1]. For a legged robot, structural damage creates a direct obstacle to continued operation because a gait developed for an intact body may no longer produce effective locomotion. Recovering useful motion with the remaining limbs is therefore an important step toward sustained autonomy [3, 4].

Post-damage adaptation has advanced through self-modeling, which revises a robot’s body model after component loss [3], and Intelligent Trial and Error (IT&E), which uses a library of behaviors computed offline to guide a small number of online tests [4]. Reset-free Trial and Error (RTE) further accounts for the physical state left by each preceding attempt [5]. RTE evaluates recovery while successive trials inherit the state produced by earlier ones, but this does not by itself characterize how well the finally selected gait performs when executed separately after adaptation. This distinction matters because every attempted gait changes the robot’s pose, velocity, and contacts. A search may eventually identify an effective gait even if some intermediate trials perform poorly, while a gait that appears promising during a short test may deteriorate during continued execution.

To address this distinction, we propose persistent profile-guided reset-free recovery (PGRR). In an offline stage, candidate gaits are repeatedly executed to learn how their performance changes beyond an initial short trial. These profiles describe survival, early-to-late locomotion quality, final quality, path-related performance, and energy use over continued execution. After damage, PGRR uses these profiles and their predictive uncertainty to select a promising gait for a short online probe. The observed performance is then used to update the predictions, while the best gait identified so far is executed between probes as the incumbent bridge. The robot is not reset between trials: each new probe starts from the physical state left by the preceding motion. In this way, PGRR uses short online tests to search for a gait that is expected to remain effective during continued execution while preserving the robot’s physical state throughout recovery.

We implement PGRR on a simulated hexapod and evaluate it on a frozen holdout of 108 matched condition–seed tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock. Locomotion quality combines forward motion, path tracking, energy use, and transition stability. We report both SRQ, which summarizes recovery under a fixed scoring budget, and the quality of a separate 3-s execution of the selected gait. Relative to the tested IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline, PGRR improves final quality by 0.106 and SRQ by 0.044, while reducing low-quality failures by 27.8 percentage points. Final quality improves in all three damage classes.

This work makes three contributions. First, we distinguish final-gait quality from the overall recovery summary in reset-free damage recovery. Second, we introduce PGRR, which combines repeated-execution profiles, conservative uncertainty-aware selection, short online probes, and incumbent bridging without resetting the robot. Third, we evaluate the method on 108 matched MuJoCo tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock. PGRR improves final-gait quality and reduces low-quality failures, while SRQ gains depend on the comparison baseline. These results show that final performance and recovery-summary performance capture complementary aspects of reset-free recovery.

title: Feasibility Ceilings Before Learning: Sizing and Timing Bounds for Drone-Mesh Interception
authors: Dmytro Babarytskyi

abstract:
A mesh of interceptors defending a fixed site must spread over the predicted
arrival point of an approaching object. This is a recurring task in multi-agent
robotics: NN agents, each covering a disc of radius rr, spread over a
probability density so that a point drawn from it falls within some agent’s
disc. We give closed forms for the quantities that bound performance before any
policy is chosen, and validate each by Monte Carlo. The uncertainty of a point
predicted by extrapolating a noisy linear track follows from least-squares
variance propagation plus a delta-method term for the uncertain arrival time,
agreeing with simulation to within 1.8%1.8\%. The coverage probability of a
packed mesh admits a closed form accurate to 0.0070.007 absolute, with a
volumetric analogue. A naive area ratio misses a ceiling: while agents stay at
least 2​r2r apart, no mesh exceeds 90.69%90.69\% coverage in the plane or 74.05%74.05\%
in a volume. This ceiling belongs to the separation constraint, not to the
problem — permitting overlap substitutes Kershner’s thinnest-covering density
and removes it, the better regime above a crossover at p=0.80p=0.80. Hexagonal
packing is optimal among five arrangements; the centroidal-Voronoi
configuration coverage control supplies reaches only half its coverage at small
budgets. The Gaussian assumption is conservative under heavy tails and
anisotropy but fragile under bias: a one-sigma aim-point offset costs 1414
points of coverage. A repositioning team must also choose a commit time, and
the admissible window can be empty. Against the applicable ceiling, analytic
placement attains 85%85\% of what the configuration permits while centralised
PPO averages 15%15\% over three trainer seeds, with a paired bootstrap against a
null policy containing zero at every seed. We argue such ceilings should be
computed before any learning experiment and quoted alongside every result.
introduction:
A fixed site is approached by an airborne object on a ballistic or
near-ballistic course. A sensor tracks the object and predicts where it will
cross a defensive plane standing off from the site, with an error that shrinks
as the track lengthens. A mesh of small interceptors, each able to engage
whatever comes within a radius rr of it, must spread itself across that
predicted crossing point and be on station before the object arrives. Three
questions decide whether the concept is viable at all, and none of them is
about control: how many interceptors the prediction’s uncertainty demands, how
early the mesh must commit to a position, and whether any commit time satisfies
both the sharpness of the prediction and the distance the vehicles must fly.
All three can be answered from geometry, before a controller exists.

We strip the application to that geometry. Consider a team of NN agents
constrained to a plane, each able to cover a disc of radius rr centred on
itself. A point of interest will arrive somewhere in that plane at a known
future time; the agents hold a noisy prediction of where.
The team must distribute itself so that the arriving point falls inside some
agent’s disc. This is a coverage problem in the sense of Cortés
et al. [1], specialised in two ways that turn out to
matter a great deal. The density is a prediction with a quantified and
time-varying error rather than a static importance map. And success is binary
and instantaneous — a point either lands within rr of some agent or it does
not — rather than an integrated sensing cost.

Tasks of this shape invite a multi-agent reinforcement-learning treatment, and
the recipe is easy to follow: define an environment, shape a reward, train a
policy, report a success rate. The difficulty is that a bare success rate on a
hand-designed task carries almost no information. Whether 16%16\% is a failure
or a near-optimal result depends on what the configuration permits, and that
quantity is rarely computed. Henderson et al. [30],
Colas et al. [31] and Agarwal
et al. [32] have each documented how fragile deep
reinforcement-learning comparisons are to precisely this kind of missing
context — unreported baselines, too few seeds, and point estimates quoted
without dispersion.

This paper supplies the missing context for the coverage task above, in closed
form, and then validates the assumptions the closed form rests on. We
contribute:

the uncertainty σ\sigma of the predicted arrival point, propagated from
per-fix sensor noise through a least-squares track fit, with a
delta-method term that a common heuristic omits at a cost of up to
9.5×9.5\times (Section IV);

the uncertainty σ\sigma of the predicted arrival point, propagated from
per-fix sensor noise through a least-squares track fit, with a
delta-method term that a common heuristic omits at a cost of up to
9.5×9.5\times (Section IV);

the coverage probability attainable by NN agents at given σ\sigma and
rr, in the plane and in a volume, including a ceiling no mesh can exceed
at any size (Section V);

an empirical check that hexagonal packing is the right arrangement, and a
quantification of how far the standard coverage-control answer falls
short of it on this objective (Section VI);

a robustness study of the Gaussian assumption, separating departures that
make the law conservative from the one that breaks it
(Section VII);

the admissible window of commit times for a team that must physically
reposition, which can be empty (Section VIII).

Section X reports what happened when a learned placement
policy was trained on this task, across three trainer seeds, and argues that
the outcome is better explained by these bounds than by any property of the
learner. Section XI states what the analysis omits.

Each individual result applies standard material — ordinary least squares,
the delta method, densest packing of equal spheres. The claim is that
computing them first, and reporting them alongside learned
results, changes what those results mean, and that this is not current
practice.

title: Navigation by Skylight Polarization via Rayleigh Model Optimization on a Road Vehicle
authors: Ben Potter,Eslam Mounier,Aboelmagd Noureldin,Yahia Antar,Muhammad Alam
abstract:
Reliable absolute heading estimation is critical for road-vehicle navigation, particularly when magnetic, inertial, or GNSS-based references are degraded.
This paper presents a skylight-polarization navigation method that estimates vehicle heading by globally optimizing a Rayleigh sky model against measurements from a division-of-focal-plane polarimetric camera.
The proposed framework combines a pinhole camera model, a single-scattering Rayleigh polarization model, and a solar position algorithm to synthesize the expected full-image angle-of-polarization distribution for candidate vehicle states.
A degree-of-polarization-weighted root-mean-square error objective function compares measured and simulated polarization patterns, allowing the estimator to use all available sky information while attenuating low-confidence pixels caused by clouds, buildings, foliage, and other depolarizing occlusions.
Experimental evaluation is performed using three urban road-vehicle trajectories collected with a roof-mounted polarimetric camera and a high-precision dual-antenna GNSS/INS reference system.
Results show sub-degree RMS yaw error across all trajectories, ranging from 0.718 °0.718\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} to 0.889 °0.889\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}.
Compared with representative feature-based and model-based polarization navigation methods, the proposed approach reduces RMS heading error by up to 87 %87\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} and demonstrates improved robustness to partial sky occlusion.
introduction:
Modern mobile platforms spanning driver assistance systems, manned tactical vehicles, autonomous road transportation, and industrial robotics depend on accurate, continuous, and highly resilient navigation systems for safe and reliable operation.
Among the core parameters governing vehicle state estimation and trajectory control, absolute heading determination plays a pivotal role.
In dynamic, real-world operational environments, maintaining an uncompromised orientation reference is essential to prevent cumulative dead-reckoning drift, ensuring operational continuity and human safety, particularly when external positioning infrastructure is degraded or unavailable.

Despite significant advances in navigation instrumentation, conventional sensors utilized for absolute heading determination suffer from severe physical and environmental limitations.
Gyrocompasses and inertial measurement units provide self-contained dead-reckoning capabilities, but their orientation estimates suffer from unbounded error integration over time [1, 2, 3], and a loss of power permanently destroys the reference orientation.
Magnetic compasses provide absolute heading but are highly susceptible to local electromagnetic interference [4, 5, 6], structural ferromagnetic distortion from the vehicle chassis [7, 8], and ambient anomalies in the Earth’s magnetic field [9, 10].
Dual-antenna global navigation satellite system configurations can deliver high-precision heading solutions under open skies; however, their performance degrades in complex operational environments.
Natural and artificial obstructions such as tall buildings and dense foliage cause signal multipath and line-of-sight shadowing [11, 12, 13].
Furthermore, global navigation satellite system signals are increasingly vulnerable to deliberate radio frequency jamming and spoofing [14, 15], which poses failure risks in high-reliability civilian and defense scenarios.
Although multi-sensor fusion strategies aim to combine complementary sensor modalities to mitigate individual weaknesses, effective fusion relies on the availability of a passive, drift-free, and infrastructure-independent absolute orientation reference.

Skylight polarization offers a compelling physical foundation for self-contained, passive, and drift-free navigation.
As unpolarized sunlight enters the Earth’s atmosphere, atmospheric scattering interactions impart a predictable, structured linear polarization pattern across the sky.
The spatial distribution of this polarization pattern depends solely on the solar position relative to an observer on the Earth’s surface.
Biological organisms, including desert ants [16, 17], honeybees [18, 19], desert locusts [20, 21], and monarch butterflies [22], exploit this skylight polarization pattern via specialized optical structures to perform long-distance navigation with remarkable precision [23].
Inspired by these biological visual systems, polarization-based navigation systems measure skylight polarization parameters across observed sky points to infer the absolute orientation of the observer.

Recent developments in polarimetric imaging, particularly division-of-focal-plane polarimeters, have enabled real-time, high-resolution capture of spatial polarization patterns.
Traditional polarization navigation algorithms predominantly rely on extracting specific geometric landmarks, such as the solar meridian line or neutral points, using line-fitting or transformation techniques such as the Hough transform [24].
However, these local feature-based methods suffer from three primary drawbacks when applied to ground vehicle navigation.
In urban canyons, buildings, bridges, and tree canopies obscure significant portions of the sky. When local geometric features (e.g., the solar meridian) are occluded, feature-based algorithms experience performance degradation or failure.
Existing studies often assume a strictly horizontal polarimeter orientation. In mobile vehicle applications, dynamic pitch and roll motions introduce non-horizontal measurement tilts. Transforming angle of polarization measurements from the sensor frame into ray coordinate frames under non-horizontal conditions incurs systematic errors that are rarely modeled or compensated in literature.

To overcome these challenges, this paper presents a global model optimization framework for absolute heading determination on road vehicles using a wide-field division-of-focal-plane polarimetric camera.
Rather than relying on local feature extraction, our method formulates heading estimation as an optimization problem evaluated over the full polarimetric image.
By integrating a pinhole camera model with single-scattering Rayleigh sky theory and an accurate solar position algorithm (Plataforma Solar de Almeria) [25, 26], we simulate superpixel-level expected angle of polarization distributions for candidate vehicle poses.
We construct an objective function that compares simulated and measured angle of polarization distributions, weighted by the degree of polarization, across all visible sky pixels.
The degree of polarization weighting naturally attenuates low-polarization noise from depolarizing cloud cover and solid occlusions.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We develop a full-image polarimetric camera simulation combining a pinhole camera model with the Rayleigh sky model to synthesize expected superpixel-level angle of polarization distributions for division-of-focal-plane sensor hardware under arbitrary camera orientations and solar positions.
Additionally, we formulate our simulation based exclusively on the state (i.e., position, time, orientation) of a virtual polarization camera in the horizontal coordinate system, which enables its application to conventional trajectory data where the position of the sun is not immediately recorded.

We formulate a coordinate transformation between the division-of-focal-plane measurement coordinate system and individual ray coordinate systems used by the Rayleigh sky model.
We explicitly account for non-horizontal camera tilt and document the errors incurred from such tilted measurements in vehicle-mounted schemes.

We propose a weighted root mean squared error objective function for heading extraction that evaluates global skylight polarization patterns and incorporates degree of polarization weighting to suppress measurement noise and depolarizing occlusions such as cloud cover, buildings, and foliage.

We perform experimental evaluations on an urban vehicle dataset collected under dynamic road conditions using a high-precision dual-antenna global navigation satellite system/inertial measurement unit reference system. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves up to an 87 %87\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} decrease in the root mean squared error of the heading estimate compared with traditional Hough transform-based methods and up to a 73 %73\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} decrease compared with other model optimization methods.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows.
Section II provides a review of relevant literature on bio-inspired skylight polarization navigation.
Section III presents the physical theory of skylight polarization, representations of linearly polarized light, and the Rayleigh sky model.
Section IV details the proposed model optimization framework, objective function formulation, camera projection model, and polarimetric measurement scheme.
Section V describes the experimental vehicle instrumentation and the urban trajectory dataset.
Section VI presents the experimental results, performance evaluations, and comparative analyses against existing methods.
Finally, Section VII concludes the paper and highlights directions for future research.
