title: Multi-Dimensional Featurizers Yield Fine-Grained Steering and Data Shaping in Robot Foundation Models
authors: Aiden Swann,Mozes Jacobs,Mathilde Papillon,Siddharth Boppana,David Chanin,Dron Hazra,Usha Bhalla,Curt Tigges,Mac Schwager,Owen Lewis,Jack Merullo,Ekdeep Singh Lubana,Atticus Geiger,Thomas Fel,Matthew Kowal
abstract:
Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn.
We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model’s computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than 1.4% of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.
introduction:
A vision-language-action (VLA) model maps visual observations, language instructions, and robot state to actions in the physical world (Black et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Black et al., 2024; Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Deshpande et al., 2026). Although today’s VLAs rarely perform consequential real-world tasks, fully learned robotics models may soon see widespread deployment. Yet little is known about the computations underlying their actions. Understanding these internal representations will be essential for safe deployment.

One way to understand the internal representation of a learned model is through the perspective of features, which are recurring internal variables that encode concepts, states, relationships and ultimately underlie the process by which the model converts input to output. A promising line of work, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAEs), leverages the linear representation hypothesis (LRH) (Park et al., 2023a; Huben et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025; Elhage et al., 2022) and assume that activations are composed of a sparse set of vectors. These methods have been well studied in language and vision modalities (Huben et al., 2024; Templeton et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2025). Examining models in the basis of the features that they express is useful for a plethora of problems, such as to study generalization (Gallifant et al., 2025; Olson et al., 2025), steer model behavior (Templeton et al., 2026; Prasad et al., 2026; Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024), attribute behaviors to training data (Kowal et al., 2026; Bergen et al., 2026; Koh & Liang, 2017), and identify safety-relevant computation (Templeton et al., 2026; Marks et al., 2025).

However, a featurizer is ultimately a hypothesis about the data-generating process of the activations (Fel et al., 2026a). The LRH is particularly questionable for visual domains involving perception, since continuous factors such as viewpoint, illumination, position, and motion naturally generate low-dimensional manifolds that are reflected in learned representations (Cohen et al., 2020; Kvinge et al., 2024; Fel et al., 2026a; Engels et al., 2025; Michaud et al., 2025). Despite this, the majority of work in VLA interpretability assumes the LRH, with varying degrees of success. Early studies showed that specific MLP directions can offer limited control of variables like speed and height (Häon et al., 2025). Complementary studies use linear probes and activation interventions to characterize the contributions of visual, language, and action pathways and identify representations of environmental dynamics and task progress (Molinari et al., 2025; Grant et al., 2026; Bhardwaj et al., 2026; Buurmeijer et al., 2026). More recently, SAEs have been applied to recover semantic concepts, motion primitives, task structure, and episode-specific memorization, demonstrating that interventions on individual features can alter policy behavior (Swann et al., 2026; Khan et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2026; Grant et al., 2026).Prior work has improved our understanding of VLA policies, but precise behavioral steering remains challenging, with interventions often producing inconsistent, off-target, or weak effects. Much of this work relies on pooled visual activations or small activation corpora, leaving open whether training SAEs on individual token activations at greater scale improves feature discovery and steering.

In this work, we apply recent methods for multi-dimensional feature discovery—block-sparse featurizers (BSFs) (Fel et al., 2026a)—to frontier open-source VLA models, training BSFs and baseline SAEs on the largest corpora of unpooled VLA token activations to date. BSFs represent features as sparse low-dimensional blocks (Yuan & Lin, 2006; Eldar & Bölcskei, 2009; Jenatton et al., 2010; Bach et al., 2012) rather than single directions, making them a natural fit for robotic representations. Across models and layers, we recover a broad vocabulary of task-relevant features spanning visual perception, language, proprioceptive state, task variables and episode progress. BSFs outperform matched SAEs on recovering and intervening on task-relevant structure, suggesting that the additional geometry is useful rather than simply excess representational capacity. We then causally validate them through fine-grained steering experiments across multiple layers, inducing targeted changes at several stages of the policy: what is perceived in the observation, which object is selected, where that object is localized. Finally, we perform feature-based attribution to connect interpretable behaviors directly to the episodes in the fine-tuning dataset that shaped them. Related robot data-curation methods select demonstrations with datamodels, influence estimates, or mutual information (Dass et al., 2026; Agia et al., 2025; Hejna et al., 2025). Using a ‘failure-recovery’ feature as as case-study, we isolate fewer than 1.4% of fine-tuning tokens in DROID whose influence is disproportionately associated with this behavior.
Our contributions are:

Comparing block-sparse and linear featurizers for VLAs.
We systematically compare BSFs and SAEs in VLAs. BSFs recover features spanning perception, language, proprioception, task state and episode progress, better capturing computational geometry qualitatively and quantitatively. We also strengthen VLA SAE baselines with substantially larger, unpooled activation corpora to better evaluate multidimensional features.

Causal validation through fine-grained steering.
Across multiple layers, and computational regimes, we causally validate recovered features by steering perception, semantics, target-object selection, geometric localization, and downstream robot behavior.

Feature-based dataset attribution and shaping.
We trace behaviors captured by BSF features to the data that caused them. For failure recovery, masking ∼1.4%\sim 1.4\% of fine-tuning tokens qualitatively transforms robot behavior, demonstrating precise control over robot datasets and learned policies.

title: Causal Analysis of Robot Foundation Models Enables Efficiency Gains
authors: Aiden Swann,Mathilde Papillon,Mozes Jacobs,Siddharth Boppana,Tal Haklay,Eric Bigelow,Andrew Lee,Conor Watts,Thomas Icard,Mac Schwager,Owen Lewis,Jack Merullo,Ekdeep Singh Lubana,Atticus Geiger,Thomas Fel,Matthew Kowal
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising approach to general purpose robot manipulation. While the internal computation of vision-language models, which compose the backbone of VLAs, has been studied extensively, less is known about how their perceptual and semantic representations are transformed into action in VLA models. We study this question mechanistically in three frontier VLA models (π0.5\pi_{0.5}, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot) by analyzing the causal pathways through which the input image and the instruction shape actions. Across the three models, activation patching shows that causally relevant information influences the action expert (AE) through a narrow band of mid-to-late cross-attention layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface. The content of this information changes with token and layer within the model. Early-to-mid layer representations of the target noun token determine which object is selected, whereas mid-to-late layers carry the spatial information in text tokens that redirects the movement when patched. Where spatial information is stored in prompt tokens various based on the architecture. In MolmoAct2 the model forms task-conditioned representations at the text positions that follow the instruction, whereas π0.5\pi_{0.5} additionally stores this information at image token positions. We show that these findings can be translated directly into improving model efficiency. We find that restricting MolmoBot’s action expert conditioning to only 3 out of 36 layers reduces inference FLOPs by up to 33%33\% while maintaining comparable task success with the default model across 3,000 evaluation episodes (46.7% vs. 46.9%), and the same principle carries over to real-robot deployment of π0.5\pi_{0.5}.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising route to achieve general-purpose robot manipulation. By adapting large pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to action (Driess et al., 2023; Beyer et al., 2024; Deitke et al., 2025), VLAs combine broad visual and semantic knowledge with continuous control and increasingly handle manipulation tasks across objects, environments, and robot embodiments (Brohan et al., 2022; Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025).

Architecturally, VLAs typically combine a pretrained VLM backbone (Chi et al., 2023; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Deshpande et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2025a; Wen et al., 2025b) with a separate diffusion or flow-matching action expert that produces continuous control. The two modules are typically joined through a dense, layer-wise interface that conditions the expert on the backbone at every layer. Despite their growing real-world efficacy and partially due to the multi-modal architecture design, these models remain black boxes. VLAs transform thousands of image, language, and proprioceptive tokens through billions of parameters before producing a small set of continuous action tokens, leaving the internal mapping from perception to action an open area of study.

We study three frontier open-source VLAs: π0.5\pi_{0.5}, MolmoBot, and MolmoAct2 (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Deshpande et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026). Across all three models, we find that perception and action communicate through a surprisingly narrow channel (1-3 cross-attention layers). Causal influence concentrates in a middle-to-late band of VLM layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface. This suggests that the action expert ingests representations which already encode task-relevant spatial information, rather than depending equally on every stage of backbone computation.

We apply our findings of the narrow action-conditioning interface between the AE and VLM to improve VLA efficiency. Many prior works have attempted to reduce VLA computation, by skipping or exiting backbone layers (Yue et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b), pruning redundant layers or parameters (Yang et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a), or conditioning the action head on only a subset of backbone layers (Bjorck et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025). These methods decide what to remove using heuristics such as representational similarity or benchmark success. We offer a more mechanistic account of why these designs work. Our results show that the representations necessary for action are stored sparsely across tokens and layers.

In this work we show that by leveraging causal analysis we can choose exactly the relevant areas of the model to prune. Restricting conditioning to the causally important layers removes 92%92\% of MolmoBot’s cross-attention parameters and reduces the estimated VLM–action-expert floating-point operation count by up to 33%33\% with a similar change in real world measured latency. The simplified architecture achieves task success comparable to the vanilla policy across 3,000 evaluation episodes. The same approach carries over to preliminary trials on a real robot, where sparse and dense π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies achieve comparable success rates (67 and 64 of 100 trials). We view these results as a step toward intentional design (McGrath, 2026) of VLA models, where the internal mechanisms connecting perception to control directly inform how robot policies are built and trained.

Beyond just leveraging the action-conditioning interface we seek to understand and explain it. There are many promising approachs to understanding VLA computation via mechanistic interpretability (Grant et al., 2026; Bhardwaj et al., 2026; Molinari et al., 2025; Khan et al., 2025; Goyal, 2026; Yang & Mokalla, 2026). In particular, activation patching (Vig et al., 2020; Geiger et al., 2021; Zhang & Nanda, 2024; Heimersheim & Nanda, 2024) approaches aim to measure the causal role of an internal representation by replacing the target representation from one rollout with a donor from another rollout, while measuring the resulting change in behavior. In language models, such interventions have localized the computations behind factual recall and uncovered computations underlying numerous tasks (Meng et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Geiger et al., 2023; Mueller et al., 2026), helping elucidate the causal relationships between internal model representations and behavior.

Recent work has begun to apply such tools to VLAs, identifying internal directions that steer movement, recovering sparse features tied to semantic concepts, and manipulating observable features to control behavior (Häon et al., 2025; Swann et al., 2026; Buurmeijer et al., 2026). Closest to our work, Grant et al. (2026) performed activation-injection experiments and showed that patching representations into a VLA can redirect movement toward the spatial location of a donor task. Shi et al. (2026) used attention knockout (Geva et al., 2023), which blocks attention from selected token positions (such as all image or all language tokens) at chosen layers and measures how the output changes, to characterize which modalities and layers action generation depends on. Together, these results establish that individual VLA representations can be causally manipulated. However, they do not address how task-relevant information is composed across the depth of the backbone and how it reaches the action expert.

We answer these questions with counterfactual comparisons that test visual, semantic, and geometric hypotheses at the interface and within the backbone. We trace how the representations read by the expert reveals a progression across depth, from transferable object selection to spatially grounded action information. The two kinds of information also reside on different tokens: semantic content is carried by the noun token of the instruction, while geometric content is spread across the other prompt tokens and, in π0.5\pi_{0.5}, the image tokens.

Our contributions are as follows:

Discovery of a narrow action-conditioning interface. Across π0.5\pi_{0.5}, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot, we identify a narrow middle-to-late region through which the backbone conditions action generation. We show that this interface mediates geometric information about the target object.

Mechanistically informed architectural improvements. We use the identified interface to design substantially sparser VLM–action-expert connections, preserving observed closed-loop performance while reducing the estimated combined operation count by up to 33%33\%. We validate the simplified architecture through direct training and adaptation in simulation, and demonstrate real-robot deployment with π0.5\pi_{0.5}.

A causal account of the information supplied to the interface. We build a counterfactual dataset with over 156 counterfactual pairs across sets of household objects. We run over 775,000 activation patching interventions across π0.5\pi_{0.5}, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot specifically designed to differentiate representations within the backbone. Visual information influences behavior through early image tokens, semantic information through the early target noun, and geometric information through later text and readout positions.

title: Perceive, Predict, and Plan: a Unified World Action Model for Egocentric Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Zirui Wu,Chen Guo,Tianjian Jiang,Zeren Jiang,Zeming Li,Lingchen Yang,Longteng Duan,Ying Xue,Handi Yin,Shenyuan Gao,Martin R. Oswald,Jun Zhang,Ping Tan,Jie Song
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
We introduce P3-WAM, a unified world action
model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns
3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary
modes: Perceive, which reconstructs articulated
hand motion and camera trajectories from video;
Predict, which generates visual futures under
prescribed actions; and Plan, which jointly
generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal.
Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual–action attention.
Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions
serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes.
Experiments show that unified training improves all three
capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision–language model evaluation.
Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized
baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned
video prediction across four datasets, while producing
goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction
adherence and action progression than video-generation
baselines.
introduction:
Dexterous manipulation requires more than mapping pixels directly to actions. An embodied model must answer three complementary questions: What happened in an observed interaction? What will happen under a specified action? What should be done to accomplish a desired goal? These questions correspond to three fundamental capabilities: perceiving the 3D motion underlying observed interactions, predicting action-conditioned world dynamics, and planning actions together with their anticipated consequences. Infants can use what they learn from observing adults’ actions to guide their own behavior (Hauf & Aschersleben, 2008). Through their own interactions, they learn to predict action outcomes and use those expected outcomes to select actions (Verschoor et al., 2013) and organize movements toward a goal (Claxton et al., 2003). Together, these findings suggest that perception, prediction, and planning are linked by knowledge of actions and their consequences.

Despite these connections, prior work on egocentric manipulation has developed along three closely related but largely separate lines. Egocentric reconstruction methods recover structured 3D interaction information, such as hand motion and camera trajectories, from observed videos (Pavlakos et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025). Action-conditioned world models predict future observations under prescribed motion trajectories (Hao et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Sun et al., 2026). World action models jointly generate actions and future observations for goal-directed control (Ye et al., 2026). These capabilities, however, are still largely learned in isolation or coupled only in subsets.

To close this loop, we introduce P3-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that integrates three complementary modes: 3D interaction reconstruction (Perceive), action-conditioned world prediction (Predict), and joint action–future planning (Plan). Reconstruction develops the model’s capacity for 3D perception by recovering 3D motion from observed interactions. Prediction teaches the model to anticipate the visual consequences of prescribed actions. Together, these capabilities provide the foundation for world–action planning, in which the model learns to jointly generate goal-directed hand action trajectories and their anticipated visual futures. We learn all three modes through unified training. Figure 1 illustrates these three modes.

We build P3-WAM on a pretrained video diffusion transformer (Wan et al., 2025) to draw on its rich visual and motion priors. We represent each action by the articulated poses of both hands and the camera pose, and encode these states as compact tokens alongside the video tokens. We integrate this representation into the video backbone through a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture with a dedicated action expert, which shares the backbone’s base weights while incorporating modality-specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022). To train this architecture across all three modes, we randomly vary the visibility of visual observations and actions: providing video while withholding actions supports perception, providing actions while withholding future video supports prediction, and withholding actions and video supports joint action–future planning, exposing the model to complete modes and partially observed interactions. Over long sequences, successive visual subgoals specify the target arrangement for each planning window.

Unified training improves all three modes over single-mode training. Our model outperforms the evaluated baselines in Perceive and Predict. Its Plan videos receive higher VLM scores for action process and instruction adherence. Robot demonstrations illustrate how generated human-hand motion can be transferred to a dexterous robot. Our main contributions are:

A unified world action model, P3-WAM, for egocentric
dexterous manipulation that integrates 3D interaction reconstruction,
action-conditioned world prediction, and goal-guided
world–action planning. We will release our code and model checkpoints.

action-conditioned world prediction, and goal-guided
world–action planning. We will release our code and model checkpoints.

A unified training framework that connects pretrained video
priors with structured 3D actions through a mixture-of-transformers
architecture and randomized modality visibility, enabling
complementary learning across perception, prediction, and planning.

Extensive experiments indicating that perception, prediction, and planning reinforce one another through unified training, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines across all three tasks.
Robot demonstrations further illustrate the transfer of generated human-hand motion to a dexterous robot.

title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling
authors: Hongchang Liu,Jian Liu,Yujuan Ding,Liang Peng,Xun Jiang,Fei Ma,Xing Xu,Yi Bin
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Project

introduction:
Learning to predict how the physical world evolves is a central goal of world modeling (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018), with direct relevance to autonomous driving, robotics, and embodied intelligence. Visual world models predict the future in pixel space (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024b; Gao et al., 2024; NVIDIA et al., 2025), which can introduce substantial representational redundancy and make geometric consistency difficult to maintain.
This has motivated increasing interest in 3D world models, which represent and predict future environments in geometrically grounded state spaces. By explicitly encoding spatial structure and 3D relationships, these representations provide a structured and geometrically grounded state space that more directly reflects the real world.

Recent 3D world models have explored a range of structured geometric state spaces, including depth, occupancy, point-based representations, and 3D Gaussians (Zheng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Zuo et al., 2025). In parallel, geometry foundation models (GFMs) have substantially advanced feed-forward 3D perception by learning rich geometric representations directly from RGB observations (Wang et al., 2024a; Yang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026). Benefiting from large-scale pretraining, these representations capture strong geometric priors that generalize across scenes and tasks, making them attractive state spaces for predictive world modeling. Building on this capability, recent approaches have begun to directly model temporal evolution in pretrained geometry feature spaces (Sun et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). In particular, VGGT-World (Sun et al., 2026) treats frozen VGGT features as world states and predicts their future evolution, demonstrating the potential of GFM representations for 3D forecasting.

Despite the strong performance achieved by recent GFM-based 3D world models, a strong representation for geometric perception is not necessarily an appropriate state representation for world dynamics. GFM features are typically constructed from and organized around the observing views, so changes in camera viewpoint can induce substantial changes in the representation even when the underlying physical scene remains unchanged. When such features are directly used as predictive states, a temporal model would account simultaneously for genuine scene evolution and camera-induced variation, although these arise from fundamentally different sources. In particular, even a static scene can undergo substantial changes in feature space as the camera moves, forcing the temporal model to predict viewpoint-dependent transformations that do not correspond to physical scene evolution. This unnecessary variation makes the latent dynamics more complex and therefore harder to predict over long horizons. FR3D (Morbitzer et al., 2026) also shows that separating ego-motion from scene forecasting can improve temporal modeling, but its predictive state still inherits the view-dependent structure of the underlying reconstruction representation. We argue that such separation should instead be built into the representation itself: the state should describe what the world is, while the camera should determine only how that world is observed.

To this end, we introduce GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry state learned from pretrained GFM features. Given multi-view observations, a scene tokenizer compresses their geometry features into a compact scene state represented in a shared scene coordinate system, while the query viewpoint is introduced only during decoding. Specifically, a geometry decoder takes the scene state together with rays from a query camera and predicts the geometry observed from that viewpoint. Consequently, the same scene state can be queried repeatedly from different viewpoints without re-encoding the scene. This transforms view-conditioned GFM features into a representation in which scene geometry is explicitly separated from camera-dependent observation.

Building on this representation, we formulate 3D world modeling directly in the scene-state space. The temporal model can therefore focus solely on predicting scene dynamics, while camera evolution is modeled independently. At inference time, a predicted future state can be decoded using either a separately predicted camera trajectory or a user-controlled camera. Our formulation also maintains a consistent scene gauge throughout temporal prediction and geometry decoding, avoiding the need for per-frame scale alignment during rollout.

We evaluate our approach on large-scale dynamic driving scenes,
using Waymo (Sun et al., 2020) for in-domain evaluation and
KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012) and nuScenes (Caesar et al., 2020)
for zero-shot transfer. Our approach outperforms the compared world
models in depth forecasting across all reported horizons, while
maintaining a consistent scale throughout the forecasting rollout.
Experiments further demonstrate geometrically consistent querying
across viewpoints and generalization across driving datasets. Ablation
results show that view decoupling makes the scene representation more predictable. Together, these findings support view-decoupled geometry states derived from pretrained GFMs as an effective representation for predictive 3D world modeling.

Our contributions are threefold:

We identify viewpoint coupling in geometry foundation model
features as a limitation when using them as predictive world
states, and introduce GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry state
derived from pretrained GFM representations that separates scene content
from how the scene is observed.

We develop a scene-state learning framework that realizes GeoState through a Scene Tokenizer that aggregates multi-view GFM features into a shared scene state and a query-conditioned Geometry Decoder that introduces the query viewpoint only at decoding time.

We formulate a 3D world model that predicts scene evolution directly in GeoState space while modeling camera evolution separately, and demonstrate long-horizon geometry forecasting, geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and zero-shot generalization across driving datasets without per-frame scale alignment.

1. We identify viewpoint coupling in geometry foundation model
features as a limitation when using them as predictive world
states, and introduce GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry state
derived from pretrained GFM representations that separates scene content
from how the scene is observed.

2. We develop a scene-state learning framework that realizes GeoState through a Scene Tokenizer that aggregates multi-view GFM features into a shared scene state and a query-conditioned Geometry Decoder that introduces the query viewpoint only at decoding time.

3. We formulate a 3D world model that predicts scene evolution directly in GeoState space while modeling camera evolution separately, and demonstrate long-horizon geometry forecasting, geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and zero-shot generalization across driving datasets without per-frame scale alignment.

title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines
authors: Florian Lercher,Karan Mahesh,Yujun Huang,Meshal Alharbi,Runyu Zhang,Hanna Krasowski,Michael R. Benjamin,Matthias Althoff,Gioele Zardini
subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract:
When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints.
These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable.
We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games).
Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario.
Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve.
We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality.
To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information.
We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters.
On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases.
These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.
introduction:
Robots that share roads, waterways, or airspace with other agents must plan their motion subject to many potentially conflicting objectives.
These objectives often include legal requirements imposed by regulators, which take precedence over individual objectives.
Since not all objectives can be satisfied simultaneously in general, minimum-violation planning prioritizes them and systematically violates lower-priority objectives when necessary to satisfy higher-priority ones [1, 2].
Legally compliant multi-agent motion planning is nevertheless difficult for at least three reasons.
First, some objectives are incomparable, in the sense that one cannot assert that either objective is more important than the other.
This is particularly relevant for legal regulations, where authorities typically specify only a partial priority order [3].
Second, many traffic laws are stated as rules between pairs of agents, so the obligations of an agent depend on which other agents are present, and obligations toward different agents might conflict (Fig. 1).
Third, in multi-agent settings, agents respond strategically to the actions of other agents [4], whose private objectives are typically unknown.
Taken together, these obstacles call for a framework that derives the preferences of the agents from the law for every scenario, preserves the partial priorities of the law, and coordinates the agents without requiring them to disclose their private objectives.

A particularly important instance of this problem is motion planning for autonomous vessels in the maritime domain.
The International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Ships [6], adopted in 2026, requires autonomous vessels to comply with the maritime traffic rules laid out in the Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGS) [5].
However, the COLREGS are only defined for pairs of vessels which may lead to conflicting requirements in encounters involving more than two vessels, as shown in Fig. 1.
While the COLREGS prioritize collision avoidance over strict compliance with the encounter rules [5, Rule 2], they do not specify which rules should be violated when conflicts arise.

Considering these challenges, we identify auditability, customizability, and deployability as key requirements for a multi-agent motion planning algorithm under legal constraints.
Auditability requires agents to exhibit predictable behavior and provide explanations for their actions, particularly when not all conflicting objectives can be satisfied.
Customizability enables regulators to revise legal priorities and manufacturers to refine priorities that laws leave unspecified.
Moreover, any deployable algorithm has to allow agents to coordinate despite their limited knowledge of the private objectives of other agents.
To meet these requirements, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first systematic method for automatically constructing legally compliant motion-planning games from scenario-independent legal guidelines.
Our framework represents objective hierarchies as partially ordered preferences, resulting in posetal games [4], for which we provide solution protocols that operate under limited information.
The key idea is to separate what the law prescribes from what a scenario instantiates.
Regulators specify a guideline, i.e., a partial order over abstract legal concerns such as collision avoidance, and every concrete scenario inherits the preferences of its agents by matching their legal metrics to these concerns.
Since every customization of the resulting preferences is a refinement, and refining preferences can only remove equilibria, legality is preserved by construction.
We demonstrate the practical applicability of the framework through a case study of COLREGS-compliant motion planning for multi-vessel encounters.

Our work lies at the intersection of formal specifications for robotics, game-theoretic motion planning with ordered objectives, and COLREGS-compliant maritime navigation.
Since formal specifications provide an interpretable representation of complex objectives and serve as the building blocks of posetal games, we first review their use in robotics, followed by specification-based approaches to multi-agent motion planning and related game-theoretic formulations with ordered preferences.
Finally, we discuss existing approaches for COLREGS-compliant multi-vessel motion planning to provide context for our case study.

Formal specifications, initially used primarily for offline monitoring and runtime verification, have become core components of learning, synthesis, and control methods [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14].
They provide interpretable representations of objectives and constraints and, in multi-agent settings, requirements governing interactions among agents.
For example, autonomous-driving systems must satisfy specifications ranging from lane-keeping requirements to appropriate responses to emergency vehicles [15, 16].
In unstructured environments, interaction requirements are commonly expressed through pairwise rules or fixed priority structures, which favor concise representations at the expense of completeness.
For instance, the airborne collision-avoidance system ACAS-X determines priorities for pairwise aircraft encounters and relies on heuristics to combine the resulting evaluations [17, 18].
Even in this pairwise setting, the precomputed lookup tables are sufficiently large to motivate dedicated compression methods [19].
This scalability challenge is further amplified in domains such as warehouse navigation and maritime robotics, where agents and interactions are more diverse [20, 21, 22, 23].
Rulebooks [3, 24] reduce the need for exhaustive specification by prioritizing objectives and permitting lower-priority objectives to be violated when necessary to satisfy higher-priority ones.
Our framework builds on this principle and extends it to multiple strategic agents whose obligations depend on the scenario.

Motion-planning methods based on formal objectives generally adopt one of two perspectives: single-agent planning, in which other agents are treated as uncooperative, or multi-agent planning, in which varying degrees of cooperation are assumed.
In single-agent settings, the behavior of surrounding agents is typically modeled using worst-case assumptions, reflecting minimal or no cooperation [25, 22].
Moreover, formal safety specifications are assigned higher priority than performance objectives to guarantee specification compliance by the ego agent [26, 27, 22].

In multi-agent settings, game-theoretic motion planning naturally models strategic interactions between agents.
Most existing approaches require the objectives of each agent to be expressed as a scalar cost function, e.g., [28, 29, 30, 31].
However, scalarization can obscure the relative priorities among objectives so that the resulting behavior becomes difficult to interpret and predict.

To increase interpretability when rich preference structures are present, game-theoretic formulations that allow for enforcing orders of preferences have been proposed. The simplest structure is a two-level hierarchy, common when constraints, such as safety requirements, have strict priority over the performance objective.
For example, in urban driving games [32], a shared collision-avoidance objective takes strict priority over individual costs.
These personal costs may only depend on the personal action of the agent, a limitation that is lifted in [33] by incorporating zero-sum components.
Games of ordered preferences [34] further generalize the objective hierarchy by allowing an arbitrary number of levels, corresponding to a total order over objectives.
An iterative best-response solver for these games is presented in [35].
However, requiring a total order over legal requirements places a significant burden on regulators.
Posetal games [4] relax this assumption by enabling objectives to remain incomparable, i.e., they admit a partial order over the objectives.
Thus, they support the most general preference structure among the methods considered here.

Although the methods in [32, 33, 4, 34, 35] compute Nash equilibria, their practical deployment remains challenging.
In particular, they assume complete knowledge of the preferences of all involved agents.
Moreover, they do not provide a mechanism for translating general legal requirements into the preferences required to model a specific scenario.

The COLREGS have been translated into formal specifications to provide a precise, machine-interpretable representation [36, 37, 38].
These formalizations support the monitoring, testing, and synthesis of behavior in pairwise vessel encounters.
However, because the COLREGS primarily specify pairwise obligations, they do not explicitly prescribe how to prioritize conflicting obligations arising from simultaneous encounters with multiple vessels, as illustrated in Fig. 1.

Specification-based approaches to maritime navigation have predominantly adopted an ego-centric perspective in which the behavior of surrounding vessels is monitored or modeled rather than strategically coordinated.
Examples include real-world monitoring of COLREGS encounter situations for collision avoidance [39] and reactive vessel simulations in which the first detected conflict determines the executed maneuver [40].
Such methods can enforce or evaluate the obligations of an individual vessel, but do not explicitly model the potentially heterogeneous preferences of multiple interacting vessels.

Existing multi-agent approaches commonly employ centralized game-theoretic methods or homogeneous reinforcement-learning controllers with scalarized objectives [41, 42, 43, 44, 45].
However, scalarization obscures the priority structure among objectives, and centralized or homogeneous formulations generally cannot accommodate private, agent-specific preferences.
To the best of our knowledge, our framework is the first to systematically lift the pairwise COLREGS rules to encounters involving an arbitrary number of vessels while preserving an interpretable hierarchy of legal objectives.
It further supports agents with private preferences and solution protocols that operate without requiring those preferences to be disclosed.

We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements with partially ordered objectives, which automates the translation of practical scenarios into the theory of posetal games [4].
Our contributions are fourfold.

Systematic construction of legal posetal games.
We introduce guidelines to represent priorities among legal concerns independently of the concrete scenario.

From the legal guideline, we automatically derive the partially ordered preferences of the agents and the corresponding multi-agent game for any concrete scenario.
This removes the need to specify preferences by hand for every scenario, which is a prerequisite for using posetal games in practice.

Customization with legality guarantees.
We enable agents to incorporate private objectives and regulators to refine legal guidelines, and we prove that such refinements can only restrict the set of legal behaviors rather than introduce new ones.
This sharply contrasts with scalarization methods (e.g., [28, 29, 30, 31]), in which changing even a single weight can alter the resulting behavior in ways that are to predict and audit.

Deployable solution protocols under private preferences.
We develop two protocols that avoid the complete-information assumption of prior work [32, 33, 4, 34, 35]. We prove that belief play, which relies on conservative local beliefs, recovers exactly the equilibria of the true game and remains legal when interrupted. The second protocol, distributed iterative best-response, requires even less information about other agents.

Auditable COLREGS-compliant multi-vessel motion planning.
We instantiate our framework for autonomous vessels and lift the pairwise COLREGS rules to encounters with any number of vessels.
We evaluate our framework empirically on seven encounters involving two to four vessels. Contrary to previous approaches [41, 42, 43, 44, 45], we can audit every rule violation and certify it as either forced by conflicting legal requirements of higher or incomparable priority or unsatisfiable within the action space.
Moreover, defectors can be identified from public information alone.

This paper is organized as follows:
In Sec. II, we provide preliminaries and our problem statement.
We present our framework for deriving posetal games from legal requirements in Sec. III before explaining our solution protocols for the resulting games in Sec. IV.
In Sec. V, we instantiate our framework for COLREGS-compliant multi-vessel motion planning and evaluate it in Sec. VI.
Finally, Sec. VII draws a conclusion and discusses future work, and Sec. -A contains the proofs of the preference refinement operations.

1. Systematic construction of legal posetal games.
We introduce guidelines to represent priorities among legal concerns independently of the concrete scenario.

2. Customization with legality guarantees.
We enable agents to incorporate private objectives and regulators to refine legal guidelines, and we prove that such refinements can only restrict the set of legal behaviors rather than introduce new ones.
This sharply contrasts with scalarization methods (e.g., [28, 29, 30, 31]), in which changing even a single weight can alter the resulting behavior in ways that are to predict and audit.

3. Deployable solution protocols under private preferences.
We develop two protocols that avoid the complete-information assumption of prior work [32, 33, 4, 34, 35]. We prove that belief play, which relies on conservative local beliefs, recovers exactly the equilibria of the true game and remains legal when interrupted. The second protocol, distributed iterative best-response, requires even less information about other agents.

4. Auditable COLREGS-compliant multi-vessel motion planning.
We instantiate our framework for autonomous vessels and lift the pairwise COLREGS rules to encounters with any number of vessels.
We evaluate our framework empirically on seven encounters involving two to four vessels. Contrary to previous approaches [41, 42, 43, 44, 45], we can audit every rule violation and certify it as either forced by conflicting legal requirements of higher or incomparable priority or unsatisfiable within the action space.
Moreover, defectors can be identified from public information alone.

title: Robust Multi-Agent Pursuit with Preemptive Communication via Reachability-Based Control Barrier Functions
authors: Madison Book,Justin Bradley
subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: . Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
abstract: Safe multi-agent coordination typically assumes what real-world, deployed, resource-constrained robots cannot provide: continuous, perfect state sharing. Robust control strategies must be complemented with robust communication strategies to deliver resilient deployments. In this work, we propose a unified control/communication strategy that provides safe control to guarantee inter-agent safety under intermittent communication and demonstrate its effectiveness in a pursuit-evasion scenario. Each agent computes the reachable set of neighboring agents based on the last state information received, then solves for a safe control input based on control barrier functions to ensure agents avoid collision. We prove that inter-agent collision avoidance is guaranteed provided communication staleness remains bounded. As the reachable set inflates between state transmissions, each agent reasons about when to preemptively transmit its state information to neighboring agents based on novel metrics characterizing uncertainty risk and kinematic risk. We implement and simulate a variety of pursuit-evasion scenarios and show that preemptive communication reduces messages by 77.5% compared to periodic and event-triggered baselines with zero collisions.
introduction:
Multi-agent safety guarantees based on Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) typically assume continuous state information [1]. This assumption fails the moment bandwidth, power, or latency issues arise. On small, resource-constrained UAVs, this failure is the norm rather than the exception, leading to event-triggered safe control methods that rely on continuous state monitoring to trigger communication when deemed necessary [2]. In this work, we invert the usual communication trigger: rather than transmitting when an agent’s own state crosses a threshold, agents transmit preemptively, when neighbors need the information to remain safe.

An alternative line of work models communication as discrete events [3] but treats control and communication as separate design problems leading to fragile real-world deployments [4]. In reality, control must account for the uncertainty growth with time under stale information.

Together, these limitations suggest a need for safety-aware communication that incorporates onboard constraints while ensuring safety. Rather than traditional event-triggered mechanisms [5], which rely on self-state thresholds to transmit state, agents should transmit state when it is needed to preserve safety guarantees. This reframes communication as a safety mechanism.

We address this by combining reachability analysis with CBFs. Reachability analysis over-approximates the set of states an agent could occupy since its last communicated state [6]. CBFs enforce safety constraints by finding control inputs that ensure the state never leaves a safe set [7]. Related to this work, they have been applied to pursuit-evasion [8, 9] and multi-agent navigation [10, 11]. CBFs have also been combined with reachability analysis [12, 13]. But these efforts have left open the opportunity to co-design CBFs with communication in a safety-preserving manner.

As reachable sets expand with time, prolonged gaps in communication may lead to the quadratic programming (QP) controller becoming infeasible. To address this, we propose a preemptive communication mechanism where an agent transmits its state when it predicts that neighboring agents don’t have enough information to remain safe. The result is agents that communicate with neighbors as needed, reducing overall communication bandwidth while still providing safety guarantees. This framework is illustrated in Figure 1.

We evaluate the proposed methods in a pursuit-evasion scenario with multiple cooperative pursuers and adversarial evaders. Pursuing agents must coordinate to capture the evaders while avoiding inter-agent collisions. The contributions of this paper are as follows:

A novel preemptive communication mechanism based on predicted uncertainty and physical risk where agents transmit state when they predict neighboring agents need updated information.

A reachability-aware control barrier function, providing formal safety guarantees under intermittent and stale information.

A unified design strategy integrating preemptive communication and reachability-aware CBFs that accounts for onboard communication and computation limitations.

Simulation results demonstrating that our unified strategy maintains safety and performance while reducing total message volume by 77.5% against comparable strategies.

title: DeciCAD: Harness-Grounded Learning of Action Policies for CAD Agents
authors: Yufeng Peng,Yixin Zhang,Ziyi Liu,Zhikun Xu,Jiarong Yang,Sijie Wang,Wenjie Feng,Qiyu Kang
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Large Language Model agents operate through closed-loop action policies whose decision space is defined by an agent harness.
We investigate how this operating space shapes agent behavior and policy learning in computer-aided design (CAD), a professional domain characterized by persistent state, geometric constraints, and long-horizon procedures.
We instantiate this perspective in DeciCAD, a domain-native harness that exposes semantic CAD actions, decision-oriented observations, environment feedback, and persistent state transitions.
Building on this harness, we develop a learning pipeline that extracts causal decision supervision from interaction trajectories and improves the policy through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and geometry-grounded online reinforcement learning (RL).
Across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD achieves the best F1 and intersection over union (IoU) while reducing model-output tokens by 45–88% relative to a general-purpose coding harness.
Under matched supervision, its SFT policy improves F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437 and outperforms the coding policy; subsequent online RL further raises geometry availability from 66.5% to 73.5% and F1 to 0.7880.
These results demonstrate that the decision space induced by a harness materially affects both agent execution and policy learning in CAD.
introduction:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as agents to operate
professional software and complete long-horizon
tasks (Achiam et al. 2023; Naveed et al. 2025; Guo et al. 2024).
Computer-aided design (CAD) is a particularly demanding setting for
such agents (Willis et al. 2020; Wu et al. 2021).
Unlike one-shot content generation, CAD modeling requires a sequence of
state-dependent operations over a persistent design document.
An agent must create and modify sketches, constraints, features, and geometric objects;
inspect intermediate results; recover from execution failures;
and maintain references across long interaction trajectories.
In this process, the model outputs are interpreted as actions:
each action changes the current CAD state, produces execution feedback, and conditions
the next decision (Yao et al. 2023; Schick et al. 2023).
The effectiveness of a CAD agent therefore depends not only on the underlying model
and its reasoning strategy,
but also on how CAD actions, states, and execution outcomes
are represented to the model.

Such a model–environment boundary is defined by an agent harness
(Yang et al. 2024). In CAD, a harness determines which design operations the
model can express, which parts of the evolving design state it can inspect, and
how execution outcomes are returned for subsequent decisions.
A general-purpose coding harness may expose the CAD system through programs,
libraries, and runtime feedback, whereas a domain-native harness may expose
structured CAD actions and object-level observations.
Consequently, even when the model, task, and CAD backend remain fixed,
different harnesses can present the model with substantially different
decision spaces, as illustrated in
Figure 1.
Existing work has studied CAD code generation, tool-using agents, execution repair,
and interactive modeling (Mallis et al. 2024; Guan et al. 2025; Doris et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2025; Barkley et al. 2026; Gong et al. 2026),
but the harness itself is typically treated as implementation infrastructure
rather than as a variable that shapes both agent execution and policy learning.
This raises a central question:
How should a CAD agent harness represent actions and states so that it
preserves the decisions required for complex modeling while avoiding
representation burden that is irrelevant to the task?

This trade-off is important in CAD.
A fine-grained coding interface gives the model broad control over the underlying software,
but the same CAD operation can often be expressed through many programs,
command sequences, variable names, temporary objects, and API combinations.
These implementations may produce the same geometric state transition,
but they appear as different generation and supervision targets.
The model must then spend capacity on implementation choices that do not affect the intended state transition.
A semantic interface can remove many of these choices by representing the intended operation directly.
However, excessive compression can hide state differences that require
different actions or remove operations needed for correct modeling and error recovery.
A useful harness must therefore reduce irrelevant representation choices
while preserving the actions and observations needed for correct decisions.

To make this trade-off explicit, we formalize the model-facing interface as a
Harness-Induced CAD Decision Space: a harness maps model outputs to
executable operations, maps internal CAD states to model-visible observations,
and returns execution results as feedback, thereby determining which
operations the agent can perform, which state differences and failures it can
identify, and which policies it can execute and learn. We then introduce the
Semantic Decision Bottleneck as a design principle for this space: it
compresses behaviorally equivalent implementations and removes state
information that does not affect the next decision, while preserving the
actions and observations needed to reach the target geometry and recover from
errors.

Following this principle, we develop DeciCAD, a domain-native harness
for closed-loop CAD agents. DeciCAD represents task-relevant design
transitions as semantic CAD actions, grounds these actions in a persistent CAD
document, and returns structured execution feedback together with
decision-oriented observations. We further develop a
harness-grounded learning pipeline that reconstructs causally conditioned
action supervision from successful and recovered interaction trajectories,
initializes CAD action policies through supervised fine-tuning (SFT),
and supports online reinforcement learning (RL) using policy-generated
trajectories and geometry-grounded rewards.
Figure 2 summarizes
this execution and learning loop.

Across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD consistently produces more
accurate final geometry than competitive CAD agents and a general-purpose
coding harness, while reducing model-output tokens by 45–88% relative to the
coding harness on text-to-CAD tasks. Observation ablations show that showing more CAD state does not always help: unfiltered state inflates the input context, and coarse feedback strips out what the agent needs in order to recover. With matched training settings, open-weight models trained in the DeciCAD decision space learn stronger long-horizon CAD action policies than the same models trained through code-level interaction.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We define the Harness-Induced CAD Decision Space and introduce the Semantic Decision Bottleneck as a design principle for CAD agent interfaces.
We design DeciCAD, which combines semantic CAD actions, compact observations, structured feedback, and persistent object state.

We develop a harness-grounded policy-learning pipeline that reconstructs causally conditioned supervision from interaction trajectories, initializes policies through SFT, and supports geometry-grounded online RL.

Experiments across four benchmarks verify
DeciCAD improves geometric accuracy, token efficiency,
error recovery, and long-horizon policy learnability significantly.

1. We define the Harness-Induced CAD Decision Space and introduce the Semantic Decision Bottleneck as a design principle for CAD agent interfaces.
We design DeciCAD, which combines semantic CAD actions, compact observations, structured feedback, and persistent object state.

2. We develop a harness-grounded policy-learning pipeline that reconstructs causally conditioned supervision from interaction trajectories, initializes policies through SFT, and supports geometry-grounded online RL.

3. Experiments across four benchmarks verify
DeciCAD improves geometric accuracy, token efficiency,
error recovery, and long-horizon policy learnability significantly.

title: CLAD: Keypoint Matching Using Global Line Correspondences
authors: Masaki Satoh
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Traditional keypoint descriptors, such as SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) and ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF), are computed from local image patches. They may be unreliable in scenes with repetitive patterns or weak textures, where patches at different locations can look similar. We propose the Contextual Line-Assisted Descriptor (CLAD), a keypoint matching method that addresses this problem by using global geometric context from line correspondences. CLAD represents each keypoint with a vector whose elements indicate its proximity to matched lines. It can therefore use the keypoint’s spatial relationships to the lines in the scene. We use HOME (Hough-space One-dimensional Matching of Extrema) to detect both clear and weak linear structures and to establish enough line-to-keypoint associations to represent this context. Evaluations on the TUM RGB-D SLAM dataset and outdoor video sequences show that CLAD provides geometrically consistent matches that complement those obtained with traditional local descriptors. In repetitive scenes, where local descriptors may not distinguish similar patches, CLAD uses global structure to improve matching reliability. The method is computationally lightweight and practical to implement.
introduction:
Keypoint detection and matching are fundamental to many computer vision applications, including image registration, 3D reconstruction, and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). A keypoint detector identifies distinctive, repeatable points in an image, such as corners and blobs. A matching algorithm then finds correspondences between images by comparing the feature vectors, or descriptors, associated with the keypoints. The number of correct matches directly affects the accuracy and robustness of later processing. We can increase this number either by improving the detector to find more repeatable points or by improving the descriptors to make matching more reliable. This paper focuses on the second approach.

In standard methods, such as the Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) [1] and Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF (ORB) [2], each keypoint descriptor is computed only from the local image patch around that keypoint. Local information alone may not distinguish keypoints at different locations if their patches look similar, making it difficult to match such keypoints correctly. Even in these cases, human observers can often establish correct correspondences by considering the scene as a whole and the geometric relationships between keypoints. For example, standard descriptors may not distinguish individual checkerboard corners, as illustrated in Fig. 1, whereas a human observer can identify them from the overall grid pattern.

We propose CLAD (Contextual Line-Assisted Descriptor), a method that uses line correspondences to capture global geometric structure and improve keypoint matching. The following simplified example illustrates the main idea. Suppose that we establish line correspondences between two images, where line ℓi\bm{\ell}_{i} in the first image corresponds to line ℓi′\bm{\ell}_{i}^{\prime} in the second. Let NN be the number of line correspondences. We represent the jjth keypoint in the first image and the kkth keypoint in the second image with NN-dimensional binary vectors 𝒗j\bm{v}_{j} and 𝒗k′\bm{v}_{k}^{\prime}, respectively. The iith element of 𝒗j\bm{v}_{j} is 11 if ℓi\bm{\ell}_{i} passes through the jjth keypoint in the first image and 00 otherwise. We define 𝒗k′\bm{v}_{k}^{\prime} in the same way for the kkth keypoint in the second image. These binary descriptors thus encode the global linear context. We use the Hamming distance to compare CLAD descriptors and match keypoints, as in standard methods. Fig. 1 shows that CLAD can match keypoints in challenging scenes where local descriptors such as ORB may fail.

title: Do VLAs Really Follow Instructions? Diagnosing How-Level Instruction Following in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Sangwu Park,Wonjoong Kim,Yeonjun In,Chanyoung Park
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Preprint
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success. To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge.11
1
          
          
          
        Our code and data are available at https://github.com/sangwu99/how-level-vla-Arxiv.
introduction:
Completing a task specified by a language instruction does not necessarily mean following instructions on how to perform it. For example, “put the carrot on the plate” specifies what a robot should accomplish, whereas “grasp the carrot by its green end” specifies how to accomplish it. This distinction is particularly important for vision-language-action (VLA) models, which generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025). Following instructions about how to act would enable VLAs to incorporate corrections, refine actions, and adjust their behavior through language, as widely practiced in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) (Ouyang et al., 2022; Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2025; Driess et al., 2023).

We distinguish these capabilities as What-level and How-level instruction following. What-level instructions specify the task itself, while How-level instructions specify how to execute an already determined task, such as where to grasp an object or which path to take. Existing VLA research has largely focused on the What level, evaluating or improving robustness to paraphrased or replaced task instructions (Zhou et al., 2025a; Fei et al., 2026; Hou and Zhao, 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Lian et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026; Zhan et al., 2026).
Meanwhile, systems requiring How-level guidance typically restrict it to predefined commands (Shi et al., 2025; Belkhale et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026) or replace language corrections with visual symbols or externally generated recovery actions (Zeng et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2025).
Consequently, whether VLAs can directly follow free-form How-level instructions, and what limits this ability, remains largely unexplored. We therefore ask: Do current VLAs reflect How-level instructions in their actions, and if not, what prevents them from doing so?

In this work, we systematically diagnose How-level instruction following in current VLAs through two complementary settings. First, in offline correction, we collect failed episodes and rerun them with three alternatives: a simple retry with a different seed, a language correction generated from the observed failure, and an inverted correction that reverses the actionable content of the original correction. Comparing these alternatives allows us to determine whether a VLA uses the information in a correction rather than merely benefiting from another attempt. Second, in online intervention, we examine a dual-system design (Shi et al., 2025) in which a VLM monitors robot execution and provides corrections or sub-step instructions to the VLA during the task. Together, these settings evaluate instruction following under favorable and controlled conditions in offline correction and under deployment conditions in online intervention.

Across general VLAs (Black et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Community, 2026) and models designed to strengthen instruction following (Yang et al., 2026; Lian et al., 2026), both settings reveal a consistent limitation, as summarized in Fig. 1(a) and (b). In offline correction, corrections succeed less often than simple retries and do not clearly outperform inverted corrections. In online intervention, How-level instructions generally fail to improve task success, while frequent interventions substantially degrade performance. These findings suggest that current VLAs do not reliably use How-level instructions to guide their actions, even when designed to follow task instructions more robustly.

To understand this limitation, we investigate the structure of VLA training data. In standard robot datasets, each episode is paired with a single instruction shared across all timesteps (Walke et al., 2023), and these instructions exhibit limited linguistic diversity (Wanna et al., 2026). Although the robot’s actions change throughout an episode, the instruction typically describes only the task. Language may therefore serve primarily as a task identifier, without teaching the model how instructions should influence task execution. We hypothesize that this training structure limits How-level instruction following. An attention-level analysis provides indirect support: models assign different amounts of attention to corrections, yet their actions fail to reflect them regardless of the attention received, suggesting that the limitation is not specific to a single architectural component.

We test this hypothesis by introducing enriched instructions that describe the robot’s movements at different segments of an episode, while keeping the underlying demonstrations unchanged. Fig. 1(c) shows how these instructions differ from the original instruction shared across an episode. Across five VLA model families, enriched instructions maintain comparable task success while substantially improving responsiveness to How-level guidance. In particular, actions follow the directions specified by corrections in about 84% of evaluated episodes. The original models and controls trained on the original instructions with the same training budget reach about 53%, close to the 50% chance level. However, this improvement does not consistently translate into higher task success. One possible explanation is that task success on standard benchmarks depends largely on the scene (Lian et al., 2026) and on chance (Jang et al., 2026), and many failures can be recovered through retries alone. Thus, task success may not reliably reflect whether a model actually follows the additional instruction.

To measure How-level instruction following more directly, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, an Instruction-Necessity benchmark built on SIMPLER (Li et al., 2024), in which the conditions required for success are given only in How-level instructions. Its tasks require following a specified path around a transparent barrier, grasping a particular part of an object, or placing an object at an instructed location. None of the evaluated models, including those trained with enriched instructions, reliably follows these instructions, suggesting that the gained responsiveness falls short under demanding conditions and does not transfer to out-of-distribution (OOD) How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge for current VLAs.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

Diagnosis of How-level instruction following.
We introduce offline correction and online intervention, revealing that current VLAs do not reliably follow How-level instructions even when designed for instruction following.

Training data hypothesis and enriched instructions.
We identify episode-level instruction supervision as a potential cause and show that enriched segment-level instructions improve action-level responsiveness without consistently improving task success.

SIMPLER-IN.
We introduce an Instruction-Necessity benchmark that requires How-level instruction following for success, revealing remaining limitations of current VLAs.

1. Diagnosis of How-level instruction following.
We introduce offline correction and online intervention, revealing that current VLAs do not reliably follow How-level instructions even when designed for instruction following.

2. Training data hypothesis and enriched instructions.
We identify episode-level instruction supervision as a potential cause and show that enriched segment-level instructions improve action-level responsiveness without consistently improving task success.

3. SIMPLER-IN.
We introduce an Instruction-Necessity benchmark that requires How-level instruction following for success, revealing remaining limitations of current VLAs.
