title: RoPE-Flow: Monocular Vision-based Robot Pose Estimation via 2D Graph-Conditioned 3D Flow Matching
authors: Liangjing Shao,Wanhao Liu,Zhiwei Fang,Rulin Zhou,Quanlu Zhang,Changjing Liu,Beilei Cui,Yiming Huang,Hongliang Ren
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: . Under Review
abstract: Camera-to-robot pose estimation from a monocular image is significant for vision-based robot navigation and control. However, recovering 3D structural features from 2D observations remains a challenging task. Existing camera-to-robot pose estimation methods either rely on time-consuming iterative rendering or involve sophisticated 2D–3D registration which suffers from projection ambiguity, accumulated errors for distal joints and imbalanced learning for different joints. In this work, we propose RoPE-Flow, an end-to-end flow matching-based framework for camera-to-robot pose estimation. From the predicted 2D heatmaps, we propose a Keypoint-centered Feature Extractor to obtain positional features along with contextual representations from keypoints-centered multi-scale patches. Moreover, we introduce Graph-guided Condition Generator, which embeds a learnable adjacency map to generate condition for flow matching based on correlation among keypoints. Besides, we introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-Depth Loss for topological consistency and scale stability, with joint-wise weighting to mitigate varied prediction difficulty across joints. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation across different types of robots with mutiple cameras. Besides, we establish a novel cross-scene benchmark to demonstrate the outstanding performance of RoPE-Flow on zero-shot cross-scene robot pose estimation. Meanwhile, animated visualizations are shown on the website: https://ropeflow.netlify.app/.
introduction:
Accurate pose estimation of articulated robots from monocular RGB is a core capability for vision-based navigation (Bultmann et al., 2023), human–robot collaboration (Zhang et al., 2025), closed-loop manipulation (Liu et al., 2026b) and multi-robot collaboration (Yun et al., 2025). Unlike rigid object pose estimation, robot pose requires recovering the configuration of a kinematic chain whose links are self-occluding and appearance-ambiguous under changing viewpoints and lighting.

Conventional approaches perform camera-to-robot calibration using externally mounted fiducial markers such as ArUco Markers (Garrido-Jurado et al., 2014) and AprilTags (Olson, 2011). The marker’s 2D image coordinates are extracted, while its corresponding 3D position on the robot is computed via forward kinematics. With a collection of across multiple robot configurations, the camera-to-robot transformation can be recovered by Perspective-n-Point (PnP) algorithms. After calibration, both the robot base and camera are assumed to remain stationary. Therefore, calibration can drift from minor impacts or repeated operation, alongside time-varying environmental conditions such as vibration.

To enable flexible camera-robot calibration for robot interaction in unstructured environments, render-based pipelines (Labbé et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2025) perform iterative rendering supervised by segmentation masks to directly reconstruct the robot body. However, these methods rely on iterative refinement and require proper initialization for the optimization loop to converge (Li et al., 2018). To boost efficiency, end-to-end models (Lu et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2025; Goswami et al., 2025) detect 2D keypoints and recover 3D structure via Perspective-n-Point (PnP), combined with robot forward kinematics (FK) and known camera intrinsics. Still, these approaches derive 3D keypoints from 2D keypoints and joint angles using PnP, with limited robustness due to high sensitivity to correspondence noise. Some recent works (Liu et al., 2026a; Ban et al., 2024) adopt 3D models for 2D–3D registration to jointly optimize 2D and 3D representations. Even so, identical 2D projections can correspond to multiple depth configurations, introducing optimization and inference ambiguity. Generative methods offer a promising alternative by modeling the conditional distribution of 3D keypoints rather than predicting single deterministic keypoints estimate(Tian et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025). Moreover, most existing methods lack zero-shot cross-scene generalization evaluation on real robots under varied backgrounds, they only conduct self-supervised sim-to-real training and tests on single-background real data captured by different cameras from DREAM (Lee et al., 2020).

We propose RoPE-Flow, the first conditioned flow matching-based model for camera-to-robot pose estimation. Method based on flow matching can face two major challenges. First, directly predicting 3D keypoints without PnP and forward kinematics (FK) fails to enforce rigid structural constraints, kinematic priors, and inter-joint relationships. Second, the prediction difficulty varies across different robot joints. To tackle these issues, we make the following contributions:

We propose a Keypoints-centered Feature Extractor to learn multi-scale contextual representations at keypoint locations together with positional embeddings.

We propose Graph-guided Condition Generator , which provides the condition for 3D flow matching based on keypoint-centric features and the relationships among keypoints.

We introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-Depth Loss during training to guarantee rigid structural consistency and scale stability, respectively. Meanwhile, Joint-wise Weighting is adopted in loss computation to balance the varied prediction difficulty over joints.

The proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art models across different types of robot with various backgrounds from DREAM dataset. We also construct a novel realistic benchmark for cross-scene robot 3D pose estimation, LabRoPE, to demonstrate outstanding zero-shot generalization of RoPE-Flow.

title: SHRED: Self-Play for Heterogeneous Road-Users without Expert Demonstrations
authors: Wei-Jer Chang,Zhouchonghao Wu,Akshay Rangesh,Weixin Li,Masayoshi Tomizuka,Wei Zhan
comment: Self-play for Autonomous Driving
abstract:
Realistic traffic simulation and autonomous planning both depend on modeling interactions among heterogeneous road users whose dynamics, constraints, and behaviors differ fundamentally. Existing approaches predominantly learn realistic interaction behavior from large-scale human driving demonstrations. In this work, we ask whether such behavior can instead emerge purely through self-play. We present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction.
On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo. For planning, SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark. Controlled ablations show that heterogeneity in self-play improves both traffic realism and planning performance, with particularly large planning gains in interaction-heavy scenarios. Together, these results establish heterogeneous procedural self-play as a scalable, demonstration-free paradigm for learning realistic and interactive traffic behavior.
introduction:
Developing autonomous vehicles that operate safely alongside human road users requires scalable and realistic closed-loop traffic simulation. Real-world traffic, however, is inherently heterogeneous: beyond vehicles, it includes pedestrians, cyclists, and other agents with distinct physical dynamics, motion constraints, and behavioral patterns. These differences shape how agents respond to one another and how their interactions unfold over time. A pedestrian or scooter yielding at a crosswalk and a vehicle merging into traffic follow fundamentally different rules of engagement. Capturing such heterogeneous interactions is therefore central to realistic closed-loop simulation. It is equally central to autonomous planning, where the ego vehicle must anticipate how diverse agents will react to its own actions.

Recent advances in traffic simulation and autonomous planning have widely adopted data-driven learning, leveraging large-scale human driving datasets to model traffic behavior and train driving policies. Tokenized and generative simulation models reproduce realistic traffic behaviors and achieve strong performance on large-scale simulation benchmarks (Wu et al., 2024; Philion et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024). However, these approaches often rely on computationally expensive centralized models, limiting throughput in large-scale closed-loop simulation (Chang et al., 2026). In parallel, learning-based planning methods have increasingly leveraged large-scale driving datasets to learn scene representations, model interactions, and optimize driving decisions, achieving strong performance across challenging driving scenarios (Huang et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025). Despite their different objectives, both lines of work remain widely dependent on logged human driving data for learning realistic and effective interaction behaviors.
Their behavior remains tied to the interaction distributions in logged datasets, which can make coverage of diverse heterogeneous interactions and cross-dataset transfer more challenging. Large-scale demonstration datasets are also expensive to collect and may not fully capture the diversity of reactive multi-agent behaviors observed in real-world traffic.

Self-play reinforcement learning offers a complementary direction: it can learn through online interaction without trajectory supervision, scales naturally to large numbers of agents, and enables diverse multi-agent interactions to emerge through closed-loop rollouts.
Recent work has shown that self-play can produce robust driving policies at unprecedented scale (Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025) and achieve competitive realism when anchored to pretrained reference models (Chang et al., 2026). However, prior self-play systems focus on vehicle policies or homogeneous dynamics and rewards across road-user types despite fundamentally different motion characteristics. Scalable, fully reactive heterogeneous self-play across vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists without relying on logged trajectory data or pretrained imitation-policy anchors therefore remains largely unexplored.

To address these challenges, we propose SHRED (Self-Play for Heterogeneous Road-Users without Expert Demonstrations), a scalable framework for learning heterogeneous traffic behavior through large-scale self-play. SHRED jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists from random initialization, with type-specific dynamics, objectives, and action spaces that reflect their distinct modes of interaction. Procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization of dynamics and reward parameters expose agents to diverse traffic configurations and behaviors throughout training. This enables a compact decentralized policy to learn realistic heterogeneous multi-agent behaviors entirely through self-play, without demonstration supervision.

We show that demonstration-free self-play can achieve both realistic
heterogeneous traffic simulation and strong interactive planning. For
simulation, we evaluate on the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge
(WOSAC) (Montali et al., 2023) while jointly controlling vehicles, pedestrians,
and cyclists. SHRED outperforms the closest demonstration-free self-play
baseline, while controlled ablations show that heterogeneous self-play
substantially improves traffic realism, including the behavior of vehicles
themselves. For planning, we evaluate SHRED on
InterPlan (Hallgarten et al., 2024), where it outperforms all compared planners
on interaction-heavy closed-loop scenarios. Complementary planning ablations
show that heterogeneous self-play substantially outperforms vehicle-only
self-play, with the largest gains on scenarios involving concentrated
interactions with other road users. Beyond these benchmarks, policies trained
on nuPlan maps transfer zero-shot to Waymo, while behavioral analyses show
that self-play produces diverse, plausible alternatives to logged trajectories
(Figure 1).

Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce SHRED, a demonstration-free heterogeneous self-play framework that jointly learns vehicle, pedestrian, and cyclist behaviors with distinct dynamics and objectives, entirely without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay.

We develop the key components for scalable heterogeneous self-play, including procedural scenario and goal generation, per-agent randomization of dynamics and objectives, and type-specific policy components that support joint learning across diverse road-user types.

We show that demonstration-free self-play is effective across both simulation and planning: SHRED achieves strong sim-agent realism on WOSAC, the highest score among compared planners on the official 80-scenario InterPlan split, and zero-shot map transfer from nuPlan to Waymo.

1. We introduce SHRED, a demonstration-free heterogeneous self-play framework that jointly learns vehicle, pedestrian, and cyclist behaviors with distinct dynamics and objectives, entirely without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay.

2. We develop the key components for scalable heterogeneous self-play, including procedural scenario and goal generation, per-agent randomization of dynamics and objectives, and type-specific policy components that support joint learning across diverse road-user types.

3. We show that demonstration-free self-play is effective across both simulation and planning: SHRED achieves strong sim-agent realism on WOSAC, the highest score among compared planners on the official 80-scenario InterPlan split, and zero-shot map transfer from nuPlan to Waymo.

title: A Response to the Reply Presented in "A Fair Comparison of Sliding-Mode and Immersion-and-Invariance Observers"
authors: Luis Cervantes-Pérez,Víctor Santibáñez,Jesús Sandoval,Romeo Ortega,José Guadalupe Romero
abstract: In response to the reply presented in [Muñoz-Vázquez and Sánchez-Torres(2026)], this technical report extends the experimental evaluation of position-feedback velocity observers and adaptive tracking controllers for a pendular system with nonlinear friction reported in [Cervantes-Pérez et al.(2026)]. The immersion-and-invariance (I&\&I) adaptive control scheme proposed in [Romero et al.(2025)], whose gains are tuned according to the guidelines presented in [Ortega et al.(2025)], is compared with a control scheme employing the adaptive modified super-twisting observer of [Dávila et al.(2006)], whose observer gains are selected according to the guidelines proposed in [Muñoz-Vázquez and Sánchez-Torres(2026)]. Although these “tuning guidelines” attenuate chattering in certain scenarios, the experimental results reported here show that they do not eliminate it in general.
introduction:
This section introduces the experimental platform used to conduct the comparative study and outlines the scope of the reported tests. The testbed consists of a direct-drive pendular device with a single vertical link, designed and built at the La Laguna Technological Institute, Mexico. A picture of the pendular device is shown in Figure 1, whereas its schematic diagram is presented in Figure 2, where qq denotes the angular position of the actuated joint.

The joint is actuated by a direct-drive motor manufactured by Yokogawa Electric Corporation, model DM1A200G. The motor operates in torque mode, providing a maximum torque of ±200​[Nm]\pm 200~\mathrm{[Nm]}. It is also equipped with a relative encoder offering a resolution of 1,024,0001{,}024{,}000 pulses per revolution. The proposed controller was implemented digitally in MATLAB using the Simulink Desktop Real-Time environment, with a sampling period of 1​[ms]1~\mathrm{[ms]}. The experiments were conducted on a PC running Windows 10, equipped with an Intel Core i5-14600K CPU, 32​GB32~\mathrm{GB} of RAM, an RTX 3060 GPU, and a 512​GB512~\mathrm{GB} M.2 SSD. Communication between the PC and the robot was established through a Sensoray 626 data acquisition card (DAQ) installed in the PCI port of the motherboard. The DAQ interfaced with the motor driver (PARKER COMPUMOTOR model DMG3-1200A) by sending analog voltage signals corresponding to the control torques. In turn, the driver transmitted pulse trains replicating the motor encoder signals to the DAQ digital inputs. The physical parameters of the link are listed in Table 1, as originally reported in [Gamez-Herrera et al.(2025), Gandarilla et al.(2022)]. The table summarizes the meaning of the parameters and their numerical values, where ll denotes link length, and ‘Dist.’, ‘Inert.’, and ‘com’ stand for distance, inertia, and center of mass, respectively.
